wrong_answers: National teams from around the world
hints: It isn't played by countries, but by teams.
Its name honors the heroes of the wars of independence.
It's the Copa Libertadores.
questions.description: A trophy so coveted that some fans get its outline tattooed on their skin.
questions.fun_fact: The first Copa Libertadores was played in 1960, and it was won by Peñarol of Uruguay.

questions.question: The referee sprays a line that vanishes on its own, so the wall can't creep forward. At which World Cup was it first used?
hints: It's more recent than you might think.
It was at a World Cup in the 2010s.
Germany won that World Cup.
questions.description: The only graffiti a referee can paint on the field without getting sent off.
questions.fun_fact: One of its inventors is Argentina's Pablo Silva, and the foam disappears by itself in a minute or two.

questions.question: What do a cat, an owl and a crocodile have in common?
wrong_answers: They see in black and white
hints: It has to do with how they protect their eyes.
It's a thin film that slides sideways across the eye.
On top of the usual two, they have one more.
questions.description: A cat, an owl and a crocodile walk into a doctor's office… and no, this isn't the start of a joke.
questions.fun_fact: You can sometimes see a cat's third eyelid when it's half asleep or sick: it's a thin white film in the corner of the eye.

questions.question: Daedalus designed it, it was on Crete, and Theseus got out of it by following Ariadne's thread. What was it?
hints: A monster was locked up inside it.
That monster was half man, half bull.
It is full of corridors and dead ends.
questions.description: A job for a king with more secrets than Grandma's junk room.
questions.fun_fact: The English word “clue” comes from “clew,” an old word for a ball of thread, like the one Ariadne gave Theseus.

questions.question: Guess who: “A goddess cursed me to repeat only the last words others say, and I fell for a young man who only looked at himself in the water.” Who am I?
hints: The young man I fell in love with was called Narcissus.
The goddess Hera punished me because my chatter kept distracting her.
Shout your name into a canyon and I’ll answer… with your name.
questions.description: A girl who always gets the last word… but never the first.
questions.fun_fact: The word “echo” comes from this nymph, and the word “narcissist” comes from the young Narcissus.

questions.question: Guess who: “I married Eros, the god of love, but I wasn’t allowed to see his face. My name means ‘soul’ in Greek.” Who am I?
hints: In the end, Zeus made me a goddess.
Artists sometimes paint me with butterfly wings.
Words like “psychology” come from my name.
questions.description: A love story where one of them couldn’t even see the other’s profile picture.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Greek, “psyche” meant both “soul” and “butterfly”.

questions.question: A kitchen knife is to a Swiss Army knife as an AI that can only play chess is to…
hints: The Swiss Army knife isn't bigger: it can do more things.
Scientists haven't managed to actually build it yet.
Its short name is AGI, and it's the opposite of a “narrow” or specialized AI.
questions.description: Machines have their own “when I grow up, I want to be…” too.
questions.fun_fact: Several AI labs, such as OpenAI, openly say that building artificial general intelligence is their main goal.

questions.question: Copilot is made by Microsoft and shows up in Windows, Word and Excel with a colorful icon. Its name comes from the person who sits next to the pilot. What is Copilot?
questions.answer: An assistant that answers your questions
wrong_answers: A checker that underlines your mistakes
A guard that blocks computer viruses
A search tool that finds your files
hints: It has nothing to do with planes, even if the name sounds like it.
You can ask it to sum up a document or help you write an email.
It's a chatbot, from the same family as ChatGPT.
questions.description: Someone has to sit next to the pilot, and it isn't always a person.
questions.fun_fact: Before it came to Windows, the name was used for GitHub Copilot, launched in 2021 to help programmers write code.

questions.question: It started in 2013 as a joke, its symbol is the Shiba Inu dog from the Doge meme, and Elon Musk has posted about it many times. What is it?
hints: Some people buy and sell it.
It doesn't exist as paper bills or metal coins.
It's a relative of Bitcoin.
questions.description: Such doggo. Very internet. Wow.
questions.fun_fact: The dog in the meme was named Kabosu and lived in Japan with her owner, a teacher.

questions.question: Samoa and American Samoa are less than 200 km (125 miles) apart. How many hours apart are their clocks?
hints: A very special imaginary line runs between the two islands.
That line marks where each new day begins on the planet.
The clocks show the same time, but on one island it's already tomorrow.
questions.description: Neighbors so close they could borrow sugar from each other, yet they never agree on the clock.
questions.fun_fact: In 2011, Samoa skipped December 30 entirely so it would end up on the other side of the International Date Line.

questions.question: The city of Bombay (now Mumbai), in India, was made by joining several islands with landfill. How many islands were there?
hints: The English took more than a century to join them all with landfill.
There were few enough to count on your fingers.
It is the same as the number of days in a week.
questions.description: A giant city that is really a jigsaw puzzle put together with dirt and patience.
questions.fun_fact: The English got Bombay as part of the dowry of a Portuguese princess who married King Charles II.

questions.question: The name of the Canary Islands comes from Latin and hides an animal. Which one?
hints: The Romans already knew about these islands in the Atlantic.
In Latin, this animal was called “canis.”
It's the animal that wags its tail when you come home.
questions.description: A name that looks obvious, but has hidden a surprise since Roman times.
questions.fun_fact: It's the other way around from what most people think: the canary bird is named after the islands, not the islands after the bird.

questions.question: What do Hong Kong, Singapore and Jamaica have in common in their history?
hints: That European empire left all three its language as an official language.
That empire had the most powerful navy in the world in the 19th century.
In all three places, people still drive on the left.
questions.description: Three places with beaches, lots of heat and a past that arrived by ship from Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Hong Kong was handed back to China in 1997, after more than 150 years under British rule.

questions.question: In the film “My Neighbor Totoro,” how many Totoros appear?
hints: He is not alone in the forest.
They are not all the same size: the biggest one is the one waiting for the bus in the rain.
It's the same number as the little pigs in the story with the big bad wolf.
questions.description: The giant cuddly toy everyone would love as a pillow on a rainy day.
questions.fun_fact: Totoro appears in the logo of Studio Ghibli, the Japanese studio that made the film in 1988.

questions.question: In a famous picture book, a turtle, an elephant, a giraffe, a zebra and even a mouse climb on top of each other. What did they all want to taste?
hints: What they want is very, very high up.
You can only see it well at night.
The book's title is about getting a taste of it.
questions.description: A tower of animals that no architect would ever approve.
questions.fun_fact: The book was written and illustrated by Polish-born Michael Grejniec, and at the end a fish can't see why they tried so hard, because it has another moon right beside it, reflected in the water.

questions.question: In a Roald Dahl book, three men named Boggis, Bunce and Bean spend days chasing a very clever fox. What are the three men?
hints: The three are neighbors, very rich and very stingy.
One is fat, one is short and one is thin, and none of them can stand the fox.
One keeps chickens, one keeps ducks and geese, and one keeps turkeys and apples.
questions.description: Three neighbors with very bad luck and one furry neighbor with very good luck.
questions.fun_fact: Wes Anderson turned “Fantastic Mr. Fox” into a 2009 movie, using puppets animated one frame at a time.

questions.question: García Márquez is to “One Hundred Years of Solitude” as Isabel Allende is to…
hints: It is Isabel Allende's first novel, from 1982.
It tells the story of several generations of the Trueba family.
Its title is about a home full of ghosts.
questions.description: A question for people who read long novels with even longer family trees.
questions.fun_fact: “The House of the Spirits” began as a letter Isabel Allende started writing to her grandfather in 1981.

questions.question: In “Love in the Time of Cholera”, Florentino Ariza waits and waits for his love, Fermina Daza. How many years does he wait, according to the novel?
hints: It's a very long time: when they finally get together, they are both old.
The novel says: “… years, nine months and four days.”
It's a number just over 50.
questions.description: The longest wait in literature, worse than the line at the bank on a Monday.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez based this novel partly on the love story of his own parents.

questions.question: In many video games, characters drink little red bottles in the middle of a battle. What does one of those bottles almost always do?
hints: Think about what happens when an enemy hits you.
When you drink it, a bar that was running low goes back up.
It's the same color as the little hearts many games show in a corner.
questions.description: A colorful little drink that's worth more than gold in video games.
questions.fun_fact: In many games, health potions are red and magic potions are blue, a color code players understand without reading a word.

questions.question: Which legendary magician from Madrid does impossible card tricks and sings “¡Tararí, que te vi!”?
hints: He is seen as one of the best card magicians in the world.
He is a master of card magic who spent decades on Spanish TV.
His surname starts with “Tam”.
questions.description: A magician who laughs more than his audience, and that's saying something.
questions.fun_fact: Many professional magicians around the world study this Spanish magician's books on how to fool the audience's memory.

questions.question: I'm the Minecraft enchanting table: I have a book that floats and opens when you come close. What happens if you surround me with bookshelves?
wrong_answers: You can enchant several items at once
You no longer need lapis lazuli
hints: The bookshelves must be nearby, but with one free block between them and the table.
Look at the numbers next to each enchantment option.
More books around it, more magical wisdom for the table.
questions.description: A piece of furniture that reads more than you do, and it doesn't even have eyes.
questions.fun_fact: With enough bookshelves around it, the Minecraft enchanting table can offer level 30 enchantments.

questions.question: On a day trip, you drink tap water, swim in a river and later row on a mountain lake. What do those three waters have in common?
hints: None of them tastes like the sea.
It's the kind people and animals can drink.
Its name uses the same word as bread just out of the oven.
questions.description: A day out in the country with three different dips and not a single wave.
questions.fun_fact: Almost all the water on Earth is salty: fresh water is only about 3%, and most of it is frozen.

previous.feedback: The question asks what three given things have in common (“What do those three waters have in common?”). That style is retired (reason 7), and it applies to the source too. The translation itself is faithful, and the new hint 3 (fresh bread) works well in English.

questions.question: A shark has several rows of teeth and loses them easily. What happens when one falls out?
questions.answer: A tooth from the row behind moves forward
wrong_answers: The gap stays there for the rest of its life
The whole row of teeth falls out with it
It stops eating until the gum heals
hints: It never runs out of teeth.
Its teeth work like a conveyor belt.
Spare teeth are already waiting behind.
questions.description: If the Tooth Fairy paid for every shark tooth, she would go broke.
questions.fun_fact: Fossil shark teeth are so common on some beaches that you can find them just by walking along the shore.

questions.question: Take a close look at this water animal. Which group of animals does it belong to?
hints: It has whiskers on its snout.
It comes up to the surface to breathe air.
The mothers feed their babies with milk.
questions.description: A calm, chubby fellow who spends all day eating grass… underwater.
questions.fun_fact: The manatee's closest living relatives are dugongs, and outside their own group, its closest relatives are elephants and hyraxes.

questions.question: He's called the father of geometry, wrote a book called “Elements” and lived about 2,300 years ago. Which civilization was Euclid from?
hints: His civilization was famous for its philosophers.
He came from the same culture as Pythagoras and Archimedes.
His civilization also invented the Olympic Games.
questions.description: The man who turned triangles into a bestseller for more than 2,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: Euclid's “Elements” is one of the most-printed books in history and was used in schools for more than 2,000 years.

questions.question: Complete: “equilateral” is to three equal sides as “scalene” is to…
hints: Its name comes from a Greek word.
The one with two equal sides is called isosceles.
You measure its three sides and get three different numbers.
questions.description: Triangles have some really strange names too.
questions.fun_fact: “Scalene” comes from the Greek word “skalenos,” which means limping or uneven.

questions.question: This lump of corroded bronze was pulled from a Greek shipwreck in 1901. What was the Antikythera mechanism used for?
questions.answer: Predicting eclipses and movements in the sky
wrong_answers: Measuring how deep the sea is
hints: It had dozens of gear wheels, like a clock.
It showed the Sun, the Moon and maybe some planets.
It is seen as the oldest known astronomical calculator.
questions.description: Divers looking for sea sponges found a 2,000-year-old bronze puzzle on the seabed.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody built a device with such complex gears again until the astronomical clocks of the Middle Ages, more than a thousand years later.

questions.question: At the beach you see a starfish, in the water a jellyfish, and in the kitchen you cut an orange in half. What do they have in common?
hints: It has to do with how their parts repeat.
Their parts spread out from a center, like the spokes of a wheel.
Its name comes from “radius,” like the radius of a circle.
questions.description: Nature is the best artist in geometry class.
questions.fun_fact: Baby starfish have bilateral symmetry, like us, and only become radial as they grow up.

questions.question: Which of these energy sources is NOT renewable?
hints: Renewable sources never run out: they come back on their own.
The one you want is dug out of a mine, like a rock.
It's used in nuclear power plants, like the one where Homer Simpson works.
questions.description: Some energy comes back by itself every day, and some is gone for good once it runs out.
questions.fun_fact: One uranium fuel pellet, about the size of a fingertip, gives as much energy as a ton of coal.

questions.question: Hyenas, vultures and condors have something in common in what they eat. What are they?
hints: None of them eats grass or flowers.
They love finding food that's already… not moving.
They eat the remains of animals that were already dead.
questions.description: Three animals that look nothing alike, but would happily order from the same dinner menu.
questions.fun_fact: An Andean condor's open wings can measure more than 3 m (10 ft), almost the length of a small car.

questions.question: Hoover in the United States, Itaipu between Brazil and Paraguay, and Three Gorges in China. What are all three?
hints: All three sit on huge rivers.
They hold back water with a giant wall.
They make electricity from the force of falling water.
questions.description: Three concrete giants so famous they have more fans than most movie stars.
questions.fun_fact: Brazil and Paraguay share Itaipu and split the electricity it makes.

questions.question: Which of these four people never won the Nobel Peace Prize?
hints: The other three won the prize between 2004 and 2014.
One of them planted millions of trees in Kenya, and she did win it.
The person you're looking for is famous for studying chimpanzees.
questions.description: An inconvenient truth: not every hero of the planet has the same medal.
questions.fun_fact: Wangari Maathai was the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, in 2004, for a movement that planted millions of trees.

questions.question: This radioactive chemical element was discovered by a Swedish chemist in the 19th century and named after the Norse god of thunder. What is it?
hints: Several elements are named after gods or planets.
The chemist was Jöns Jacob Berzelius.
Take the thunder god's name and add “-ium”.
questions.description: The thunder god sneaked onto the periodic table too, and he didn't even need his hammer.
questions.fun_fact: Years earlier, Berzelius had already used the name “thorium” for a supposed new element that turned out to be a mistake.

questions.question: Riddle: I am Brísingamen, the golden necklace of the goddess Freya. Four brothers in Norse myth forged me. What kind of beings were they?
hints: In Norse myths, these beings also made famous weapons for the gods.
They live underground and are the best blacksmiths.
They are small, bearded and work in mines.
questions.description: The shiniest jewel in Asgard, and nobody bought it at the mall.
questions.fun_fact: In the myths, dwarves also forged Mjölnir, Thor's hammer.

questions.question: Newspapers and school projects often use posters that explain facts with icons, charts and very little text. What are they called?
hints: It helps you understand something complicated at a glance.
It mixes numbers and pictures.
Its name joins “information” and “graphic.”
questions.description: For people who read the news but only look at the pictures.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1800s, the nurse Florence Nightingale used colorful charts to convince the British government to improve hospitals.

questions.question: The brown tone of old photos is called sepia. Where did that pigment originally come from?
hints: It comes from an animal.
That animal lives in the sea and is a relative of the squid.
The animal lets out a dark cloud when it gets scared.
questions.description: Your great-great-grandparents' photos hide a rather strange secret.
questions.fun_fact: The cuttlefish, whose scientific name is Sepia, can change color in less than a second to hide.

questions.question: What is an oath, like the one some people make to their flag?
hints: It is said out loud and with great respect.
Whoever makes it commits to doing something.
It's like saying “I promise”, but in a very serious way.
questions.description: When school asks you to be really serious, at least for a little while.
questions.fun_fact: In many Latin American countries, children make their oath to the flag at a special school ceremony.

questions.question: The ancient Egyptians painted this eye on their boats and wore it around their necks. What did they use it for?
questions.answer: To protect themselves and stay healthy
wrong_answers: To guide their boats along the Nile
To show that they were nobles
To measure the passing of time
hints: Both rich and poor people used it.
The living wore it, and it was also placed on mummies.
According to the myth, the falcon god's eye was healed after a fight.
questions.description: An eye that has been watching for thousands of years and still doesn't need glasses.
questions.fun_fact: The Eye of Horus is still worn today as a pendant on necklaces and shows up in many video games.

questions.question: Brazil will host the first Women's World Cup ever played in South America. In which year?
hints: Brazil had already hosted the men's World Cup in 2014.
The Women's World Cup is played every four years, like the men's.
The previous one was held in Australia and New Zealand in 2023.
questions.description: A party so long awaited that the samba is already rehearsing.
questions.fun_fact: The first Women's World Cup was played in 1991, in China.

questions.question: The “Mona Lisa” is to the Louvre as which painting is to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam?
hints: It was painted by the same artist the museum is named after.
It shows yellow flowers in a vase.
These flowers turn their heads to follow the sun.
questions.description: A museum for a painter who sold almost nothing while he was alive and is now too famous to fit through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh painted several versions of “Sunflowers” to decorate the bedroom of his friend, the painter Paul Gauguin.

questions.question: You've been in the pool for ages and suddenly start shivering and your teeth chatter. Why does your body do that?
wrong_answers: To get water out of your ears
hints: Your muscles do it without you deciding to.
It happens most when the water or the air is cold.
It's a bit like rubbing your hands together on a freezing day.
questions.description: Your body has a secret trick it switches on without asking you first.
questions.fun_fact: When you shiver, your muscles move very fast without you deciding to, just to make heat.

questions.question: The walls of the “Water Cube,” Beijing's Olympic swimming pool, are covered in irregular cells. What inspired its architects?
hints: It lasts only a very short time before it disappears.
You see it in the bathtub or when you wash the dishes.
Kids make them by blowing through a little ring.
questions.description: Architects who went looking for ideas somewhere not serious at all.
questions.fun_fact: For the 2022 Winter Olympics, the Water Cube became the “Ice Cube” and hosted the curling games.

questions.question: It's added to swimming pools to kill germs and, together with sodium, makes table salt. Which element is it?
hints: Its name comes from the Greek word for “pale green.”
It's also in the bleach people use to clean at home.
Its chemical symbol is Cl.
questions.description: The secret ingredient of the swimming pool, though your nose always finds it out.
questions.fun_fact: The famous “pool smell” doesn't come from chlorine alone, but from what forms when chlorine mixes with sweat and other things swimmers leave behind.

questions.question: In what year did Michael Phelps win 8 gold medals at the Beijing Olympics?
hints: It was in the first decade of this century.
That same year, Barack Obama was elected president of the United States.
The year ends in the same number as Phelps's gold medals.
questions.description: Eight gold medals: even a pirate's treasure chest doesn't shine that bright.
questions.fun_fact: With those 8 golds, Phelps beat Mark Spitz, who had won 7 at Munich 1972.

questions.question: Turkey is to Christmas dinner in the US as ________ is to Christmas dinner for millions of families in Japan.
hints: You buy it from a famous fast-food chain.
The custom started with an ad campaign in the 1970s.
It comes in buckets, and the brand's founder was a colonel with a white beard.
questions.description: A Christmas tradition that was born in an advertising office.
questions.fun_fact: So many families in Japan order it that they have to reserve their Christmas bucket weeks in advance.

questions.question: In the film about a man who swears he's the real Santa Claus at a New York department store, what street number is in the title?
hints: The original film is from 1947, and it was remade in 1994.
Macy's, the store famous for its Thanksgiving parade, is on that street.
It's double 17.
questions.description: In New York, even the street addresses have the holiday spirit.
questions.fun_fact: Edmund Gwenn won an Oscar for playing Santa Claus in the 1947 version.

questions.question: Who were the first to come and worship baby Jesus, on the very night he was born?
hints: They were working at night in the fields near Bethlehem.
An angel brought them the news while they watched over their animals.
Their job was looking after sheep.
questions.description: The most exclusive guest list in history, and not a single celebrity on it.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Bible, the Wise Men didn't arrive that night: the Gospel says they found the child in a house.

questions.question: At the festival in this photo, each year is named after an animal. How many different animals are in the cycle before it starts over?
hints: It is the biggest festival in China, with red lanterns and dragons.
The cycle includes the rat, the ox, the tiger, the dragon and the pig, among others.
There are as many as there are months in a year.
questions.description: A party where the year gets a mascot instead of a number.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the order of the animals was decided by a race, and the rat won by riding on the ox's back.

questions.question: Which animal has these two humps?
hints: It lives in cold deserts of Asia, like the Gobi in Mongolia.
Its one-humped cousin lives in Arabia and North Africa.
Its name starts with “C”.
questions.description: An animal that carries its packed lunch on its back, sometimes in a double portion.
questions.fun_fact: A camel's humps don't store water but fat, which the animal uses as an energy reserve.

questions.question: Which ancient people gave Mexico its name and founded their capital where Mexico City stands today?
hints: They ruled central Mexico when the Spanish arrived.
Their capital was called Tenochtitlan and was built on a lake.
They called themselves the “Mexica.”
questions.description: A city so important that it lent its name to the whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico City was built on a lake, so some of its buildings are slowly sinking.

questions.question: Which believers mainly celebrate the festival of lights in this photo, with little clay lamps and colorful patterns on the ground?
hints: It is the most famous festival in India.
It is called Diwali and celebrates the victory of light over darkness.
Their religion has gods like Ganesha, the one with an elephant's head.
questions.description: A festival where nobody fears the electricity bill, because it all runs on tiny candles.
questions.fun_fact: The word Diwali comes from the Sanskrit “Deepavali,” which means “row of lamps.”

questions.question: Guess who I am: I'm the Gym Leader of Pewter City, I use Rock-type Pokémon, and I travel with Ash, cooking for everyone. Who am I?
hints: I was one of Ash's very first travel companions.
I always fall in love with every Nurse Joy and Officer Jenny.
My first Pokémon is Onix, a giant stone snake.
questions.description: A boy who has been traveling for years and still hasn't finished school.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, Brock is called Takeshi, and Ash is called Satoshi, after Pokémon creator Satoshi Tajiri.

questions.question: Charmander is to Fire type as Lucario is to…
hints: Lucario can sense other creatures' aura, but that's not what decides its type.
Machop and Hitmonchan are this type too.
It's the type of Pokémon that throw punches and kicks.
questions.description: A dog that never barks, but can read everyone's energy.
questions.fun_fact: Lucario actually has two types at once: Fighting and Steel.

questions.question: In 1593, the Irish pirate Grace O'Malley sailed to London and met Queen Elizabeth I of England in person. Why did she go?
questions.answer: To ask for her son's release
hints: It was a family matter.
An English governor in Ireland had taken something very important from her.
Two of her relatives were in prison.
questions.description: A meeting of two bosses where nobody dared to interrupt.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Grace O'Malley refused to bow to Elizabeth I because she did not see her as Queen of Ireland.

questions.question: What links the film “Captain Phillips”, speedboats attacking cargo ships, and warships guarding oil tankers in the Indian Ocean?
hints: It's modern piracy, from this century.
It happens near the entrance to the Red Sea.
These pirates come from the country whose capital is Mogadishu.
questions.description: Pirates with no parrot and no wooden leg, but with very fast boats.
questions.fun_fact: “Captain Phillips” is based on the real hijacking of the cargo ship Maersk Alabama in 2009.

previous.feedback: The question asks what several given things have in common ("What links the film “Captain Phillips”, speedboats… and warships…?"). That is the retired "what do they have in common" style. The source uses the same style ("¿Qué tienen en común…?"), so the source has the same problem.

questions.question: They call me hardtack, and I turn up in lots of pirate stories. Sailors soaked me before biting, and I lasted months in the hold. What am I?
wrong_answers: A sponge cake of egg and sugar
An oat cake made with honey
hints: Sailors sometimes found weevils living inside me.
I was baked several times to dry out every bit of moisture.
I'm made of just flour, water and salt.
questions.description: The pirates' favorite snack, if you don't care about your teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Some pieces of hardtack more than 150 years old are still kept in museums.

questions.question: Smoke from chimneys like this one carries the gas that does the most to drive human-caused climate change. Which gas is it?
hints: Burning coal, oil and gas produces it.
You breathe it out every time you exhale.
Plants take it in, and its formula is CO₂.
questions.description: That cloud coming out of the chimney isn't cotton candy, even if it puffs up just the same.
questions.fun_fact: Forests and oceans soak up a large share of the carbon dioxide that humans release every year.

questions.question: A shop in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, offers you an ammonite, a fossil with a spiral shell. When did ammonites die out for good?
hints: They lived in the oceans for hundreds of millions of years.
No human, and no close relative of ours, ever saw a living ammonite.
They disappeared at the end of the Cretaceous, along with the non-bird dinosaurs.
questions.description: A cousin of the octopus that curled up like a snail and has been posing for photos for millions of years.
questions.fun_fact: The closest living relatives of ammonites are octopuses and squids.

questions.question: Riddle: Bogotá and Tunja sit on top of one of me, and my name is “plateau.” What am I?
wrong_answers: A mountain with a sharp peak
A lake high up in the mountains
hints: I am very high above sea level.
If you walk across me, you hardly go up or down at all.
My name comes from an old French word for “flat.”
questions.description: Bogotá and Tunja share more than chilly mornings, woolly ponchos and hot sugarcane drinks.
questions.fun_fact: The Altiplano Cundiboyacense, where Bogotá and Tunja sit, is one of the largest high, flat regions in the Andes.

questions.question: Tapioca pearls, like the ones in bubble tea, are made from the starch of which part of a plant?
hints: The plant comes from South America.
Peoples of the Amazon have grown it for thousands of years.
This part of the plant grows hidden underground.
questions.description: The little balls that get stuck in your straw and turn you into a human vacuum cleaner.
questions.fun_fact: Cassava, the plant tapioca comes from, has been grown in the Amazon for thousands of years.

questions.question: I'm the Amazon River: in the rainy season I rise several meters and spill into the rainforest. What happens then?
wrong_answers: Pink river dolphins leave for the sea
Monkeys move down to live on the ground
hints: For months, the forest is half underwater.
Down there, visitors with fins start showing up.
Some of them eat the fruit that falls from the branches.
questions.description: A river that leaves home every year without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon fish eat fruit and drop the seeds far away, so they help plant the rainforest.

questions.question: What do water lettuce, water hyacinth and the giant water lily have in common?
wrong_answers: They only grow in salt water
They are algae that live underwater
hints: All three live in rivers and lakes.
Sometimes they cover whole ponds like a green carpet.
Their leaves stay on top of the water without sinking.
questions.description: A garden where watering the plants is completely pointless.
questions.fun_fact: Water lettuce has tiny hairs on its leaves that trap air, so even if you push it under, it pops right back up.

questions.question: In which season do people in Japan have picnics under the blooming cherry trees?
hints: It comes right after the cold.
It is when the school year starts in Japan.
It is the season that brings the flowers back.
questions.description: A tree that puts on its best outfit for just a couple of weeks a year.
questions.fun_fact: The Japanese custom of gathering to admire the cherry blossoms is called “hanami”.

questions.question: Nepenthes is a plant from Asia's rainforests with pitcher-shaped leaves. Complete: “The stomach is to food as the Nepenthes pitcher is to…”
hints: What goes into the pitcher never comes out.
It lures its visitors with sweet nectar and a very slippery rim.
It is a meat-eating plant.
questions.description: A pitcher you really shouldn't pour the juice into.
questions.fun_fact: Some Nepenthes plants in Borneo have a deal with tree shrews: they give them nectar, and the shrews leave their poop behind as fertilizer.

questions.question: A woman cooks cassava bread on a budare griddle and keeps waving a palm-leaf fan. What is she using it for?
hints: It has to do with cooking, not with resting.
What she cares about is under the griddle.
Embers need air to glow red and give off more heat.
questions.description: Air conditioning in the rainforest longhouse runs on pure arm power.
questions.fun_fact: Many Amazon peoples weave their fans from palm leaves and use them almost like a kitchen bellows.

questions.question: Lope de Aguirre sailed the Amazon River in 1561, rebelled against his own king and wrote that king a very rude letter. What country was he from?
hints: He was a European conquistador.
His king also ruled cities like Bogotá and Lima.
He came from the same kingdom that paid for Christopher Columbus's voyage.
questions.description: A tourist who went for a nice boat ride down the river and ended up in a fight with the king.
questions.fun_fact: Lope de Aguirre called himself “the Pilgrim,” and history remembers him as “Aguirre the Madman.”

questions.question: Riddle: “They call me guayuco. I'm tied around the waist, and in the hot jungle I was almost all many people wore for centuries.” What am I?
hints: It's a piece of clothing.
It's worn from the waist down.
It covers just enough and nothing more.
questions.description: The coolest outfit in the jungle, with no buttons and no zipper.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional guayucos were sometimes made from tree bark, pounded until it was as soft as cloth.

questions.question: A giant tree trunk is hollowed out with fire and an ax, and left long and pointed at both ends. What is it used for?
hints: The pointed ends help it cut through something that moves.
In the rainforest, rivers are like roads.
It's going to need some paddles.
questions.description: A tree that got hollowed out and found itself a whole new career.
questions.fun_fact: Some canoes carved from a single tree trunk can carry more than ten people.

questions.question: At a school fair, one ticket buys one cupcake. In the carbon credit market, one credit stands for… what?
questions.answer: One metric ton of CO₂ kept out of the air
wrong_answers: One kilogram of CO₂ kept out of the air
One liter of CO₂ kept out of the air
100 metric tons of CO₂ kept out of the air
hints: It's an amount of greenhouse gas.
It's a fairly big unit, not one you'd use on a kitchen scale.
It's a thousand kilograms of carbon dioxide.
questions.description: Polluting with permission: the grown-up version of “I'll trade you my dessert for your homework.”
questions.fun_fact: Carbon credits became famous with the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in Japan in 1997.

questions.question: Tiny plastic beads, smaller than a grain of sand, were banned because they went down the drain into the sea. What products were they in?
hints: People bought them at the pharmacy or the supermarket.
They were used to gently scrape something.
People rubbed them on their face to remove dead skin.
questions.description: Beads so small they ended up being a giant problem.
questions.fun_fact: The United States banned plastic microbeads in rinse-off cosmetics with a law passed in 2015.

questions.question: What is the model called where products are used, repaired, recycled and used again and again, instead of being bought, used and thrown away?
hints: Many governments and companies in Europe promote it.
Its name describes a path that comes back to where it started.
Its name is the shape of a wheel or a ring.
questions.description: An economy where “throw it away” is almost a forbidden phrase.
questions.fun_fact: In a circular economy, even a fruit peel can go back to the soil as fertilizer.

questions.question: What do you call the local business that buys old metal things by the kilo, like pots, car rims and cables?
hints: Its name comes from another word for old, leftover metal.
Old cars that no longer run often end up there, crushed into cubes.
Its name starts with a word for leftover bits, like the pieces of paper you throw away.
questions.description: A place where your trash is someone else's treasure… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: Steel can be melted down and recycled again and again without losing its strength.

questions.question: If Europe's border runs along the Caucasus Mountains, as most geographers say, what is the highest mountain in Europe?
hints: It is a sleeping volcano.
It is in Russia and has two snowy summits.
Both of its summits are over 5,600 meters (18,370 ft) high.
questions.description: Europe has a rooftop too, but hardly anyone remembers where it put it.
questions.fun_fact: Elbrus is about 5,642 m (18,510 ft) tall, more than 800 m higher than Mont Blanc (4,806 m / 15,770 ft), which many people think is Europe's highest.

questions.question: Monarch butterflies fly from Canada and the United States to spend the winter in mountain forests. In which country are they?
hints: Spanish is spoken in this country.
The butterflies never cross the equator.
It's the country of mariachis and tacos.
questions.description: Travelers who need no passport, just a pair of colorful wings.
questions.fun_fact: No single monarch butterfly makes the whole round trip: its great-grandchildren finish the journey back north.

questions.question: What is the name of the old man in the Pixar movie who ties thousands of balloons to his house?
hints: He travels with a young explorer scout and a talking dog.
The movie is called “Up”.
His first name starts with C, like “cloud”.
questions.description: A mountain so strange it looks like it came from another planet… or from a movie.
questions.fun_fact: Mount Roraima is a tepui with rocks about 2 billion years old, some of the oldest on the planet.

questions.question: Off California there are underwater “forests” over 40 m (130 ft) tall that grow more than half a meter a day. What are these “trees”?
hints: They use sunlight to make food, through photosynthesis.
Sea otters wrap themselves in them to sleep without drifting away on the current.
The green film that grows in a neglected fish tank belongs to the same group.
questions.description: A forest where nobody ever has to water the trees.
questions.fun_fact: Giant kelp is the largest alga in the world, and its underwater forests are home to hundreds of species.

questions.question: On which day is the crown-shaped sweet bread with candied fruit and a hidden surprise inside traditionally eaten?
hints: By that day, Christmas and New Year's are already over.
Its crown shape is a clue about who is celebrated that day.
It's the day of Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar.
questions.description: A bread with a prize inside, like cereal boxes used to have.
questions.fun_fact: A tiny baby Jesus figure is hidden inside the bread, and in Mexico whoever finds it must treat everyone to tamales on February 2.

questions.question: What is the best-selling album of all time?
wrong_answers: The Dark Side of the Moon
hints: It came out in the early 1980s.
Its singer was famous for a dance move that made him look like he was walking backward on stage.
It's by the King of Pop.
questions.description: Music from the days when people still bought their albums in a store.
questions.fun_fact: The music video for “Thriller” is almost 14 minutes long, longer than many short films.

questions.question: How high did Cuba's Javier Sotomayor jump in 1993 to set the high jump world record?
hints: He jumped well over the height of a normal door.
He didn't reach three meters.
It's almost exactly the height of the crossbar on a full-size soccer goal.
questions.description: A man who could get over your front door without bothering to open it.
questions.fun_fact: Sotomayor is the only human ever to clear 8 feet (2.44 meters).

questions.question: Methuselah, a pine in California’s White Mountains, is one of the oldest trees in the world. About how old is it?
hints: It is far older than any person or tortoise.
It was already growing while the pyramids of Egypt were being built.
Its age has four digits.
questions.description: A grandpa with more birthdays than candles could ever fit on a cake.
questions.fun_fact: Methuselah’s exact location is kept secret to protect it from visitors and souvenir hunters.

questions.question: “Horseshoe Falls is to Niagara Falls as ___ is to Iguazu Falls.” What fills the blank?
hints: You're looking for the most famous and spectacular part of a group of waterfalls.
It sits on the border between Argentina and Brazil, and it is shaped like a U.
Its name points to a body part of someone with horns and a tail.
questions.description: A challenge for travelers who aren't afraid of getting soaked right down to their socks.
questions.fun_fact: Iguazu Falls is made up of about 275 separate waterfalls, and Devil's Throat is the tallest and most powerful of them all.

questions.question: What is the longest river in France?
hints: It doesn't flow through Paris.
Its valley is full of castles built for kings and nobles.
Its name starts with L.
questions.description: A river so French it surely has a croissant for breakfast every day.
questions.fun_fact: The Loire is just over 1,000 km (about 625 miles) long, and its valley, with dozens of castles, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: iCub is a robot the size of a small child, built at an institute in Genoa. Which Italian scientist co-led its development?
hints: He has worked in Genoa for most of his career.
He became scientific director of the Italian Institute of Technology.
His first name is the Italian form of “George”.
questions.description: A baby that never cries, never sleeps and comes with an instruction manual anyone can read.
questions.fun_fact: Dozens of iCub copies are spread across labs around the world, and they all share their design freely.

questions.question: In which year did “The Wild Robot” come out, the animated film where the robot Roz raises an orphaned gosling?
hints: It's a fairly recent film.
It was made by DreamWorks, the studio behind “Shrek” and “Kung Fu Panda”.
It came out the same year as the Paris Olympic Games.
questions.description: A robot who showed up to work and ended up as a mother goose, without even asking for parental leave.
questions.fun_fact: The film is based on an illustrated book by Peter Brown, published in 2016.

questions.question: This is Robby the Robot from the film “Forbidden Planet” (1956). Its story was inspired by a play by which writer?
hints: The original play doesn't have a single robot in it.
The original play takes place on an island, with a magician and a storm.
He also wrote “Romeo and Juliet”.
questions.description: A robot from the 1950s that already had more style than most of today's kitchen appliances.
questions.fun_fact: Robby cost a fortune for his time, so the studio got its money's worth by putting him in many other films and TV shows.

questions.question: This robot is Maria, from the silent film “Metropolis” (1927). Her design inspired a very famous robot from another film series. Which one?
hints: That robot is shaped like a human, just like her.
It appears in “Star Wars”.
It speaks a huge number of languages and is always with a short friend who beeps.
questions.description: A robot so stylish that almost 100 years later, people are still copying her look.
questions.fun_fact: “Metropolis” was the first film ever added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

questions.question: Which of these places will you NOT find in Patrick Star's neighborhood at the bottom of the sea?
hints: Patrick lives in Bikini Bottom, next door to SpongeBob.
One of these places is from a Disney movie, not from SpongeBob.
The father of a red-haired mermaid lives there.
questions.description: He lives under a rock and still has a better social life than you.
questions.fun_fact: Real sea stars can grow back an arm they have lost.

questions.question: How many wheels does Curiosity have, the robot NASA sent to explore Mars?
hints: It has more wheels than a normal car.
Each wheel has its own motor and a special suspension for climbing over rocks.
It's the same as the number of legs an ant has.
questions.description: A toy car that cost more than every car on your street put together.
questions.fun_fact: Curiosity's wheels have holes that spell “JPL” in Morse code, so it leaves that message in the Martian sand as it drives.

questions.question: The Bismarck was a famous German ship of World War II. What type of ship was it?
hints: It was a warship that sailed on the surface.
Its strength was in its giant guns, not in planes.
Its type is named after the “line of battle” that the biggest gun ships once formed.
questions.description: A ship named after a man with a big mustache and a temper to match.
questions.fun_fact: The wreck of the Bismarck was found in 1989 by Robert Ballard, the same explorer who found the Titanic.

questions.question: Newton's apple is to gravity as Archimedes' bathtub is to…
hints: Archimedes noticed that the water rose when he got in.
His famous principle is taught in physics class with water and objects of different weights.
It has to do with water pushing things upward.
questions.description: The only time in history that taking a bath led to a scientific discovery.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says Archimedes jumped out of the bath and ran off shouting “Eureka!”, which is Greek for “I found it!”.

questions.question: I'm the name of the horsemen of the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, and I come from a Turkic word. What did my name, “Cossack”, first mean?
hints: The same word gave its name to a country in Central Asia.
The name tells how they lived, not where they lived.
The opposite of a serf or a slave.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a Russian dance, but has more galloping in it than squatting.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Cossack” has the same origin as the name of the Kazakhs, the people of Kazakhstan.

questions.question: I'm a warrior of the First Crusade, and people call me a “crusader”. Where does my name come from?
questions.answer: From the cross sewn on their clothes
wrong_answers: From crossing the sea by ship
hints: Before setting out, they made a vow in a religious ceremony.
They wore it on them, where everyone could see it.
It is a Christian symbol.
questions.description: A warrior name so tangled it could have come straight out of a crossword.
questions.fun_fact: The First Crusade set out in 1096, and many of its warriors walked thousands of kilometers to reach Jerusalem.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this shiny round part with a small arm on top sits inside a device. What device is it?
hints: It's hidden inside many computers.
It keeps your photos and files even when you turn the computer off.
The first word of its name is the opposite of “soft”.
questions.description: Something that spins faster than you do when you hunt for the remote under the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The arm of a hard drive floats above the spinning disk at a gap far smaller than the width of a hair.

questions.question: What technology does the super-fast train between Shanghai and its airport use?
hints: It floats a tiny bit above the track.
It works with the same force that sticks things to the fridge door.
It uses very powerful magnets.
questions.description: A train that gets you to the airport before you've finished looking for your passport.
questions.fun_fact: Shanghai's maglev train covers about 30 km (19 miles) in under 8 minutes.

questions.question: I'm hidden at the end of level 1-2 in Super Mario Bros.: run across the ceiling and you'll find me, with three pipes waiting. What am I?
hints: I let you skip whole levels.
My name uses a word that science fiction uses for super-fast space travel.
A sign inside me says “WELCOME TO ... ZONE!”.
questions.description: A secret so famous it's not a secret anymore, yet everyone still goes looking for it.
questions.fun_fact: Using the warp zones, you can finish Super Mario Bros. by playing only 8 of its 32 levels.

questions.question: It's named after a Greek philosopher, fools your touch rather than your eyes, and you can test it on your nose. What is “Aristotle's illusion”?
questions.answer: Feeling two objects where there is only one
wrong_answers: Feeling warm water as cold after touching hot water
Feeling your phone buzz in your pocket when it doesn't
Feeling itchy when you see someone else scratch
hints: You need two fingers of the same hand.
The fingers must be in a position that isn't their normal one.
Cross your index and middle fingers and touch a marble with the tips.
questions.description: A Greek philosopher who also ran experiments you can repeat from your couch.
questions.fun_fact: Aristotle described this illusion more than 2,300 years ago, and brain scientists still study it today.

questions.question: Which key nutrient found in meat can you also get from beans, lentils and chickpeas?
hints: Meat and eggs have this nutrient too.
Your body uses it to build and repair itself.
Athletes drink shakes full of it.
questions.description: Never eaten a burger in its life, and still nobody beats it in a race.
questions.fun_fact: Rice and beans eaten together give a more complete protein than either one eaten alone.

questions.question: In many sushi restaurants, the “wasabi” is really a different spicy root dyed green. Which one?
hints: It grows underground and gets really hot when you grate it.
In Europe it goes into sauces served with meat.
Its name puts a small red salad vegetable together with a farm animal.
questions.description: An impostor hiding out in sushi restaurants.
questions.fun_fact: Real wasabi is so expensive and rare that even in Japan many restaurants serve the imitation.

questions.question: In “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban,” how many years did Peter Pettigrew hide as Scabbers, the Weasleys' pet rat?
hints: A normal rat lives about 3 years, and Scabbers lived much longer.
It's the same amount of time Sirius Black spent in Azkaban.
It's more than ten years, but less than 15.
questions.description: The oldest pet in the wizarding world, and not because of a healthy diet.
questions.fun_fact: Lupin learned that Pettigrew was still alive when he saw his name moving on the Marauder's Map.

questions.question: I'm Sinestro, Green Lantern's great enemy, and I wear a yellow ring. What emotion gives my ring its power?
hints: The green ring runs on willpower.
Scarecrow, one of Batman's enemies, also uses this emotion as a weapon.
My followers scare people to grow stronger.
questions.description: A villain so vain he grew a movie-star mustache and put on a ring the color of a baby chick.
questions.fun_fact: Before he turned villain, Sinestro was a Green Lantern himself and even trained Hal Jordan.

questions.question: Jafar's parrot in “Aladdin” has the same name as the traitor in Shakespeare's “Othello”. What is that name?
hints: He is a red parrot who never stops talking.
The name is an old form of James.
It has four letters, starting with “I” and ending with “O”.
questions.description: A name so sneaky that Shakespeare used it first, and then someone gave it to a parrot.
questions.fun_fact: Comedian Gilbert Gottfried voiced Iago in the 1992 film, and Alan Tudyk voiced him in the 2019 remake.

questions.question: Complete this: “Bowser is to Super Mario Bros. as M. Bison is to…”
hints: It's a one-on-one fighting video game.
Ryu, Ken and Chun-Li are characters in this game.
One of its fighters shouts “Hadouken!”
questions.description: A final boss in a red cape and military cap who won't even let you win at rock, paper, scissors.
questions.fun_fact: In Japan, M. Bison is called Vega, and the name M. Bison belongs to the boxer there.

questions.question: We are the Borg from “Star Trek”: we travel in a cube-shaped ship and always say “Resistance is futile.” What do we want to do to you?
hints: We are half living beings, half machines.
For us, the word “I” doesn't exist: there is only “we.”
We would give you implants so you think exactly like us.
questions.description: Space neighbors who aren't here to borrow sugar, or to say hello.
questions.fun_fact: The Borg Queen first appeared in the 1996 movie “Star Trek: First Contact.”

questions.question: I'm a skinny old horse. My owner took four days to pick my name, because he wanted one worthy of a great knight-errant's horse. What's my name?
hints: My owner read far too many books about knights.
I live in La Mancha.
My rider is Don Quixote.
questions.description: A horse showing more bones than any desire to gallop.
questions.fun_fact: Sancho Panza's donkey has a name too: Dapple (el Rucio in Spanish).

questions.question: The rose is to the kings of England as the fleur-de-lis is to the kings of…
hints: Many of these kings were crowned in Reims Cathedral.
Their royal banners were blue with golden flowers.
Its capital is Paris.
questions.description: A flower that has spent centuries on flags, coats of arms and even American football helmets.
questions.fun_fact: The fleur-de-lis is also the symbol of the Scouts all over the world.

questions.question: In what year was the Obelisk of Buenos Aires unveiled, as a kind of birthday present for the city?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
It was in the first half of that century.
It marked 400 years since Buenos Aires was first founded, in 1536.
questions.description: A giant pencil that nobody has ever managed to sharpen.
questions.fun_fact: The Obelisk is about 67 m (220 ft) tall and was built in just over a month.

questions.question: What nickname is given to the city where this monument stands?
hints: The nickname comes from poets of ancient times.
A famous saying claims that all roads lead to this city.
It is the opposite of “temporary.”
questions.description: A city with so much history that even its ruins have ruins.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman poet Tibullus was already calling it that in the 1st century BC.

questions.question: What has been special about public transportation in Luxembourg since 2020?
wrong_answers: It runs only on solar power
hints: Tourists and the people who live there enjoy it just the same.
No other country had done this before across its whole territory.
You can leave your wallet in your pocket.
questions.description: A tiny country with a very big idea for getting around town.
questions.fun_fact: In 2020, Luxembourg became the first country in the world with free public transportation across its whole territory.

questions.question: Complete: “Buster the dog is to Andy as Scud the dog is to…”
hints: Scud is a fierce dog who chases toys.
His owner lives in the house next door to Andy.
His owner wears a skull T-shirt and takes toys apart.
questions.description: A question for people who even know the names of the characters' pets.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of Toy Story 3, a grown-up Sid shows up working as a garbage collector.

questions.question: Which of these movies did NOT win the Oscar for Best Animated Feature?
hints: The odd one out was nominated, but it lost.
It lost to a movie about dancing penguins.
Its hero is a red race car.
questions.description: A golden statuette that lots of cartoon characters dream of hugging.
questions.fun_fact: The first Oscar for Best Animated Feature went to Shrek, in 2002.

questions.question: In a village near Burgos, Spain, at Corpus Christi, a man dressed as a devil jumps over people lying on mattresses in the street. Who are they?
hints: The festival is called El Colacho and is several centuries old.
Their families dress them in their best clothes before laying them on the mattresses.
All of them were born during the past year.
questions.description: A festival where the one who jumps highest is also the ugliest guy in town.
questions.fun_fact: By tradition, the devil's leap “cleanses” the children of original sin and protects them from illness.

questions.question: I'm a famous saint of Ireland. Legend says I taught with a three-leaf clover, and on my day, March 17, half the world wears green. Who am I?
hints: I lived more than a thousand years ago.
A huge cathedral in New York is named after me.
In Irish, my name is Pádraig.
questions.description: A saint so green that even his symbol is a plant.
questions.fun_fact: In Chicago, the city's river is dyed green to celebrate Saint Patrick's Day.

questions.question: At the harvest festival called Pongal, people boil rice and milk in a pot until it spills over, for good luck. In which country is it celebrated?
hints: It's a country in Asia.
The Ganges River is sacred there.
Diwali, the festival of lights, is also celebrated there.
questions.description: A festival where letting the pot boil over isn't a kitchen disaster, it's good luck.
questions.fun_fact: “Pongal” comes from a Tamil word meaning “to boil” or “to overflow”, which is exactly what the pot does.

questions.question: Every February 2 in the US, Phil the groundhog comes out of his burrow. Depending on whether he sees his shadow, what does he “predict”?
wrong_answers: Whether the corn harvest will be good
Whether the year will bring good luck
How many hurricanes there will be
hints: Phil lives in a town in Pennsylvania called Punxsutawney.
It has to do with the weather in the coming weeks.
If he sees his shadow, he hides back in his burrow… and the cold sticks around.
questions.description: The only celebrity in the world whose job is to climb out of a hole once a year.
questions.fun_fact: The tradition inspired the movie “Groundhog Day” (1993), in which Bill Murray lives the same February 2 over and over again.

questions.question: The Seven Dwarfs are to Snow White as the ___ are to Gru.
hints: They are small and very mischievous.
They are yellow, and many of them wear goggles.
They love bananas.
questions.description: A villain so bad that everyone ends up loving him, especially his little helpers.
questions.fun_fact: The Minions speak a made-up language that mixes words from many languages, including Spanish.

questions.question: Olive oil is made from olives, and balsamic vinegar of Modena is made from…
hints: It's a fruit that grows in bunches.
It's a small, round fruit, green or purple.
The same fruit is used to make wine.
questions.description: A dark dressing that makes any salad feel important.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena is aged in wooden barrels for at least 12 years.

questions.question: Raffaele Esposito, Naples in 1889 and the colors of the Italian flag. According to the most famous story, which dish links all three?
hints: The flag's colors were red, white and green, just like its ingredients.
It is baked in a wood-fired oven.
It was named after the queen of Italy at the time.
questions.description: A tale of royalty, patriotism and a lot of hunger in the 19th century.
questions.fun_fact: The pizzeria where Esposito worked still exists in Naples and is now called Pizzeria Brandi.

questions.question: At the store you see butterfly-shaped pasta called “farfalle”. If “farfalle” is to “butterflies”, “orecchiette” is to…
hints: It's a part of the body.
You have two of them, one on each side of your head.
You use them to listen to music.
questions.description: A pasta so tiny it fits on the tip of your finger.
questions.fun_fact: In Bari, in southern Italy, women make orecchiette by hand right in the street, pressing each piece of dough with their thumb.

questions.question: You just picked olives in an olive grove in Italy, as people have done since ancient Rome. Where do you take them to make oil?
hints: That's where they get crushed with stones or machines.
The old ones had big stone wheels that turned round and round.
The same kind of place is used to grind wheat.
questions.description: A fruit so oily that people squeeze the oil right out of it.
questions.fun_fact: Some olive trees in Italy are more than a thousand years old and still grow olives.

questions.question: Minestrone, ribollita and pasta e fagioli: what do they have in common?
hints: They are served hot in a deep bowl.
They contain vegetables, beans and sometimes pasta.
Minestrone is the one with lots of chopped vegetables.
questions.description: Three names that sound like opera singers, but you eat them.
questions.fun_fact: “Ribollita” means “reboiled”: it was made by heating up the previous day's soup with stale bread.

questions.question: It has sushi rice tucked inside a sweet fried tofu pouch, and legend says it's the favorite food of a Japanese god's fox messengers. What is it called?
hints: It has no raw fish and no seaweed on the outside.
Its pouch is golden or brown and tastes sweet.
Its name comes from the Japanese god of rice, guarded by foxes.
questions.description: A sushi that climbed into a little bag and refuses to come out.
questions.fun_fact: Inari shrines in Japan have fox statues, and people leave fried tofu for them as an offering.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: shōjin ryōri, the traditional cooking of the monks in Japan's temples, is completely…
hints: It has to do with what the monks choose not to eat.
It uses tofu, vegetables, seaweed and mushrooms.
It has no meat and no fish.
questions.description: A menu so calm it meditates before it's served.
questions.fun_fact: Many Japanese temples still serve shōjin ryōri to visitors, on lacquered trays.

questions.question: At a Japanese restaurant, the menu lists “nigiri” and “onigiri.” Besides rice, what do they have in common?
questions.answer: They are shaped by squeezing by hand
wrong_answers: They are fried in hot oil
They are served in a broth
They are eaten with a spoon
hints: The clue is in the part of the name they share.
“Nigiru” is a Japanese verb that has to do with your fingers.
It means something like “to grip” or “to squeeze.”
questions.description: Two dishes with almost twin names, like cousins who dress alike.
questions.fun_fact: A good nigiri chef presses the rice just enough to hold together, but still melt in your mouth.

questions.question: Finish the translation: “okonomiyaki,” the grilled Japanese pancake with cabbage, means roughly “grilled the way you…”
hints: The missing word is about the person who is going to eat it.
Everyone adds whatever they enjoy most.
“Okonomi” means “to your taste.”
questions.description: A Japanese pancake that took the whole cabbage thing very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: In many okonomiyaki restaurants, the table has a hot griddle and each customer cooks their own.

questions.question: It's a Japanese lunch box with food decorated to look like characters such as Pikachu or Totoro, and its name blends “character” and “bento.” What is it called?
hints: Many parents in Japan make it for their kids to take to school.
They use rice, seaweed and vegetables as if they were modeling clay.
“Kyara” comes from the English word “character.”
questions.description: A lunch so cute it feels mean to eat it.
questions.fun_fact: Japan holds contests for decorated lunch boxes, and some look like real works of art.

questions.question: Caesar salad, with romaine lettuce, croutons and Parmesan cheese, is famous all over the world. In which country was it invented?
hints: It's not the country the name makes you think of.
It was born in a border city, very close to California.
It was invented in Tijuana.
questions.description: A salad with an emperor's name and a passport full of surprises.
questions.fun_fact: Italian chef Caesar Cardini invented it at his restaurant in Tijuana in the 1920s, which is why it's called “Caesar”.

questions.question: I'm a Mexican breakfast: fried eggs on a tortilla, covered in tomato and chili sauce. I'm called huevos rancheros. What does “rancheros” mean?
hints: Think of Mexican ranchera music.
It comes from the Spanish word “rancho”.
Farm workers used to eat it.
questions.description: A breakfast with so much personality it even has a last name.
questions.fun_fact: It was the hearty breakfast of farm workers, to keep them going through a long day in the fields.

questions.question: I'm fried dough eaten at Christmas. In Mexico I'm flat and crunchy with honey; in Colombia I'm a little cheese ball. What am I?
hints: I'm fried in very hot oil.
In Spain I'm sometimes filled with cream.
My name starts with “Bu”.
questions.description: Dough, hot oil and a little patience: the recipe for happiness in December.
questions.fun_fact: Buñuelos came to the Americas with the Spanish, and each country changed them in its own way.

questions.question: I'm the pib, the traditional Maya oven of Yucatán, and cochinita pibil comes out of me. What am I made of?
wrong_answers: An adobe dome with a chimney
hints: The Maya used me long before modern kitchens existed.
The food is covered and cooks slowly for hours.
People dig me and fill me with stones and embers.
questions.description: A kitchen so old it isn't in any appliance catalog.
questions.fun_fact: “Pibil” means “cooked in the pib”, in other words, buried underground.

questions.question: According to the most common story, the first cheeseburger was made in Pasadena, California. In which decade?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
It was the age of jazz and silent films.
It was the same decade that radio became popular.
questions.description: Someone looked at a burger and thought: “It needs a little yellow blanket.”
questions.fun_fact: The cheeseburger is usually credited to Lionel Sternberger, who, the story goes, was only 16 or 17 years old when he made it.

questions.question: The most common story says mayonnaise got its name from the French capture of Mahón, Menorca, in 1756. Which noble led those troops?
hints: It happened during the reign of King Louis XV.
He was a Marshal of France, and one of his relatives had been a very powerful cardinal.
That cardinal relative is the villain in “The Three Musketeers”.
questions.description: A sauce with more military history than many generals.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this story, many people in Spain still call it “mahonesa”.

questions.question: My face, with a white suit and a little goatee, is on buckets of fried chicken. Which US state is in my chain's name?
hints: The chain is known by three letters.
The state is famous for racehorses and a race called the Derby.
KFC stands for “… Fried Chicken”.
questions.description: A gentleman in a white suit who spent his whole life thinking about chicken.
questions.fun_fact: Sanders was never a real colonel: “Colonel” was an honorary title given to him by the state of Kentucky.

questions.question: Croquettes, small breaded and fried bites that are golden outside and creamy inside, get their name from the French verb “croquer”. What does it mean?
hints: It has to do with a sound.
Think of the first bite.
The French word imitates a sound, a bit like “crack” or “crisp”.
questions.description: A little snack that vanishes from the party tray before anyone even sees it.
questions.fun_fact: The same French word gave its name to the “croque-monsieur”, a hot ham and cheese sandwich.

questions.question: In “The Jungle Book,” the animals almost never call Mowgli a “boy.” What nickname do they use?
hints: They call him as if he were one of the wolf family, but they also say what he really is.
It's made of two words joined together, and one of them says what species Mowgli is.
The second part is the word for a baby bear, lion or wolf.
questions.description: Raised by wolves, he learns to howl before he learns to say “Mom.”
questions.fun_fact: In Kipling's original book, Mother Wolf calls him “Mowgli the Frog” because the baby had no fur at all.

questions.question: Which country is the original Pinocchio book from?
hints: The book came out in Europe in the 19th century.
In the original language, “Pinocchio” means something like “pine nut”, the seed of the pine tree.
It's the country shaped like a boot.
questions.description: A bug who works full-time as a conscience and doesn't charge a single cent.
questions.fun_fact: In the original book the cricket has no name: he's simply “the Talking Cricket”. The name Jiminy Cricket came with the Disney film.

questions.question: This black panther found Mowgli as a baby and took him to live with the wolves. What is its name?
hints: It's not the bear who sings or the tiger who hunts Mowgli.
It's the one who keeps telling Mowgli off and urging him to go back to the humans.
Its name starts with B, just like its bear friend's.
questions.description: The jungle's most stylish babysitter, dressed all in black.
questions.fun_fact: Black panthers are leopards or jaguars with lots of dark pigment: in the right light, you can still see their spots.

questions.question: About how wide can a leaf of the giant Amazon water lily grow?
hints: It's much bigger than the leaf of any plant in your home.
A grown-up could lie down on it, stretched out.
It's about as long as a small car.
questions.description: A plate so big that not even a whole family barbecue could fill it.
questions.fun_fact: The ribs under this leaf inspired the gardener Joseph Paxton when he designed London's Crystal Palace.

questions.question: What do Mickey Mouse's 1928 cartoon, the writer Mark Twain and the inventor Robert Fulton have in common?
hints: All three have to do with a way of traveling.
Mark Twain worked as a river pilot on the Mississippi.
They run on a boiler and a big paddle wheel.
questions.description: A museum where everything puffs out smoke, except the tour guide.
questions.fun_fact: The pen name “Mark Twain” was a call of Mississippi boatmen meaning the river was two fathoms deep, enough to sail safely.

questions.question: In southern Vietnam, the Mekong splits into many branches before reaching the sea. There it's called the “River of ___ Dragons.” What number is missing?
hints: The number is hidden in the river's Vietnamese name, Cửu Long.
It's a single-digit number.
It's the number just before 10.
questions.description: A river so stylish it dresses up as a whole bunch of dragons at the end.
questions.fun_fact: The Mekong Delta has floating markets where people buy fruit straight from one boat to another.

questions.question: I'm called “the river of five colors,” and in some months my riverbed turns bright red. What gives me that color?
hints: It's something alive.
It grows stuck to the rocks on the riverbed and needs sunlight to change color.
It isn't an animal: it has leaves and even flowers.
questions.description: A river that looks like someone painted it in art class.
questions.fun_fact: The plant that paints Caño Cristales is called Macarenia clavigera, named after the Serranía de La Macarena mountains where the river flows.

questions.question: In the movie WALL·E, what does EVE come to Earth to find?
hints: Finding it would prove that people can live on Earth again.
What she finds fits inside an old boot.
It's something green that grows out of the soil.
questions.description: A visitor from space with more style than a brand-new phone and a worse temper than a Monday morning.
questions.fun_fact: Apple designer Jony Ive helped shape EVE's look so she would seem like a sleek, modern gadget.

questions.question: A robot walks on six legs, moving three at a time while the other three hold it up. Which group of animals is it copying?
hints: Look at the number of legs.
Spiders have eight, so it isn't them.
Ants, beetles and cockroaches belong to this group.
questions.description: A robot that would need three pairs of shoes just to leave the house.
questions.fun_fact: Walking with three legs always on the ground makes a tripod, so the robot never loses its balance, just like a cockroach.

questions.question: In which decade did the Roomba, the disc-shaped robot vacuum, first go on sale?
hints: It's younger than your parents, but older than many kids playing today.
It came out before the first iPhone.
It came out in 2002.
questions.description: The only worker in the house who never complains about cleaning the floor, but still gets stuck under the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Roomba, iRobot, the company that made it, built robots to explore dangerous places.

questions.question: In what year did the animated series “PAW Patrol” first air?
hints: It's from this century.
It came out when touchscreen phones were already common everywhere.
It first aired the same year the movie “Frozen” hit theaters.
questions.description: Six puppies and a boy with a tablet handle more emergencies than real firefighters.
questions.fun_fact: Its creator, Keith Chapman, also came up with the series “Bob the Builder.”

questions.question: I have pointy ears, I'm half human and half Vulcan, and I greet people with my fingers split in a V, saying “Live long and prosper.” Who am I?
hints: I travel through space on a ship called the Enterprise.
I'm famous for being very logical and almost never showing emotions.
My show is “Star Trek” and my name has five letters.
questions.description: A hand greeting so tricky that some people practice it in front of the mirror.
questions.fun_fact: Actor Leonard Nimoy based the Vulcan salute on a blessing gesture he saw in a synagogue as a boy.

questions.question: I delivered pizza in New York, got frozen on New Year's Eve 1999 and woke up a thousand years later, in the year 3000. Who am I?
hints: My show was made by the same creator as “The Simpsons.”
Now I work for a space delivery company.
My best friend is a robot, and my full name starts with Philip J.
questions.description: The longest nap in history: a thousand years, and the pizza didn't even get cold.
questions.fun_fact: In a time-travel episode of “Futurama,” Fry ends up becoming his own grandfather.

questions.question: I'm a lab mouse with a huge head, every night I plan to take over the world, and my buddy keeps shouting “Narf!”. Who am I?
hints: I live in a cage at Acme Labs.
I'm very serious and very smart; my buddy is the total opposite.
My name is the organ you think with.
questions.description: One evil plan a day, every day, for years: now that's dedication.
questions.fun_fact: “Pinky and the Brain” started as a segment of the show “Animaniacs” before getting its own series.

questions.question: I'm a secret agent in a hat, living with two inventor stepbrothers who don't know my double life. My kind lives wild in only one country. Which?
hints: I'm Perry, from “Phineas and Ferb.”
My kind has a duck's bill and lays eggs, even though it's a mammal.
It's the land of kangaroos and koalas.
questions.description: Lazy pet by day, secret agent in a hat by night: every cat's dream.
questions.fun_fact: The platypus is one of the very few mammals in the world that lay eggs.

questions.question: I'm a dog who can stretch, grow huge or tiny, and I go on adventures in the Land of Ooo with my human brother Finn. Who am I?
hints: I'm on a Cartoon Network show.
My friend Finn wears a white hat with little ears.
I'm yellow and my show is “Adventure Time”.
questions.description: The perfect dog: stretches like chewing gum and never needs a walk.
questions.fun_fact: “Adventure Time” started as a short cartoon in 2007, years before it became a series.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm the brain of the computer, I do billions of calculations per second and I live on a tiny chip. What am I made of inside?
hints: My parts are tiny switches that turn on and off.
Each of my parts lets electric current through or stops it: that's how I count in ones and zeros.
Before chips, these parts came one by one, and they gave their name to your grandparents' portable radios.
questions.description: It thinks faster than you, but it still has no idea where you left your keys.
questions.fun_fact: The transistors in a modern processor are so small that they're tinier than most viruses.

questions.question: The tech region in California where companies like Apple and Google were born has a nickname. Which material is it named after?
hints: It's an element on the periodic table, not something you buy at a hardware store.
It sits right below carbon on the periodic table.
Computer chips are made from it.
questions.description: A valley where, instead of cows grazing, you find engineers drinking coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust, after oxygen: it's in almost all sand.

questions.question: Riddle: I read the tiny lines on your finger to unlock your phone. If only one identical twin registers a finger, what happens when the other twin tries?
hints: Identical twins share their genes, but not everything is genetic.
The lines on our fingers form before we're born, shaped by our movements inside mom's belly.
Not even identical twins have the same fingerprints.
questions.description: Your finger is your password, so don't lend it to anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Koalas have fingerprints so similar to human ones that they are hard to tell apart.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a space probe. I left Earth in 1977, flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and now travel beyond the planets. What do I carry in case aliens find me?
questions.answer: A record of sounds and music from Earth
wrong_answers: A flag from every country in the world
Seeds from plants that grow on Earth
A letter written by children of the world
hints: A team led by the astronomer Carl Sagan put it together.
It comes with drawn instructions showing how to use it.
It's golden and shaped like your grandparents' old vinyl LPs.
questions.description: The slowest letter in the universe, sent with no address and no stamp.
questions.fun_fact: The Voyager Golden Record carries greetings in 55 languages and even the song of a humpback whale.

questions.question: What do the trains run on along most lines of the Mexico City Metro?
hints: It isn't future technology: it has been in use for more than seventy years.
