The idea came from the Paris Metro, which wanted quieter trains.
It's the same thing a mechanic pumps up when a car gets a flat.
questions.description: A metro that rolls with more style than you walk.
questions.fun_fact: The little pictures for each Mexico City Metro station were made so that anyone could find their way, even people who couldn't read.

questions.question: In Madrid, you board a train called the AVE, short for “Alta Velocidad Española” (Spanish High Speed). About how fast can it carry passengers at most?
hints: It goes much faster than a car on the highway.
But not as fast as a plane in mid-flight.
It's about the top speed of a Formula 1 car.
questions.description: In Spanish its name means “bird,” and it doesn't just flap around.
questions.fun_fact: The first AVE line, between Madrid and Seville, opened in 1992, the year Seville hosted the World's Fair.

questions.question: At the movie theater, the stadium and the train station, you line up at a window to pay before you go in or travel. What is that window called?
hints: You usually find it near the entrance.
It's often a window with glass and a little gap to pass the money through.
Its name says exactly what you buy there.
questions.description: The place where the line is always longest just when you're in a hurry.
questions.fun_fact: At movie theaters and stadiums, the ticket office is often called the box office, which is why a very successful movie is called a “box-office hit”.

questions.question: It's 6 p.m., everyone is leaving work, and the subway is so packed you can't move. What is this time of day called?
hints: It's when the most people travel at the same time.
It's the opposite of off-peak, when trains are almost empty.
The first word of its name also means “to hurry”.
questions.description: The time of day when the subway turns into a can of sardines.
questions.fun_fact: In Tokyo, station staff sometimes help squeeze passengers into packed trains during the morning rush.

questions.question: This is the Big Boy, one of the largest steam locomotives ever built. What was it made for?
hints: A US company built it in the 1940s.
Its huge pulling power mattered more than speed.
It had to pull very heavy trains up the mountains of the western United States.
questions.description: If this were a toy train, you'd need a living room the size of a stadium.
questions.fun_fact: Only 25 Big Boys were ever built, and one of them, No. 4014, ran again in 2019.

questions.question: In the Harry Potter books and films, what do wizards use Platform 9¾ at King's Cross station for?
questions.answer: To catch the train to Hogwarts
wrong_answers: To reach the Ministry of Magic
hints: It's part of the world of Harry Potter.
Students use it at the start of every school year.
A red train leaves from there for a school of magic.
questions.description: A platform where running straight into a wall is part of the plan.
questions.fun_fact: J. K. Rowling has said her parents met on a train leaving King's Cross station.

questions.question: Which luxury train ran from Paris to Istanbul and is the setting of an Agatha Christie novel with Hercule Poirot?
hints: Its route went from Western Europe toward the east.
Istanbul sits at the gateway to Asia.
Its name means “the express to the East”.
questions.description: A luxury train where nobody gets off until a detective has asked them a few questions.
questions.fun_fact: The Orient Express made its first trip in 1883.

questions.question: A paper clip floating on water, an insect walking on a puddle, food coloring fleeing from soap in milk: what do they have in common?
hints: It all happens on the surface of a liquid.
It's as if the water had a very thin “skin”.
Soap “breaks” the tension of that skin on the liquid.
questions.description: An experiment where milk sets off fireworks without asking anyone's permission.
questions.fun_fact: With whole milk the effect is even more spectacular, because the soap also starts “chasing” the fat in the milk.

questions.question: I'm a famous character. So I never forget a detail, I keep each fact in a room of my “mind palace” and walk through it in my imagination to find it. Who am I?
hints: I'm a detective.
I live in London, and a doctor friend writes down my adventures.
My address is 221B Baker Street.
questions.description: For anyone who can never remember where they left their keys: someone keeps a whole building inside their head.
questions.fun_fact: The mind palace is the ancient “method of loci”, which legend says the Greek poet Simonides invented about 2,500 years ago.

questions.question: The finger trick for the 9 times table gives 27, 63 and 72. What do these results have in common?
hints: Look at each number on its own, one digit at a time.
Try adding: 2 + 7, 6 + 3, 7 + 2.
It always gives you the same number as the times table you're practicing.
questions.description: Ten fingers, one times table and zero calculators: the oldest technology at school.
questions.fun_fact: The trick works because 9 is 10 minus 1: each time you add 9, the tens go up by one and the ones go down by one.

questions.question: With toothpaste and a cloth, you can make something shiny again after it turns black over time. What is it?
hints: It's something that used to be very shiny.
It gets darker because it reacts with the air.
It's a precious metal, cheaper than gold.
questions.description: A bathroom product with a secret second job in the dining room.
questions.fun_fact: Silver turns black because it reacts with sulfur in the air and forms a layer of silver sulfide.

questions.question: Roughly how many Scoville units does pure capsaicin, the substance that makes chili peppers hot, measure?
hints: It's far more than any chili pepper you've ever tasted.
A jalapeño measures only a few thousand units.
It's a number with six zeros.
questions.description: Some spicy things you feel on your tongue, and some you feel in your soul.
questions.fun_fact: Birds don't feel the burn of capsaicin, so they eat chili peppers and spread the seeds everywhere.

questions.question: The Fertile Crescent, shaped like a half-moon and watered by the Tigris and Euphrates, saw farming begin 10,000 years ago. Which countries cover much of it today?
hints: It's in the Middle East, in Asia.
Ancient Mesopotamia was there.
One of these countries has Baghdad as its capital.
questions.description: A half-moon that lives on a map instead of in the sky, and invented the vegetable garden.
questions.fun_fact: Wheat, barley, lentils, peas and chickpeas are among the first plants humans learned to grow in that region.

questions.question: Which insects ooze a yellow liquid from their legs when disturbed and are set loose in vegetable gardens to eat aphids?
hints: These insects are hunters.
Farmers use them as a natural way to control pests.
They are usually red with black spots.
questions.description: A tiny bug that drinks your plants' juice without asking first.
questions.fun_fact: Some ants look after aphids like cows, so they can drink the sweet liquid the aphids give off.

questions.question: Look at these leaves: they're rich in folic acid, which doctors recommend during pregnancy. What is it for?
questions.answer: Helping the baby's spine and brain form well
wrong_answers: Helping the baby be born with more hair
Helping the baby be born with light eyes
hints: It helps build new cells.
It matters most in the first weeks, when the baby is only just forming.
It has to do with the nervous system.
questions.description: Leaves that work hard for someone who hasn't even been born yet.
questions.fun_fact: “Folic” comes from the Latin “folium”, meaning leaf, because it was discovered in spinach leaves.

questions.question: Vitamin A is to sight as vitamin K is to…
hints: It's plentiful in leafy greens like spinach and kale.
It has to do with blood.
It helps a cut stop bleeding.
questions.description: Vitamins are named with letters, and this one skipped a big part of the alphabet.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “K” after the German word “Koagulation”.

questions.question: Riddle: “I left Lisbon, sailed around Africa past the Cape of Good Hope and was the first European to reach India by sea, looking for pepper.” Who am I?
hints: He was Portuguese.
He reached India in 1498.
His family name starts with G.
questions.description: A really, really long trip just to get something to make dinner tastier.
questions.fun_fact: In the Middle Ages pepper was so expensive that it was sometimes used to pay off debts.

questions.question: I live in a cave under the mountains, eat raw fish, ask a hobbit riddles and call a ring “my precious.” Who am I?
hints: I appear in “The Hobbit” and “The Lord of the Rings.”
I talk to myself, as if there were two of us.
My name used to be Sméagol.
questions.description: The worst roommate ever: lives in a cave, eats raw fish and talks to his jewelry.
questions.fun_fact: The character is called Gollum because of the gulping noise he makes in his throat.

questions.question: In “The Lion King”, Scar bosses the hyenas. In “The Little Mermaid”, the sea witch Ursula bosses two…
hints: They live in the sea.
They are long and look like snakes.
Their names are Flotsam and Jetsam.
questions.description: Every villain needs helpers who laugh at their jokes, even the bad ones.
questions.fun_fact: Scar's hyenas are called Shenzi, Banzai and Ed, and Ed never says a word: he only laughs.

questions.question: You walk into Dolores Umbridge's office at Hogwarts. Which of these would you NOT find there?
hints: Umbridge's office is pink and overly cute.
Look for the thing that belongs to another teacher.
That animal is the pet of the Hogwarts headmaster.
questions.description: An office so pink that even bubble gum would look dull next to it.
questions.fun_fact: In the movies, the kittens on Umbridge's plates move and meow.

questions.question: Complete this: “Lex Luthor is to Superman as Ming the Merciless is to…”
hints: He is a comic-strip hero from the 1930s.
Ming rules the planet Mongo.
In 1980 he got a movie with music by the band Queen.
questions.description: A space emperor with a soap-opera villain mustache and a nickname that doesn't win friends.
questions.fun_fact: Queen's song for the 1980 movie made the shout “Flash! Ah-ah!” famous.

questions.question: You buy shares in a famous sports shoe company. What do you become?
hints: Now you own a tiny piece of the company.
If the company does well, you might do well too.
The word comes straight from what you bought.
questions.description: Owning a piece of a giant company without ever sitting through a boring meeting.
questions.fun_fact: The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, is considered the first company to sell shares to the public.

questions.question: I have no handles and no wicker, but I hold rice, milk, rent and bus fares, and I'm checked every month. What am I for?
questions.answer: To measure how much prices go up
wrong_answers: To work out how much tax you pay
To count how many people live in the country
hints: I'm a list of what a typical household buys.
Economists compare what I cost before with what I cost now.
I'm how inflation gets calculated.
questions.description: The most famous basket in the country, and nobody has ever seen it.
questions.fun_fact: The basket used to measure inflation holds hundreds of goods and services, from potatoes to haircuts.

questions.question: We're brothers, we wear masks and prison numbers, and we keep trying to rob Scrooge McDuck's money bin. Who are we?
hints: We show up in the adventures of DuckTales.
Our mom is a thief too.
Our name comes from a breed of dog, the same breed as Snoopy.
questions.description: A very close family, especially when they're planning something they shouldn't.
questions.fun_fact: The Beagle Boys were created by cartoonist Carl Barks and first appeared in a comic book in 1951.

questions.question: He's a billionaire, lives in a mansion in Gotham, and his butler is named Alfred. Where did his fortune come from?
hints: We're talking about the man behind Batman's mask.
He didn't have to earn it all by himself.
His family was already rich and owned a big company before he was born.
questions.description: A butler, a mansion and a secret cave don't come cheap.
questions.fun_fact: Bruce Wayne has appeared on Forbes magazine's lists of the richest fictional characters.

questions.question: This bird stars in the old saying “Grain by grain, the hen fills her crop.” What does the saying teach?
questions.answer: That saving bit by bit adds up
wrong_answers: That food is worth more than money
hints: The hen doesn’t eat everything in one bite.
Think of a piggy bank where you drop in a coin every day.
Lots of small things together make something big.
questions.description: A bird that has been teaching money lessons for centuries without charging a cent.
questions.fun_fact: The crop is a little pouch in a bird’s neck where it stores food before digesting it.

questions.question: M-Pesa, a service for sending money by phone, launched in 2007 in an African country. Which one?
hints: It's a country in East Africa.
It's famous for its safaris and its marathon runners.
Its capital is Nairobi.
questions.description: Sending money by text message before it was cool.
questions.fun_fact: “Pesa” means “money” in Swahili, and the “M” stands for “mobile.”

questions.question: Complete this: an umbrella is to rain as an emergency fund is to…
hints: You need an umbrella for something you can't be sure when it will come.
Think of a fridge that breaks down or a trip to the doctor.
It's something you never planned to pay for.
questions.description: Money you put aside for when life decides to play a prank on you.
questions.fun_fact: Many experts say an emergency fund should be big enough to cover three to six months of expenses.

questions.question: I'm an airline, and my name, QANTAS, is an acronym that starts with “Queensland.” Which country am I from?
hints: My country is in the Southern Hemisphere.
Queensland is a region famous for a huge coral reef.
A red kangaroo is painted on the tail of my planes.
questions.description: An airline whose name sounds like a tongue twister but is really a geography lesson.
questions.fun_fact: Qantas was founded in 1920 and is one of the oldest airlines in the world that is still flying.

questions.question: At airports, “BOG” is to Bogotá as “MAD” is to…
hints: These codes appear on luggage tags.
Look at the first letters of the city's name.
It's the capital of Spain.
questions.description: Cities have nicknames too, but only three letters long.
questions.fun_fact: Chicago's airport code is ORD because the airport used to be called Orchard Field.

questions.question: I'm a Caribbean beach where planes land almost right over the swimmers' heads. Which island am I on?
hints: My name is Maho Beach, and I star in lots of viral videos.
My airport is named after a Dutch princess.
My island is split between France and the Netherlands.
questions.description: A place where sunbathing comes with free hair styling by jet engine.
questions.fun_fact: Saint Martin is one of the smallest islands in the world shared by two countries.

questions.question: The white lines airplanes leave in the sky form very high up, where it is extremely cold. What are they made of?
hints: They are close cousins of clouds.
The engine releases hot water vapor that cools down all at once.
It’s the same thing that forms frost in a freezer.
questions.description: Airplanes can draw too, but only in straight lines.
questions.fun_fact: When the air is very humid, these trails can last for hours and turn into real clouds.

questions.question: I'm four gold stripes on a pilot's sleeves. What am I for?
questions.answer: To show the pilot is the captain
wrong_answers: To count the years spent flying
To show how many languages they speak
To show how many engines the plane has
hints: The stripes change with the job in the cockpit.
The co-pilot usually wears three.
They show who is in charge of the plane.
questions.description: A uniform that speaks without saying a single word.
questions.fun_fact: Pilots' stripes come from navy uniforms, where they also show rank.

questions.question: After a run, what does a drink with electrolytes help your body get back?
wrong_answers: The sugar the body uses to sleep
hints: Think about what comes out of your skin when you exercise a lot.
Sweat tastes a little salty.
They are minerals like sodium and potassium.
questions.description: After a race, even the bravest runner stares at the bottle like it's buried treasure.
questions.fun_fact: Sweat tastes salty because it carries sodium, one of the electrolytes a sports drink puts back.

questions.question: I wear a huge hat, drink tea with a hare and celebrate a “happy unbirthday” with Alice. Who am I?
hints: I live in Wonderland.
My tea party never ends.
My name says what I make… and how things are going in my head.
questions.description: The perfect party: no presents, no cake and no sense at all.
questions.fun_fact: In the book, it is always six o'clock at the Hatter's party: teatime.

questions.question: I'm a fermented milk from the Caucasus, made with little white grains that look like tiny cauliflower. What am I?
hints: My grains are a mix of bacteria and yeasts.
I taste a little sour and a bit fizzy.
My name starts with K and ends with R.
questions.description: A milk that comes with its own little pets.
questions.fun_fact: Kefir grains grow and multiply, so you can give some away for others to make their own kefir.

questions.question: Strictly speaking, chamomile isn't a tea but an herbal infusion, because it doesn't come from this plant. Which plant is it?
hints: Green, black and white tea all come from it.
It is related to a very popular garden flower.
The second part of its Latin name means “from China.”
questions.description: A family feud: chamomile insists it's tea, and tea says it's no child of hers.
questions.fun_fact: Green and black tea come from the same plant; the difference is how much the leaves oxidize after they are picked.

questions.question: You boil dried hibiscus flowers, called “flor de Jamaica” in Mexico, in water to make a drink. What color does the water turn?
hints: It is a very popular drink in Mexico, served ice cold.
It tastes tart, a bit like cranberry.
It's the same color as a ripe tomato.
questions.description: A flower that jumps into the pot and comes out as a soft drink.
questions.fun_fact: The part of the hibiscus used for the drink isn't the petals but the calyces, the cup of leaves around the flower.

questions.question: I'm about 5 mm (0.2 in) long, I raise a colorful fan on my abdomen and dance for the female. What spider am I?
hints: I live in Australia, and videos of my dances go viral online.
I'm a jumping spider: I don't spin webs to hunt, I pounce on my prey.
I'm named after a blue and green bird that spreads its tail like a fan.
questions.description: An eight-legged dancer with zero shyness and plenty of sparkle.
questions.fun_fact: If his dance doesn't win the female over, the male has to run fast, or he could end up as her lunch.

questions.question: When a male peacock spreads its tail like a fan, about how many long feathers does it show off?
hints: That's far more than all the fingers in your whole family put together.
Many of them have a colorful “eye” at the tip.
It's more than a hundred, but less than a thousand.
questions.description: The only animal that carries its own fan wherever it goes.
questions.fun_fact: Every year the peacock loses its long tail feathers, and they grow back again.

questions.question: I'm a talking raccoon, and I travel with a tree that only says three words. What am I an expert at?
hints: I'm one of the Guardians of the Galaxy.
I love anything that goes “boom!”.
I always carry a huge gun that I built myself.
questions.description: A garbage-can raider who ended up saving the universe.
questions.fun_fact: Rocket was inspired by “Rocky Raccoon”, a song by the Beatles.

questions.question: The male builds a bower of twigs and decorates it with blue objects, even plastic bottle caps, to attract a mate. Where does it live?
hints: It lives in the Southern Hemisphere.
This region is famous for its marsupials.
Koalas and kangaroos live there too.
questions.description: The most obsessive interior decorator in the whole animal kingdom.
questions.fun_fact: Some male bowerbirds steal blue decorations from their neighbors' bowers.

questions.question: Its flat head looks like a dead leaf, it breathes through a tube-shaped nose and it catches fish by sucking them in. Where does this turtle live?
hints: It lives in the warm, slow waters of a tropical rainforest.
It is called the mata mata.
It shares its river with piranhas and pink dolphins.
questions.description: A turtle that dressed up as a dry leaf and forgot to take off the costume.
questions.fun_fact: The mata mata doesn't chew: it snaps its mouth open so fast that the fish gets swallowed along with the water.

questions.question: This river, with its finger-shaped mountains, is shown on a banknote worth 20. Which country is it in?
hints: It's in Asia.
New Year there is celebrated with dragons and red lanterns.
It's the country of the Great Wall.
questions.description: A view so pretty that someone decided a whole country should carry it in their pockets.
questions.fun_fact: Many tourists take a photo holding up a 20-yuan banknote in front of the same view of the Li River.

questions.question: In which country is the world's oldest central bank that is still working?
hints: The bank's name contains the local word for “realm” or “kingdom.”
Today this country is famous for flat-pack furniture and pop music.
Its capital is Stockholm.
questions.description: The great-grandpa of every bank that prints money, and it still hasn't retired.
questions.fun_fact: Sweden's Riksbank was founded in 1668, 26 years before the Bank of England.

questions.question: Euro banknotes went into circulation in 2002. Which of these currencies was NOT replaced by the euro?
hints: It belongs to a country that joined the European Union after 2002.
That country is in the European Union but still has its own currency.
Its capital is Budapest.
questions.description: In 2002, half of Europe emptied its wallets and started over with brand-new money.
questions.fun_fact: Hungary joined the European Union in 2004, but people there still pay in forints.

questions.question: In a New York store, prices are marked with $. If € stands for the euro, $ stands for the…
hints: Its name comes from an old European silver coin, the “thaler”.
Scrooge McDuck has millions of them.
Its most famous banknote is green.
questions.description: An S that got a stripe and suddenly became a millionaire.
questions.fun_fact: The $ sign was used for the peso before the dollar, and today both use it.

questions.question: The Eiffel Tower is to Paris as the Red Fort is to…
hints: It's in Asia.
It's a city in India.
The country's capital is there.
questions.description: A fort so red that even its name is blushing.
questions.fun_fact: The Red Fort in Delhi appears on the back of India's 500-rupee banknote.

questions.question: The Spanish children's song “La farolera” goes: “six and two are eight, and eight sixteen, and eight twenty-four, and eight…”. What number comes next?
hints: The song keeps adding the same number.
Each step adds 8 to the number before.
It's 24 plus 8.
questions.description: A song where someone falls down and, instead of getting up, starts doing math homework.
questions.fun_fact: Before electric light bulbs, there were people whose job was to light the street lamps by hand every night.

questions.question: Finish the song: “Old MacDonald had a farm…”
hints: It's a chorus with no meaning, just made for singing.
It's made only of vowels, with no consonants at all.
You sing the same sounds again right after “And on that farm he had a cow…”
questions.description: A farm so noisy that the farmer can't even hear his alarm clock.
questions.fun_fact: The song is sung around the world: in the Spanish version, the farm belongs to “my uncle” and the chorus goes “ia, ia, o”.

questions.question: I'm a dry, hollow gourd with ridges, and you play me by scraping me with a stick. What am I?
hints: I'm a percussion instrument.
People don't shake me or hit me: they scrape me.
You hear me a lot in salsa and cumbia, and my name sounds like “GWEE-roh”.
questions.description: An instrument that loves getting its belly scratched.
questions.fun_fact: A traditional güiro is made from the dried, hollow fruit of a plant in the squash family.

questions.question: You do it with both hands, it makes noise, and the song “If You're Happy and You Know It” asks you to do it. What is it?
hints: The audience does it at the end of a show.
Your hands hit each other.
People say “Give them a big hand!” just before doing it.
questions.description: A song that turns being happy into a workout.
questions.fun_fact: In later verses, the song also asks you to stomp your feet and shout “Hooray!”

questions.question: Look at this pipe at the back of a vehicle. What comes out of it when the engine is running?
hints: It comes from what the engine has already used and doesn't need anymore.
Sometimes it looks gray or white, especially on cold mornings.
It smells bad and you shouldn't breathe it in.
questions.description: Even cars need somewhere to let out what didn't agree with them.
questions.fun_fact: The exhaust system has a muffler that makes the engine sound much quieter.

questions.question: A cyclist’s legs are to the pedals as an engine’s pistons are to…
hints: Pedals turn an up-and-down push into a spin.
In the engine, this part takes the push from the pistons and turns it into rotation.
It’s a long metal shaft bent into a zigzag of elbows.
questions.description: A cyclist and a gasoline engine have more in common than you’d think.
questions.fun_fact: A bicycle’s pedal arms work like a tiny crankshaft, which is why bike mechanics call that part the “crankset”.

questions.question: You sit behind the wheel of a car with a manual gearbox. How many pedals are at your feet?
hints: One of them makes the car go faster.
Another one makes the car stop.
Besides those two, there is one you press to change gears: the clutch.
questions.description: Driving a car with gears means your feet have to know how to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Automatic cars have no clutch pedal, just an accelerator and a brake.

questions.question: This windshield cracked, but it didn’t shatter into pieces. What is it made of?
hints: It isn’t a single piece: it has several layers.
Between two layers of glass there is a sheet of plastic.
Its name is the same word used for sealing a paper ID card in clear plastic.
questions.description: A glass that breaks but flatly refuses to fall apart.
questions.fun_fact: Side windows are usually made of tempered glass, which breaks into lots of small pieces without sharp edges.

questions.question: Three of these luxury car brands were founded in Germany. Which one wasn't?
hints: The one we want was founded in another European country.
It was founded in 1906 by two partners, Charles and Henry.
It's as British as afternoon tea.
questions.description: Four luxury cars walk into a party, and one of them doesn't speak the same language as the others.
questions.fun_fact: The little silver statue on the hood of every Rolls-Royce is called the “Spirit of Ecstasy.”

questions.question: You're in Matsumoto, Japan, in front of one of the country's oldest castles. Which bird gives it its nickname?
hints: The nickname comes from the color of its walls.
Himeji Castle, all white, is nicknamed after a white bird: the heron.
It's a black, clever, noisy bird, and its bigger cousin, the raven, guards the Tower of London in legend.
questions.description: A Japanese castle with a bird for a nickname, just like athletes who get named after animals.
questions.fun_fact: Matsumoto Castle still has its original wooden main tower from more than 400 years ago, which is very rare in Japan.

questions.question: When the castle was attacked, soldiers gathered in me: open to the sky and surrounded by walls. What am I?
hints: I'm inside the walls, but I have no roof.
Many cities in the Americas, like Lima and Cusco, have a main square, the “Plaza de Armas”, named after the same idea.
Big houses and schools often have one of me too: an open space in the middle of the building.
questions.description: The only place in the castle where nobody complained there was no room for the horse.
questions.fun_fact: The “Plazas de Armas” (“squares of arms”) of many Latin American cities got their name because troops gathered there in colonial times.

questions.question: Its giant stones fit together without mortar, it watches over Cusco, and Inti Raymi is celebrated there. What language does the name Sacsayhuamán come from?
hints: It's the language of the people who built it.
It was the main language of the Inca Empire.
Millions of people in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador speak it today; English got words like “llama” and “puma” from it.
questions.description: A stone puzzle put together so well that not even a sheet of paper fits between its pieces.
questions.fun_fact: Its name is often translated as “satisfied falcon”, though experts argue about other meanings.

questions.question: Look at this detail of a fairy-tale castle in Germany. Which king, nicknamed “the Swan King”, had it built?
hints: He ruled a region in the south of Germany.
He was a huge fan of Wagner's operas.
The capital of his kingdom was Munich.
questions.description: A king who spent more on dreams than on armies.
questions.fun_fact: Neuschwanstein inspired Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland.

questions.question: It's a French word, it's on many wine labels, and there are hundreds along the Loire River. What does “château” mean?
hints: It's a large building.
Many French kings and nobles lived in one.
It comes from the Latin “castellum”, just like the English word for it.
questions.description: A word that sounds super fancy just because it's in French.
questions.fun_fact: In Bordeaux, many wineries call themselves “château” even if they only have a country house and not a single tower.

questions.question: Darth Vader is to a black helmet as a Star Wars stormtrooper is to…
hints: Think of the Empire's soldiers marching in rows.
Their suit covers them from head to toe and makes them all look the same.
They look like they're made of plastic the color of snow.
questions.description: A thousand identical soldiers and not one can aim: the great mystery of the galaxy.
questions.fun_fact: The name “stormtrooper” was borrowed from German shock troops of World War I.

questions.question: Which of these Star Wars characters is NOT a Sith?
hints: Three of them are villains from the dark side of the Force.
The one we want sat on the Jedi Council.
He uses a purple lightsaber.
questions.description: Dark Side Club: cape, yellow eyes and a bad attitude required.
questions.fun_fact: Under the “Rule of Two” in Star Wars, there can only be two Sith at a time: a master and an apprentice.

questions.question: You're driving the DeLorean in “Back to the Future”. What speed must you reach for the flux capacitor to send you through time?
hints: The speed is in miles, not kilometers.
It's about 141 km per hour.
The number is two eights in a row.
questions.description: A car that runs on a calendar instead of gasoline.
questions.fun_fact: Besides the speed, the flux capacitor needs 1.21 gigawatts of power, which Doc gets from plutonium or a bolt of lightning.

questions.question: It has Gungans living underwater, Padmé was its queen and its capital is Theed. Which planet is Palpatine from?
hints: It's a green planet with lakes and elegant palaces.
Jar Jar Binks comes from there too.
It appears at the start of “The Phantom Menace”.
questions.description: A very friendly senator with big weekend plans: taking over the galaxy.
questions.fun_fact: The scenes in the palace on Naboo were filmed at the Royal Palace of Caserta in Italy.

questions.question: Chewbacca is to Wookiee as the furry little bears of the moon of Endor are to…
hints: They appear in “Return of the Jedi”.
They live in little houses up in the forest trees.
One of them is named Wicket.
questions.description: Cuddly toys with spears that won a war against an empire.
questions.fun_fact: The forest of Endor was filmed among the giant redwoods of California.

questions.question: In which decade did Stanisław Lem publish his novel “Solaris”?
hints: It's about scientists on a space station studying a planet covered by a living ocean.
It came out the same year Yuri Gagarin flew into space.
Tarkovsky turned it into a film in 1972, a decade later.
questions.description: A planet that's all ocean and reads your mind too: a terrible vacation spot.
questions.fun_fact: “Solaris” has two famous films: Andrei Tarkovsky's (1972) and Steven Soderbergh's with George Clooney (2002).

questions.question: In which US state is Area 51?
hints: It lies deep in the desert of the American West.
It borders California and was home to a famous nuclear test site.
Its largest city is Las Vegas.
questions.description: The most secret base in the world, which somehow everyone has heard of.
questions.fun_fact: The US government only officially admitted that Area 51 exists in 2013.

questions.question: Joseph Lister introduced it in 1867. It used carbolic acid and keeps wounds from getting infected. What is it called?
hints: It has to do with killing germs.
The alcohol and iodine you put on a cut do exactly this.
Its name means “against rotting.”
questions.description: Before this, surgeons operated in the same stained coat they wore last week.
questions.fun_fact: Listerine mouthwash is named in honor of Joseph Lister.

questions.question: In an animated film, food like this falls from the sky thanks to a young inventor's machine. What is his name?
hints: He lives in a small town on an island.
His machine turns water into food.
The film is called “Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs.”
questions.description: Today's weather forecast: grab an umbrella and a fork.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, Flint's machine has a very long name, shortened to FLDSMDFR.

questions.question: Henry Cavendish discovered it in 1766, called it “inflammable air,” and it is the lightest element there is. What is it?
hints: It's a gas.
Stars like the Sun are made mostly of it.
It's the H in H₂O.
questions.description: A scientist so shy he left notes for his housekeeper so he wouldn't have to talk to her.
questions.fun_fact: Cavendish also “weighed” the Earth with an experiment using lead balls and a thin wire.

questions.question: In which century did Hippocrates, the Greek known as the father of medicine, live?
hints: It was before the birth of Christ.
It was around the same time as Socrates.
It was about a hundred years before Alexander the Great.
questions.description: The doctor every doctor swears an oath to, even though none of them ever met him.
questions.fun_fact: Hippocrates was one of the first to say that diseases have natural causes and are not punishments from the gods.

questions.question: I was the first dog to circle the Earth, aboard a Soviet satellite in 1957. Who am I?
hints: Before I was famous, I lived on the streets of Moscow.
I traveled on Sputnik 2.
My name means something like “barker” in Russian.
questions.description: A little dog who went farther than any ball anyone ever threw for her.
questions.fun_fact: Laika was the first animal to orbit the Earth, more than three years before the first human.

questions.question: Which German physicist discovered that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance?
hints: He published his law in 1827.
Today the unit of electrical resistance is named after him.
That unit is written with the Greek letter omega.
questions.description: A law that puts up resistance, but only to the current.
questions.fun_fact: When Ohm published his law, many fellow scientists dismissed it, and he lost his job as a teacher.

questions.question: Oppenheimer led the lab that tested the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In which year?
hints: It happened during the Second World War.
The United States built it in secret as part of the Manhattan Project.
It was in the middle of the 20th century, in the 1940s.
questions.description: A scientist Hollywood gave three hours of film and zero minutes of jokes.
questions.fun_fact: The test was called “Trinity”, and its flash was seen more than 200 km (124 miles) away.

questions.question: In which decade was “A Beautiful Mind”, the movie about mathematician John Nash, released?
hints: The lead actor is Russell Crowe.
It won the Oscar for Best Picture.
It came out the same year as the first Harry Potter movie.
questions.description: A movie where the equations have more suspense than the villains.
questions.fun_fact: John Nash won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994 for his ideas on game theory.

questions.question: In which century did Washington Irving publish “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” the tale of the Headless Horseman?
hints: Irving was one of the first famous writers from the United States, a country born in 1776.
It was the same century the telephone was invented.
It came out in 1820, one year before Napoleon died.
questions.description: A rider who lost his head long before there were phones to distract him.
questions.fun_fact: Irving published the story in the same book as “Rip Van Winkle,” the man who slept for 20 years.

questions.question: A 2004 British comedy with zombies in London and a plan to hide out at the local pub. Which film is it?
hints: Its director later made “Baby Driver.”
Its star is Simon Pegg, Scotty in the newer “Star Trek” films.
Its title is a play on “Dawn of the Dead” and the hero's name.
questions.description: The world is ending, and plan B is going out for a drink.
questions.fun_fact: George A. Romero, the father of zombie films, liked it so much that he invited its creators to play zombies in “Land of the Dead.”

questions.question: I'm the monster in a 2006 animated film: my door is my mouth, my rug is my tongue, and I swallow balls. What am I?
hints: I don't walk: I never leave my street.
I have windows that look like eyes.
I have a roof, a chimney and a yard that nobody dares to enter.
questions.description: The grumpiest grumpy neighbor in the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: “Monster House” was produced by Steven Spielberg and Robert Zemeckis and was nominated for the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

questions.question: “Vampyr” (1932) is a classic vampire movie. Which country was its director, Carl Theodor Dreyer, from?
hints: It's a Scandinavian country.
Its capital has a famous statue of a little mermaid by the sea.
It's the home country of Lego.
questions.description: Long before vampires sparkled, there were vampires who barely said a word.
questions.fun_fact: The lead actor in “Vampyr” was a baron who paid for the movie and acted under a fake name.

questions.question: I scare people in their dreams and wear a red-and-green striped sweater, a hat and a glove with blades. Who am I?
hints: I'm a movie villain from the 1980s.
Director Wes Craven created me.
My first name is short for Frederick.
questions.description: Counting sheep won't help you one bit against this gentleman.
questions.fun_fact: Wes Craven is said to have picked red and green for the sweater because those two colors clash and are hard on the eye when put together.

questions.question: Who composed the famous two-note theme from “Jaws” (1975)?
hints: He is American and has worked with Spielberg on almost all of his films.
He composed the music for “Jurassic Park”.
He also wrote the famous march from “Star Wars”.
questions.description: Two notes were enough to make sure nobody ever swam calmly in the sea again.
questions.fun_fact: That music won John Williams the Oscar for Best Original Score.

questions.question: I wrote the novel about a snowy haunted hotel that Stanley Kubrick made into a film in 1980, though I didn't like his version. Who am I?
hints: I'm American and I live in Maine.
I wrote “Carrie” and “Misery”.
I also wrote “It”, the one with Pennywise the clown.
questions.description: A vacation at a mountain hotel: what could possibly go wrong?
questions.fun_fact: Stephen King disliked Kubrick's version so much that in 1997 he made his own TV miniseries of “The Shining”.

questions.question: “Found footage” films pretend to be real recordings discovered later. Which of these movies is NOT in that style?
hints: Look for the one that seems like a normal movie, with no handheld camera.
In [REC], everything is filmed by a TV reporter.
The one you want is about the paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren.
questions.description: Movies shot as if the camera operator had never heard of a tripod.
questions.fun_fact: “The Blair Witch Project” cost about $60,000 to make and earned more than $240 million.

questions.question: In “Madagascar 3,” the zoo animals join a circus in Europe. Which of these characters is NOT in that movie?
hints: Three of them lived in the New York zoo.
The odd one out comes from another movie series about prehistoric animals.
He's a mammoth from “Ice Age.”
questions.description: A zoo that ran away from home to do acrobatics in Europe.
questions.fun_fact: In “Madagascar 3,” Marty the zebra sings the catchy song “Afro Circus.”

questions.question: He wears a costume of colorful diamonds and a black mask, and he was born in Italian comedy theater. Who is he?
hints: He is a playful, very nimble servant.
His costume looks like it's made of colorful patches.
His name starts with “Harle-”.
questions.description: The character who made diamonds fashionable four hundred years ago.
questions.fun_fact: A pattern of colorful diamonds is still called a “harlequin” pattern.

questions.question: The Wallendas are a famous circus family who walk on wires high up in the air, like in the photo. What are these performers called?
hints: Their secret is never losing their balance.
Sometimes they carry a long pole so they don't fall.
Their name describes exactly what they do: step along a stretched line.
questions.description: A family that walks to school on a wire instead of the sidewalk.
questions.fun_fact: Nik Wallenda walked across Niagara Falls on a wire in 2012.

questions.question: It's sweet, full of cream, and clowns smash it into each other's faces. What is it?
hints: You can buy it at a bakery.
It's a dessert that you usually cut into slices shaped like wedges.
In old silent films, comedians threw them at each other's faces.
questions.description: The most wasted dessert in the history of comedy.
questions.fun_fact: Silent comedy films made the pie in the face famous, and a single scene once used up thousands of pies.

questions.question: What material is this circus tent made of?
hints: It's a very thick, strong fabric.
It keeps the rain out without letting water through.
It's also used for awnings and camping tents.
questions.description: A roof that folds up, packs away and goes on tour.
questions.fun_fact: Old circus tents were made of cotton; today they're made of polyester canvas coated with PVC.

questions.question: I'm the brain trick that makes you see faces in outlets and clouds; my name joins the Greek words for “beside” and “image.” What am I?
hints: Your brain is so well trained to spot faces that it finds them even where there are none.
That's why many people see a rabbit or a face on the Moon.
It starts with “pare-” and has the word “idol” hidden inside.
questions.description: That wall outlet is staring at you with a surprised look, and it's not your fault.
questions.fun_fact: Some people see a famous figure's face in a piece of burnt toast, and one such snack even sold at auction for thousands of dollars.

questions.question: I'm nicknamed “golden blood,” and only a few dozen people in the world have me. What blood type am I?
hints: I'm not one of the eight common types (A, B, AB and O, positive or negative).
My red blood cells lack every antigen of one very well-known system.
That system is the same one that makes blood “positive” or “negative.”
questions.description: Blood so exclusive it has no one to share with.
questions.fun_fact: People with Rh null blood can donate to many people with rare Rh types, but they can only receive blood from another Rh null donor.

questions.question: When you're cold, tiny bumps appear on your arms and the little hairs stand up. What did this do for our hairy ancestors?
questions.answer: Trapped warm air in their fur
hints: A cat does something similar and looks fluffier.
Birds fluff up their feathers in winter for a similar reason.
The raised hair worked like a coat.
questions.description: Your skin doing a goose impression, and nobody asked it to.
questions.fun_fact: You can also get goosebumps from hearing a song that really moves you.

questions.question: I'm oily, I come from tiny glands attached to each hair, and when there's too much of me, pimples appear. What am I for?
hints: Without me, your skin would crack like dry ground.
When there's too much of me, hair looks shiny and greasy very quickly.
I work like a natural cream.
questions.description: The oil your face makes for free, and nobody ever thanks it.
questions.fun_fact: This oil is called sebum, the Latin word for tallow: the animal fat once used to make candles.

questions.question: Roughly how many muscles does the human body have?
hints: There are many more muscles than bones.
An adult body has 206 bones.
It's a three-digit number.
questions.description: A whole gym hidden under your skin.
questions.fun_fact: The smallest muscle in the body, the stapedius, sits inside the ear and is just over 1 millimeter long.

questions.question: There were twelve of us, set up in the Roman Forum about 2,500 years ago for everyone to read. What was written on us?
hints: Before us, only a few people really knew what was forbidden.
We said what punishment someone got for stealing or hurting others.
Judges had to follow what we said.
questions.description: Before social media, the Romans posted the important stuff in the town square.
questions.fun_fact: Roman children learned the Law of the Twelve Tables by heart at school.

questions.question: From the port of Marseille you can see a small island with a fortress: the Château d'If. What was it used as for centuries?
hints: The fortress was built in the 16th century on the orders of King Francis I.
A famous French writer set part of an adventure novel there.
Edmond Dantès spent fourteen years there in “The Count of Monte Cristo.”
questions.description: A tiny rock in the middle of the sea that took the whole castle thing very seriously.
questions.fun_fact: Dantès never existed, but tourists at the Château d'If can still visit a “Monte Cristo cell” today.

questions.question: In lawyer movies, you sometimes hear someone ask for “habeas corpus.” What is it?
questions.answer: A prisoner's right to be brought before a judge
wrong_answers: Bail paid to get out of jail
A DNA test taken from a suspect
hints: It protects people from being locked up without explanation.
In Latin, it means something like “you may have the body.”
It forces the authorities to present the arrested person so a court can check whether the arrest is legal.
questions.description: Two Latin words that sound like a magic spell in lawyer movies.
questions.fun_fact: England made it law with the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679.

questions.question: I sparkle with diamonds, I'm kept in the Tower of London, and I only come out on very special occasions. Who wears me on their head?
hints: I'm golden and round.
I'm put on during a big ceremony.
The person who wears me lives in a palace.
questions.description: A piece of jewelry so important it has its own tower and its own guards.
questions.fun_fact: In 1671, a man named Thomas Blood tried to steal the Crown Jewels and squashed the crown flat to hide it.

questions.question: Today, what is the longest a Test match, cricket's classic format, can last?
hints: It is much longer than a soccer game.
It is played over several days in a row, with breaks for lunch and tea.
It lasts about as long as a school week.
questions.description: A sport where they stop for tea, and that's no joke.
questions.fun_fact: A Test match can go on for five days and still end in a draw.

questions.question: It's long, round and made of wood or aluminum, and in baseball it's used to hit the ball. In cricket it's flat. What is it?
hints: You hold it with both hands.
The player trying to send the ball far away uses it.
The player who swings it is named after it.
questions.description: The sport where running in circles (well, a diamond) earns you points.
questions.fun_fact: Professional baseball bats are made from woods like maple or ash.

questions.question: In cricket and baseball, what word is used when a batter is dismissed?
hints: It's a very short word.
It has only three letters.
It's the opposite of “in.”
questions.description: The saddest word anyone holding a bat can hear.
questions.fun_fact: In cricket, the umpire signals that a batter is out by raising one index finger.

questions.question: In cricket, players shout “Howzat!” (“How's that?”) to ask for the batter to be given out. Who do they shout it at?
hints: It's someone who doesn't play for either team.
It's the person who decides whether the batter is out or not.
They raise a finger when the answer is yes.
questions.description: A shout that's half question, half begging, and all cricket.
questions.fun_fact: If nobody shouts “Howzat”, the umpire can't give the batter out, even if they saw it happen.

questions.question: Hatzegopteryx, a huge flying reptile, probably hunted small dinosaurs on an island in what is now Romania. In which period did it live?
hints: It was a pterosaur, a relative of the pterodactyls, not a dinosaur.
It shared the Earth with Tyrannosaurus rex, which lived on another continent.
It's the period that ended when an asteroid hit the Earth 66 million years ago.
questions.description: A real airplane, but with a beak, wings made of skin and a very bad temper.
questions.fun_fact: Its open wings measured about 10 m (33 ft) across, and standing on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe.

questions.question: In Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs, the mammoths face Rudy, a Baryonyx. In real life, how much time separates Baryonyx from the first mammoths?
hints: Mammoths appeared long after the dinosaurs.
The last giant dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.
Baryonyx lived about 125 million years ago, and the first mammoths only about 5 million years ago.
questions.description: A dinosaur party where one guest showed up very, very late.
questions.fun_fact: Baryonyx had a snout a lot like a crocodile's and probably ate plenty of fish.

questions.question: In 1888, I split the dinosaurs into two groups by their hips and named the ornithischians. Who am I?
hints: I was a British paleontologist of the 19th century.
I called the other group saurischians, “lizard-hipped.”
I didn't invent the word “dinosaur”; a more famous Briton did.
questions.description: The big question of the Jurassic world: bird hips or lizard hips?
questions.fun_fact: Even though ornithischians are “bird-hipped,” birds actually descend from the other group, the saurischians.

questions.question: In Jurassic World, Blue leads the pack of velociraptors that Owen trains. How many raptors were in that pack?
hints: Owen controls them with a snap of his fingers and a clicker.
Besides Blue, there are Charlie and Delta…
Charlie and Delta have one more sister named after a letter of the radio alphabet, just like them.
questions.description: A gang with real claws and a very brave trainer.
questions.fun_fact: Real velociraptors were about the size of a turkey and had feathers, much smaller than the ones in the movies.

questions.question: I'm the colored ring in your eyes, blue, green or hazel, and I share my name with the Greek goddess of the rainbow. What am I?
hints: It's why some people have green eyes and others have dark eyes.
It surrounds the little black dot in the middle of the eye.
It's also the name of a flower that comes in many colors.
questions.description: A goddess whose eyes follow you everywhere.
questions.fun_fact: The iris flower is also named after the rainbow goddess, because it comes in so many colors.

questions.question: Tantalus is to the water he can never drink as Sisyphus is to…
hints: His punishment takes place on a hill.
He always gets close to the top, and then it all starts over.
Albert Camus wrote an essay about him pushing something heavy uphill.
questions.description: Some punishments are worse than going to bed without dessert, and this question proves it.
questions.fun_fact: Albert Camus ended “The Myth of Sisyphus” (1942) by saying we must imagine Sisyphus happy.

questions.question: It was named after a Greek god, it launched on a Saturn V rocket, and in 1969 it reached its big goal. What was that goal?
wrong_answers: Putting the first satellite in orbit
hints: Its destination can be seen in the sky almost every night.
Astronauts left footprints and a flag there.
Neil Armstrong said there: “That's one small step for man…”
questions.description: A Greek god who traveled farther than all the others put together.
questions.fun_fact: The astronauts' footprints are still on the Moon, because there is no wind there to blow them away.

questions.question: I'm a warrior princess from a '90s TV series: I throw a chakram and travel with my friend Gabrielle. Where do most of my adventures take place?
hints: My world is an ancient, mythical age, full of kings and warlords.
The places I travel through are near the Aegean Sea.
Zeus and the gods of Olympus show up there too.
questions.description: A heroine with a battle cry loud enough to wake up the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: Although “Xena: Warrior Princess” is set in Greece, it was filmed in New Zealand.

questions.question: Adidas is to three stripes as Nike is to…
hints: Look at the sneakers of someone near you.
It looks like the mark a teacher draws when an answer is right.
It's like a comma lying on its side.
questions.description: A Greek goddess who now lives on the feet of half the planet.

questions.question: In which century did Charles Darwin publish his famous book “On the Origin of Species”?
hints: It was the same era when steam trains were spreading around the world.
His ideas came from a long voyage around the world that stopped at the Galápagos Islands, and he waited many years to publish them.
The book came out in 1859.
questions.description: A book so controversial that half the world looked in the mirror searching for the monkey.
questions.fun_fact: The first printing of “On the Origin of Species” sold out on the very day it went on sale.

questions.question: Columbus thought he had reached Asia, so the Spanish called the Americas “the Indies.” What name set them apart from the Asian ones?
hints: The name has to do with a compass direction.
From Spain, you had to sail toward the sunset to get there.
The ones in Asia were the East Indies.
questions.description: Columbus's GPS was a little out of date: by about half a planet.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that mistake, the native peoples of the Americas were called “Indians,” even though they had never been to India.

questions.question: Which of these islands was NOT settled by Polynesian sailors before Europeans arrived?
hints: Three of them form the great “Polynesian Triangle.”
The right answer is much closer to South America.
Darwin studied finches and giant tortoises there.
questions.description: Sailors who crossed the ocean with no compass, just stars, waves and birds to show them the way.
questions.fun_fact: The Galápagos had no human inhabitants when Spanish sailors found them by accident in 1535.

questions.question: They're in Indonesia, Magellan set out to reach them, and the Dutch controlled them for centuries. What were Europeans after there?
hints: They are the Maluku Islands, also called the Moluccas.
What they wanted was used to give food flavor.
They were known as “the Spice Islands.”
questions.description: Tiny islands that empires fought over like kids fighting over the last piece of cake.
questions.fun_fact: In 16th- and 17th-century Europe, nutmeg cost many, many times more than on the islands, and only the rich could afford it.

questions.question: According to a famous story, who made an egg stand on its end by crushing its tip, to silence his critics?
hints: His critics said anyone could have done his great feat.
His feat had to do with crossing an ocean.
He reached the Americas in 1492.
questions.description: The easiest solution in the world… once someone shows it to you.
questions.fun_fact: Today an idea that seems hard but turns out very simple once you know how is called an “egg of Columbus”.

questions.question: On which date do many Latin American countries celebrate the Día de la Raza, which marks Columbus's arrival in the Americas?
hints: It's in the second half of the year.
It falls in the month of Halloween.
It's the 12th of that month.
questions.description: A holiday that shows up on time every year, unlike a ship that set out looking for Asia.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain the same day is called Día de la Hispanidad, and in some other countries it is the Day of Cultural Diversity.

questions.question: Which people sailed longships, long boats with a dragon's head on the prow?
hints: They came from northern Europe.
They hung round shields along the sides of their ships.
Like Hiccup's dad in “How to Train Your Dragon.”
questions.description: A ship with a face that says “stay away,” literally.
questions.fun_fact: The Vikings reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.

questions.question: They never grow old, they can see incredibly far, and Legolas is one of them. What are these people called?
hints: They live in beautiful forests and valleys.
They have pointed ears.
Santa's little helpers go by the same name.
questions.description: An archer who never needs glasses, not even at two thousand years old.
questions.fun_fact: In the movies, Orlando Bloom wore a blond wig and blue contact lenses to play Legolas.

questions.question: Its name comes from Greek, in Harry Potter you must bow to it, and one is called Buckbeak. What is the hippogriff a mix of?
hints: It has wings and feathers.
Its back half is made for galloping.
“Hippos” is Greek for horse.
questions.description: An animal built by someone who just couldn't choose between two.
questions.fun_fact: The Italian poet Ariosto made the hippogriff famous in his 1516 poem “Orlando Furioso”.

questions.question: Galadriel keeps one of the elves' rings of power. How many rings were made for the elves?
hints: The elves forged them themselves, and Sauron never touched them.
The dwarves got more, and men got even more.
There are fewer of them than fingers on one hand.
questions.description: An elf whose jewelry outshines any emerald on Earth.
questions.fun_fact: Galadriel's ring is called Nenya and is known as the Ring of Water.

questions.question: Who is the lord of Rivendell, the hidden valley of the elves?
hints: He is half-elven and very wise.
The Council that formed the Fellowship of the Ring met at his house.
He is Arwen's father.
questions.description: A mountain hotel where every guest shows up either wounded or carrying a dangerous ring.
questions.fun_fact: In the films, Elrond is played by Hugo Weaving, the same actor who played Agent Smith in “The Matrix”.

questions.question: He's called Strider, he's the heir to a lost kingdom, and he falls in love with the elf Arwen. Which people is Aragorn from?
hints: He is not immortal, though he lives longer than usual.
His people were given nine rings of power.
He is the same species as you.
questions.description: A king who spent years as a wanderer before he ever tried on a crown.
questions.fun_fact: In Tolkien's story, Aragorn lives to 210 thanks to the blood of the Dúnedain in his veins.

questions.question: I have fangs, I hate sunlight, and I march in armies for the Dark Lord. Which writer made me famous?
hints: He was a professor at the University of Oxford.
He studied languages and invented whole new ones, like the languages of the elves.
His most famous work is “The Lord of the Rings.”
questions.description: Monsters who have never once been to the dentist.
questions.fun_fact: Since Tolkien, orcs have shown up in countless video games and role-playing games.

questions.question: Look at this tall Egyptian crown, shaped like a bowling pin. What did it stand for?
hints: Egypt began as two kingdoms that later joined together.
It was called the “hedjet,” and its partner was a red crown.
It was the crown of the southern kingdom, up the Nile River.
questions.description: A hat shaped like a bowling pin, but with political power.
questions.fun_fact: Once the two kingdoms were united, the pharaoh wore the white crown set inside the red one: the double crown, or “pschent.”

questions.question: I'm braided, I was tied to the chin with a strap, and even Queen Hatshepsut wore me. What was I for?
wrong_answers: To cover the face at funerals
hints: Pharaohs usually shaved their faces.
You can see it on many statues and on Tutankhamun's gold mask.
It was a fake beard: a symbol of sacred power.
questions.description: The accessory a pharaoh wore to look wiser, even at 9 years old.
questions.fun_fact: In 2014, the beard fell off Tutankhamun's mask and was badly glued back with resin; experts later restored it.

questions.question: The Colossi of Memnon are two giant statues of a pharaoh in Egypt. About how old are they?
hints: They date from the time of the pharaohs.
Tutankhamun lived at roughly the same time.
They are older than the Roman Empire, but not from the Stone Age.
questions.description: Two giants sitting and waiting for a bus that never comes.
questions.fun_fact: After an earthquake, one of the statues “sang” at sunrise, and travelers in ancient times came to hear it.

questions.question: In the movie “Cleopatra” (1963), Elizabeth Taylor set a costume record. How many times did she change outfits?
hints: It was a Guinness World Record for an actress in a single film.
It's more outfits than you'd wear in a normal week.
It's more than 50 but less than 100.
questions.description: A queen of Egypt with more outfits in her closet than years on the throne.
questions.fun_fact: “Cleopatra” cost so much that it nearly bankrupted the studio that made it.

questions.question: The Great Migration of wildebeest makes a full loop every year. How many countries does it pass through?
hints: It starts and ends in the Serengeti.
Once a year, the herds cross the Mara River, which is full of crocodiles.
These countries are Tanzania and its northern neighbor, Kenya.
questions.description: A traffic jam of millions of legs that happens again every single year.
questions.fun_fact: About 1.5 million wildebeest take part in the Great Migration, along with zebras and gazelles.

questions.question: It's a kind of grasshopper that changes color when crowded and forms clouds that destroy crops in Africa. What is it?
hints: Its swarms appear in ancient stories as a disaster.
In a swarm, it can fly hundreds of kilometers.
In the Bible, swarms of them were one of the ten plagues of Egypt.
questions.description: An insect that turns into someone else when it hangs out with friends.
questions.fun_fact: A swarm of desert locusts can hold billions of insects and eat as much food in one day as millions of people.

questions.question: These monkeys with a red patch on their chest live in the mountains of just one country in the world. Which one?
hints: It is a country in the Horn of Africa.
They live in high grasslands, more than 3,000 m (9,800 ft) up.
Its capital is Addis Ababa.
questions.description: A monkey that wears its heart on its chest, where everyone can see it.
questions.fun_fact: Geladas eat almost nothing but grass: they are the only primates that live mainly on grass.

questions.question: About how long is an adult Egyptian cobra?
hints: It's much longer than a pencil or a ruler.
But it's not as gigantic as an anaconda.
Stretched out, it would be as long as a tall person (about 6 ft).
questions.description: The snake that pharaohs wore as decoration on their foreheads.
questions.fun_fact: The cobra on the pharaohs' headdress is called the “uraeus,” and it stood for royal protection.

questions.question: It's reddish, it comes out of a hippo's skin, and it isn't blood. Which human product does it act like?
hints: Hippos spend many hours under the African sun.
Their skin is delicate and cracks easily.
You'd put it on at the beach so you don't get burned.
questions.description: The hippo has its own beauty line, and it refuses to sell it.
questions.fun_fact: This “red sweat” also helps keep the hippo's wounds from getting infected.

questions.question: Which animals can pull in their claws when they walk, so their footprints almost never show claw marks?
hints: Tucked away, the claws don't wear down on the ground and stay sharp.
They hunt by creeping up quietly and then pouncing on their prey.
They belong to the same family as the lion and the leopard.
questions.description: Claws that fold away by themselves, like a pocketknife.
questions.fun_fact: The cheetah is the exception: it can't fully pull in its claws, and it uses them like cleats when it runs.

questions.question: In a museum, you see a huge elephant bird egg. Which of these labels does NOT fit it?
hints: It was a giant bird that walked, like an ostrich.
It no longer exists: it died out centuries ago.
It lived in the forests and fields of an island, not at sea.
questions.description: A bird so big that even its name seems too small for it.
questions.fun_fact: One elephant bird egg could hold the contents of more than 100 chicken eggs.

questions.question: “Kangaroo” is to “jumping forward” as “sifaka” is to “jumping…”
hints: The sifaka is a lemur from Madagascar that lives in the trees.
When it comes down to the ground, it looks like it's dancing.
It moves like a crab, with its arms up in the air.
questions.description: A lemur that dances like nobody's watching.
questions.fun_fact: The name “sifaka” copies the alarm call this lemur makes: “shi-fak!”

questions.question: I'm a tiger: to everyone else, a stuffed toy; to my friend Calvin, a real one. I share my name with an English philosopher. Who am I?
hints: I appear in a newspaper comic strip, not in a movie.
My creator is Bill Watterson.
My name is that of the philosopher who wrote “Leviathan”.
questions.description: A stuffed toy that has read more philosophy than most grown-ups.
questions.fun_fact: Calvin is named after a thinker too: the theologian John Calvin.

questions.question: Saint Augustine is to “Confessions” as Thomas Aquinas is to…
hints: It is a huge work that was never finished.
He wrote it in the 13th century.
Its title says it is a “summary” of what is known about God.
questions.description: A book so long that not even its author got to the end of it.
questions.fun_fact: Because he was quiet and heavyset, his classmates nicknamed Thomas Aquinas “the Dumb Ox.”

questions.question: This 1787 painting shows a famous Greek philosopher surrounded by his students. Who is he?
hints: He was Plato's teacher.
He is credited with the saying “I know that I know nothing”.
A way of teaching by asking questions is named after him.
questions.description: A get-together of friends where nobody asked for popcorn.
questions.fun_fact: David painted Plato as an old man at the foot of the bed, even though Plato was actually young at the time.

questions.question: I'm a 19th-century German philosopher who wrote “Phenomenology of Spirit” and spoke of “absolute spirit”. Who am I?
hints: I lived at the same time as Napoleon.
When I saw Napoleon in Jena, I called him “the world soul on horseback”.
As a young man, Karl Marx was one of my most famous followers.
questions.description: A philosopher so hard to follow that even his students asked for subtitles.
questions.fun_fact: Hegel finished “Phenomenology of Spirit” in Jena just as Napoleon was winning a battle there in 1806.

questions.question: The Florentine Marsilio Ficino named it after a Greek philosopher, and it means love for someone you idealize. What is it called?
hints: It shows up in countless songs and soap operas.
The Greek philosopher was a student of Socrates.
That philosopher wrote “The Symposium”, a dialogue about love.
questions.description: That crush who never knew you existed, now with a philosophy diploma.
questions.fun_fact: For Ficino, platonic love wasn't love that goes unreturned, but a love of beauty that lifts the soul toward the divine.

questions.question: I seem logical, but I lead to something absurd: thanks to me, Zeno said, swift Achilles never catches a tortoise. What am I?
hints: Zeno of Elea came up with several of them to defend his teacher Parmenides.
Another very famous one is the sentence “This sentence is false.”
My name starts with “para-”.
questions.description: Why you're never on time, explained by an ancient Greek.
questions.fun_fact: Math untangled the puzzle centuries later: infinitely many tiny pieces of a path can add up to a finite distance.

questions.question: A track switch lever like this one is the star of a famous moral dilemma. What is that dilemma called?
hints: It became a hugely popular internet meme.
You must decide whether to change the path of a vehicle with no brakes.
The vehicle runs on rails through a city.
questions.description: A lever that has ruined more family dinners than politics.
questions.fun_fact: British philosopher Philippa Foot came up with this dilemma in 1967.

questions.question: Inside an igloo you can stay warmer than outside. What job does the packed snow of its walls do?
hints: Packed snow is full of tiny trapped air bubbles.
It does the same job as the wool in a good winter coat.
It barely lets your body heat escape to the outside.
questions.description: A house made of ice that, against all odds, is not a refrigerator.
questions.fun_fact: Inside an igloo, with nothing but the warmth of the people in it, the temperature can be tens of degrees higher than outside.

questions.question: Complete: one hertz equals one vibration or oscillation per…
hints: The hertz measures frequency: how often something repeats.
It is the basic unit of time in the International System of Units.
A clock shows it with its fastest hand.
questions.description: A unit with a German last name that buzzes more than a phone on silent.
questions.fun_fact: Human ears hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and dogs can hear much higher frequencies.

questions.question: In what year did the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius propose his temperature scale?
hints: It was after Galileo built his first thermoscopes, around 1600.
It was before the French Revolution.
It was in the middle of the 18th century.
questions.description: A Swede who got half the world talking about the weather in his own numbers.
questions.fun_fact: Celsius's original scale was upside down: water boiled at 0 degrees and froze at 100.

questions.question: You drop a stone and a flat sheet of paper at the same time, and the stone lands first. What slows the paper down most?
hints: If you crumple the sheet into a ball, it falls much faster.
On the Moon, both would land at the same time.
A parachute uses the very same thing.
questions.description: A race between a stone and a sheet of paper, and everyone already knows how it ends.
questions.fun_fact: In 1971, an Apollo 15 astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, and they hit the ground at the same time.

questions.question: In what year did Albert Einstein publish his theory of special relativity?
hints: Einstein was only about 26 years old.
At the time, he worked in a patent office in Switzerland.
It was early in the 20th century, before the First World War.
questions.description: A year so busy that even time started to stretch.
questions.fun_fact: People call 1905 Einstein's “miracle year”: he published four papers that changed physics.

questions.question: I'm shaped like a cone: speak into my narrow end and your voice comes out louder and carries far. What am I?
hints: People use me at marches, sports games and fire drills.
Many of me run on batteries and have a trigger.
My name starts with “mega”, which means big.
questions.description: The best friend of every gym teacher on a school field trip.
questions.fun_fact: Before they had batteries, megaphones were just simple cones of cardboard or metal, and they still worked pretty well.

questions.question: Its symbol is the Greek letter omega, it measures electrical resistance, and body fat scales use it. Which unit is it?
hints: It is named after a German physicist.
It tells you how hard it is for current to flow through something.
Its symbol looks like a horseshoe: Ω.
questions.description: A unit that resists everything, even being easy.
questions.fun_fact: Fat carries electricity less well than muscle does, which is how those scales can estimate how much body fat you have.

questions.question: The Koch snowflake is built by repeating the same step over and over. What shape does it start from?
hints: At each step, every side grows a little spike in the middle.
After the first step, the shape looks like a six-pointed star.
The starting shape has three equal sides.
questions.description: A snowflake that never melts, but never finishes being drawn either.
questions.fun_fact: The Koch snowflake has an infinitely long edge, yet the area inside it is finite.

questions.question: It has one point, one curved edge and two equal straight edges: a party hat, unrolled and flattened. What shape is it?
hints: The bottom edge of the hat is round, so the flat shape can't be made of straight lines only.
It looks like a slice of pizza.
It's a piece of a circle cut out from the center.
questions.description: The accessory that turns any serious adult into a birthday unicorn.
questions.fun_fact: From the same circle of cardboard you can make taller or wider hats, depending on how big a slice you cut out.

questions.question: Pentagon, hexagon, heptagon… keep going and you reach the dodecagon. How many sides does it have?
hints: “Dodeca” comes from Greek.
It has more sides than a decagon, which has 10.
It's the number of eggs in a dozen.
questions.description: A shape with so many corners it almost thinks it's a circle.
questions.fun_fact: The British one-pound coin in use since 2017 is shaped like a dodecagon.

questions.question: These shapes have the same form and the same size, and they match exactly when you put one on top of the other. What are they called?
hints: Looking alike isn't enough: they must also be the same size.
Similar shapes have the same form, but they can be different sizes.
The word starts with “con”.
questions.description: Two shapes so alike that even their mom can't tell them apart.
questions.fun_fact: Fold a sheet of paper in half and cut out a shape through both layers: the two pieces you get are congruent.

questions.question: The architect Buckminster Fuller made this dome built from triangles popular. What is it called?
hints: It is very light and strong for its size.
Disney's Epcot park has a giant sphere built the same way.
Its name shares a root with the science that measures the shape of the Earth.
questions.description: A roof that is all triangles and zero tiles.
questions.fun_fact: Ball-shaped carbon molecules are called “fullerenes” in honor of Buckminster Fuller.

questions.question: The track in the photo, near Barcelona, first hosted Formula 1 in 1991. Who won that race?
hints: At that point he had never been world champion.
The next year he would win his only world title.
He was a British driver with a famous mustache who raced wheel to wheel with Senna down the main straight in that race.
questions.description: A racetrack so Catalan that even its corners have an accent.
questions.fun_fact: In that 1991 race, Mansell and Senna raced down the straight with their wheels almost touching at more than 300 km/h (186 mph).

questions.question: At a Formula 1 pit stop, how long does a good team take to change all four tires?
hints: About twenty people work at the same time.
It's less time than it takes you to say your full name.
You could barely blink twice.
questions.description: Faster than Mom slipping on her sandals to run out the door.
questions.fun_fact: In 2023, McLaren changed all four tires in just 1.80 seconds, a record at the time.

questions.question: The Imola racetrack in Italy is named after the founder of a famous sports car brand and his son. What is their last name?
hints: This brand is the oldest team in Formula 1.
Its factory is in Maranello, in the same region of Italy as Imola.
Its cars are famous for being red.
questions.description: A racetrack named after a family, like Grandpa's farm.
questions.fun_fact: Its official name is Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari.

questions.question: It's shown to a driver about to be lapped, asks them to let the faster car pass, and the back of the field sees it most. Which flag is it?
hints: It doesn't warn of danger or a crash.
It's also shown at the pit exit when cars are coming down the track.
It's the color of Italy's national soccer team shirt.
questions.description: The color of good manners on the track, even if the driver isn't one bit amused.
questions.fun_fact: If a driver ignores the blue flag several times, the race stewards can give them a penalty.

questions.question: In classic 35 mm film, each photo is 36 × 24 mm, like a “full-frame” sensor. What does that “35 mm” measure?
questions.answer: The total width of the film strip
wrong_answers: The focal length of the lens
hints: It has nothing to do with the lens, only with the film itself.
The name came from movies, long before anyone talked about photo sizes.
Lay the strip flat and measure it from one edge to the other: that's exactly the number.
questions.description: The little roll Grandpa's camera used to swallow, which today costs more than a restaurant lunch.
questions.fun_fact: 35 mm film came from the movies, and Oskar Barnack's Leica brought it to still photography in the 1920s.

questions.question: Which of these photography books is NOT by the Brazilian Sebastião Salgado?
hints: Salgado spent years on huge projects shot around the world, always in black and white.
The odd one out is a famous 1950s book about a road trip.
It was made by the Swiss photographer Robert Frank while traveling across the United States.
questions.description: An economist who swapped numbers for black-and-white photos.
questions.fun_fact: Salgado and his wife Lélia replanted millions of trees on the family farm in Brazil, which had lost its forest.

questions.question: Three of these camera shots show a person at least down to the knees. Which one does NOT?
hints: Look for the closest shot.
It's the one soap operas use when someone cries.
It shows the face and little else.
questions.description: It's all about distance: some show all of you, others get close enough to count your pores.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain and France, the medium long shot is called the “American shot”, after Hollywood westerns, where it showed the cowboy's gun at the hip.
