questions.question: In a scene like this, with a very bright sky and very dark areas, what is your phone's HDR mode for?
questions.answer: To show detail in highlights and shadows at once
wrong_answers: To zoom in without losing quality
To make the photo file smaller
To take photos in black and white
hints: Without it, the sky turns white or the ground turns black.
The phone takes several photos with different amounts of light and combines them.
The letters stand for “high dynamic range.”
questions.description: Three letters your phone turns on when the sky and the shadows can't agree.
questions.fun_fact: As early as the 1850s, Gustave Le Gray combined two negatives to capture both the sky and the sea in one picture.

questions.question: This boot print was photographed in 1969. Where exactly was it made?
hints: It was on the Moon, during Apollo 11.
The Moon’s “seas” are dark plains without a single drop of water.
The landing site was named after that same sea.
questions.description: The most famous footprint in the universe, and it isn’t on any Walk of Fame.
questions.fun_fact: Buzz Aldrin photographed his own footprint to study how moon dust packs down, not for the family photo album.

questions.question: I was the first human to travel to space, and from up there I said: “The Earth is blue.” Who am I?
hints: My trip was in 1961, before anyone had walked on the Moon.
I came from the Soviet Union.
My first name starts with Y, and my spaceship was called Vostok 1.
questions.description: The first tourist who looked out the window and found out home had a whole new paint job.
questions.fun_fact: Gagarin's trip around the Earth lasted only about 108 minutes.

questions.question: In which century was the book published that begins “Somewhere in La Mancha, in a place whose name I do not care to remember…”?
hints: It is a Spanish novel about a knight who reads too many books.
It came out more than a hundred years after Columbus reached America.
Its first part came out in 1605.
questions.description: A place so famous that its author didn't even want to say its name.
questions.fun_fact: Cervantes and Shakespeare died in 1616, only one day apart by their official dates.

questions.question: At my farewell match I said: “I made mistakes and I paid for them, but the ball doesn't get stained.” Who am I?
hints: I said goodbye at Boca Juniors' stadium, in 2001.
I was a World Cup champion in Mexico in 1986.
I became famous for “the Hand of God” and the “Goal of the Century.”
questions.description: A ball with more dignity than plenty of the people who kick it.
questions.fun_fact: Maradona's farewell match was at La Bombonera in November 2001, in front of a packed stadium.

questions.question: Which country's national anthem begins with the words “Gloria al bravo pueblo” (“Glory to the brave people”)?
hints: It is a neighbor of Colombia.
Simón Bolívar was born there.
Its capital is Caracas.
questions.description: An anthem that opens by congratulating everyone, just in case.
questions.fun_fact: “Gloria al bravo pueblo” became the official national anthem in 1881, though the song dates from the time of independence.

questions.question: I was the second man to walk on the Moon, and I called it “magnificent desolation.” Who am I?
hints: I flew on Apollo 11 in 1969.
I stepped onto the Moon a few minutes after my crewmate.
A famous toy from “Toy Story” has my first name.
questions.description: A five-star review for a place with no air, no water and no Wi-Fi.
questions.fun_fact: Buzz Lightyear from “Toy Story” was named after Buzz Aldrin.

questions.question: Which video game character has the motto “Gotta go fast!”?
hints: He runs so fast he curls up into a little ball.
He collects golden rings.
He is a blue hedgehog.
questions.description: Someone who has never once had to wait for anything to load.
questions.fun_fact: Sonic is blue because that was the color of the logo of Sega, the company that created him.

questions.question: I wore braces on my legs until a friend shouted, “Run!” Later I ran across the United States. Who am I?
hints: My movie came out in 1994.
Tom Hanks plays me.
My mama always said life is like a box of chocolates.
questions.description: The man who turned a bit of playground advice into the longest jog in movie history.
questions.fun_fact: In the movie, Forrest runs for three years, two months, fourteen days and sixteen hours.

questions.question: You're at a party in the United States and everyone is dancing to rock and roll, which was just born. What decade is it?
hints: It was a few years after World War II.
It's the time of cars with tail fins and jukeboxes in diners.
Elvis Presley became famous in that decade.
questions.description: A time when parents were shocked because young people moved their hips way too much.
questions.fun_fact: Bill Haley's song “Rock Around the Clock” became a worldwide hit in 1955 after it was played in a movie.

questions.question: It is the holiest day in Judaism, spent fasting, and in 1973 it gave its name to a war. Which day is it?
hints: Its name is in Hebrew.
It is also called the Day of Atonement.
Its name starts with “Yom”, which means “day”.
questions.description: A day so serious that even a war ended up taking its name.
questions.fun_fact: In 1973, Egypt and Syria attacked Israel on exactly that day, when almost the whole country was fasting and the streets were empty.

questions.question: The Sandinista Revolution won in this country in 1979. Which country is it?
hints: It is in Central America.
It has the largest lake in Central America.
Its capital is Managua.
questions.description: A land of lakes and volcanoes that changed hands almost overnight in 1979.
questions.fun_fact: The Sandinistas took their name from Augusto César Sandino, a rebel fighter who fought against US Marines in the 1920s and 1930s.

questions.question: Cold War spies hid microfilm everywhere. In which century was microfilm invented?
hints: It's older than it looks.
It was invented soon after photography.
Back then, steam trains were running, but the electric light bulb didn't exist yet.
questions.description: The tiniest thing a spy could hide inside a hollow coin.
questions.fun_fact: During the Siege of Paris in 1870, thousands of messages on microfilm were sent tied to carrier pigeons.

questions.question: In 1956 this yacht carried Fidel Castro and Che Guevara from Mexico to Cuba, and today Cuba’s official newspaper bears its name. What was it called?
hints: It set sail from Tuxpan, on the Gulf of Mexico.
It was a pleasure yacht bought from an American.
Its English name was a fond nickname for a grandmother.
questions.description: An overloaded little boat that ended up giving its name to a whole province.
questions.fun_fact: The yacht was built for about 12 people, but 82 men squeezed aboard for a week-long trip.

questions.question: In what year did the US and the Soviet Union sign the START I treaty to cut their nuclear weapons?
hints: On the Soviet side, it was signed by the leader who launched perestroika.
On the US side, it was signed by George H. W. Bush, president since 1989.
It was just a few months before the Soviet Union ceased to exist.
questions.description: A treaty for fewer bombs, signed at almost the last minute.
questions.fun_fact: It was signed in July 1991, and in December of that same year the Soviet Union ceased to exist.

questions.question: The CIA is the famous secret service of the United States. What does the “I” in CIA stand for?
hints: The word describes the agency's job: secretly finding out what other countries are planning.
It is also a word used for spying in general.
It is what an IQ test measures.
questions.description: Three letters that always show up in dark sunglasses in the movies.
questions.fun_fact: The CIA was founded in 1947, just as the Cold War was beginning.

questions.question: Who is this singer, still called “the King”?
hints: He lived in Memphis, in the United States, and became famous there.
He lived in a mansion called Graceland.
His first name starts with E, and he is known as “the King of Rock and Roll”.
questions.description: A singer whose hips were censored on television.
questions.fun_fact: Elvis did his military service in West Germany from 1958 to 1960, in the middle of the Cold War.

questions.question: Which creatures run Gringotts, the wizarding bank?
hints: They are short, very clever and brilliant with gold and metalwork.
One of them, Griphook, helps Harry get into a vault.
They have long fingers, pointy ears and very grumpy faces.
questions.description: The only bank where nobody complains about the line, because complaining looks like a bad idea.
questions.fun_fact: To reach the deepest vaults at Gringotts, you ride down in little carts that race along like a roller coaster.

questions.question: I'm a Hogwarts subject: in my class, students read tea leaves, and a centaur teaches by watching the planets. What am I?
hints: My main teacher lives at the top of a tower full of incense.
That teacher is Sybill Trelawney, who keeps predicting terrible things for Harry.
My goal is to see the future.
questions.description: A class where you can get top marks if you already know what's on the test.
questions.fun_fact: The centaur Firenze teaches this subject in a classroom that looks like a forest, with moss on the floor.

questions.question: I was Quidditch captain and Keeper, and I cried with joy when we won the cup in my last year. Which Hogwarts house was I in?
hints: My name is Oliver Wood.
I'm obsessed with tactics and wake my team at dawn to practice.
My house has a lion as its symbol.
questions.description: A captain who talks about Quidditch even in his sleep.
questions.fun_fact: After leaving Hogwarts, Oliver Wood signed with the reserve team of Puddlemere United.

questions.question: What is the magic game, a bit like marbles, where the pieces squirt a smelly liquid at a player who loses a point?
hints: Harry sees other students playing it at Hogwarts.
Snape's mother, Eileen Prince, was captain of this game's club at Hogwarts.
Its name ends with what the pieces are usually made of.
questions.description: Marbles, but with really bad manners.
questions.fun_fact: The pieces of this game can be made of stone or even solid gold.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer is right. The smelly squirt, the marbles comparison and Eileen Prince as club captain are confirmed. Two claims are not supported. Rowling's site says the stones may be made of 'precious metals', not specifically 'solid gold'. I also found no source for 'Harry sees other students playing it at Hogwarts'. The Gobstones Club first appears in Order of the Phoenix.

questions.question: I'm an object: if you write on my pages, the ink disappears and a young man named Tom Riddle writes back. What am I?
hints: I appear in “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets.”
Ginny Weasley found me and wrote her secrets in me.
Harry destroyed me with a basilisk fang.
questions.description: An object that keeps secrets… and talks back.
questions.fun_fact: The letters of “Tom Marvolo Riddle” can be rearranged to spell “I am Lord Voldemort.”

questions.question: Dr. Dre co-founded the headphone brand Beats. In which decade was it founded?
hints: It came after Dr. Dre was already a 1990s rap legend.
The iPod already existed, but the iPhone hadn't come out yet.
It was founded in the middle of the decade when the 21st century began.
questions.description: Headphones so expensive they should come with their own bodyguard.
questions.fun_fact: In 2014, Apple bought Beats for about $3 billion.

questions.question: At a party, the DJ moves the record back and forth so it goes “wikka-wikka.” In which decade was this trick invented?
hints: It was invented in the Bronx, New York, when hip hop was being born.
It was the same era as disco music and mirror balls.
A teenager invented it in the middle of that decade, while his mother was scolding him about the volume.
questions.description: A record getting pushed back and forth like it's being told off.
questions.fun_fact: Scratching was discovered by Grand Wizzard Theodore when he was about 12, as he stopped a record with his hand while his mother was talking to him.

questions.question: I'm a video series by an Argentine DJ in a cap and dark glasses; Shakira sang about Piqué in me. What am I called?
hints: Each video has a number, and the guest singer sits facing the producer in his small studio.
Quevedo, Nathy Peluso and Residente have also been guests.
Its name starts with the consonants of the producer's nickname: B, Z, R, P.
questions.description: A producer who hides behind his sunglasses and makes everyone else famous.
questions.fun_fact: Bizarrap got his start uploading edited videos of freestyle rap battles from his bedroom.

questions.question: I'm a street dance, named for the “pop” the body makes. What move am I based on?
wrong_answers: Spinning on your head on the floor
Tapping your feet in metal-soled shoes
Jumping nonstop with a jump rope
hints: When you watch me, the dancer looks a bit like a robot.
The move happens in the arms, legs, neck and chest, like tiny jolts.
It means tightening your muscles all at once, as if something taps you from inside.
questions.description: A dance where your body seems to have the hiccups, but with style.
questions.fun_fact: Popping was born in the 1970s in Fresno, California, with a group called the Electric Boogaloos.

previous.feedback: Hint 1 ("When you watch me, the dancer can look like a robot.") keeps the first-person voice of the source riddle ("Soy un baile…"). The English question isn't in the first person, so "me" doesn't refer to anything. Reword it, e.g. "Watching it, the dancer can look like a robot."

questions.question: I'm a party right in the street of a Bronx neighborhood; DJs plugged their speakers into the lampposts. What am I called?
hints: I'm a bit like a neighborhood street fair.
The whole street was closed to traffic so people could dance on it.
My name comes from the stretch of city street between two crossroads.
questions.description: A party where the neighbors can't complain about the noise, because they're all invited.
questions.fun_fact: Many people date the birth of hip hop to a back-to-school party that DJ Kool Herc played in the Bronx in August 1973.

questions.question: Eminem's “Lose Yourself” was the first rap song to win an Oscar. In which decade did it come out?
hints: It came out when people still bought music on CDs.
The 21st century had already begun.
It came out just a couple of years after the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: A song that tells you that you only get one shot, so think carefully about your answer.
questions.fun_fact: Eminem didn't go to collect his Oscar: reportedly he was asleep at home.

questions.question: Its bass makes you move, James Brown was its big star, and its drum beats fed hip hop. What genre is it?
hints: It was born in the United States in the 1960s.
DJs in the Bronx looped its drum parts so people could dance.
George Clinton's band Parliament and bassist Bootsy Collins were also huge stars of this style.
questions.description: Music that makes even your grandpa shake his shoulders without noticing.
questions.fun_fact: The drum break in James Brown's “Funky Drummer” is one of the most sampled pieces of music in history.

questions.question: I'm a very tall hairstyle from the court of Versailles. I carried ships, gardens and birds, and Marie Antoinette made me fashionable. What am I?
hints: It was typical of 18th-century France, before the Revolution.
It was built with pads, wire, fake hair and lots of powder.
My name sounds like a low, padded footstool.
questions.description: Up there, there was room for everything except modesty.
questions.fun_fact: One of the most famous poufs carried a tiny warship to celebrate a French naval battle.

questions.question: The founder's son created it in 1896, with flowers and the letters LV. Why was the Louis Vuitton pattern invented?
wrong_answers: To hide stains on the leather
To win a contest in Paris
hints: The brand already had a problem that it still has today.
In 1888 the brand had tried a checkered design, but it didn't solve that problem.
Think of the knockoff bags sold on the street.
questions.description: Letters so famous that even people who can't read know them.
questions.fun_fact: Louis Vuitton started out making flat travel trunks, which stacked better than the ones with curved lids.

questions.question: In the 1920s, party dresses were straight and short, and they swung when people danced the Charleston. What were they usually decorated with?
hints: The decoration had to move with every dance step.
It sparkled under the lights of the jazz clubs.
Thin hanging strips, like on a curtain or a poncho.
questions.description: A decade when even the clothes wanted to dance.
questions.fun_fact: Some 1920s dresses had so many glass beads that they weighed more than a kilogram (over 2 lb).

questions.question: In a museum you see a 1960s dress made of small plastic discs joined with metal rings. Which designer invented it?
hints: He said he made “unwearable dresses.”
He was born in the Basque Country, in Spain, and made his name in Paris.
Today his name is famous for perfumes shaped like a gold bar.
questions.description: A dress that rattles like a cookie tin every time you take a step.
questions.fun_fact: He made his metal dresses with pliers and a blowtorch, working more like a jeweler or a blacksmith than a tailor.

questions.question: My husband crowned himself emperor, I made high-waisted dresses fashionable, and I loved the roses in my garden. Who am I?
hints: I lived in France in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
That style of dress is still called the “Empire style”.
My husband was defeated at Waterloo and exiled to an island.
questions.description: Behind every great emperor stood a woman with an even greater wardrobe.
questions.fun_fact: Josephine is said to have spent fortunes on clothes and owned hundreds of cashmere shawls.

questions.question: I wear a uniform with blue, yellow and red stripes, a plumed helmet and a spear, and I protect the Pope. Who am I?
hints: I work in the smallest country in the world.
I live in the Vatican, inside Rome.
My name includes a country famous for its chocolate and its watches.
questions.description: The most colorful bodyguards on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: People often say Michelangelo designed their uniform, but that's a myth: today's version dates from 1914.

questions.question: I shine like a pirate's gold, but inside I'm sweet. If you leave me in the sun, what happens to me?
hints: Inside, I'm not made of metal.
I'm made of something brown that kids love.
The same thing happens to ice cream on a hot day.
questions.description: The only pirate treasure you can eat without a trip to the dentist… well, almost.
questions.fun_fact: The gold foil on chocolate coins copies real gold coins, and in many countries people give them as gifts at Christmas.

questions.question: I'm made of paper and you pay with me. I was invented over 1,000 years ago in a country in Asia. Which one?
hints: That country also invented paper.
Gunpowder and the compass were invented there too.
It's the country with the Great Wall.
questions.description: A little piece of paper worth more than all your school notebooks put together.
questions.fun_fact: When Marco Polo told people in Europe that the Chinese paid with paper, many found it hard to believe.

questions.question: The bank gives you money, you pay it back bit by bit, and at the end you pay a little extra. What is that called?
hints: The money isn't yours forever.
That “little extra” is called interest.
It's just like when someone lends you something and you have to give it back.
questions.description: Money that arrives fast, leaves fast, and comes back… with little friends.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Mesopotamia, people were already lending barley and silver more than 4,000 years ago, and they wrote the deals down on clay tablets.

questions.question: The shekel, which gives its name to Israel's currency today, began as a weight of silver in Mesopotamia. How long ago?
hints: Its name comes from an ancient word meaning “to weigh.”
It already appears in the Code of Hammurabi.
Mesopotamia is the same region where writing was invented.
questions.description: A currency older than your grandpa's oldest joke.
questions.fun_fact: At first the shekel wasn't a coin but a unit of weight: people weighed silver on a scale to pay.

questions.question: I'm a colorful glass bead, and in Africa people used me as money. Which European city did the finest of us come from?
hints: It's a city in southern Europe, by the sea.
It was the capital of a powerful trading republic in the Mediterranean.
In this city, people get around by gondola.
questions.description: Costume jewelry that, for centuries, was worth more than plenty of real jewels.
questions.fun_fact: The glassmakers of Murano guarded their secrets so closely that for centuries they were forbidden to leave the republic.

questions.question: There were 450 of us. On Mount Carmel, we begged our god all day to send fire, but it never came. Who are we?
hints: The prophet Elijah challenged us.
We worshipped a Canaanite god of rain and storms.
Our god's name starts with B.
questions.description: History's first cooking contest held without a stove.
questions.fun_fact: In the story, Elijah soaked his altar with water three times before the fire came down, so no one could doubt the miracle.

questions.question: I'm made of wood, I turned into a snake in the desert, and with one strike I made water flow from a rock. What am I?
hints: My owner looked after sheep before he became a leader.
I was held out over the Red Sea.
I'm a long stick you can lean on when you walk.
questions.description: The most useful thing to carry in the desert, after a water bottle.
questions.fun_fact: Moses was a shepherd, so his famous staff was really just a shepherd's walking stick.

questions.question: At the wedding at Cana, the wine ran out. According to the Gospel, what did Jesus turn into wine?
hints: It came out of some large stone jars.
Jesus told the servants to fill the jars to the brim.
It has no color and no taste.
questions.description: The trick every waiter wishes they could learn.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Gospel of John, this was Jesus's first miracle, and the new wine turned out better than the first.

questions.question: The prophet Samuel anointed the first king of Israel. Who was he?
hints: He was from the tribe of Benjamin.
He was so tall he stood head and shoulders above everyone.
He was later replaced by the young David.
questions.description: He had to pick a king with no elections, no debates and no polls.
questions.fun_fact: Samuel later anointed David too, while he was still a boy looking after sheep.

questions.question: What is the name of the garden that Adam and Eve were sent out of?
hints: It is also called paradise on Earth.
The tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil grew there.
It starts with E.
questions.description: The only garden you get thrown out of for eating the fruit.
questions.fun_fact: According to the story, God placed cherubim with a flaming sword at the garden's entrance so no one could ever get back in.

questions.question: Samurai is to Japan as… is to the army of ancient Rome.
hints: He was a foot soldier.
In Asterix, Obelix knocks them over by the dozen.
His name comes from the big unit of the Roman army: the legion.
questions.description: Sandals, a helmet and a 30-kilometer (19-mile) walk every day: the least relaxing vacation plan in history.
questions.fun_fact: A legionary carried about 30 kg (66 lb) of gear on his back, including a shovel for digging the camp every night.

questions.question: Complete: the word “basilica” comes from the Greek basiliké, meaning “the … hall.”
hints: In Rome, a basilica wasn't a temple: people held trials and did business there.
The Greek word “basileús” has to do with whoever ruled.
Basileús meant “king.”
questions.description: Today it's a fancy church, but it started its career as a courthouse and a shopping mall.
questions.fun_fact: The first Christians copied the shape of Roman basilicas for their churches because they were huge halls that could hold lots of people.

questions.question: Palatine, Aventine and Capitoline are three of them, and they give Rome its nickname. What are they?
hints: Rome's nickname comes with the number seven.
Legend says Romulus founded the city on the Palatine.
From the top of each one, you can see the whole city.
questions.description: Rome has more nicknames than Grandma has for you when she can't remember your name.
questions.fun_fact: The word “palace” comes from the Palatine Hill, where the Roman emperors lived.

questions.question: I'm the pilum, the Roman legionary's javelin, and my iron tip bent when it hit something. What was that for?
questions.answer: So it couldn't be thrown back
wrong_answers: So it was lighter to carry
So it could hook walls for climbing
So it wouldn't rust in the rain
hints: Think about what the enemy would do after it landed.
A bent javelin doesn't fly straight.
The enemy couldn't reuse it against the Romans.
questions.description: A weapon designed to break on purpose, like an umbrella on a windy day.
questions.fun_fact: If a pilum stuck in a shield, the shield became so heavy and awkward that many warriors chose to drop it.

questions.question: When graphite was found in England in the 1500s, people thought it was a metal. Which metal, whose name we still use for a pencil's core?
hints: It's a gray, soft and very heavy metal.
That's why people say a pencil tip isn't poisonous: it never had this metal in it.
When your pencil breaks, people say you snapped this metal.
questions.description: A lie so old you've even written with it in your notebook.
questions.fun_fact: Shepherds in Borrowdale used that graphite to mark their sheep long before anyone thought of writing with it.

questions.question: I'm a crunchy, orange, triangle-shaped snack, born at a Disneyland restaurant so leftovers wouldn't go to waste. What am I made of?
hints: My name comes from a Spanish word meaning “little golden ones.”
The restaurant had leftover Mexican tortillas.
It's the same ingredient as in arepas and popcorn.
questions.description: Leftovers that skipped the trash can and went straight to fame.
questions.fun_fact: According to the most popular story, the Casa de Fritos restaurant at Disneyland cut stale tortillas into triangles and fried them instead of throwing them away.

questions.question: This dark blue dye once came from a plant, and today it colors almost all jeans. What is it called?
hints: This dye was so valuable that people called it “blue gold”, and ships carried it across oceans.
The plant's leaves are green: the blue only shows up after you soak them and let the air get to them.
In the rainbow, it sits between blue and violet.
questions.description: A color with a name so fancy it sounds royal, yet it lives in your pants.
questions.fun_fact: Isaac Newton added this color to the rainbow partly because he wanted seven colors, like the seven notes of the musical scale.

questions.question: The putty that bounces, stretches and copies pictures from the newspaper was an accident in the search for fake rubber. In which decade?
hints: Its inventor worked in the lab of a big US electric company.
Only a few years passed between its discovery and its sale as a toy.
Rubber was scarce because of the war, and in 1950 it went on sale in plastic eggs.
questions.description: A failed experiment that bounces, stretches and never did its job, but kept millions of people busy.
questions.fun_fact: No engineer found a serious use for it, until a salesman packed it in plastic eggs and turned it into a toy.

questions.question: Warfarin, a medicine against blood clots, was discovered by studying this moldy plant that cattle ate. What is it?
hints: Its mold made a substance that kept the blood from clotting.
The research was done at the University of Wisconsin in the 1930s and 1940s.
It is also called melilot.
questions.description: From the cows' field to Grandpa's nightstand: a very unusual journey.
questions.fun_fact: Warfarin was first sold as rat poison, and its name comes from WARF, the University of Wisconsin's research foundation.

questions.question: Which actor took over from Pierce Brosnan as 007 and began by playing poker at a casino in Montenegro?
hints: His first Bond film was “Casino Royale” in 2006.
He is English and was the sixth actor to play Bond in the official series.
He played Bond in five films; the last one was “No Time to Die” in 2021.
questions.description: A spy whose first day on the job starts with a game of cards.
questions.fun_fact: The “Montenegro” scenes in “Casino Royale” were actually filmed in Karlovy Vary, in the Czech Republic.

questions.question: I'm British, I work for the secret service, and I order my vodka martini “shaken, not stirred.” Who am I?
hints: I'm a spy, not a detective.
I work for MI6, and my boss is called M.
My agent number is 007.
questions.description: A very stylish gentleman who is extremely fussy about how his drink is served.
questions.fun_fact: In Ian Fleming's novels, Bond invents his own cocktail and names it the “Vesper,” after a Bond girl.

questions.question: Which of these actresses has NOT played Miss Moneypenny in the James Bond films?
hints: One of them had an even more important job at MI6.
That actress played Bond's boss in several films.
She played M from “GoldenEye” to “Skyfall”.
questions.description: Cinema's most famous secretary, still waiting decades later for a date with 007.
questions.fun_fact: Lois Maxwell played Moneypenny in 14 films, starting with “Dr. No” in 1962.

questions.question: In “You Only Live Twice,” what fish did Blofeld keep in the pool of his secret lair inside a volcano?
hints: They are small fish, not giants.
Blofeld punishes helpers who fail him by sending them into the pool.
They are famous for their sharp teeth and for feeding in groups.
questions.description: A pet no villain should keep in the living room, and yet every one of them wants some.
questions.fun_fact: Red-bellied piranhas make barking-like noises when they are caught.

questions.question: Which actor was the first to drive this car in a James Bond movie?
hints: It's a British sports car that became one of the most famous cars in movie history.
The movie was “Goldfinger,” from 1964.
He was the first actor to play 007 on the big screen.
questions.description: A car with more tricks up its sleeve than a magician at a kids' birthday party.
questions.fun_fact: The DB5 in “Goldfinger” had an ejector seat, machine guns, and revolving license plates.

questions.question: The famous ice rink at Rockefeller Center in New York first opened on Christmas Day of which year?
hints: The rink is older than TV sets in most homes.
Your great-grandparents could already have skated there.
It was a few years before World War II.
questions.description: Skating in New York: the only place where you fall down surrounded by skyscrapers.
questions.fun_fact: The giant Christmas tree next to the rink has been an official tradition since 1933.

questions.question: All four push at the start, jump in within seconds and race down at over 140 km/h (87 mph). What are the positions on a four-person bobsled?
questions.answer: A pilot, two pushers and a brakeman
wrong_answers: A pilot, one pusher and two brakemen
Two pilots, one pusher and a brakeman
A pilot, three pushers and no brakeman
hints: Only one of the four steers.
The last one to jump in sits at the very back.
Someone has to stop the sled after the finish line.
questions.description: Four people squeezed into a carbon-fiber bullet, and they volunteered for it.
questions.fun_fact: A four-person bobsled with its crew can weigh up to 630 kg (about 1,390 lb).

questions.question: I'm Lillehammer: I hosted the 1994 Winter Olympics and the 2016 Winter Youth Olympics. Which country am I in?
hints: I'm in Scandinavia.
My country has won more gold medals at the Winter Games than any other.
My capital is Oslo.
questions.description: A tiny town that threw a giant party on the snow.
questions.fun_fact: The mascots of Lillehammer 1994 were two children, Håkon and Kristin: the first Olympic mascots in human form.

questions.question: In Scotland, it's good luck when a tall, dark-haired man arrives at your home with coal, salt and bread. When must he arrive?
questions.answer: Just after midnight on New Year's
wrong_answers: On the morning of Christmas Day
hints: He has to be the first person to enter the home on that date.
Scots call this celebration “Hogmanay.”
It's when everyone counts down and the calendar starts over.
questions.description: A surprise visitor that nobody in Scotland wants to see arriving empty-handed.
questions.fun_fact: People often say the visitor shouldn't be blond, because that reminded people of the Viking invaders of long ago.

questions.question: One tradition says that if you fold a thousand paper figures like this one, you can make a wish. Which country is it from?
hints: It's a country made up of islands.
There, the crane is a symbol of long life and good luck.
Its flag is white with a red circle.
questions.description: A bird that will never fly, but grants wishes if you're patient.
questions.fun_fact: The crane was said to live a thousand years, so people fold a thousand of them, and the whole set is called “senbazuru.”

questions.question: This little man loaded with tiny objects is a good-luck charm for plenty and wealth. Which region does he come from?
hints: It's a cold region, high above sea level.
His most famous festival, Alasitas, is held in La Paz.
Lake Titicaca is there.
questions.description: A man carrying so many shopping bags he looks like he just left the mall.
questions.fun_fact: At the Alasitas fair, people buy tiny houses, cars or banknotes so the Ekeko will bring them the real, full-size thing.

questions.question: According to tradition, why is this object hung with its ends pointing up?
questions.answer: So the luck doesn't spill out
wrong_answers: So the devil slips off it
So it brings rain to the house
hints: Think about its shape: it looks like a container.
Turn it upside down and whatever is inside falls out.
It works like a cup that holds on to something good.
questions.description: A horse's shoe that retired to hang on a wall.
questions.fun_fact: An English legend says Saint Dunstan, a blacksmith, nailed a horseshoe to the devil's hoof and only took it off once the devil promised never to enter a place where one was hanging.

questions.question: The bride carries it at the wedding, throws it backward at the end, and whoever catches it is next to marry. What is it?
hints: She holds it in her hands as she walks down the aisle.
It smells very nice.
It's made of roses, lilies or other plants.
questions.description: The only throwing sport played in fancy clothes.
questions.fun_fact: It's said that guests once tore little pieces off the bride's dress for good luck, and throwing the bouquet was a way to distract them.

questions.question: Finish the wedding tradition for brides: “Something old, something new, something borrowed, something…”
hints: It's a color.
It's not the color of the dress.
It's the color of a clear sky.
questions.description: The most famous shopping list at any wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The full old English rhyme ends with “and a silver sixpence in her shoe”.

questions.question: In “The Goonies,” a group of kids hunts for the treasure of the pirate One-Eyed Willy. In which decade did the movie come out?
hints: It's from the time of the Walkman and early console video games.
The series “Stranger Things” pays tribute to it many times.
It's from the same decade as “Back to the Future.”
questions.description: A group of kids with more treasure maps than finished homework.
questions.fun_fact: The story of “The Goonies” was Steven Spielberg's idea, but Richard Donner directed it.

questions.question: Guess: I was born in 1873 for California's miners, I have copper rivets, and on my label two horses try to tear me apart. What am I?
hints: You wear me on your legs.
I'm almost always made of a blue cloth called denim.
I have pockets, a zipper or buttons, and two legs.
questions.description: A piece of clothing so tough that not even the cavalry could beat it.
questions.fun_fact: Levi's has used its two-horse logo since 1886 to show off that not even two horses could tear its jeans apart.

questions.question: Guess who: I have stripes, wear a red scarf around my neck, and on the cereal box I say “They're Gr-r-reat!”. Who am I?
hints: You always see me full of energy and playing sports.
My cereal is sugar-frosted flakes.
I'm orange with black stripes.
questions.description: A breakfast so sugary that even the box is smiling.
questions.fun_fact: Tony the Tiger was born in 1952 and beat a kangaroo named Katy for the mascot job.

questions.question: In which century did the hermit Ivan of Rila found the famous Bulgarian monastery that bears his name?
hints: It was in the Middle Ages, long before the Ottomans reached the Balkans.
It happened shortly after Bulgaria became Christian.
It was in the 900s.
questions.description: A hermit wanted to be alone on a mountain and ended up with his country's most visited monastery.
questions.fun_fact: Rila Monastery has appeared on Bulgarian banknotes and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

questions.question: Which place is NOT inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, according to tradition?
questions.answer: The grotto where Jesus was born
hints: The church remembers the end of Jesus's life, not the beginning.
The church's name already speaks of a tomb.
That place is in another town: Bethlehem.
questions.description: A church so busy that several Christian communities have to take turns looking after it.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, two Muslim families have kept the keys to the Holy Sepulchre and opened its door every morning.

questions.question: I played the organ in German churches, and the famous “Toccata and Fugue in D minor” is credited to me. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the Baroque era, before Mozart.
I was German and had a huge family, with many children who became musicians.
My surname has only four letters.
questions.description: A musician who worked in church and ended up playing in every villain movie.
questions.fun_fact: As a young man, Bach walked about 400 km (250 miles) to hear the organist Dietrich Buxtehude play.

questions.question: What is the town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee where Peter's house stood and where Jesus lived while preaching?
hints: It's not where Jesus was born or where he grew up.
Today visitors can see the ruins of a white stone synagogue there.
Its name means “village of Nahum” in Hebrew.
questions.description: A fishing village more famous than many of the world's capitals.
questions.fun_fact: A modern church stands on pillars right above the ruins said to be Peter's house, so it looks like a spaceship hovering over them.

questions.question: The Maya city of Tulum sits on a cliff above Mexico's Caribbean coast, and its name describes what surrounds it. What does “Tulum” mean?
hints: The name describes something people built around the city.
It protected the city on three sides; the sea guarded the fourth.
It's the same thing that rings the old towns of Cartagena in Colombia and Dubrovnik in Croatia.
questions.description: Ruins with an ocean view: the Maya really knew how to pick a spot.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya seem to have called Tulum “Zamá”, thought to mean “dawn”, because from there you can watch the sun rise over the sea.

questions.question: This is Mount Tabor, in Galilee. According to Christian tradition, what happened on its summit?
wrong_answers: The giving of the Ten Commandments
hints: It happened during the life of Jesus, not in the Old Testament.
Moses and Elijah appeared there next to Jesus.
The Gospels say his face shone like the sun and his clothes turned white.
questions.description: A nice round mountain that looks like it came out of a pudding mold.
questions.fun_fact: To drive up to the top of Mount Tabor, you take a road full of hairpin bends.

questions.question: If I don't draw the plans, nobody knows how to build the house. I design houses, buildings and skyscrapers. Who am I?
hints: I work a lot with pencils, rulers and plans on a screen.
My work starts before the first brick is laid.
I went to university to learn how to design buildings.
questions.description: Without this person, buildings would just be piles of bricks with good intentions.
questions.fun_fact: The word “architect” comes from Greek and means something like “chief builder.”

questions.question: Which of these statements is NOT true about Saint Basil's Cathedral?
questions.answer: It is made entirely of white marble
hints: Inside, it is actually several small chapels joined together.
Its domes look like ice cream or candy.
From the outside, you can see a lot of red brick.
questions.description: A church that looks like it was designed by a very excited bakery.
questions.fun_fact: Tsar Ivan the Terrible ordered the cathedral built in the 16th century to celebrate a military victory.

questions.question: These carved figures are at Monte Albán in Oaxaca, Mexico. Which people built this city?
hints: It was one of the first great cities of Mesoamerica.
This people still exists and speaks its own language in Oaxaca.
Their name starts with Z.
questions.description: Stone figures that have been posing for the camera for more than 2,000 years.
questions.fun_fact: Monte Albán was built by flattening the top of a mountain, about 400 m (1,300 ft) above the Oaxaca Valley.

questions.question: I was an Inca emperor, I turned my people into a great empire, and I had Machu Picchu built. Who am I?
hints: I ruled in the 15th century, from Cusco.
My name means something like “he who transforms the world”.
My name starts with “Pacha”.
questions.description: An emperor who wasn't happy with just a little cottage in the country.
questions.fun_fact: Many historians think Machu Picchu was a country retreat for Pachacuti and his family.

questions.question: Roughly how long ago was the Great Pyramid of Giza built?
hints: It is much older than the time of Jesus.
It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
It was finished around 2560 BC.
questions.description: A building so old that when it was finished, mammoths were still wandering around.
questions.fun_fact: For about 3,800 years, the Great Pyramid was the tallest structure ever built by humans.

questions.question: I'm white and chubby, and my body is made of stacked tires. Who am I?
hints: I don't live in a movie: I show up in ads.
My brand sells something round that vehicles roll on.
My French brand starts with “Mich…”.
questions.description: A guy so puffed up he looks like he swallowed the whole repair shop.
questions.fun_fact: The Michelin Man is called Bibendum and was born in 1898, making him one of the oldest brand mascots in the world.

questions.question: Juanito, a boy in a Mexican sombrero, was the mascot of a FIFA World Cup. Which year?
hints: It was the first World Cup played in North America.
At that World Cup, Brazil and Pelé won their third title.
It came right at the start of a new decade.
questions.description: A boy in a hat who never played a single match but showed up in every sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico hosted the World Cup again in 1986, and that time the mascot was Pique, a jalapeño pepper with a mustache.

questions.question: Before some movies, a little hopping lamp squashes a letter of the logo. Which of these movies does NOT start that way?
hints: The little lamp is the mascot of an animation studio.
That studio belongs to Disney and is based in California.
The answer stars a green ogre from another studio.
questions.description: A desk lamp with more bounce than a kangaroo on coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Pixar's little lamp is called Luxo Jr. and starred in a short film in 1986, before Toy Story even existed.

questions.question: A famous ad says “A Diamond Is Forever.” Which chemical element is this gem made of?
hints: It's the same element found in the graphite of pencils.
It's the basis of the chemistry of all living things.
Its chemical symbol is the letter C.
questions.description: Anything promised “forever” usually comes in a very small box.
questions.fun_fact: Frances Gerety wrote the line for De Beers in 1947, and in 1999 it was named the best advertising slogan of the 20th century.

questions.question: Which of these characters did NOT live in McDonaldland, the fantasy world of McDonald's commercials?
hints: Three of them were Ronald McDonald's friends.
The answer is the mascot of a different burger chain.
She is a red-haired girl with pigtails.
questions.description: A kingdom where hamburgers grow on trees and nobody pays taxes.
questions.fun_fact: In 2023, a purple shake made in honor of Grimace went viral on social media.

questions.question: In which of these countries does the boa constrictor NOT live in the wild?
hints: The boa constrictor lives on just one continent... well, two that are joined together.
It likes warm, humid tropical jungles and forests.
The answer is in Asia, where pythons take this boa's place.
questions.description: A snake that gives the longest hugs in the world, and nobody asked for them.
questions.fun_fact: The boa constrictor isn't venomous: it catches its prey by squeezing it with its body.

questions.question: Listen: this animal is one of the most rescued from illegal wildlife trade in Latin America. What is it?
hints: It's a bird from the rainforest.
It has very bright feathers and a very long tail.
It's a big parrot, sometimes red, blue and yellow.
questions.description: A bird so colorful that smugglers want it, and so do the people who rescue it.
questions.fun_fact: Macaws can live more than 50 years, so a rescued macaw needs care for a very, very long time.

questions.question: In 1975, a “pet” that was just a stone in a box went on sale in the United States. About how many were sold?
hints: It was a huge craze, even though it lasted only a few months.
Its inventor became a millionaire.
It was more than a million.
questions.description: The perfect pet: it doesn't eat, doesn't bark and never runs away.
questions.fun_fact: The stone came with a manual explaining how to teach it to “sit” and “play dead.”

questions.question: Look at this crest and those orange cheeks: which group of birds does this bird belong to?
hints: It is a very common pet bird kept in cages.
It raises and lowers its crest depending on its mood.
It is related to some large white birds from Australia with a big crest.
questions.description: A bird that always looks like it just styled its hair with gel.
questions.fun_fact: The cockatiel is the smallest cockatoo in the world, and many males learn to whistle songs.

questions.question: Look at this hill in Rome: it gave its name to capitols around the world. To which god was its great temple dedicated?
hints: He was the most important god in Rome.
His favorite weapon fell from the sky during storms.
He is the Roman version of Zeus.
questions.description: The hill that lent its name to half the world's domed buildings.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the sacred geese of the Capitol woke the Romans with their honking and saved the hill from a night attack by the Gauls.

questions.question: In the Roman Forum stood a round temple with a sacred fire that must never go out. Which goddess was it dedicated to?
hints: She was the goddess of the home and hearth.
Priestesses looked after her temple and vowed to serve her for 30 years.
Those priestesses were called the Vestals.
questions.description: The only place in Rome where nobody was allowed to turn off the stove.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans believed that if Vesta's fire ever went out, something bad would happen to the whole city.

questions.question: The Apollo program took humans to the Moon in 1969. Which twin sister of Apollo gives her name to the new Moon program?
hints: She is a hunting goddess with a bow and arrows.
Like her brother, she is a daughter of Zeus.
The Romans called her Diana.
questions.description: Even NASA has trouble choosing names for its kids.
questions.fun_fact: The Apollo program's Saturn V rocket was about 110 meters (360 ft) tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty with its pedestal.

questions.question: Diana was the “Princess of Wales”. Where is Wales?
hints: It is a place in Europe.
It is on a big island, right next to England.
It is part of the same country as London.
questions.description: A title so grand that you need a map just to understand it.
questions.fun_fact: People in Wales speak Welsh, a very old language with words like “cwtch”, which means a hug.

questions.question: In what year was “Spare,” Prince Harry's memoir, published?
hints: It came out in this decade.
It was published a few months after his grandmother, Elizabeth II, died.
It came out in January, the year after his grandmother's funeral.
questions.description: A book with more family gossip than a Sunday lunch at Grandma's.
questions.fun_fact: The title “Spare” comes from the saying “the heir and the spare”: the child who will be king, and the backup.

questions.question: I was never meant to be king, but my brother gave up the crown for love, so it fell to me. I also had a stammer. Who am I?
hints: I reigned during the Second World War.
My story is told in the film “The King's Speech.”
I was the father of Elizabeth II.
questions.description: A king who came off the bench, like a backup goalkeeper sent on in the final minute.
questions.fun_fact: His first name was actually Albert, and his family called him “Bertie.”

questions.question: The Sovereign's Orb is a hollow gold sphere covered in jewels, given to the monarch at the coronation. What sits on top of it?
hints: It is a religious symbol.
Remember that the monarch is also head of the Church of England.
It is made of two short bars, one upright and one sideways.
questions.description: A golden ball that nobody would ever dare to kick around.
questions.fun_fact: The orb was made in 1661 for Charles II, because the earlier crown jewels had been melted down while England was a republic.

questions.question: You're on the banks of the River Thames and see white swans with no markings. By an old tradition, who owns them?
hints: Their owner wears a crown.
Every year they are counted in an official ceremony.
They used to belong to Elizabeth II; today they belong to her son.
questions.description: Some very fancy ducks with a very important owner.
questions.fun_fact: Every summer there is “Swan Upping”, a ceremony where people in boats count and check the swans on the Thames.

questions.question: In what year was Charles III crowned at Westminster Abbey?
hints: It was in this decade.
It wasn't the same year he became king.
It was about eight months after the death of Elizabeth II.
questions.description: A king who waited so long for his turn that the line at the bank feels short.
questions.fun_fact: Charles III was 74 when he was crowned, the oldest British monarch ever to be crowned.

questions.question: I was king of England, in 1215 I was forced to accept the Magna Carta, and I'm the villain in the Robin Hood stories. Who am I?
hints: I ruled while my brother was far away.
My brother was a king famous for his bravery in the Crusades.
My nickname says I ended up with no land of my own.
questions.description: A king that not even children's stories have a soft spot for.
questions.fun_fact: Only four copies of the 1215 Magna Carta survive today, and two of them are in the British Library in London.

questions.question: This man appears on every banknote in Vietnam. Who is he?
hints: He was a political leader of the 20th century.
He founded modern Vietnam and was its president.
The old city of Saigon is now named after him.
questions.description: A banknote where the same man always shows up, whatever its value.
questions.fun_fact: Saigon, Vietnam's largest city, has officially been called Ho Chi Minh City since 1976.

questions.question: I was Ecuador's currency until 2000, and I'm named after the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho. Which currency am I?
hints: My hero fought alongside Simón Bolívar.
One of Bolivia's capitals has the same name.
Colombia has a department with my name, and its capital is Sincelejo.
questions.description: A currency named after a hero, which retired as soon as the dollar showed up.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2000, Ecuador has used the US dollar as its official currency.

questions.question: I'm Japan's lowest-value coin and I weigh exactly 1 gram. What metal am I made of?
hints: It's a very light, silver-colored metal.
Many drink cans are made of it.
It's also used for the shiny foil that wraps food in the kitchen.
questions.description: A coin so light it nearly flies out of your pocket on its own.
questions.fun_fact: This coin is so light that it can float on water, held up by surface tension.

questions.question: Three of these Roman structures are in Italy. Which one is NOT?
hints: One of them is on an island far to the north, where it rains a lot.
It's very far from Rome, in a land the Romans called Britannia.
It runs across the north of England.
questions.description: The Romans built so much that they left things lying around half of Europe.
questions.fun_fact: Some say Hadrian's Wall inspired the giant Wall of ice in “Game of Thrones.”

questions.question: It has white domes, a princess lives there with a tiger, and a genie visited it. Which real monument inspired this Disney palace?
hints: It's in Asia.
It's a white marble tomb.
It's in India.
questions.description: Even cartoon palaces copy someone else's homework.
questions.fun_fact: The story of Aladdin wasn't even in the oldest Arabic versions of “One Thousand and One Nights”: a French translator added it.

questions.question: This building was built as a Christian church almost 1,500 years ago. What was its city called back then?
hints: The city lies on a famous strait, where two continents meet.
Later another empire renamed it, and today it is the largest city in its country.
Its name comes from a Roman emperor called Constantine.
questions.description: A city so important it ended up with more names than a dog shared by three families.
questions.fun_fact: Hagia Sophia was the largest cathedral in the world for almost a thousand years.

questions.question: You're inside a Gothic cathedral and you don't go out. Which of these parts can you NOT see?
hints: This part does its work on the outside of the building.
It's like a stone arm pushing against the walls.
It's an outside arch that helps hold up the tall walls.
questions.description: Some parts of a cathedral can only be admired by people who skip going inside for Mass.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to those outside arches, Gothic cathedrals could have thinner walls and giant stained-glass windows.

questions.question: It stands on an island in the Seine, caught fire in 2019, and a novel has a hunchbacked bell-ringer living in it. What is it?
hints: It's in France.
Disney made a movie about its hunchback.
The hunchback is called Quasimodo, and he lives in Paris.
questions.description: A building with more gargoyles than tourists, and that's saying something.
questions.fun_fact: After the fire, the cathedral opened its doors again in December 2024.

questions.question: This marble sculpture is in the Vatican. Who made it?
hints: He was an Italian artist of the Renaissance.
He carved it when he was only about 24 years old.
He also sculpted the famous David in Florence.
questions.description: A sculpture so perfect that its maker just couldn't resist signing it.
questions.fun_fact: The Pietà is the only work Michelangelo ever signed: his name is carved on the sash across the Virgin Mary's chest.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which piece of music plays when the owner of this helmet appears?
hints: A full orchestra plays it, with very loud brass and a marching beat.
You hear it in Star Wars.
Its name is about emperors and armies on parade.
questions.description: When this gentleman walks in, even the soundtrack gets serious.
questions.fun_fact: The Imperial March was first heard in “The Empire Strikes Back” in 1980, not in the first film.

questions.question: They called me “The Voice” and I sang “New York, New York.” I was born in the US, but my parents came from another country. Which one?
hints: My parents moved to the United States in the early 1900s, like millions of other Europeans.
Many immigrants from that country settled in New York and New Jersey.
It's the country of pizza and pasta.
questions.description: A gentleman so elegant he even sang in a bow tie.
questions.fun_fact: Frank Sinatra was born in Hoboken, a New Jersey city just across the river from New York.

questions.question: Mariachi is to ranchera as cowboy is to…
hints: Its songs are about pickup trucks, horses and broken hearts.
It's sung with guitar, banjo and lots of longing for life out on the land.
Dolly Parton and Johnny Cash are among its biggest stars.
questions.description: Music with boots, a big hat and a whiff of the stable.
questions.fun_fact: Nashville, Tennessee, is so famous for country music that it's nicknamed “Music City.”

questions.question: I'm Brazil's most famous festival, with feathers, sequins and giant floats. Who competes by parading in me?
hints: They dance and play drums for hours.
They prepare all year to win the contest.
Their name sounds like a place where kids learn, but there's no homework, only Brazil's most famous dance.
questions.description: A party with more feathers than a henhouse.
questions.fun_fact: The Rio Carnival parades take place in the Sambadrome, an avenue built just for them.

questions.question: There are seven of them, they're from South Korea, and in 2020 “Dynamite” made them the first South Korean group to hit No. 1 on Billboard. Who are they?
hints: They are the most famous K-pop group in the world.
Their fans call themselves ARMY.
Their name is just three letters.
questions.description: Seven guys who blew up the charts, literally.
questions.fun_fact: “Dynamite” was the first BTS song sung entirely in English.

review.feedback: Source: the claim is wrong as stated, in both the source and the translation. BTS already reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200 album chart in 2018 with "Love Yourself: Tear". "Dynamite" was their first No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, the singles chart. The source should say "Hot 100" (for example "the first all-South Korean act to top the Billboard Hot 100"), and the translation should then follow it.

questions.question: I moved from Cancún to Buenos Aires, I deliver food on roller skates and I dream of shining at the Jam & Roller rink. Who am I?
hints: I'm the main character of a Disney Channel series.
The series is named after me.
My first name is the Spanish word for Earth's natural satellite.
questions.description: A girl who can't seem to walk anywhere without wheels under her feet.
questions.fun_fact: Luna was played by Mexican actress and singer Karol Sevilla.

questions.question: They call me a “single,” but I'm not looking for a partner. In music, what am I?
questions.answer: A song released on its own
hints: Artists put me out before their album.
I'm used to promote a record.
On old vinyl records, I often had a B-side.
questions.description: In music, this word has nothing to do with dating apps.
questions.fun_fact: Singles used to be sold on small vinyl records that spun at 45 revolutions per minute.

questions.question: In a black-and-white movie, a dancer in a tailcoat tap-dances with Ginger Rogers. They made 10 movies together. Who is he?
hints: He was a Hollywood star in the 1930s.
He's not the one who dances in the rain with an umbrella.
His stage surname starts with “A”.
questions.description: A man who made the floor look like it was made of clouds.
questions.fun_fact: People say Ginger Rogers did everything he did, but backwards and in high heels.

questions.question: I'm a cheerleader in Seabrook, I hide my white hair under a wig, and I fell in love with Zed, a zombie. Who am I?
hints: I'm in the Disney Channel movie “Zombies”.
My cousin Bucky is the captain of the cheerleaders.
My name starts with “A”.
questions.description: A love story where one of the two needs a wristband to stop craving brains.
questions.fun_fact: The first “Zombies” movie premiered on Disney Channel in 2018 and got several sequels.

questions.question: At a Broadway concert: “Don't Cry for Me Argentina” is to “Evita” as “Memory” is to…
hints: Both musicals are by Andrew Lloyd Webber.
The song is sung by Grizabella, a faded old star.
Its characters have whiskers and tails.
questions.description: Songs so famous that people sing them in the shower, even if they've never seen the show.
questions.fun_fact: The musical “Cats” grew out of a book of poems about cats by T. S. Eliot.

questions.question: Olaf from Frozen is made of snow, loves warm hugs and sings about dreaming of one season. Which one?
hints: It's a season he has never lived through.
He pictures himself on the beach, soaking up the sun.
It's the hottest season of the year.
questions.description: A snowman whose big dream is, honestly, a terrible plan.
questions.fun_fact: In the song, Olaf has no idea what heat would do to snow.

questions.question: In which decade did “Singin' in the Rain”, starring Debbie Reynolds and Gene Kelly, come out?
hints: The film was already in color.
It was the golden age of Hollywood's big studio musicals.
It came out early in that decade, soon after 1950.
questions.description: It was pouring down, and someone still danced happily in the street: that's how cheerful those days were.
questions.fun_fact: Debbie Reynolds was the mother of Carrie Fisher, who played Princess Leia in Star Wars.

questions.question: I played detective Sam Spade in “The Maltese Falcon” and Philip Marlowe in “The Big Sleep”, both film noir classics. Who am I?
hints: I was an American actor of the 1940s.
I also starred in a famous romance set in a café in Morocco.
There I said “We'll always have Paris,” in “Casablanca.”
questions.description: Hat, trench coat, cigarette and zero smiles: the official uniform of the black-and-white detective.
questions.fun_fact: The name “film noir” came from French critics, inspired by a French series of crime novels with black covers.

questions.question: At a trial, “lawyer” is to “defend” as “witness” is to…
hints: A witness is not a judge or a police officer.
They were there when something happened.
Their job at the trial is to use their memory and their voice.
questions.description: Wrong place, wrong time, eyes wide open.
questions.fun_fact: The words “testify” and “testimony” come from the Latin “testis,” meaning someone who is present as a third party.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel where ten strangers are stuck on an island and drop out one by one?
hints: She is an English author.
She created Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple.
She is called “the Queen of Crime.”
questions.description: A vacation on a private island that nobody would recommend in a review.
questions.fun_fact: “And Then There Were None” is one of the best-selling novels of all time, with more than 100 million copies sold.

questions.question: I open the mansion door and serve the tea, and in the old mystery-novel joke, I'm always the guilty one. Who am I?
hints: I work in the house, but I'm not part of the family.
I wear a smart suit and white gloves.
I'm the head of the mansion's staff.
questions.description: An English mansion with 40 rooms, three suspects and the same old culprit as always.
questions.fun_fact: The line “The butler did it” is world-famous, but in classic mystery novels the butler is almost never the culprit.

questions.question: One of Van Dine's famous 20 rules for detective novels says: “The detective must never turn out to be the…”
hints: The rules are meant to keep the game fair for the reader.
It would be a huge cheat at the end of the book.
It's exactly the person the detective is hunting for.
questions.description: A rulebook to stop authors from cheating their readers… or at least from cheating too much.
questions.fun_fact: S. S. Van Dine published his 20 rules in 1928, and another one bans the culprit from being a servant.

questions.question: In a mystery novel, a detail makes you suspect the gardener, but the author was tricking you. What is this device called?
hints: It's there to throw the reader off the trail.
It's the opposite of a real clue.
Its name comes from a strong-smelling smoked fish.
questions.description: The author pointed left while the culprit slipped out to the right.
questions.fun_fact: The story goes that the name comes from using smoked herrings to throw hunting dogs off a scent.

questions.question: I'm an Italian professor, and I wrote a mystery novel set in a medieval abbey, with a friar as the detective. Who am I?
hints: My novel was made into a film starring Sean Connery.
Its title mentions a flower.
I wrote “The Name of the Rose.”
questions.description: A professor who decided the best medieval history lesson was a murder mystery full of monks.
questions.fun_fact: The friar detective in “The Name of the Rose” is called William of Baskerville, a nod to Sherlock Holmes.

questions.question: For years, people believed human cells had 48 chromosomes. In which decade was it shown that they have 46?
hints: It was in the 20th century, when microscopes and staining methods had already improved a lot.
The count was done in a Swedish lab, with a new method that spread the chromosomes out clearly.
It was a few years after the end of the Second World War.
questions.description: For decades, science miscounted and nobody dared to say a word.
questions.fun_fact: Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan found the right number in Sweden in 1955, after more than 30 years of people believing it was 48.

questions.question: In the number 4,725, which place does the 7 sit in?
hints: It's about the position a digit holds inside a number.
Counting from the right, it's the third place.
The 7 in 4,725 is worth 700.
questions.description: Every number lives in a building, and each digit has its own floor.
questions.fun_fact: Our place-value system, with ones, tens and hundreds, came to Europe from India through Arab mathematicians.

questions.question: A normal year of 365 days starts on a Thursday. How many Thursdays does that year have?
hints: Think about how many full weeks fit into 365 days.
52 weeks are 364 days, so exactly one day is left over.
That extra day is the same day of the week the year started on.
questions.description: A whole calendar counted with the 7 times table and a little patience.
questions.fun_fact: That's why in every normal year one day of the week comes up 53 times; in leap years, two days do.

questions.question: There's a party in the town square because the city is celebrating its bicentennial. How many years old is it turning?
hints: “Bi” means two, as in “bicycle.”
“Centennial” has to do with a hundred, like “century.”
It's two times a hundred.
questions.description: A birthday cake with so many candles that you need a firefighter to blow them out.
questions.fun_fact: Many countries in Latin America celebrated 200 years of independence between 2009 and 2024.

questions.question: They counted cards at blackjack, won millions in Las Vegas and inspired the movie “21”. Which university were they from?
hints: It is a US university famous for engineering and technology.
It is in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Its name is an abbreviation that includes the word “Technology”.
questions.description: Some students took their math homework to the casino and got a top grade.
questions.fun_fact: Mathematician Edward Thorp proved card counting works in his 1962 book “Beat the Dealer”.

questions.question: I'm a string quartet, but one of my musicians went on vacation. What do I become?
hints: The names of these music groups come from Latin numbers.
Do the math: count the musicians in a quartet and take away the one who left.
My new name starts the same way as “tricycle”.
questions.description: A band loses a member and suddenly needs a new name.
questions.fun_fact: Haydn is called the “father of the string quartet”: he wrote about 68 of them.

questions.question: One of the founders of Western Union used his telegraph fortune to start a university bearing his last name. Who was he?
hints: The university is in New York State.
It is one of the Ivy League universities.
His first name comes from the Bible and starts with E.
questions.description: Before it sent money around the world, this company sent dots and dashes.
questions.fun_fact: Western Union began in the 1850s as a telegraph company and sent its last telegram in 2006.

questions.question: In which decade did Post-it Notes first go on sale in stores?
hints: Your grandparents didn't have them as kids.
They came before smartphones.
They arrived around the time of the first personal computers.
questions.description: A note that sticks, unsticks and sticks again without losing its dignity.
questions.fun_fact: They grew out of a “failed” glue that barely stuck, plus someone who wanted to mark pages without the paper falling out.

questions.question: Where does the name of the Japanese brand Casio come from?
wrong_answers: From the name of a Japanese volcano
From the name of an Italian city
hints: Many brands got their names this way.
It was founded by several brothers.
The brothers' surname was Kashio.
questions.description: A Japanese brand that has been on the wrists and in the backpacks of half the planet.
questions.fun_fact: In 1957, Casio launched one of the world's first compact, fully electric calculators.

questions.question: I'm made by the Swiss brand Omega, and I went to the Moon on the astronauts' wrists. What am I?
hints: I go tick, tock.
I have hands.
I tell you what time it is.
questions.description: Something that flew all the way to the Moon without paying for extra baggage.
questions.fun_fact: Buzz Aldrin wore an Omega Speedmaster when he walked on the Moon in 1969.

questions.question: Look at this huge fossil tooth with saw-like edges. What kind of animal did it come from?
hints: Its owner lost teeth all its life and kept growing new ones.
Its owner had no bones, only cartilage.
It was a giant sea hunter with fins, and its living relatives still hunt in every ocean.
questions.description: This owner would have needed a very big toothbrush, and a whole box of spares.
questions.fun_fact: A shark can go through thousands of teeth in its life: the spare ones move forward in rows, like on a conveyor belt.

questions.question: Look at this small striped aquarium fish. Outside the fish tank, what is it famous for around the world?
questions.answer: For research on genes and human diseases
wrong_answers: For cleaning algae out of ponds
For making a cheap kind of caviar
hints: Its embryos are see-through, so you can watch them grow inside.
It can regrow part of its heart.
Thousands of biology labs raise it.
questions.description: A fish in striped pajamas with a very busy schedule.
questions.fun_fact: GloFish, the glowing aquarium fish, were at first zebrafish given a gene from a jellyfish or a coral.

questions.question: This gas-filled organ, taken from a fish, helps it float without effort. Which group of fish has it?
hints: It's called the swim bladder.
Sharks don't have one: they stay afloat thanks to a liver full of oil.
It's the group most fish belong to: sardines, tuna and trout.
questions.description: A party balloon that some fish carry inside them all year round.
questions.fun_fact: The swim bladder and our lungs are related organs: they share an evolutionary origin.

questions.question: Look at this eye. Most fish sleep with their eyes open because they have no…
hints: You use them many times a minute without noticing.
They are like little skin curtains for the eye.
They come down every time you blink.
questions.description: An eye that will never wink at you.
questions.fun_fact: Some sharks have a special membrane, called the nictitating membrane, that covers the eye when they bite.

questions.question: This aquarium gourami has an organ called the “labyrinth” above its gills. What is it for?
hints: Thanks to it, the fish can live in puddles with little oxygen.
You'll see it swim up to the surface every now and then.
If it can't reach the top, it can drown.
questions.description: A fish with a maze in its head, and somehow it never gets lost.
questions.fun_fact: In many gourami species, the males build a nest of bubbles at the surface for the eggs.

questions.question: In “Finding Nemo”, which shark is NOT in Bruce's club of sharks who promise not to eat fish?
hints: Bruce is the biggest and smiliest member of the club.
One of his friends has a head shaped like a tool.
The missing one is a giant that eats plankton and wouldn't need the club at all.
questions.description: A club full of sharp teeth and very good intentions.
questions.fun_fact: Bruce is named after the mechanical shark from the film “Jaws”, which the film crew nicknamed Bruce.

questions.question: The alligator gar, with a crocodile-like snout and scales like armor, is a “living fossil.” How long have its relatives been around?
hints: They are far, far older than humans.
You have to count in millions of years.
They swam in rivers where dinosaurs came to drink.
questions.description: Half fish, half crocodile, and older than all your grandparents put together.
questions.fun_fact: Alligator gar eggs are poisonous to people.

questions.question: This rainbow trout is common in the cold rivers of the Andes, but it isn't native there. Where does it originally come from?
hints: It was brought to South America more than a hundred years ago for fishing and fish farming.
Its original home is rivers that flow into the Pacific Ocean.
It's native to places like California, Canada and Alaska.
questions.description: A tourist so well settled in that nobody asks for her passport anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Some rainbow trout travel out to sea and come back to the river much bigger; these are called steelhead.

questions.question: In an official agility competition under FCI rules, the dog zigzags through the weave poles. How many poles are there?
hints: It's an even number.
It's more than 10.
It's the same as the number of months in a year.
questions.description: A dog that dodges obstacles better than you do at the mall on the first day of a big sale.
questions.fun_fact: Agility was born in England in the late 1970s, inspired by show jumping competitions for horses.

questions.question: The virus behind this dog disease is a cousin of measles. Measles is to child as ___ is to puppy.
hints: Puppies are protected against it by their vaccines.
It often starts with discharge from the nose and eyes.
Cats can get a disease with the same name, though a different virus causes it.
questions.description: A trip to the vet: the only walk no dog ever asks to repeat.
questions.fun_fact: The distemper virus is such a close relative of measles that a measles vaccine was once used to protect dogs.

questions.question: Complete the famous Spanish saying used when people criticize you: “The dogs bark, Sancho, a sign that…”
hints: Sancho Panza travels with a knight-errant.
The saying means that criticism is a sign you are moving forward.
It's what someone does when they are on horseback.
questions.description: A quote so famous that many people swear they read it in a book where it never appears.
questions.fun_fact: Although people credit it to Cervantes, this saying doesn't appear anywhere in “Don Quixote.”

questions.question: It has no owner, sleeps wherever it can and finds food wherever it can. What word describes this dog?
hints: The word tells you how it lives.
You see it walking along the sidewalks.
The same word means to wander away from where you belong.
questions.description: It has no address, but it knows every address in the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the world's dogs are thought to live not inside a home, but freely on the streets or in the countryside.

questions.question: An old Spanish saying goes: “Once the dog is dead, the rabies is gone.” What does it teach?
questions.answer: Remove the cause and the problem ends
hints: The saying is about solving problems, not about pets.
Think about who spreads the illness in the saying.
If what causes it disappears, so does the trouble.
questions.description: A saying with a nasty bite, but a lot of logic.
questions.fun_fact: Louis Pasteur created the rabies vaccine and first used it successfully on a boy in 1885.

questions.question: Canine parvovirus mostly strikes unvaccinated puppies and can survive for months in the ground. Which body system does it harm most?
hints: The puppy stops eating.
The puppy loses a lot of fluid and becomes dangerously dehydrated.
It's the system of the stomach and intestines.
questions.description: A tiny virus that sends shivers through every dog breeder.
questions.fun_fact: Canine parvovirus appeared in the late 1970s, and within just a couple of years it had spread all over the world.

questions.question: During a long race through the snow, how many calories does a sled dog burn in a day?
hints: Far more than an adult human, who needs about 2,000.
It runs for many hours a day and also has to stay warm.
It's a five-digit number.
questions.description: A furry athlete who eats breakfast like there's no tomorrow.
questions.fun_fact: In races, sled dogs wear fabric booties to protect their paw pads from the ice.

questions.question: I'm the oldest written papyrus from Egypt, and I describe the daily work of the inspector Merer. What was his team carrying?
questions.answer: Limestone blocks for the Great Pyramid
wrong_answers: Granite for the obelisks of Karnak
Cedar from Lebanon for royal ships
Gold from Nubia for the pharaoh's treasury
hints: I was found in 2013 at an ancient port on the Red Sea.
I was written in the time of the pharaoh Khufu.
My team crossed the Nile from the Tura quarries to Giza.
questions.description: The world's oldest work notebook, and nobody checked its spelling.
questions.fun_fact: The Diary of Merer shows that the stone reached Giza by boat along canals of the Nile, not dragged across the whole desert.

questions.question: Narrow “air shafts” lead out from two chambers inside this pyramid. How many of these shafts are there in total?
hints: The chambers are called the “King's Chamber” and the “Queen's Chamber.”
Each chamber has the same number of shafts.
From each chamber, one shaft heads north and one heads south.
questions.description: Tunnels so narrow that not even a cat would squeeze in, but a robot would.
questions.fun_fact: In 1993, a small robot called Upuaut climbed up one of these shafts and found a tiny stone door with two copper handles.

questions.question: These are the pyramids of Meroë, in today's Sudan. Which people built them?
hints: They are smaller, steeper and newer than the ones at Giza.
Their kings copied Egyptian customs, like hieroglyphs and burial under pyramids, but they also wrote their own language.
Their kingdom had the name of a son of Ham in the Bible.
