questions.description: Pointy pyramids that never make it onto the postcards from Egypt.
questions.fun_fact: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: Meroë alone has about 200.

questions.question: I'm a giant temple in Nubia, carved into the rock for Ramesses II. In the 1960s, I was cut into blocks and moved up a hill. Why?
questions.answer: A huge dam was going to flood me
wrong_answers: The desert sand was burying me
They wanted to take me to a museum
hints: The problem came from the Nile River.
Something enormous was built at Aswan.
Behind that project, the gigantic Lake Nasser formed.
questions.description: A move so heavy that even calling every cousin you have wouldn't help.
questions.fun_fact: The Abu Simbel temple was cut into more than a thousand blocks and rebuilt about 65 meters (213 feet) higher up.

questions.question: You're singing the Spanish kids' song “I Had Ten Little Puppies”, and one falls in the snow. How many puppies are left?
hints: It's a really easy take-away sum.
At the start there were ten.
It's the number that comes just before ten.
questions.description: A song where puppies vanish faster than candy from a piñata.
questions.fun_fact: The song helps kids practice counting down: in every verse one puppy goes away, until none are left.

questions.question: This Spanish Baroque style is full of fancy words and Latin borrowings, and Luis de Góngora was its great master. What is it called?
hints: It belongs to the Golden Age of Spanish literature.
Its great rival was Quevedo's style, which played more with ideas than with words.
Its name comes from the Spanish word “culto”, meaning “learned” or “refined”.
questions.description: Writing so complicated that even the dictionary asks for hints.
questions.fun_fact: Góngora and Quevedo disliked each other so much that they wrote poems to make fun of each other.

questions.question: In which century did Quevedo write his mocking sonnet “Érase un hombre a una nariz pegado” (“Once there was a man stuck to a nose”)?
hints: Quevedo is a figure of the Spanish Golden Age.
It was the time of the Baroque.
Quevedo died in 1645.
questions.description: A poem that poked its nose where nobody asked it to: right into someone's face.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the giant nose in the poem belonged to Quevedo's rival, the poet Luis de Góngora.

questions.question: Mercedes Sosa was nicknamed “La Negra”, sang “Gracias a la vida” and “Alfonsina y el mar”, and wore a poncho. Which country was she from?
hints: It's a country in the south of the Americas.
“Gracias a la vida” was written by a Chilean woman, but Sosa wasn't Chilean.
She was born in Tucumán.
questions.description: A voice too big for just one country, but she still needed a passport.
questions.fun_fact: “Alfonsina y el mar” is a tribute to the poet Alfonsina Storni.

questions.question: I eat up words that are understood anyway: in “I ordered coffee; you, tea” a verb is missing. Which figure of speech am I?
hints: I am a figure of speech.
The missing word is “ordered”.
My name comes from Greek and means “omission” or “leaving out”.
questions.description: A figure of speech so thrifty it thinks even words are too expensive.
questions.fun_fact: Movies use ellipsis too: when the story suddenly jumps several years ahead.

questions.question: In ancient Greece, someone takes power by force, rules without limits and governs only for himself. What is this kind of government called?
hints: Only one person is in charge.
Aristotle called it the corrupt form of monarchy.
Today we call a ruler like this by a word that fits a storybook villain.
questions.description: A government that mixes up “the people” with “me, me and only me.”
questions.fun_fact: In Greek, “tyrannos” was not an insult at first: it just meant someone who came to power without inheriting it, and some of them were quite popular.

questions.question: Two doors, two guards: one always lies, the other never does. You ask one which door the other would say is the exit. What do you do?
hints: It doesn't matter which of the two guards you ask.
The lie passes through the answer exactly once.
The answer always points to the wrong door.
questions.description: Two guards, two doors and one question: harder than picking an ice cream flavor.
questions.fun_fact: This riddle shows up in the film “Labyrinth” (1986), where Sarah faces two guards watching over two doors.

questions.question: Which 19th-century English mathematician created an algebra where everything is either true or false, the basis of today's computing?
hints: He worked as a professor in Ireland.
In programming, true-or-false variables are named after him.
Programmers type his surname every day, shortened to four letters.
questions.description: A man who boiled the whole world down to “yes” or “no,” and your phone thanks him for it.
questions.fun_fact: Boole was almost entirely self-taught: he left school very young and learned mathematics on his own while working as a teacher.

questions.question: It studies what is right and wrong, asks how we should behave, and is a school subject in many places. What is it?
hints: It is a branch of philosophy.
It deals with values like honesty and fairness.
Many doctors and lawyers must follow a professional code named after it.
questions.description: The subject that asks whether it's okay to eat the last slice of cake without telling anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Greek “êthos”, which means “custom” or “character”.

questions.question: Take away one grain of sand and I stay the same. And another, and another… until one is left. “At which grain did I lose my name?” Which paradox am I?
wrong_answers: The paradox of the Ship of Theseus
The paradox of Achilles and the tortoise
hints: It comes from ancient Greece.
The same goes for someone losing hairs one by one: when do they become bald?
It's about how many grains it takes before you can call something by a certain name.
questions.description: A question that turns a day at the beach into an existential crisis.
questions.fun_fact: It is credited to Eubulides of Miletus, the same Greek philosopher credited with the liar paradox.

questions.question: This mistake in arguing uses the conclusion as proof of itself, like “I'm right because I'm never wrong.” What is it called?
hints: The argument gives you no new information.
In Latin it is called “petitio principii.”
The argument ends right where it started, like a wheel.
questions.description: An argument as confident as a kid saying “because I said so.”
questions.fun_fact: In English it is also called “begging the question,” and many people use that phrase as if it meant “raising the question.”

questions.question: You're standing in front of a dolmen: big upright stones with a flat slab on top. How long ago were Europe's first ones built?
hints: They are older than the pyramids of Egypt.
They were built in the Neolithic, when people already farmed.
It's thousands of years, but fewer than ten thousand.
questions.description: A table so heavy that the whole family together couldn't move it to sweep underneath.
questions.fun_fact: The word “dolmen” comes from Breton and means “stone table.”

questions.question: This skull, about 430,000 years old, came from the Sima de los Huesos (“Pit of the Bones”) in Spain. Which human lineage did it belong to?
hints: It isn't our species: it's far too old for that.
DNA from these bones links them to humans who later lived in Europe.
They are ancestors of humans with heavy brow ridges who vanished about 40,000 years ago.
questions.description: A pit where the family tree was traced with DNA almost half a million years old.
questions.fun_fact: Remains of at least 28 people turned up in the Sima, and their DNA is among the oldest human DNA ever read.

questions.question: A relative of the elephant, it lived in the Americas in the Ice Age, and its Greek name means “nipple tooth.” What animal is it?
hints: It browsed on leaves, twigs and shrubs in forests rather than grazing on open grassland.
Its back teeth had round, cone-shaped bumps.
Its name starts with the same four letters as “masticate.”
questions.description: Its smile was so odd that it got named after its teeth.
questions.fun_fact: French naturalist Georges Cuvier gave it its name in the early 19th century.

questions.question: Three of these human groups are named after the place where their fossils were found. Which one is NOT?
hints: Look for the name that describes a skill, not a spot on the map.
The others come from a cave in Siberia, a valley in Germany and an island in Indonesia.
Its Latin name means something like “the one who is skilled with his hands.”
questions.description: Naming your family after your home address: a very prehistoric habit.
questions.fun_fact: Very few Denisovan bones are known: almost everything we know about them came from the DNA in a single finger bone.

questions.question: The Stone Age is to stone as the first stage of the Metal Age is to…
hints: It is a reddish metal.
Today it is inside almost every electric cable.
The Statue of Liberty is covered in it, which is why it turned green.
questions.description: A caveman swapped his stone tools for something shinier and never looked back.
questions.fun_fact: Ötzi the Iceman, who lived about 5,300 years ago, carried an axe made of copper.

questions.question: A newspaper called Alfred Nobel “the merchant of death.” Which of his inventions earned him that name?
hints: It was widely used to dig tunnels and mines.
It comes in sticks and has a fuse.
It goes BOOM in lots of Road Runner cartoons.
questions.description: A man who tried to clean up his name with the most famous prize on the planet.
questions.fun_fact: The newspaper ran the story by mistake: the one who had died was his brother Ludvig, not Alfred.

questions.question: Colombia's peace deal with which guerrilla group earned Juan Manuel Santos the 2016 Nobel Peace Prize?
hints: It was Colombia's largest and oldest guerrilla group.
The peace talks took place in Havana, Cuba.
Its name begins with “Revolutionary Armed Forces”.
questions.description: A signature with a very special pen that made headlines around the world.
questions.fun_fact: The deal was signed with a pen made from a bullet.

questions.question: The Curies discovered it, it glows faintly in the dark, and its name starts like a device for listening to music. Which element is it?
hints: It is a chemical element.
It was once used on watches that glowed at night.
The device is used to listen to stations.
questions.description: A family where prizes were handed down like grandma's recipes.
questions.fun_fact: The Curie family won five Nobel Prizes in total, shared between Marie, Pierre, their daughter Irène and their son-in-law Frédéric.

questions.question: Which Indian economist won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on famines and well-being?
hints: He was born in Bengal, India, in 1933.
As a child, he lived through the great Bengal famine of 1943.
His first name was chosen by the poet Rabindranath Tagore, also a Nobel Prize winner.
questions.description: An economist who counted not just dollars, but also plates of food.
questions.fun_fact: Sen argued that no major famine has ever happened in a democracy with a free press.

questions.question: Guess: I'm a giant black hole, and Andrea Ghez won the Nobel Prize for proving I exist. Where do I live?
questions.answer: At the center of the Milky Way
hints: I live very, very far from Earth.
Stars spin around me.
I sit at the heart of our own galaxy.
questions.description: An astronomer who spent years keeping an eye on a neighbor nobody can see.
questions.fun_fact: That black hole, called Sagittarius A*, has about four million times the mass of the Sun.

questions.question: It was founded in 1950, helps refugees and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981. In which city is its headquarters?
hints: It is a UN agency called UNHCR.
It is in a country famous for staying neutral.
It is the same city as the International Red Cross, on a big Swiss lake.
questions.description: An organization that won the same prize twice and still has no time to celebrate.
questions.fun_fact: When UNHCR was created in 1950, it was meant to last only three years; today it works in more than 100 countries.

questions.question: Which of these books was NOT written by Albert Camus, winner of the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature?
hints: The odd book out was written by an author from Prague.
In that book, a man wakes up to find he has turned into an insect.
Its author was Franz Kafka.
questions.description: A writer who wondered about the meaning of life, and played goalkeeper on the side.
questions.fun_fact: As a young man in Algiers, Camus played goalkeeper, and he said soccer taught him what he knew about morals.

questions.question: In 2010, Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Oscar for Best Director. How many Oscar ceremonies came before?
hints: The Oscars are given out once a year.
The first awards were handed out in 1929.
Subtract 1929 from 2010.
questions.description: Hollywood took longer on this than your brother takes in the bathroom.
questions.fun_fact: Bigelow won for “The Hurt Locker”, beating her ex-husband James Cameron, who was nominated for “Avatar”.

questions.question: At 73, actor Jack Palance did one-armed push-ups when he accepted his Oscar. In which decade did this happen?
hints: He won for a modern Western comedy, “City Slickers.”
It was a few years before “Toy Story” came out.
It was in 1992.
questions.description: The most muscular thank-you speech in history.
questions.fun_fact: Billy Crystal, the host, spent the rest of the night making jokes about Palance's push-ups.

questions.question: I hosted the first Oscars shown on TV, in 1953, and I have hosted the show more times than anyone else. Who am I?
hints: I was a very famous comedian from Hollywood's golden age.
I hosted the show 19 times.
My last name is the word for wishing that good things will happen.
questions.description: A host who felt as at home at the Oscars as on the living-room couch.
questions.fun_fact: Bob Hope never won an Oscar for acting, but the Academy gave him several honorary awards.

questions.question: The Oscars were first handed out in 1929. In which city was that first ceremony held?
hints: It was in the United States.
It's in California, on the Pacific Ocean.
It's home to the Hollywood neighborhood.
questions.description: A little golden man who never works out but is always standing up.
questions.fun_fact: The first ceremony, at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel, lasted only about 15 minutes.

questions.question: Who was the first Mexican-born actor to win an Oscar?
hints: He won in the 1950s.
He won twice for Best Supporting Actor.
He is famous for “Zorba the Greek.”
questions.description: An actor who had more roles than a bakery has rolls.
questions.fun_fact: Anthony Quinn was born in Chihuahua and won his first Oscar for “Viva Zapata!”.

questions.question: In what year did the slogan “Yes we can” become famous in a US presidential campaign?
hints: It was in the 21st century.
That year, the first African American president of the United States won the election.
It was the year of Barack Obama's campaign, four years before he was reelected.
questions.description: Three little words that fit on a cap, on a T-shirt and on the lips of millions.
questions.fun_fact: Obama had already used “Yes we can” in 2004, when he ran for senator in Illinois.

questions.question: When the US Civil War broke out in 1861, about how many people were enslaved in the country?
hints: It was more than one in every ten people in the country.
Nearly all of them lived in the Southern states, on cotton and tobacco plantations.
It is a number in the millions, but with just one digit.
questions.description: A number so big it changed a whole country forever.
questions.fun_fact: Slavery was abolished across the whole US by the 13th Amendment, ratified in December 1865.

questions.question: In 1962, in a stadium in Texas, I said: “We choose to go to the Moon in this decade.” Who am I?
hints: I am a US president of the 1960s.
My wife was named Jacqueline and was famous for her elegance.
My initials are JFK, like an airport in New York.
questions.description: A speech so ambitious that someone had to build a rocket to keep its promise.
questions.fun_fact: The speech was given at Rice University in Houston, and the Moon landing came in 1969, right on schedule.

questions.question: Which of these did NOT happen while Andrew Johnson was US president?
hints: Johnson became president in April 1865.
The one you're looking for happened before Johnson took office, while the war was still going on.
It was an order signed by the president before him, Abraham Lincoln.
questions.description: The man who inherited the hardest job at the worst possible moment.
questions.fun_fact: Johnson escaped removal from office in the Senate by just one vote.

questions.question: The first impeachment of a US president was in 1868. In which decade did the second one come?
hints: More than a hundred years passed between the first and the second.
Nixon resigned in 1974 before his could be voted on, so it doesn't count.
It was against Bill Clinton.
questions.description: When the boss of the whole country gets sent to the principal's office.
questions.fun_fact: No US president has ever been removed from office by impeachment: every one was acquitted by the Senate.

questions.question: In Spain, the defeat by the US that cost the country Cuba and Puerto Rico is called “the Disaster of ’…”. Which number completes the name?
hints: It happened at the end of the 19th century.
The US president at the time was William McKinley.
It's the year of the war, without the 18 in front.
questions.description: The day Spain looked at the map and found a few islands missing.
questions.fun_fact: After that war, the US also took the Philippines and Guam.

questions.question: In what year did Donald Trump win his first presidential election?
hints: It came after Barack Obama's two terms.
His opponent was Hillary Clinton.
The Olympic Games were held in Rio de Janeiro that same year.
questions.description: He used to fire people on TV; then he moved into a very white house.
questions.fun_fact: Trump is the second president to serve two terms that were not back to back; the first was Grover Cleveland in the 19th century.

questions.question: I was US president and later Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, something no one else has done. I got a giant bathtub. Who am I?
hints: I was president from 1909 to 1913.
I was the first president to throw out the first pitch of a baseball season.
My last name has only four letters.
questions.description: A president who found the White House, quite literally, a bit of a tight fit.
questions.fun_fact: A famous photo shows four workmen sitting together inside the bathtub made for Taft.

questions.question: It's only done for trusted customers, written down in a notebook, and typical of the corner shop. What is it?
questions.answer: Selling now so you pay later
wrong_answers: Giving a free extra with your purchase
Selling in bulk at a lower price
Keeping a product aside for tomorrow
hints: It has to do with money and trust.
It's a favor the shopkeeper only does for regular customers.
You take the bread today and pay for it at the end of the month.
questions.description: The corner shop, where the shopkeeper knows your name and even your favorite bread.
questions.fun_fact: The word “credit” comes from the Latin “credere”, which means “to believe” or “to trust”.

questions.question: Hellmann's is to mayonnaise as Tabasco is to…
hints: Tabasco comes in a very small bottle.
A few drops are all you need.
It's made from red chili peppers.
questions.description: A question for people who put sauce on everything, even their cereal.
questions.fun_fact: Tabasco sauce has been made since the 1800s on Avery Island, in Louisiana, in the United States.

questions.question: It's a soft white powder that goes on a baby's skin after a bath, and Johnson's has sold it for over 100 years. What is it?
hints: It comes in a bottle with tiny holes in the lid.
It keeps skin dry so it doesn't get sore.
Its name comes from a very soft mineral.
questions.description: The powder that makes babies smell like babies.
questions.fun_fact: Since 2023, Johnson's baby powder has been made with cornstarch instead of the mineral talc.

questions.question: It was born in Brazil, it scrubs burnt pots, and people once hung it on TV antennas. What is Bombril made of?
hints: If you leave it wet for a long time, it rusts.
The antenna trick worked because it carries electricity.
It's a metal made into very thin threads, like hairs.
questions.description: The only thing in the kitchen that can beat a pot burnt during Sunday lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Bombril became so famous in Brazil that “bombril” now means any metal scrubbing pad.

questions.question: It's a powder you mix with water, and it tastes like orange. In the 1960s, who made the drink Tang famous?
hints: They drank it in a place with no refrigerators and no fresh fruit.
They drank it far, far away from Earth.
It flew on the spacecraft of the Gemini program.
questions.description: A drink that has traveled more miles than your aunt.
questions.fun_fact: NASA didn't invent Tang: it was created in 1957 by William Mitchell, the same chemist who invented Pop Rocks popping candy.

questions.question: If you walk across the Pons Fabricius in Rome, you step on stones laid there about… how many years ago?
hints: It crosses the Tiber River to reach an island in the middle of the river.
It was already standing when Julius Caesar lived in Rome.
It was finished in 62 BC.
questions.description: These stones have seen more feet go by than the front door of a shopping mall.
questions.fun_fact: The Pons Fabricius is the oldest bridge in Rome still in use almost exactly as it was built.

questions.question: An acoustic guitar has a part called the “bridge.” What is it?
questions.answer: The piece on the body where the strings are attached
wrong_answers: The long part with frets where your fingers go
The top end where the tuning pegs are
The round hole in the middle of the body
hints: It is glued to the guitar's wooden top.
It passes the strings' vibration to the body.
It is at the opposite end from the tuning pegs.
questions.description: A bridge nobody ever walks across, yet it gets everyone singing.
questions.fun_fact: On classical guitars the strings are tied at the bridge; on steel-string guitars they are held in place with small pins.

questions.question: A Tibetan bridge crosses a deep gorge between mountains and sways as you walk. What is it mainly made of?
hints: It's a material that can bend.
Kids also use it to jump at recess.
You can tie knots in it.
questions.description: A bridge for the brave that moves more than your uncle on the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: In the Andes, the Incas wove hanging bridges out of grass; the Q'eswachaka bridge in Peru is rewoven every year.

questions.question: In which century did the Ottomans build the Stari Most, the famous stone bridge of Mostar?
hints: It was destroyed in 1993, then rebuilt, and today it is a World Heritage Site.
At that time the Ottoman Empire was at the height of its power.
Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent ordered it built.
questions.description: A bridge that comes with show divers included, at no extra charge.
questions.fun_fact: Divers jump from the Stari Most into the Neretva River from more than 20 m (65 ft) up, a tradition that goes back centuries.

questions.question: In “Shrek”, Shrek and Donkey cross a swaying bridge of wooden planks over lava. What type of bridge is it?
hints: It has no pillars underneath.
It is held up from both ends.
It seems to float in midair, hanging from ropes.
questions.description: An ogre, a donkey who won't stop talking and a creaking bridge: what could go wrong?
questions.fun_fact: When Donkey freezes with fear halfway across, Shrek keeps him arguing and walks him backward to the other side without Donkey noticing.

questions.question: On farms around Bogotá, you see lots of Holstein cows, white with black spots. What are they mainly raised for?
hints: What they give comes every morning, not just once.
It's used to make cheese, yogurt and butter.
Farmers get it when they milk them.
questions.description: A cow dressed up as a Dalmatian, working a double shift on the farm.
questions.fun_fact: A Holstein cow can give more than 30 liters (about 8 gallons) of milk in a single day.

questions.question: It's French, has a white rind, is named after a region near Paris, and legend says it was crowned “king of cheeses” in 1815. Which is it?
hints: It's soft and creamy inside.
Its rind is white and velvety, not blue and not hard.
Its name is short: just four letters.
questions.description: A cheese with a crown, a white cape and the airs of French royalty.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says diplomats at the Congress of Vienna held a cheese contest, and Brie won.

questions.question: Which animal's milk is used to make French Roquefort and Italian Pecorino Romano?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It lives in flocks, often watched over by herding dogs.
Its coat is used to make wool.
questions.description: Two famous cheeses with the same fluffy mom.
questions.fun_fact: Sheep's milk has almost twice as much fat as cow's milk, which is why sheep's milk cheeses are so creamy.

questions.question: Where do the round holes in Swiss Emmental cheese come from?
hints: They form on their own while the cheese ripens.
Tiny living things cause them.
It's a bit like how yeast puffs up bread.
questions.description: A cheesy mystery that cartoon mice have always gotten wrong.
questions.fun_fact: The bacterium behind it is Propionibacterium, which gives off carbon dioxide, the same gas that makes fizzy drinks bubbly.

questions.question: Which Spanish cheese is named after Don Quixote's home region?
hints: Don Quixote was a gentleman from a village in… where?
His region is in the middle of Spain and full of windmills.
The cheese takes its name from La Mancha.
questions.description: A cheese wearing a knight's shining armor.
questions.fun_fact: Its rind has a zigzag pattern because it used to be shaped with braided grass bands.

questions.question: A water strider, the insect that walks on water, is in a puddle and someone adds dish soap. What happens to it?
hints: The water strider is held up by a kind of “skin” on the surface of the water.
That “skin” is called surface tension.
Soap breaks that “skin”, and the insect has nothing left to stand on.
questions.description: What cleans your pots can ruin the day of a very nimble little bug.
questions.fun_fact: Surface tension is so strong that a sewing needle, placed gently, can float on water.

questions.question: I'm the fat your body burns when you exercise. I don't just vanish: which way does almost all of my mass leave?
hints: Matter is never created or destroyed, only changed.
When it burns, fat turns mostly into carbon dioxide and water.
Carbon dioxide leaves your body every time you breathe out.
questions.description: In nature nothing is lost, not even what you lose at the gym.
questions.fun_fact: A 2014 study worked out that more than 80% of lost fat leaves the body breathed out as carbon dioxide.

questions.question: It sits in a car's exhaust system, contains metals like platinum and isn't used up as it reacts. What does a catalytic converter do?
wrong_answers: It makes the car go faster
hints: A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
Its job has to do with what comes out of the tailpipe.
It turns poisonous gases into ones that are less harmful to the air.
questions.description: A hidden part under the car that works hard all day and never wears out.
questions.fun_fact: The enzymes in your body are catalysts too: without them, digesting your lunch would take an extremely long time.

questions.question: The head of a soap molecule is to water as its tail is to…
hints: Soap molecules are called surfactants.
The tail is the part that “hates” water.
That's why soap gets the oily grime off your dishes.
questions.description: A molecule with a split personality: half best friends with water, half best friends with something else.
questions.fun_fact: The soap tails surround the grease and form tiny balls called micelles, which the water carries down the drain.

questions.question: In “pH”, the H stands for hydrogen. What does the p stand for?
hints: The scale goes from 0 to 14.
It tells you the capacity or strength of the hydrogen ions.
It's the same word as in “… energy”: energy stored up and waiting to be used.
questions.description: Two letters that measure how sour everything is, and one of them has a mysterious past.
questions.fun_fact: The pH scale was invented in 1909 by the Danish chemist Søren Sørensen while he worked in a brewery's laboratory.

questions.question: I'm Mario Molina, the first Mexican to win a Nobel Prize in science. I warned that gases from spray cans and fridges were destroying the ozone layer. Which gases?
hints: They are known by a three-letter abbreviation.
For decades they were used in fridges because they are neither toxic nor flammable.
Their abbreviation is CFC.
questions.description: A Mexican who put a bandage on the sky.
questions.fun_fact: His work led to the Montreal Protocol, and today the ozone layer is slowly healing.

questions.question: It comes as a bar, makes lots of bubbles, and you wash your hands with it. What is it?
hints: You find it next to the bathroom sink.
It slips out of your hands when it’s wet.
It rhymes with “rope” and “hope.”
questions.description: Your hands’ best friend after playing in the mud.
questions.fun_fact: More than 4,000 years ago, people in ancient Mesopotamia were already making soap by mixing fat with ashes.

questions.question: A team of window cleaners washes every pane of glass on the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building. How long does it take?
hints: The building has more than 24,000 windows.
About 36 people do the job, hanging from platforms.
By the time they finish, it's almost time to start again at the top.
questions.description: A job with the best view in the city and zero desire to look down.
questions.fun_fact: When the cleaners finally finish the Burj Khalifa, the first windows are already dirty again, so they start over.

questions.question: You go from the ground floor to the top floor of the Cayan Tower in Dubai, and each floor is turned a little. How many degrees does it turn in total?
hints: Each floor turns just over one degree from the one below it.
It doesn't even make half a turn.
It's the same angle as the corner of a square.
questions.description: A building that did so much yoga it got stuck in a twist forever.
questions.fun_fact: The Cayan Tower has 75 floors, and each one turns about 1.2 degrees to give it its corkscrew shape.

questions.question: In the video game Mirror's Edge, which character delivers messages by leaping across the rooftops of a city of white skyscrapers?
hints: She is a messenger and a parkour expert.
She has a tattoo near her right eye.
Her first name is a word for strong belief or trust.
questions.description: Someone who thinks elevators are for cowards.
questions.fun_fact: Mirror's Edge shows almost nothing on screen to guide you: you find your way because useful objects are colored red.

questions.question: After the Great Chicago Fire, the city rebuilt and the first skyscrapers were born there. In what year was the fire?
hints: It happened in the 19th century.
It was a few years after the American Civil War.
It happened a few years before Edison's light bulb was invented.
questions.description: A city that burned down and, instead of crying about it, started building upward.
questions.fun_fact: Legend blames Mrs. O'Leary's cow for kicking over a lantern, but it was never proven.

questions.question: The neo-Gothic style, which copies medieval cathedrals, had its heyday in buildings like London's Houses of Parliament. In which century?
hints: “Neo” means new: it came long after the original Gothic style.
It was the age of steam trains.
It's the century of Queen Victoria.
questions.description: A style that copied medieval cathedrals and showed up a few centuries late to the party.
questions.fun_fact: New York's neo-Gothic Woolworth Building was nicknamed “the Cathedral of Commerce.”

questions.question: If you walk all the way up Chicago's Willis Tower, how many floors do you climb?
hints: It was the tallest building in the world for more than 20 years.
It's more than a hundred.
It's a three-digit number that starts with 1.
questions.description: A leg workout you can do without leaving the couch.
questions.fun_fact: Fazlur Khan designed the tower as a bundle of nine tubes joined together, an idea that saved a huge amount of steel.

questions.question: From 300 m (984 ft), a skyscraper is called “supertall”. If it keeps growing past 600 m (1,969 ft), what is it called?
hints: Only a handful of buildings in the world have earned it.
The Burj Khalifa belongs in it.
Its prefix is the same one as in “megaphone”.
questions.description: When “tall” just isn't enough, engineers borrow prefixes from superheroes.
questions.fun_fact: The world has more than a hundred supertall skyscrapers, but you can count the megatall ones on your fingers.

questions.question: Benidorm, on the coast of Spain, boasts a world record for its skyscrapers. Which one?
hints: It's not about the height of a single building.
It's a small city with a huge number of towers.
You have to divide buildings by people.
questions.description: A fishing village that one day decided the beach could be stacked too.
questions.fun_fact: Benidorm is nicknamed “the New York of the Mediterranean” for its skyline packed with towers by the sea.

questions.question: You're in the middle of a skyscraper floor, inside its central concrete core. What is usually NOT found there?
hints: The core is like the building's backbone.
Everything that goes up and down passes through it.
The windows are on the outside walls, far from the center.
questions.description: The heart of a skyscraper: it doesn't beat, but without it everything falls down.
questions.fun_fact: In many skyscrapers, the concrete core is built first and rises several floors ahead of the rest of the building.

questions.question: You're watching “Dancing with the Stars” on TV. Who are the “stars” who dance?
questions.answer: Famous people from TV and sports
wrong_answers: Real stars from the night sky
hints: They don't come from space or from the sea.
You've probably seen them before on TV, in movies or at games.
Very famous people are also called “stars.”
questions.description: A show where nobody looks up at the sky, but everyone talks about stars.
questions.fun_fact: The show started in the United Kingdom in 2004 as “Strictly Come Dancing” and has been made in dozens of countries.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: a singer who “has the X factor,” like in the famous talent show, has…
questions.answer: A special talent that is hard to explain
wrong_answers: A very deep and very loud voice
Lots and lots of social media followers
A last name that starts with X
hints: In math, x stands for something we don't know yet.
It's what makes you unable to stop watching someone on stage.
The judges look for it, but nobody can quite describe it.
questions.description: A letter so mysterious that mathematicians have spent centuries looking for it.
questions.fun_fact: Simon Cowell created “The X Factor” in the United Kingdom in 2004, and Colombia had its own very popular version.

questions.question: In reality shows like “Survivor”, immunity is won in a challenge, lasts one round and is sometimes a necklace. What does it give you?
wrong_answers: A phone call to your family
hints: The word comes from when your body doesn't get sick.
It's what everyone wants to have before a vote.
With it, nobody can send you home that week.
questions.description: Every contestant's favorite vaccine: no needle, but it can save your life in the game.
questions.fun_fact: In “Survivor”, hidden “immunity idols” are tucked away around the island, and contestants search for them in secret.

questions.question: I was an unknown Scottish woman, the audience laughed when they saw me, and in 2009 I sang “I Dreamed a Dream” on a “Got Talent” show. Who am I?
hints: It was the British version of the show.
Millions of people watched the video of my audition online.
My first name starts with S.
questions.description: Proof that you should never judge a song by its cover.
questions.fun_fact: Susan Boyle’s audition got more than 100 million views online in just a few days.

questions.question: On your phone, the little blue bird was Twitter's, and the phone inside a green speech bubble belongs to…
hints: It's an app for sending messages.
Lots of families have a group there with all the aunts and uncles.
Its name sounds like a casual way to ask “How's it going?”.
questions.description: A green bubble that never stops buzzing.
questions.fun_fact: The name WhatsApp is a play on “What's up?”, a casual English way to say “How's it going?”.

questions.question: What does a YouTube channel have to do to get this silver plaque?
wrong_answers: Be on YouTube for one year
hints: You don't earn it with time or with the number of videos.
It has to do with people who press a red button under your videos.
The gold one is for a million; the silver one is for a number with five zeros.
questions.description: A trophy you don't win by running, but by talking to a camera.
questions.fun_fact: After gold comes the Diamond Play Button, given to channels that reach 10 million subscribers.

questions.question: Guess who: I was born in 1996, my name sounds like “I seek you,” and my logo is a green flower. What was I for?
hints: It was a computer program, not a phone app.
When something arrived, it made a famous “uh-oh” sound.
It's like a grandparent of WhatsApp and Messenger.
questions.description: From the days when the internet made strange noises just to connect.
questions.fun_fact: ICQ was created by a small Israeli company called Mirabilis, and AOL bought it in 1998.

questions.question: Facebook, the social network whose logo is a white “f” on a blue background, was founded in 2004. Who created it?
hints: He created it while he was a university student.
He was studying at Harvard University.
Today he runs Meta, which also owns Instagram and WhatsApp.
questions.description: A single lowercase letter that changed your aunts' lives forever.
questions.fun_fact: Facebook is blue because Zuckerberg has trouble telling red from green, and blue is the color he sees best.

questions.question: “Like” is to “dislike” as “follow” is to…
hints: You use it when you no longer want to see what an account posts.
It's built the same way as “dislike”: with a prefix in front.
It starts like “undo”.
questions.description: The quietest way to end a modern friendship.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, the New Oxford American Dictionary chose “unfriend” as its Word of the Year.

questions.question: Its name comes from the Latin for “edge.” In old Catholic tradition it lay at the edge of hell, and today being there means being stuck and undecided. What place is it?
hints: You won't find this place on a map.
People say plans are here when they're on hold and nobody has decided yet.
It has the same name as a dance where you bend backward to pass under a low bar.
questions.description: The perfect place to wait after your parents answer “We'll see.”
questions.fun_fact: The limbo dance from Trinidad and Tobago has nothing to do with it: dancers bend backward to pass under a bar that keeps getting lower.

questions.question: Complete this Spanish saying: “Bread for today, hunger for…”
hints: The saying warns about fixes that only last a little while.
The second half is about what comes after today.
It's the opposite of “yesterday.”
questions.description: A saying for anyone who eats the whole pack of cookies on Monday.
questions.fun_fact: Bread is one of the oldest foods: people in ancient Egypt were already baking it thousands of years ago.

questions.question: I'm a saying: “Sow the wind, reap the whirlwind.” What do I teach?
questions.answer: Causing trouble brings you worse trouble
wrong_answers: You should plant seeds on windy days
Storms help the harvest grow bigger
Hard work always brings a big harvest
hints: It isn't advice for farmers.
It's about what happens after you behave badly.
What you do comes back to you, only bigger.
questions.description: A farming saying that won't help you grow a single tomato.
questions.fun_fact: This saying comes from the Bible, from the book of the prophet Hosea.

questions.question: According to a popular saying, money “makes” something. What does it make?
hints: People often say it when talking about rich people or business.
It sounds like good news for anyone who already has savings.
The missing word is the same word the saying starts with.
questions.description: A saying that explains why your piggy bank never fills up on its own.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to bank interest, saved money sometimes really does “make” a little more money.

questions.question: What does the saying “A closed mouth catches no flies” advise?
questions.answer: Keep quiet to stay out of trouble
wrong_answers: Keep your mouth shut while eating
hints: It's not really about hygiene or bugs.
It's said to someone who talks too much.
Sometimes it's better to say nothing at all.
questions.description: Advice your grandma would have given you just before you spilled that bit of gossip.
questions.fun_fact: Flies can taste with their feet, because they have taste sensors on them.

questions.question: Complete the saying: “Money doesn't grow on…”
hints: The missing word is something from nature.
Leaves, fruit and flowers do grow there.
Birds build their nests in their branches.
questions.description: Parents' favorite line when you ask for the most expensive toy in the store.
questions.fun_fact: Many banknotes aren't made from wood-pulp paper but from cotton fibers.

questions.question: What is this piece of clothing, made by winding a long cloth around the head?
hints: It is worn on the head.
It is very common in India and the Middle East.
Aladdin and many characters from Arabian tales wear one.
questions.description: Several meters of cloth that never end up in the closet.
questions.fun_fact: A Sikh turban can take several meters of cloth, and it has to be wound again every day.

questions.question: What does it mean when a food is “kosher”?
wrong_answers: It was cooked without salt or sugar
hints: This label is printed on food packages in many supermarkets.
Under these rules, meat and milk can't be mixed.
It is the Jewish version of what Islam calls “halal”.
questions.description: A food label that matters even more than the expiration date.
questions.fun_fact: Under kosher rules, pork and shellfish such as shrimp are not allowed.

questions.question: The hermit crab is named after hermits. What is a hermit?
questions.answer: Someone who lives alone, away from others
wrong_answers: Someone who travels without ever stopping
Someone who fishes out at sea
Someone who builds houses for others
hints: Many did it so they could pray in peace.
They lived in caves, deserts or mountains.
The word comes from an old Greek word meaning “person of the desert.”
questions.description: A sea tenant who moves out every time the house gets too small.
questions.fun_fact: A hermit crab doesn't make its own shell: it uses empty snail shells and moves into a new one when the old one gets too small.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are the three ___ religions.
hints: The name comes from a figure that all three see as their great ancestor.
This figure left the city of Ur, in Mesopotamia.
His wife was called Sarah and his son was Isaac.
questions.description: Three religions with the same great-grandpa on the family tree.
questions.fun_fact: According to the Bible, God promised Abraham as many descendants as there are stars in the sky.

questions.question: I'm a spiritual teacher whose title comes from India. Today it's also used for experts in any field. What am I?
hints: My title comes from Sanskrit.
People talk about a money one, a fashion one, a tech one…
My word has two syllables and ends in “u”.
questions.description: The only teacher whose students keep following them, even with no final exam.
questions.fun_fact: In Sanskrit, “guru” means “heavy” or “weighty”: someone carrying a lot of knowledge.

questions.question: I'm a handwritten scroll, the holiest text of Judaism. Tradition says a prophet received me on Mount Sinai. Who?
hints: He led his people out of Egypt.
He also came down the mountain carrying stone tablets.
According to the Bible, he parted the Red Sea.
questions.description: A book where you don't turn the pages: you roll them.
questions.fun_fact: A scribe takes about a year to copy a Torah by hand, and one mistake in the name of God means the whole sheet must be redone.

questions.question: Lonesome George is to the Galápagos Islands as Jonathan, the giant tortoise born around 1832, is to…
hints: It is a small, remote island in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
It is a British territory.
Napoleon spent his last years there in exile.
questions.description: A grandpa who was already old when your great-grandparents were babies.
questions.fun_fact: Jonathan arrived on his island in 1882 and appears in a photo from that time, already a fully grown tortoise.

questions.question: Take a close look at this tail. Which snake does it belong to?
hints: Its rings are made of keratin, just like your fingernails.
When it feels in danger, it shakes it like a maraca.
Its name includes a noisy baby toy.
questions.description: A tail that comes with its own soundtrack.
questions.fun_fact: Every time the snake sheds its skin, a new segment is added to its rattle.

questions.question: These wide scales on a snake's belly: what are they mainly for?
questions.answer: Gripping the ground to move forward
hints: Snakes have no legs.
They work a bit like the tread on the soles of your shoes.
Without them, it would slip in place and get nowhere.
questions.description: An armored belly that works harder than any tire.
questions.fun_fact: Reptile scales are made of keratin, the same material as your nails and hair.

questions.question: This alligator snapping turtle fishes with a pink “worm” on its tongue. Where does it live in the wild?
hints: It lives in freshwater rivers and swamps.
It shares its swamps with alligators and herons.
Its home is in the rivers that flow into the Gulf of Mexico.
questions.description: A turtle that never goes anywhere without its fishing gear, packed right in its mouth.
questions.fun_fact: It is one of the heaviest freshwater turtles in the world: some males weigh over 80 kg (176 lb).

questions.question: It was about 11 m (36 ft) long, one of the biggest crocodiles ever, and was nicknamed “SuperCroc.” Where were its most famous fossils found?
hints: 110 million years ago, this place was full of rivers.
Today it hardly ever rains there.
Paleontologist Paul Sereno dug it up in Niger, on a big expedition in 1997.
questions.description: The crocodile family's distant uncle, in bus size.
questions.fun_fact: Sarcosuchus had a strange bump on the tip of its snout, and scientists still argue about what it was for.

questions.question: Guess who: “I'm Pascal, a chameleon who lives in a tower with my best friend.” Who is she?
hints: She is a Disney princess.
She has never left her tower.
She has very, very long magic hair.
questions.description: A green buddy who can turn any color he likes, except boring.
questions.fun_fact: Pascal never says a single word in the whole film: he tells everything with gestures and color changes.

questions.question: Eyes are to light as the pits on a pit viper's face are to…
hints: The pits are two little holes between the eye and the nostril.
They help it hunt mice in complete darkness.
They work like an infrared camera.
questions.description: Night-vision goggles that come built into the face.
questions.fun_fact: Snakes with these pits can sense the warmth of their prey even in total darkness.

questions.question: I sound like a cowboy's name, but I go up and down every day. I'm the Dow Jones. What am I?
hints: The business news talks about me every day.
I follow the share prices of 30 big companies in the United States.
I'm used to measure how the stock market is doing.
questions.description: A name that goes up and down more than your mood on a Monday morning.
questions.fun_fact: The Dow Jones was first calculated in 1896, and at the start it included only 12 companies.

questions.question: Many investors split their money among stocks, bonds, property and gold instead of putting it all in one thing. Why?
hints: They think about what would happen if one investment goes wrong.
A saying tells you not to put all your eggs in one basket.
If one thing loses value, the others can make up for the loss.
questions.description: Let’s talk about money, that guest who always leaves before the month is over.
questions.fun_fact: This strategy is called diversification, and economist Harry Markowitz won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1990 partly for studying it.

questions.question: Listen: birds like this one forced Captain Sully to land his plane on the Hudson River in 2009. Which bird is it?
hints: They were flying in a flock and hit both engines.
The story became a movie starring Tom Hanks.
It's a big bird, related to the duck, that often migrates in a V shape.
questions.description: Passengers with no ticket who climbed into the wrong part of the plane.
questions.fun_fact: Only about 208 seconds passed between the bird strike and the landing on the Hudson.

questions.question: If a plane has an emergency on the runway, what is the longest the airport firefighters may take to get there?
hints: An international aviation rule sets this limit.
That's why the fire station sits right next to the runways.
It's less time than it takes a pot of water to boil.
questions.description: Firefighters who can't even wait for their coffee to cool down.
questions.fun_fact: Airport fire trucks can spray foam while racing along at full speed.

questions.question: Its bark gives tonic water its bitter taste, and it grows in the forests of the Andes. Which tree is it?
hints: Quinine is taken from its bark.
For centuries it was used against malaria.
It is also called the “quina tree”, and it appears on Peru's coat of arms.
questions.description: A drink so bitter it tastes less like a soda and more like grandma's home remedy.
questions.fun_fact: The quinine in tonic water glows blue under ultraviolet light.

questions.question: Which of these coffees was NOT born in Italy?
hints: Three of them are made with an espresso machine.
The odd one out is served cold, with lots of foam.
It was invented in Greece in 1957 by shaking instant coffee with cold water.
questions.description: An international coffee shop where one of the customers doesn't speak Italian.
questions.fun_fact: The frappé was born at a trade fair in Thessaloniki in 1957, when a Nescafé employee shook instant coffee with cold water in a cocktail shaker.

questions.question: Runner Marion Jones admitted to doping at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. How many medals did she have to give back?
hints: She was the big star of those Games.
It was more than most athletes win at a single Olympics.
More than half of them were gold.
questions.description: Reaching the finish line first is easy when you cheat along the way.
questions.fun_fact: Marion Jones ended up spending six months in prison for lying to investigators about her doping.

questions.question: In 2009, a scandal broke out because members of parliament billed taxpayers for things like a duck house and cleaning a moat. In which country?
hints: This country has a very old parliament.
Its currency is neither the euro nor the dollar.
Big Ben stands in its capital.
questions.description: Some lawmakers sent the public the bill for everything, even the ducks.
questions.fun_fact: The famous floating duck house cost about £1,645 and became the symbol of the whole scandal.

questions.question: The Salem witch trials of 1692 began when some people said they had been bewitched. Who were they?
hints: It all happened in a Puritan village during the cold winter of 1692.
It started with strange fits: screaming, shaking and twisting.
One of them was the minister's daughter, only 9 years old.
questions.description: In 1692, gossip in this village flew faster than any broomstick.
questions.fun_fact: Today Salem makes the most of its fame: every October, thousands of tourists dressed as witches come to visit.

questions.question: I'm a sign that glows red thanks to a gas, and I light up shops at night. Which inventor showed me off in Paris in 1910?
hints: He was a chemist and engineer, not a light bulb maker.
He was born in the same country where he gave the demonstration.
His first name is the French form of George.
questions.description: Before screens took over, this was the brightest thing on the street at night.
questions.fun_fact: The first neon advertising sign is said to have been sold in 1912 to a barbershop in Paris.

questions.question: I'm a German sportswear brand and my slogan is “Impossible is Nothing.” Who founded me?
hints: My founder made shoes in a small town in Bavaria.
His brother founded my big rival, the brand with the big cat.
My name joins my founder's nickname and the start of his last name.
questions.description: A sentence your math teacher would never accept as an answer.
questions.fun_fact: The Dassler brothers fell out and started two rival brands in the same German town, Herzogenaurach.

questions.question: Its can is blue, and in the 1980s its slogan was “The Choice of a New Generation.” Which drink is it?
hints: It's a cola drink.
Its logo is a red, white and blue circle.
Its name starts with P.
questions.description: A question for anyone who always orders “whatever cola you have.”
questions.fun_fact: In 1984, Michael Jackson starred in the “New Generation” ads.

questions.question: It is made from pieces of broken tile or pottery, set like a mosaic, and Gaudí used it a lot. What is this technique called?
hints: It is more a way of recycling than of making new pieces.
It is used to cover benches, walls and curved shapes in many colors.
In Catalan, the word comes from “trencar”, which means “to break”.
questions.description: Finally, someone found a use for the plate Grandma dropped.
questions.fun_fact: For his trencadís, Gaudí even used tiles that factories had thrown away, along with broken dishes.

questions.question: The Alhambra in Granada is full of muqarnas. What are they?
wrong_answers: Wooden lattice screens covering the windows
Geometric tiles along the lower part of walls
Water channels running across the courtyards
hints: They are made of many small pieces fitted together.
They decorate domes, vaults and arches.
They look like the formations that hang from a cave ceiling.
questions.description: At the Alhambra, even the decoration looks like it was made by bees who studied geometry.
questions.fun_fact: The dome of the Hall of the Two Sisters in the Alhambra is made of thousands of muqarnas pieces.

questions.question: The stadium of the Beijing 2008 Olympics is wrapped in crisscrossing steel beams. What nickname did it get?
hints: The nickname comes from something in nature.
What it looks like is made of crisscrossed twigs.
It's where baby chicks live before they can fly.
questions.description: A stadium with a much cuter nickname than its tons of steel deserve.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first stadium to host the ceremonies of both a Summer and a Winter Olympics (2008 and 2022).

questions.question: At Eurovision 2012, Russia came second with a group that baked bread right on stage. Who were they?
hints: They wore headscarves and traditional costumes.
They came from a small village in Udmurtia, a republic of Russia.
They were older ladies, many of them with grandchildren.
questions.description: While other acts brought fireworks, this group brought the oven.
questions.fun_fact: The Buranovskiye Babushki wanted to raise money to rebuild their village church.

questions.question: You're in front of the TV, watching Eurovision in color for the first time, live from London. What year is it?
hints: It was in the 1960s.
It was broadcast from the Royal Albert Hall.
It was one year before humans first landed on the Moon.
questions.description: The day Eurovision outfits finally stopped being gray.
questions.fun_fact: In 1968 several countries broadcast the contest in color, but almost nobody at home had a color TV yet.

questions.question: In 1947, someone threw a stone into a cave near the Dead Sea and found the famous scrolls. Who was it?
hints: He wasn't looking for treasure: he was looking for a lost animal.
He was a young man from a nomadic desert people.
The lost animal was a goat.
questions.description: A badly aimed throw that landed in the history books.
questions.fun_fact: The Dead Sea Scrolls are more than 2,000 years old and survived thanks to the dry desert air.

questions.question: Of the three ships on Columbus's first voyage, how many were caravels?
hints: A caravel was a light, fast ship of that time.
The popular phrase “the three caravels” isn't quite accurate.
The Santa María was a larger “nao”, a different kind of ship from the other two.
questions.description: Three ships left Palos in 1492, and not one of them had GPS.
questions.fun_fact: It was from the Pinta that the sailor Rodrigo de Triana shouted “Land!” in 1492.

questions.question: I'm a little talking flame. I live in the fireplace and I make the wizard Howl's castle walk. What's my name?
hints: I'm a fire demon.
I love eating logs and eggshells.
My name starts with “Cal”.
questions.description: The chattiest fireplace in movie history.
questions.fun_fact: Calcifer comes from a novel by British author Diana Wynne Jones, which Miyazaki turned into a movie.

questions.question: How old was Christopher Paolini when he started writing “Eragon”?
hints: It was very early to write such a long book.
He had already finished high school, studying at home.
He was a teenager, younger than many of his readers.
questions.description: A dragon saga born in a house in Montana, among books and mountains.
questions.fun_fact: Paolini's parents published the first edition of “Eragon” through their own small publishing company.

questions.question: Tolkien is to Middle-earth as George R. R. Martin is to…
hints: It's a continent with seven kingdoms.
People there fight over the Iron Throne.
It's the setting of “Game of Thrones.”
questions.description: Books so thick they double as gym weights.
questions.fun_fact: George R. R. Martin drew on England's Wars of the Roses for his story.

questions.question: In hieroglyphs, what was written inside a “cartouche”, the oval with a line at its base?
hints: It stands for a knotted rope wrapped around something very important.
Champollion compared the ones on the Rosetta Stone with those on an obelisk from Philae to read his first signs.
It shows who the king is.
questions.description: An oval so important that the Egyptians gave it its own safety rope.
questions.fun_fact: It's called a “cartouche” because Napoleon's soldiers thought it looked like the paper gunpowder cartridges for their rifles, which are “cartouches” in French.

questions.question: This is Hathor, the Egyptian goddess of love and music. Which animal's horns does she wear on her head?
hints: It's a farm animal.
Sometimes she was painted entirely as this animal.
Most of the milk people drink comes from this animal.
questions.description: A goddess wearing a hat you won't find in any fashion store.
questions.fun_fact: The Egyptians believed Hathor, as a heavenly cow, fed the pharaoh with her milk.

questions.question: You're at the Temple of Edfu, one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt. Which god was it built for?
hints: It was built by the Ptolemies, Cleopatra's family.
He is the son of Isis and Osiris.
He has the head of a falcon.
questions.description: A temple so well preserved that its god could still collect the rent.
questions.fun_fact: Its walls tell the story of this god's battle against his uncle Seth, like a comic book carved in stone.

questions.question: “White rhino” is to “grass” as “black rhino” is to…
hints: Both rhinos eat only plants.
The black rhino has a pointed upper lip that grabs like a finger.
It feeds from bushes, not from the ground.
questions.description: Two rhinos named after colors, and neither one is that color.
questions.fun_fact: Neither rhino is white or black: both are gray, and you tell them apart by the shape of their lips.

questions.question: The galago got its English nickname because its calls at night sound like the crying of…
hints: It's a high, whiny sound.
Lots of parents get woken up at night by a sound like it.
Its nickname starts with “bush”, followed by this little crier.
questions.description: A primate with giant eyes that works the night shift.
questions.fun_fact: A galago can leap several meters between branches, as if it had springs in its legs.

questions.question: In which century did Pico della Mirandola write his famous “Oration on the Dignity of Man”?
hints: He was a friend of the Medici in Florence.
He was a young Italian count who read Hebrew, Arabic and Greek.
He died two years after Columbus reached America.
questions.description: A young man who, at 23, already wanted to debate everyone… on 900 topics at once.
questions.fun_fact: Pico della Mirandola offered to debate 900 theses in public at once, but the pope banned the debate.

questions.question: Philosophers talk about the famous “Buridan's ass”. What happened to this donkey?
questions.answer: It couldn't choose between two equal piles of hay
wrong_answers: Its load of salt dissolved in a river
It disguised itself in a lion's skin
It spoke to its owner on the road
hints: The name comes from a 14th-century French philosopher.
It is used to debate whether the will is truly free.
It was hungry, with plenty of food on both sides.
questions.description: A donkey famous at medieval universities, and not for its grades.
questions.fun_fact: The donkey example doesn't appear in any of Buridan's surviving writings: his critics probably made it up to mock his ideas.

questions.question: Inventors tried to build one for centuries, and patent offices usually reject it. What is a “perpetual motion machine”?
questions.answer: A device that would keep moving with no energy supply
wrong_answers: A clock that sets itself by radio signal
A magnet that never loses its strength
A vehicle that runs only on sunlight
hints: “Perpetual” means it never ends.
It would break the law of conservation of energy.
It would run nonstop without anyone ever giving it fuel.
questions.description: Inventors chased it for centuries, with about as much luck as you have finding the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: The US Patent and Trademark Office can ask anyone who tries to patent a perpetual motion machine to send in a working model.

questions.question: Absolute zero is the lowest temperature possible. About how many degrees Celsius is it?
hints: It is far colder than any winter on Earth.
It is 0 on the Kelvin scale.
It is between −200 and −300 degrees.
questions.description: So cold that even the atoms can't be bothered to move.
questions.fun_fact: In labs, scientists have cooled atoms to within a billionth of a degree of absolute zero, but no one has ever reached it exactly.

questions.question: “Circle” is to a coin as “annulus” is to…
hints: It's the region between two circles that share the same center.
A CD has this shape too.
It's a flat metal piece with a hole that goes under a nut.
questions.description: A math word so fancy it should come with a top hat and a monocle.
questions.fun_fact: To find the area of an annulus, you subtract the area of the small circle from the area of the big one.

questions.question: My name is “Klein bottle,” and a German mathematician described me in 1882. What am I really?
questions.answer: A surface with only one side
wrong_answers: A curve that fills a plane
A shape with a fractional dimension
hints: I'm related to the Möbius strip.
You make me by joining the ends of a tube in a very special way.
I have no inside and no outside.
questions.description: A bottle that can't hold a single drop, and not because it's already full.
questions.fun_fact: A true Klein bottle can only exist in four dimensions; the glass ones you can buy pass through themselves.

questions.question: At the Indianapolis 500, the winner doesn't celebrate with champagne. What do they drink instead?
hints: It's a tradition almost a hundred years old.
It's a drink full of calcium.
It's served in a bottle, and it comes from a cow.
questions.description: When you win the most famous race in the United States, you quench your thirst in style.
questions.fun_fact: Louis Meyer started the custom by drinking buttermilk after winning in 1933, and by 1936 it had become a tradition.

questions.question: After becoming F1 world champion, Austrian driver Niki Lauda started his own company. What kind of company was it?
hints: His company had nothing to do with racing.
The company carried his own last name, and he liked to take part in person.
He held a license to fly passenger planes himself.
questions.description: A champion who never learned to sit still, not even after he retired.
questions.fun_fact: Lauda won the F1 title three times and sometimes flew the planes of his own airline, Lauda Air, himself.

questions.question: In F1, which green-striped tires are used when the track is wet but not flooded?
hints: In F1, they are made by Pirelli.
The tires for heavy rain have a blue stripe.
Their name says they sit between the dry tires and the rain tires.
questions.description: For those days when the sky can't make up its mind about raining.
questions.fun_fact: Dry-weather slick tires have no grooves, so in the rain they can't clear the water and the car slides.

questions.question: At the 24 Hours of Le Mans, how many drivers usually share each car in the top class?
hints: They take turns to sleep and rest.
One driver alone could never last a whole day.
As many as the musketeers in the famous novel.
questions.description: A whole day of driving, and there isn't even a lunch break.
questions.fun_fact: At Le Mans, the winning cars usually cover between 4,500 and 5,500 km (2,800 to 3,400 miles) in a single day.

questions.question: I'm a small pastel-colored camera, and at parties everyone lines up for a photo. What's special about me?
hints: My photos don't stay on a screen.
After you take a shot, something comes out of a slot.
The photo comes out on paper in a few seconds, like a Polaroid.
questions.description: The favorite camera at birthday parties, right after your aunt's phone.
questions.fun_fact: An Instax photo comes out almost white, and the picture slowly appears over one or two minutes.

questions.question: What is it called when a photo can be split into two matching halves, like in a mirror?
hints: Butterflies have it on their wings.
A calm lake reflecting a mountain creates it.
The word starts with “sym”.
questions.description: What you hope to see when you fold a paper with wet paint and open it again.
questions.fun_fact: Many studies have found that people tend to find more symmetrical faces more attractive.

questions.question: In photography, what is special about a “fisheye” lens?
questions.answer: It sees a huge, curved view
hints: It is a type of wide-angle lens.
Straight lines look bent, like in a bubble.
It can take in about 180 degrees.
questions.description: A lens named after an aquarium resident, and not a single scale on it.
questions.fun_fact: Skateboarding videos from the 1990s made the fisheye lens famous, because it made the jumps look bigger.

questions.question: Eadweard Muybridge took this series of photos in 1878. What did he want to find out?
questions.answer: If a horse lifts all four legs off the ground at once
wrong_answers: How fast a racehorse can really run
How many steps a horse takes each second
If a horse always lands on the same leg first
hints: Look closely at the legs in each frame.
The human eye couldn't catch it at full gallop.
In one of the frames, the horse seems to fly.
questions.description: The first time anyone checked the video replay on a horse.
questions.fun_fact: Muybridge used a row of cameras that fired one after another, and his photos are ancestors of the movies.

questions.question: I wrote a play in which a character says: “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.” Who am I?
hints: I'm English, but that play takes place in a Danish castle.
That play is about a prince who wants to avenge his father.
I also wrote “Romeo and Juliet.”
questions.description: A strange smell in the castle, and it's not a snack someone forgot in their backpack.
questions.fun_fact: Hamlet's castle really exists: it's Kronborg Castle, in Denmark.

questions.question: When the Gallic chief Brennus took Rome, he shouted “Vae victis!” (“Woe to the conquered!”). When did this happen?
hints: Rome did not yet rule even all of Italy.
It was long before the time of Julius Caesar.
It happened around 390 BC.
questions.description: The oldest rule in the game: the loser pays, and has to listen to the winner gloat too.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that when the Romans complained the weights were rigged, Brennus threw his sword onto the scales as well.

questions.question: Switzerland has built nuclear shelters since the Cold War. What share of its people can they hold today?
hints: A law required shelters in many new buildings.
There are shelters in the basements of homes, schools and hospitals.
If every Swiss person went down at once, there would be places left over.
questions.description: A country famous for its watches and chocolate, but it also hides a few surprises underground.
questions.fun_fact: Many Swiss shelters are now used as storage cellars, rehearsal rooms for bands, or even hotels.

questions.question: My notes on every story, written before I died, are printed in “The Tales of Beedle the Bard”. Who am I?
hints: I was a Gryffindor student and later taught Transfiguration.
In my will, I left this book to a Gryffindor student.
I have a long white beard and I love lemon drops.
questions.description: Bedtime stories that come with notes from a very, very wise reader.
questions.fun_fact: J.K. Rowling handwrote seven copies of the book, and one sold at auction for almost 2 million pounds for charity.

questions.question: In Quidditch, how many hoops does each team's Keeper defend?
hints: They are tall hoops on poles at each end of the field.
There is only one Keeper, but more than one hoop to guard.
It's the same number as the Chasers on each team.
questions.description: Quidditch's goalkeeper: no gloves, but a broom.
questions.fun_fact: Each goal with the Quaffle is worth 10 points, but catching the Golden Snitch gives 150 and ends the match.

questions.question: Which character from the next generation is the main character of “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child”?
hints: He is Harry and Ginny's middle child.
His best friend is Scorpius, Draco Malfoy's son.
He is named after two Hogwarts headmasters.
questions.description: Nineteen years later, the Boy Who Lived has become the Dad Who Worries.
questions.fun_fact: “The Cursed Child” is a stage play that opened in London in 2016.

questions.question: Nearly Headless Nick throws a “Deathday Party” on Halloween. How many years has he been a ghost?
hints: It happens in “Chamber of Secrets.”
It's more years than Dumbledore's age, but fewer than Hogwarts's.
Nick died on October 31, 1492, the same year Columbus reached America.
questions.description: A party where nobody eats the cake, because it's rotten on purpose.
questions.fun_fact: The party had an orchestra playing musical saws and rotten food, so the ghosts could at least smell it.

questions.question: I'm the most famous music award. I'm golden, and my name comes from the device I'm shaped like. What shape am I?
hints: That device is very old: your great-great-grandparents used it.
It played records and had a big horn shaped like a flower.
My name, “Grammy”, is almost the start of that device's name.
questions.description: A golden trophy that many artists dream of putting on their shelf.
questions.fun_fact: Grammy trophies are made by hand, one by one, in a workshop in a small town in Colorado.

questions.question: I grew up in Brooklyn, sang “Empire State of Mind” and was the first billionaire rapper, according to Forbes. Who am I?
hints: Besides rapping, I run businesses in clothing, drinks and sports.
When no record label wanted me, I started my own with some partners: Roc-A-Fella.
I'm married to Beyoncé.
questions.description: A rapper with more businesses than songs, and he has a lot of songs.
questions.fun_fact: Jay-Z's real name is Shawn Carter.

questions.question: Coco Chanel made it popular in 1926, and Audrey Hepburn made it timeless. What was the little black dress meant for?
questions.answer: To look elegant on almost any occasion
wrong_answers: To mourn the death of a relative
To dress ballet dancers on stage
To keep warm in the winter cold
hints: Chanel wanted something simple, practical and easy to match.
Vogue compared it to the Ford Model T, a car that everyone could own.
It works for daytime, evening, a dinner or a party.
questions.description: A piece of clothing so famous that in English it even has its own initials: LBD.
questions.fun_fact: Before Chanel, black was mostly linked to mourning; she turned it into the most elegant color of all.

questions.question: I'm a soft leather shoe with no heel that wraps around the foot like a glove. I'm called a moccasin. Who invented me?
questions.answer: The Indigenous peoples of North America
hints: My makers walked through forests and prairies to hunt.
My name comes from an Algonquian language.
I come from the native peoples of what is now the United States and Canada.
questions.description: The perfect shoe for anyone who hates tying their laces.
questions.fun_fact: Many traditional moccasins were decorated with dyed porcupine quills and, later, with glass beads.

questions.question: “Poulaines” (meaning “Polish-style”) were shoes with toes so long they were sometimes tied to the leg. When were they all the rage?
hints: It was long before there were any shoe factories.
It was the time of the Black Death and the Hundred Years' War.
It was the late Middle Ages, before Columbus reached America.
questions.description: Shoes for people who always wanted to arrive first, at least with their toes.
questions.fun_fact: In England, laws limited how long the toe could be, depending on the wearer's social class.

questions.question: I'm a flower, and in the 17th century one of my bulbs was worth more than a house. Who went crazy for me?
hints: It's seen as one of the first speculative bubbles in history.
That country has won a lot of land back from the sea.
Today that country still exports millions of these flowers from Amsterdam.
questions.description: An investment so pretty you could put it in a vase.
questions.fun_fact: In 1637, tulip bulb prices suddenly crashed, and many buyers were left with flowers that were worth almost nothing.

questions.question: In colonial Spanish America, what was a “macuquina”?
hints: It was a very common part of daily life in the colonies.
It had an irregular shape and was almost never perfectly round.
It was cut from a metal bar and then struck with a stamp.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a tongue twister, but in colonial times everyone knew it.
questions.fun_fact: Because macuquinas, known in English as “cobs”, were irregular, some cheats clipped little bits of silver off the edges to keep the metal.

questions.question: For centuries they were used as money in Africa and Asia; they were small, shiny and hard to fake. What were they?
hints: They came from islands in the Indian Ocean.
People collected them from the water around the Maldives.
They were left behind by an animal that carries its house on its back.
questions.description: A wallet full of this money sounded like a maraca.
questions.fun_fact: In ancient Chinese, the character linked to money and wealth is shaped like one of these shells.

questions.question: Its name means “handful,” it already existed in ancient times, and in 2002 it was replaced by the euro. Which country used the drachma?
hints: It is a country on the Mediterranean Sea.
Its capital is one of the oldest cities in Europe.
The Olympic Games were born there.
questions.description: A coin so old it has been changing hands for thousands of years.
questions.fun_fact: The Greek 1-euro coin still shows the owl that appeared on the ancient drachmas of Athens.

questions.question: Where did Joseph's brothers throw him after taking away his coat of many colors?
hints: It's a deep hole in the ground.
People usually pull water out of it with a bucket.
It rhymes with “bell”.
questions.description: Being the favorite brother has its perks… until it doesn't.
questions.fun_fact: Later his brothers sold Joseph to traders who took him to Egypt, where he became the most powerful man after Pharaoh.

questions.question: If someone is called “a real Samson,” like the hero from the Bible, what do they have plenty of?
hints: It helps you carry all the grocery bags in without help.
The Samson of the Bible beat a lion with his bare hands.
It's what you train at the gym.
questions.description: A compliment that comes with a hairstyle attached.
questions.fun_fact: According to the story, Samson's secret was never cutting his hair; when Delilah had it cut, he lost his power.

questions.question: Joseph explained Pharaoh's dream: years of plenty would come, then years of hunger. How many years of hunger?
hints: In the dream there were fat cows and skinny cows, the same number of each.
It's the same number as the years of plenty.
It's the number of days in a week.
questions.description: The first harvest forecast in history came with skinny cows.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to that dream, Joseph stored up grain during the good years, and Egypt could even feed other peoples.

questions.question: I'm named after the first emperor of Rome. Which month am I?
hints: I'm a month with 31 days.
In many countries in the Northern Hemisphere, I'm a summer vacation month.
The emperor was Julius Caesar's adopted heir, and I'm the eighth month of the year.
questions.description: An emperor so important he still shows up on every calendar in the world.
questions.fun_fact: Before it was called August, the month was named “Sextilis,” because it was the sixth month of the old Roman calendar.

questions.question: What shape is a round arch, the typical arch of the Romans?
hints: Look closely at the name.
It's the shape of a rainbow.
Put two of them together and you get a whole wheel.
questions.description: The Romans put it everywhere, the way Grandma puts salt on everything.
questions.fun_fact: Round arches let the Romans build bridges and aqueducts that are still standing after 2,000 years.
