questions.question: You climb too fast to a place like this and get a headache, dizziness and shortness of breath. What is this illness called?
hints: It happens because the air up high has less oxygen.
In the Andes people also call it soroche.
You avoid it by climbing slowly and drinking lots of water.
questions.description: Going up fast is fine in an elevator, not in the Andes.
questions.fun_fact: The entrance to Nevado del Ruiz is above 4,000 m (13,100 ft), higher than any city in Colombia.

questions.question: How many medals did Colombia win at the Athens 2004 Olympics?
hints: None of them was gold.
One was won by weightlifter Mabel Mosquera.
The other went to track cyclist María Luisa Calle.
questions.description: The Greeks invented the Games, and in 2004 they welcomed them back home.
questions.fun_fact: Both of Colombia's medals at Athens 2004 were bronze, and both were won by women.

questions.question: In 2020, Mauricio Ortega from Antioquia threw over 70 m (230 ft) and broke the South American record. In which event?
hints: It's a track and field event that was already part of the ancient Greek Olympic Games.
The athlete spins inside a circle protected by a cage.
The object is flat, round and weighs 2 kg (4.4 lb), like a heavy plate.
questions.description: A man from Antioquia who made a living throwing things far away… and people cheer him for it.
questions.fun_fact: The men's discus weighs 2 kg (4.4 lb), while the women's weighs just 1 kg (2.2 lb).

questions.question: Surfers travel to Nuquí, in Chocó, for the Pacific waves. Which of these surf spots is NOT on the Pacific coast?
hints: Three of them face the same ocean as Nuquí.
The odd one out is near the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
It is in La Guajira, beside the Caribbean Sea.
questions.description: Pack your board, your sunscreen and a map, because if you pick the wrong sea, you get no waves.
questions.fun_fact: Between July and October, humpback whales come to the waters off Nuquí to have their calves.

questions.question: Which of these Colombian athletes is NOT a golfer?
hints: Three of them have played in the big golf tournaments in the United States.
The odd one out was born in Cúcuta.
He was the top scorer of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil with Colombia's national team.
questions.description: Someone showed up at the golf club in the wrong uniform, and nobody dared to tell him.
questions.fun_fact: Camilo Villegas is nicknamed “Spider-Man” because he crouches almost flat on the ground to read the green, like the superhero.

questions.question: This tennis player was born in Cúcuta, won the junior US Open in 2019 and won the WTA tournament in Bogotá in 2021. Who is she?
hints: She is one of Colombia's highest-ranked tennis players in recent years.
She was born in 2001, so she is the youngest of the four options.
Her first name starts with C and her last name with O.
questions.description: From the heat of the border to clay courts around the world, racket in hand.
questions.fun_fact: The Bogotá tournament is played on clay at about 2,600 m (8,500 ft) above sea level, where the ball flies faster.

questions.question: Out in the countryside, you brush against a pringamosa, the nettle of Colombian farms, and your skin burns. What causes the burning?
hints: You see them better with a magnifying glass.
They cover the leaves and stems, and they're super thin.
They're like tiny needles that snap when you touch them and release substances into your skin.
questions.description: A plant that doesn't need fingernails to keep you scratching all afternoon.
questions.fun_fact: The tips of nettle hairs are made of silica, almost like glass, and break like tiny needles when you brush against them.

questions.question: On the flower farms of the Sabana de Bogotá, this flower is called “pompón.” Look at the close-up: which flower is it?
hints: It comes from Asia.
It's the symbol of the emperor of Japan.
Its name means “golden flower” in Greek.
questions.description: A flower so round it looks like it got its hair done for export.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the world's biggest exporters of chrysanthemums, and almost all of them come from the Sabana de Bogotá and Antioquia.

questions.question: Every February, Colombia ships flowers abroad for Valentine's Day. About how many stems does it send?
hints: Full cargo planes take off for weeks.
It's far more than the number of people living in Colombia.
It's hundreds of millions.
questions.description: Cupid works abroad, but his arrows come with Colombian flowers.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the big day for sweethearts isn't in February: it's Día del Amor y la Amistad, in September.

previous.feedback: Source: the 600 million figure is out of date. Recent seasons were about 700 million stems in 2024 and more than 900 million in 2025, nearing 1 billion, so the answer should become about 900 million or 1 billion, with wrong answers rebuilt around it. The English translation itself is faithful and natural ("6 billion" is the correct US rendering of 6000 millones), so it only needs updating once the source changes. Fact check: wrong. The 600 million figure is outdated. A 2023-era Portafolio piece cited a 600 million stem target. Reports for 2024 cite about 700 million stems, and Forbes and Portafolio coverage of 2025 cites more than 900 million (over 60,000 tonnes). La República's 2026 projection converts to about 980 million.

questions.question: Look at this white puff from a plant grown in Córdoba and Tolima. What is it?
hints: It's used to make T-shirts and socks.
It's white, soft and fluffy.
It's also made into little balls for cleaning cuts.
questions.description: A cloud that turns into a T-shirt instead of rain.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1970s, cotton was called “white gold” in Córdoba and Cesar because of all the money it brought in.

questions.question: Which of these will you NOT find at the Medellín Botanical Garden?
hints: Three of them have to do with plants and animals.
The odd one out is full of pieces made by Indigenous peoples.
That one is in Bogotá.
questions.description: A paisa stroll where the flowers play host.
questions.fun_fact: The Medellín Botanical Garden is named after Joaquín Antonio Uribe, a naturalist from Antioquia, and it's free to get in.

questions.question: In Medellín, whole bars and festivals are devoted to this dance. Which dance is in the photo?
hints: It reached Medellín on records from the south of the continent.
It is danced in a close embrace, with long, unhurried steps.
Its most famous singer, Carlos Gardel, is an idol in Medellín.
questions.description: For this question, knowing isn't enough: you also need rhythm in your feet.
questions.fun_fact: Every year, Medellín holds an international tango festival that draws dancers from many countries.

questions.question: In which town in Caldas is the Festival Nacional del Pasillo Colombiano held every year?
hints: It's in northern Caldas.
Its town center has steep streets with colonial architecture.
It's famous for hats handwoven from iraca palm.
questions.description: A town where even the steep streets move in 3/4 time.
questions.fun_fact: Aguadas is also the home of the aguadeño hat, handwoven from iraca palm fiber.

questions.question: In Barranquilla and Cartagena you hear it all the time: “¿Qué más, vale?”, “¡Ajá, vale!” What does “vale” mean there?
hints: It has nothing to do with saying “OK.”
You say it to someone you go everywhere with.
It comes from “valedor,” the one who keeps you company and stands up for you.
questions.description: In Spain it's how you say “OK”; on the Coast it's a different story.
questions.fun_fact: “Vale” comes from “valedor,” an old word for a person who protects and supports you.

questions.question: You're crossing the Sabana de Bogotá and you pass Chía, Zipaquirá and Facatativá. Which Indigenous people gave them those names?
hints: They lived on the high plateau of Cundinamarca and Boyacá.
Their language belonged to the Chibchan family.
They worshipped Bachué, the mother of humanity, and Sué, the Sun.
questions.description: Long before the traffic jams, the sabana already had names of its own.
questions.fun_fact: Chía was the Muisca goddess of the Moon, and the town of Chía is named after her.

questions.question: On the street you hear “vos sabés que sí, ¿cierto?”. Which of these groups does NOT usually speak with “vos”?
hints: The other three say “sabés” and “querés” all day long.
The group that doesn't use it prefers “usted” or “tú”.
They live in the country's capital.
questions.description: A verb form that divides the country almost as much as soccer does.
questions.fun_fact: Paisas mix “vos” with “pues” so often that it's almost their signature: “¿Y vos qué, pues?”.

questions.question: In the department highlighted on this map, people say “usted” (the formal “you”) even to their kids and partners, in a strong, direct tone. Which one is it?
hints: It is famous for its hormigas culonas (big-bottomed ants).
The Chicamocha Canyon is there.
Its capital is Bucaramanga, the “Ciudad Bonita.”
questions.description: A department where even “good morning” sounds like it means business.
questions.fun_fact: “Usted” comes so naturally to people from Santander that many even use it with their pets.

questions.question: I'm a custom from Colombia's Pacific coast: when a baby's umbilical cord falls off, I add powder from an animal, plant or mineral to pass on its strengths. What am I?
hints: It's done in the baby's first weeks of life.
The idea is that the child inherits the strength, cleverness or skill of what's applied.
My name comes from the Spanish word for the body part where the cord was.
questions.description: On the Pacific coast, babies get superpowers straight from the factory.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, what's used in the ombligada shapes the child's character: some families do it so the child becomes a good swimmer or a hard worker.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which Indigenous people of Colombia's Pacific coast coated their blowgun darts with this frog's poison?
hints: They live in the rainforest, not in the desert or the mountains.
Many of their communities live along the rivers of Chocó.
Their name starts with “E.”
questions.description: Tiny, shiny and more dangerous than a scalding-hot tinto in your hand.
questions.fun_fact: Just rubbing a dart's tip on the frog's back was enough to load it with poison.

questions.question: It's Colombia's rainiest region, its jungles lie next to an ocean, and humpback whales visit its beaches. Which region is it?
hints: It's not the region of the mountains.
Buenaventura and Tumaco are there.
It shares its name with the ocean on its shore.
questions.description: Here an umbrella isn't an accessory, it's part of your body.
questions.fun_fact: Lloró, in Chocó, is among the rainiest places on the planet.

questions.question: In a parade of traditional dress, the ruana is to the Andean region as… which item is to the Caribbean region?
hints: It goes on your head.
It is woven from caña flecha and has black and white stripes.
It is a symbol of Córdoba and of all Colombia.
questions.description: A fashion show where the runway is the whole map of Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: In 2004 the sombrero vueltiao was declared a cultural symbol of the Colombian nation.

questions.question: It's Colombia's largest coastal lagoon, between the Magdalena River and the Caribbean Sea, and home to Nueva Venecia, a village on stilts. What is it called?
hints: It's in the department of Magdalena.
Salamanca Island separates it from the sea.
It's named after Colombia's oldest city.
questions.description: A village with houses on the water: here, if you can't paddle, you can't get to the store.
questions.fun_fact: The Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta is a Ramsar wetland and a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

questions.question: You're at a gathering of nothing but vallunos. Which guest sneaked in because they are NOT from Valle del Cauca?
hints: Three of them come from cities in Valle del Cauca.
The gatecrasher comes from the south, near Ecuador.
The gatecrasher's city is the capital of Nariño.
questions.description: A party where the salsa is playing and someone doesn't know the steps.
questions.fun_fact: Buga is famous for the Basilica of the Lord of Miracles, which draws pilgrims from all over the country.

questions.question: You travel the department of Cauca from end to end. Which of these places will you NOT find there?
hints: An island, a volcano and an archaeological park really are in Cauca.
The odd one out is farther north in the Cordillera Central, far from Popayán.
On clear days you can see it from Manizales, and it sits between Caldas and Tolima.
questions.description: A trip around Cauca with a map in your hand and no asking Google.
questions.fun_fact: Gorgona Island used to be a prison, and today it is a national park where you can see humpback whales.

questions.question: It's a small rodent, many homes in Nariño raise it, and in Pasto it is eaten roasted at festivals. Which animal is it?
hints: In other countries it is kept as a pet.
It is also eaten a lot in Ecuador and Peru.
Its name has only three letters.
questions.description: In other countries they buy it an exercise wheel; in Pasto they buy charcoal.
questions.fun_fact: The cuy has been raised in the Andes for thousands of years, since long before the Spanish arrived.

questions.question: Look at the map: what is the capital of the highlighted department?
hints: The department borders Ecuador and Peru.
It's the capital of Putumayo.
Its name starts with “M.”
questions.description: A capital surrounded by so much green that the GPS gets nervous.
questions.fun_fact: Mocoa sits where the Andes start to drop down toward the Amazon rainforest.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the Farallones de Cali are part of one of Colombia's mountain ranges. Which one?
wrong_answers: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
hints: It's the range closest to the Pacific Ocean.
It's the lowest of the three cordilleras.
Its name tells you it lies to the west.
questions.description: Peaks that look down on Cali like a mother-in-law who came to visit.
questions.fun_fact: The Western Cordillera separates the Cauca River valley from the Pacific rainforest.

questions.question: It's a department of the Llanos, its capital is Yopal, and it's famous for the Cusiana oil field. Which department is it?
hints: It borders Boyacá.
Its name comes from a river.
It starts with “C”.
questions.description: Land of joropo, herons and horses that work harder than you do.
questions.fun_fact: Casanare has more head of cattle than people.

questions.question: In which century did the Spanish found Santa María la Antigua del Darién, near the Gulf of Urabá?
hints: It was a few years after Columbus's first voyage.
It was one of the first Spanish towns on the American mainland.
It was in the year 1510.
questions.description: A town so old that not even Grandma remembers when it was founded.
questions.fun_fact: Vasco Núñez de Balboa, the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas, set out from the Darién area.

questions.question: It's the highest and coldest piso térmico (climate zone), almost nothing grows there, and in Colombia only a few mountains have it, like Nevado del Ruiz. Which is it?
hints: It lies higher up than the frailejones.
It is also known as the zone of “nieves perpetuas” (perpetual snow).
Its name comes from the slow rivers of ice found on high peaks.
questions.description: Up here, not even a tinto stays hot for more than a minute.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's glaciers have shrunk enormously in recent decades.

questions.question: This animal is a Christmas dish in many Colombian homes. Which continent does it originally come from?
hints: Although it's eaten in Colombia today, it doesn't originally come from Colombia.
Wild turkeys still live in the forests of the continent it comes from.
It comes from the same continent as corn and potatoes.
questions.description: The star of Christmas dinner, who never asked to be invited.
questions.fun_fact: Ancient peoples of Mexico tamed the turkey about 2,000 years ago.

questions.question: In the novena de aguinaldos, right after the prayer to the Virgin Mary, who is the next prayer to?
hints: He's a saint who is in the pesebre (nativity scene).
He is part of the Holy Family.
He was a carpenter and Mary's husband.
questions.description: The moment in the novena when even the most restless cousins have to lower their voices.
questions.fun_fact: After the prayer to Saint Joseph come the gozos, the most sung and noisiest part of the novena.

questions.question: We live on very long wires, we blink on and off in colors, and in December we're hung on balconies and in Medellín's alumbrado. What are we?
hints: We run on electricity.
We go on the tree, in windows and in parks.
Each of us is a tiny bulb, and together we form long strands.
questions.description: December in Colombia: the season when even the balconies get dressed up.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín's Christmas alumbrado uses millions of bulbs, and people come from all over the country to see it.

questions.question: In May, Colombian schools celebrate their teachers with cards and flowers. What day in May is Teacher's Day?
hints: It's the day the Church named the patron saint of teachers.
It's closer to 10 than to 25.
It's half of 30.
questions.description: The one day teachers get more nice homework than they hand out.
questions.fun_fact: On May 15, 1950, Pope Pius XII named Saint John Baptist de La Salle the patron saint of teachers.

questions.question: In Circasia, Quindío, a cemetery from the 1930s buries anyone, whatever their religion or beliefs. What is it called?
hints: It was pushed for by Braulio Botero Londoño, a radical Liberal leader.
It was created because other cemeteries turned away people who weren't Catholic.
Its Spanish name is the opposite of “prisoner”.
questions.description: A Quindío graveyard where the flowers share the hills with the coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Because of this cemetery, Circasia is nicknamed “the free town of Colombia”.

questions.question: Barón Rojo Sur sings in the south stand and is named after a famous German pilot. What is it?
hints: It's a group of fans with bass drums, flags and lots of red.
Its team is also called “los Diablos Rojos”.
Its fans call their team “la Mechita”.
questions.description: A war pilot who swapped his plane for drums and flags.
questions.fun_fact: The original Red Baron, Manfred von Richthofen, was the most famous pilot of World War I.

questions.question: Look at this trophy. With its 2016 title, how many times in total had Atlético Nacional won it?
hints: No other Colombian club has won it as many times.
Its first title came in 1989, with Francisco Maturana as coach.
It didn't win it again between 1989 and 2016.
questions.description: A cup that has its own shrine of memories in Medellín.
questions.fun_fact: In 1989, Atlético Nacional became the first Colombian club to win the Copa Libertadores.

questions.question: The mita was forced labor in shifts that sent people to the silver mines of Mariquita. Who had to serve it?
hints: They were not the ones in charge in colonial times.
The Spanish copied the idea from an Inca custom.
Those who served it were called “mitayos”, and many came from the resguardos (Indigenous reserves).
questions.description: The toughest work shift in history, and you couldn’t swap it with anyone.
questions.fun_fact: The word “mita” comes from Quechua and means something like “turn” or “shift”.

questions.question: It sticks out from the second floor of colonial houses. In Cartagena it's often wooden and full of flowers, and people watched processions from it. What is it?
hints: It's on the outside of the house, up high.
You reach it through a door from a second-floor room.
Romeo climbed up to one to see Juliet.
questions.description: In the Walled City, the houses have more flowers than a flower shop on Mother's Day.
questions.fun_fact: Cartagena's historic center, full of colonial houses with balconies, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.

questions.question: He was the first Colombian to win a stage of the Giro d'Italia, in 1973, and earlier he had broken the amateur hour record. Which city was he from?
hints: He broke that hour record in Mexico City, in 1970.
His nickname was “Cochise”.
It's the city of eternal spring.
questions.description: Pasta, pedals, and a Colombian who showed the Italians how to climb.
questions.fun_fact: Martín Emilio “Cochise” Rodríguez got his nickname from an Apache chief in Western movies.

questions.question: It's Cali's most typical drink: served with ice and made with a mashed sour fruit, lime and sugar. What is it?
hints: It's cold and very refreshing.
It has little pieces of fruit in it, because it isn't fully blended.
Its name comes from the sour, orange-colored fruit it's made with.
questions.description: When a caleño gets hot from dancing salsa, they already know what to order.
questions.fun_fact: In some places, lulo is called “naranjilla” (“little orange”) because on the outside it looks like a small orange.

questions.question: Take a close look at this long, woody fruit: it's cañandonga, whose dark pulp is drunk with milk on the Caribbean coast. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Inside, it has many flat seeds in separate compartments.
It grows on a big tree with pink flowers, not on a palm.
It's the same family as beans, peas and tamarind.
questions.description: A fruit that looks like a club and smells like dirty socks, yet people still blend it with love.
questions.fun_fact: Cañandonga pulp smells so strong that many people hold their nose to drink it, but on the coast it's a traditional drink with milk.

questions.question: The palenqueras of Cartagena sing it, and sometimes it rhymes: it's the pregón. What is it for?
wrong_answers: To signal the stall has closed
hints: It's said before the customer shows up, not after.
It usually names fruits, sweets or fish.
It's like a commercial, but shouted in the street.
questions.description: Long before loudspeakers, the neighborhood already had its own sound system: a good pair of lungs.
questions.fun_fact: Street vendors' pregones have inspired many salsa and Caribbean songs.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in Colombia, these seeds go into tamales and rice. What are they used for?
hints: They barely change the taste of the food.
If you touch them, your fingers get stained.
They're why many dishes come out reddish or orange.
questions.description: Tiny little seeds with a permanent spot in the Colombian kitchen.
questions.fun_fact: The same achiote that colors rice also gives many cheddar-style cheeses around the world their orange color.

questions.question: Take a close look: this fruit makes breakfast jam and juice blended with milk. Which fruit is it?
hints: It's small and grows on thorny bushes.
It's made of lots of little balls stuck together.
When ripe it's almost black, and its name says so.
questions.description: The fruit that's always in grandma's fridge for the lunchtime juice.
questions.fun_fact: The Andean blackberry (mora de Castilla), the most grown in Colombia, is native to the Andes mountains.

questions.question: Complete the saying: “Yo no creo en brujas, pero…” (I don't believe in witches, but…)
questions.answer: de que las hay, las hay
hints: People say it when they have doubts, but just in case…
The ending sounds almost like a tongue twister.
It ends by saying that they really do exist.
questions.description: The favorite saying of people who swear they aren't superstitious, but knock on wood anyway.
questions.fun_fact: Galicia, in Spain, has its own version with “meigas”, the local witches: “Eu non creo nas meigas, mais habelas, hainas.”

questions.question: It's built right into the showerhead, heats the water just as it comes out, and is common in tierra fría. What is it called?
hints: It needs no gas cylinder and no sun.
It runs on electricity from the wall.
Touch it with wet hands and you might get a small shock.
questions.description: In tierra fría, the morning shower is an act of bravery… or of technology.
questions.fun_fact: Many electric showers have a knob for cold, warm or hot water, which really just changes how much power it uses.

questions.question: Before school, you have to iron your uniform. Why do people iron clothes?
hints: You do it on a long, narrow board.
You have to be careful not to burn yourself.
Afterward, the shirt is nice and smooth.
questions.description: On Sunday night, the school uniform goes to the spa.
questions.fun_fact: Before electric irons, people used heavy metal irons that were heated on the stove.

questions.question: In which city of the Viceroyalty of New Granada was the first government junta formed, in 1809?
hints: Its junta was formed on an August 10.
It was the seat of a royal audiencia in the south of the viceroyalty.
Today this city is the capital of Ecuador.
questions.description: In the race to set up government juntas, someone took off before the whistle.
questions.fun_fact: The Quito junta of August 10, 1809, is known as the “Primer Grito de Independencia” of Spanish America.

questions.question: At the Battle of Pantano de Vargas in 1819, a charge by horsemen from the llanos saved the day. What are those riders known as?
hints: Today a giant monument near Paipa, Boyacá, honors them.
Colonel Juan José Rondón charged with fourteen of them.
Their weapon was a very long pole with an iron tip.
questions.description: A sculpture so huge the horses look ready to gallop right out of Boyacá.
questions.fun_fact: The monument, by sculptor Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt, is one of the largest sculptures in Colombia.

questions.question: Every July 20 I move through the streets with bands and flags, and the president watches me from a stand. What am I?
hints: I am shown on TV across the whole country.
The participants rehearse for weeks to stay perfectly in step.
The Army, Navy, Air Force and Police all march.
questions.description: A July 20 plan that half of Colombia prefers to enjoy from the couch.
questions.fun_fact: July 20 is also the day each year when Colombia's Congress opens its new session.

questions.question: On July 20, 1810, in Santafé, a Spanish merchant refused to lend a flower vase and a fight broke out. Who was he?
hints: He had his shop on the main square.
The criollos asked him for the vase to decorate a dinner honoring the commissioner Antonio Villavicencio.
People remember him in the phrase “el florero de…”.
questions.description: Never has a refused loan turned out so expensive.
questions.fun_fact: The original vase is on display today at the Museo de la Independencia - Casa del Florero in Bogotá.

questions.question: The cardón grows in La Guajira and the Tatacoa, stands several meters tall, and the Wayuu use its wood to build their homes. What is it?
hints: It lives in very dry areas.
It stores water inside and is shaped like a column.
It has spines instead of leaves.
questions.description: A neighbor of the goats in La Guajira, and quite a bit taller than them.
questions.fun_fact: The Wayuu use the dried core of the cardón, called yotojoro, to build the walls and roofs of their rancherías.

questions.question: It comes from mines like Muzo and Chivor in Boyacá, and Colombia's are famous worldwide. What precious stone is it?
hints: The Muisca were using it long before the Spanish arrived.
The ones from Muzo are famous for their intense color.
Its color is the same as the mountains of Boyacá.
questions.description: The stone that makes even movie dragons jealous of Boyacá.
questions.fun_fact: Many experts consider the stones from Muzo the best in the world for their deep color.

questions.question: The first verse of Colombia's anthem says: “The horrible night has ended! Sublime liberty pours out the auroras of its invincible light.” What time of day does it describe?
hints: Look at who wins the fight: darkness or light.
“Has ended” tells you the night has just finished.
An “aurora” here is the glow in the sky before the sun comes up.
questions.description: A song every Colombian knows by heart, even if they've never stopped to think about what it means.
questions.fun_fact: The “horrible night” in the anthem stands for the time of Spanish rule before independence.

questions.question: Which Colombian national symbol has the motto “Libertad y Orden” written on it?
hints: You can see it on official documents and government buildings.
A condor holds a ribbon with the motto on it.
It has three sections and some flags on each side.
questions.description: Two words every teacher would love to see written on the classroom board.
questions.fun_fact: The coat of arms shows the Isthmus of Panama because when it was designed in 1834, Panama was part of Colombia.

questions.question: It poisons rivers with mercury, leaves dredge holes in Chocó and the Amazon, and led to the Atrato River being declared a subject of rights. What is it?
hints: Park rangers and the security forces go after it.
It's looking for something at the bottom of rivers.
Its main goal is to get gold.
questions.description: A problem that leaves the rivers of the Pacific coast looking like they never want to get out of bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2016, Colombia's Constitutional Court declared the Atrato River a subject of rights, something almost no river in the world had.

questions.question: Which of these colors does NOT appear in the Olympic rings?
hints: There are five rings of different colors on a white background.
All three colors of Colombia's flag are in the rings.
It's the color of grapes and eggplants.
questions.description: Five rings and not a single wedding.
questions.fun_fact: The ring colors, together with the white background, were chosen because they could be used to draw the flag of every country in the world at the time.

questions.question: Ingrit Valencia won bronze at Rio 2016, the first Colombian female boxer with an Olympic medal, fighting in the lightest women's class of those Games. Which was it?
hints: At those Games, her class had a limit of 51 kg (112 lb).
It's named after an animal.
It's an insect that buzzes.
questions.description: A weight class where every gram counts and the scale is the most feared opponent.
questions.fun_fact: At Rio 2016, women had only three boxing classes: 51, 60 and 75 kg (112, 132 and 165 lb).

questions.question: Its champions race on tracks and streets, and Colombia has topped the country table at its World Championships again and again. What sport is it?
hints: Many Colombian children join clubs for it at a very young age.
The athletes wear helmets and special boots.
Under each boot is a row of small wheels.
questions.description: In this sport, Colombia is like Brazil in soccer, just without the samba.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has skating clubs in almost every city, and many champions started skating before the age of 6.

questions.question: Elite runners from around the world say the Bogotá Half Marathon is one of the toughest on the planet. Why?
questions.answer: It's run at about 2,600 meters of altitude
wrong_answers: It goes up and down the eastern hills
It's always run in the rain
It has more than a hundred sharp turns
hints: The problem isn't the course, it's the air.
Runners who come from the coast feel it from the very first kilometer.
Bogotá is much closer to the clouds than to the sea.
questions.description: 21 kilometers (13 miles) that leave even the world's best distance runners begging for mercy.
questions.fun_fact: At Bogotá's height of about 2,600 m (8,500 ft), every breath brings in quite a bit less oxygen than at sea level, which is why many athletes train in the mountains.

questions.question: Its flowers look like a monkey's face, it grows in cloud forests, and it is most diverse in Colombia and Ecuador. Which orchid genus is it?
hints: Its name comes from Latin.
Its sepals end in long, pointed tails.
It shares its name with the most famous vampire in the movies.
questions.description: An orchid that poses for photos with the face of a cheeky monkey.
questions.fun_fact: “Dracula” means “little dragon” in Latin, after the long tails of its sepals, not after any vampire.

questions.question: In Medellín's Desfile de Silleteros, how much can a giant silleta weigh?
hints: One single person carries it on their back.
It can be more than 2 meters (6.5 ft) wide.
It can weigh more than the person carrying it.
questions.description: The prettiest and heaviest backpack ever carried in Antioquia.
questions.fun_fact: The silleteros of Santa Elena learn the craft from their families, and some children parade with kid-size silletas from a very young age.

questions.question: Colombia is one of the world's biggest exporters of this flower. Look at the close-up: which flower is it?
hints: Its petals have jagged edges.
It smells a little spicy.
Its Spanish name comes from the same word as the clove spice that goes into natilla.
questions.description: It flies more often than most business travelers, and always in refrigerated class.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish the carnation is called “clavel” after the “clavo de olor” (clove), because its scent is a reminder of it.

questions.question: In the Desfile de Silleteros, which category of silleta carries only bunches of flowers, with no figures or signs?
hints: It has no brands or ads.
It doesn't spell out messages or make pictures with flowers either.
It's put together the way the old silleteros of Santa Elena used to do it.
questions.description: A whole garden walking through Medellín on somebody's back.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Feria existed, the farmers of Santa Elena used the silleta to carry flowers down to sell in Medellín.

questions.question: There's a tiple requinto, a requinto guitar and a requinto clarinet. What does “requinto” tell you about an instrument?
wrong_answers: It's an old version from colonial times
It only keeps the rhythm, never the melody
hints: The word comes from old Spanish, not from an Indigenous language.
In carranga, the requinto plays the picked melody above the tiple.
Think of a “child” instrument that sounds higher than its “parent.”
questions.description: A word that shows up in three families of instruments, and nobody ever asks what it's doing there.
questions.fun_fact: In carranga, the tiple keeps the rhythm while the requinto decorates it with picked melodies.

questions.question: Paisa is to “vos” as costeño is to…
hints: It's the word for talking to a friend, in a relaxed and familiar way.
It's the same one used in most songs.
It's the one Carlos Vives and Shakira use when they sing to someone.
questions.description: A question that tastes of sea breeze and arepa de huevo.
questions.fun_fact: On the Caribbean coast “tú” is so common that many costeños use it even with people they've just met.

questions.question: In Pasto, in Boyacá and in Mexico, when someone calls your name, you answer “¿Mande?”. What does it mean?
hints: You say it to Mom, to the teacher and to your elders.
It comes from the Spanish verb “mandar,” to give orders.
It's like saying “I'm at your service.”
questions.description: In Pasto, answering when someone calls you comes with its own etiquette.
questions.fun_fact: “Mande” comes from “mandar”: it's like saying “give me your orders, I'm here to serve you.”

questions.question: Which of these Colombian expressions does NOT mean that something is good or fun?
hints: You'd say three of them at a great party.
You'd say the other one in a class that never ends.
In Colombia you say it when something is really boring or annoying.
questions.description: Colombian words have more moods than a Monday holiday.
questions.fun_fact: “Jartera” comes from “jartarse”, the popular form of “hartarse”: to be full of something or fed up with it.

questions.question: In Bogotá, this is the word for someone no longer a child but not yet an adult: in high school and always falling in love. What is it?
hints: This person is roughly between 12 and 17 years old.
Adults say it half fondly, half teasing, about kids starting to go to parties and have a boyfriend or girlfriend.
Its feminine form comes in a can.
questions.description: Too big for the piñata, too small for a tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Rolos also say “chino” or “china” for a child or a young person.

questions.question: Most Colombians live in this region, three mountain ranges cross it, and Bogotá is there. Which region is it?
hints: It's the region of the mountains.
Medellín and Cali are there too.
It's named after the longest mountain range in South America.
questions.description: So many people live here that even the tinto has to wait in line.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the Andes split into three ranges: the Western, Central and Eastern Cordilleras.

questions.question: At the Festival del Bambuco in Neiva, every candidate for queen must perform a sanjuanero. What is the sanjuanero?
hints: The candidates practice it for months.
It comes with band music and a handkerchief.
It's the signature tradition of Huila, and you need a partner for it.
questions.description: In Neiva in June, even the heat puts on a hat.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival del Bambuco falls during the feasts of Saint John and Saint Peter, the most joyful celebrations of the year in Huila.

questions.question: At the Festival Nacional del Porro in San Pelayo, Córdoba, bandas sabaneras compete. Which instruments make up these bands?
questions.answer: Clarinets, trumpets, bass drum and cymbals
wrong_answers: Gaitas, maracas, tambor alegre and llamador
hints: They're the same bands that liven up corralejas and town fiestas.
Elsewhere they're called bandas papayeras.
They mix brass and woodwind instruments with band percussion.
questions.description: In Córdoba, when they say a band is about to play, they don't mean a rock band.
questions.fun_fact: The bands of San Pelayo have played porro for generations, and the festival has been held every year since the late 1970s.

questions.question: A very famous cumbia tells the story of a boat like this one: the one belonging to Guillermo Cubillos. Who composed it?
hints: He was from El Banco, Magdalena.
He also composed “El gallo tuerto”.
The Festival Nacional de la Cumbia in El Banco is named after him.
questions.description: A song that has spent more than half a century sailing down the river without sinking.
questions.fun_fact: In “La piragua”, the boat travels between El Banco and Chimichagua, driven by twelve bogas (boatmen).

questions.question: I'm oval and sour, with red or orange skin. I'm blended into juice and ground with ají for empanadas. What am I?
hints: I grow in the Andes mountains, hanging from a small tree.
Inside I have little dark seeds and orange pulp.
My name puts together a salad vegetable and the place where I grow.
questions.description: The fruit that would rather end up in hot sauce than in dessert.
questions.fun_fact: Tomate de árbol is also called tamarillo, and it's a relative of the tomato and the potato.

questions.question: In Colombia, if people say someone “es como el arroz blanco” (is like white rice), what do they mean?
hints: The saying compares a person to the place rice has on the Colombian table.
It’s said jokingly and fondly about someone people know.
Just like rice at a Colombian meal, this person is never missing from anything.
questions.description: A saying that came straight out of the lunch pot.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia grows its own rice, mostly in the Llanos Orientales and in Tolima.

questions.question: Which freshwater fish, the most famous of the Magdalena River's subienda, is the star of a coastal sancocho?
hints: It's very bony, and on the coast people eat it fried or in sancocho.
It lives in the swamps and feeds on the mud and algae at the bottom.
Its mouth is very small.
questions.description: A fish that ends up in the pot after swimming upstream with the whole family.
questions.fun_fact: The “subienda” is the season when thousands of bocachicos swim up the Magdalena River and fishermen get a huge catch.

questions.question: I'm skinny and long, made of wheat dough rolled in a spiral around cheese, and I get fried for parties. What am I?
hints: I'm served on trays of party snacks at birthdays.
I'm crunchy on the outside, and the cheese melts inside.
I'm shaped like a part of your hand.
questions.description: The skinniest guest at the party, and the first one to vanish from the tray.
questions.fun_fact: In Venezuela, a very similar snack is called a tequeño.

questions.question: Emiliano Zuleta wrote it to mock Lorenzo Morales, and Carlos Vives made it famous in 1993. What did “La gota fría” grow out of?
hints: The song dates from the late 1930s and comes from the La Guajira and Cesar region.
Lorenzo Morales had sung something at Zuleta first, and this song was the reply.
Two juglares answer each other in verse to see who is better.
questions.description: A story from La Guajira that crossed borders with an accordion in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Emiliano Zuleta and Lorenzo Morales ended up as friends, and their rivalry became one of the most famous stories in vallenato.

questions.question: What is the head of the caja vallenata (vallenato drum) traditionally made of?
hints: It comes from a farm animal.
It's a small animal, very common in La Guajira and Cesar.
It says “baa” and its baby is called a kid.
questions.description: A drum small enough to fit between your knees, but it sounds like a giant.
questions.fun_fact: People often say vallenato's three instruments mix three heritages: the accordion is European, the caja African and the guacharaca Indigenous.

questions.question: Vallenato accordion players take great care of their instrument's bellows. What are the bellows of an accordion?
questions.answer: The folding part that moves the air
wrong_answers: The strap that holds up the accordion
The wooden box of the treble buttons
hints: Without them, the accordion wouldn't make a sound.
They stretch and squeeze while you play.
They work like the tool people use to blow air on a cooking fire.
questions.description: Some accordion players care for their instrument more than for their sombrero vueltiao.
questions.fun_fact: On a vallenato accordion, the same button plays one note when the bellows open and a different one when they close.

questions.question: On a bus, you hear someone say: “¡Ala, qué pena con usted!” Which region is that “ala” most typical of?
hints: It's a cold, high region of Colombia.
People there also love to say “sumercé.”
It's the area around Bogotá and Boyacá.
questions.description: A tiny word that means “wing” in Spanish, yet never takes flight.
questions.fun_fact: In Bogotá and Boyacá people often say “sumercé,” a warm, respectful way of saying “usted” (formal “you”).

questions.question: A Colombian teen says: “El domingo me toca almorzar con los cuchos.” Who is he having lunch with?
hints: In Colombia, Sunday lunch is usually a family plan.
“Cucho” is said of someone older.
He calls his mom “la cucha.”
questions.description: Teenagers have their own dictionary, and adults almost never understand it.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “cucho” or “cucha” can also mean any older person.

questions.question: They talk to their plants, go grocery shopping in pajamas and sing at the top of their lungs on the bus. In Colombia, what do people say about them?
hints: It has nothing to do with money or with flirting.
It's said of someone who seems to have lost their mind.
The phrase is about something slipping out of place on a roof.
questions.description: For when someone's head is overdue for urgent maintenance.
questions.fun_fact: To say the same thing, Colombians also say someone «le falta un tornillo»: they're missing a screw.

questions.question: In Colombia, what is a “tajalápiz”?
hints: You use it with pencils and colored pencils.
When you use it, little wood shavings come out.
It makes a pencil pointy again.
questions.description: A tiny object that lives in every school pencil case.
questions.fun_fact: “Tajar” means to cut, so a tajalápiz is literally a “pencil cutter.”

questions.question: In Colombia, if a student “perdió el año,” what happened?
questions.answer: They have to repeat the same grade
wrong_answers: Their grades for the year got lost
They missed almost the whole school year
They had to switch to another school
hints: It has nothing to do with actually losing something.
It happens when the grades aren't good enough.
Next year they'll take the very same subjects again.
questions.description: Final report cards arrive, and the house feels as tense as a telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: Other Spanish-speaking countries say “repetir el año,” “repetir curso” or “reprobar el grado.”

questions.question: In Colombia, if someone “le tocó bailar con la más fea” (had to dance with the ugliest one), what happened to them?
questions.answer: They got stuck with the worst part
wrong_answers: They fell in love by accident
They arrived late to the party
hints: The saying isn't about real dancing.
It's said to whoever ends up washing all the dishes after the party.
It's the opposite of being lucky when things are handed out.
questions.description: A party saying that, oddly enough, almost never gets used at a party.
questions.fun_fact: The saying is used for any thankless task: the worst part of the job, the hardest shift or the chore nobody wants.

questions.question: In Antioquia you often hear “¡Ome, no me diga!”. Which Spanish word does that “ome” come from?
hints: It's a word that got shortened from people talking fast.
The original word starts with a letter that is silent.
It's the opposite of “mujer”.
questions.description: Three very paisa letters that get used for everything except staying quiet.
questions.fun_fact: Paisas also shorten “para” to “pa'”, as in “¿pa' dónde va, ome?”.

questions.question: In Colombia, which verb means going out with friends to dance and party until late?
hints: It has nothing to do with working or getting up early.
You do it at clubs, parties and casetas.
It comes from a word for a party with music and dancing.
questions.description: A word so Colombian it isn’t in Grandpa’s dictionary… or maybe it is.
questions.fun_fact: Rumba is also a Cuban rhythm, but in Colombia the word came to mean any party with dancing.

questions.question: How often, and in which month, is the Carnaval de Riosucio in Caldas held?
hints: It isn't held every year.
During the festival, the matachines recite teasing verses.
It takes place in odd-numbered years, in the first days of the year.
questions.description: A party so good that even the devil asks permission to show up.
questions.fun_fact: The star of the Carnaval de Riosucio is the Devil, a cheerful, teasing character, not an evil one.

questions.question: The gaitas at the Ovejas gaita festival have a beeswax head and a duck-feather mouthpiece. What plant is their body made from?
hints: It's a plant of dry lands.
The craftsman scoops out its soft inner pulp.
It's a tall cactus that gets hollowed out to make the flute.
questions.description: In Ovejas (Spanish for “sheep”), Sucre, the sheep don't bleat: they blow.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival Nacional de Gaitas Francisco Llirene has been held in Ovejas, Sucre, since 1985.

questions.question: It's a piece of guadua (giant bamboo) with a strip of its bark lifted up as a string, struck with a small stick to play the bass. What is it called?
hints: It belongs to the traditional folk music of the Colombian countryside.
It isn't scraped: the strip is struck and vibrates.
Its name sounds a bit like “caramba”.
questions.description: A rural folk band that lost its bass player and built a new one from whatever grew in the hills.
questions.fun_fact: Instruments like this one, where the string comes from the tube itself, also exist in Africa and Asia, such as the valiha of Madagascar.

questions.question: A chirimía band with clarinet, euphonium, snare drum, bass drum and cymbals is typical of one Pacific department. Which one?
hints: It is one of the rainiest places in the world.
It gets the Fiestas de San Pacho going.
Its capital is Quibdó.
questions.description: A band so loud that even the neighbors three blocks away end up dancing.
questions.fun_fact: The Fiestas de San Pacho in Quibdó, chirimía and all, are Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: Finish what Colombians say about a song that gets everyone happily dancing: “Esa canción tiene…”
hints: It’s something good, not something that makes you feel bad.
It has to do with flavor and grace when you move.
It comes from the same word used for really tasty food.
questions.description: A word you pronounce with your hips.
questions.fun_fact: On Colombia’s Pacific coast, “vivir sabroso” means living in peace, as a community, and enjoying life.

questions.question: At a party where everyone dances, sings and has a great time, Colombians say: “¡Esto es una…!”
hints: It's something very cheerful.
It's said of a party nobody wants to leave.
It's also the title of a famous song by Gente de Zona and Marc Anthony.
questions.description: The exact opposite of an afternoon spent doing homework.
questions.fun_fact: “La Gozadera,” by Gente de Zona and Marc Anthony, names several Latin American countries, Colombia among them.

questions.question: Look at this island in Colombia's Pacific. Which conqueror named it Gorgona because it was full of snakes?
hints: He passed by on one of his trips south, looking for a very rich empire.
The snakes reminded him of Medusa, the Gorgon from Greek myth with snakes instead of hair.
He later conquered the Inca Empire in Peru.
questions.description: A christening with salt water, no godparents and plenty of snakes.
questions.fun_fact: Gorgona still has lots of snakes, so visitors to the national park must wear tall boots.

questions.question: You climb the Azufral volcano in Nariño and reach the Laguna Verde inside its crater. About how high up are you?
hints: It feels as cold as the páramo, and breathing is a little hard.
You are higher than Bogotá, which sits at about 2,600 m (8,500 ft).
You are almost at the top of the volcano, but there is no snow like on the highest snow-capped peaks.
questions.description: A lake so green it looks like someone went overboard with the food coloring.
questions.fun_fact: The lake's green color comes from sulfur and other minerals from the volcano, which is why you can't swim in it.

questions.question: Riddle: “I come from the Indian and Pacific Oceans and slipped into the Colombian Caribbean. I have stripes and venomous spines, and in San Andrés people eat me.” What am I?
hints: I eat the little reef fish, and almost nobody hunts me.
My long fins look like a mane.
I'm named after the king of the African savanna.
questions.description: A Caribbean reef where every neighbor dresses up like it's carnival.
questions.fun_fact: In San Andrés and on other Caribbean coasts, people hold lionfish fishing contests and cooking contests to keep this invasive species under control.

questions.question: A prisoner escaping the old prison on Gorgona Island had to swim to the mainland. About how far away is the coast?
hints: You couldn't swim it from the island in one calm afternoon.
Malpelo, the other famous island in Colombia's Pacific, is much, much farther away.
By speedboat from Guapi, you get there in a couple of hours.
questions.description: The prison with the best sea view and the worst reasons to stay.
questions.fun_fact: The Gorgona prison was open from 1960 to 1984; today the island is a national park, and the jungle covers the ruins.

questions.question: Look at the map of Colombia. Which sea washes its northern coast, the one at the top?
hints: Cartagena, Santa Marta and Barranquilla are there.
Its waters are warm and turquoise blue.
It's the sea you cross to reach the islands of San Andrés and Providencia.
questions.description: The warm water where half of Colombia goes on vacation to lie in the sun.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is the only country in South America with coasts on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean.

questions.question: Englishman Quantic and Mario Galeano formed Ondatrópica in 2012 and recorded their first album at the legendary Discos Fuentes studios. In which city?
hints: It's not a coastal city, although the label recorded lots of coastal music there.
Discos Fuentes was born in Cartagena, but moved to another city in the 1950s.
It's the city of eternal spring.
questions.description: An Englishman and a guy from Bogotá walked into an old studio and came out with the most tropical record on the block.
questions.fun_fact: Ondatrópica brought together veterans of Colombian tropical music and young musicians, in the same studio where Fruko y sus Tesos recorded their classics.

previous.feedback: source: the fact check says Ondatrópica began in late 2011, and only the album was recorded in early 2012 at Discos Fuentes in Medellín. The source repeats "created Ondatrópica in 2012", so the error comes from the source and not from the translation. The source should be reworded first, for example "Quantic and Mario Galeano recorded Ondatrópica's first album in 2012 at the legendary Discos Fuentes studios. In which city?", and then translated again. Fact check: wrong. The question says Ondatrópica was formed in 2012. Sources say the project began at the end of 2011, and the album was recorded in January 2012 at Discos Fuentes in Medellín. The answer, Medellín, is right.

questions.question: La Sonora Dinamita, with hits like “Mi cucu” and “Escándalo,” took a Colombian rhythm all over Latin America. Which one?
hints: It doesn't need a star accordion or a llanero harp.
It's so loved in Mexico that many people there feel it's their own.
On the coast, it's danced holding lit candles.
questions.description: A band named after an explosive that has been blowing up dance floors for decades.
questions.fun_fact: La Sonora Dinamita was founded in Cartagena in 1960 by Antonio Fuentes, the founder of Discos Fuentes.

questions.question: In the Gran Cabalgata, thousands of riders parade on Paso Fino horses at a fair that starts in late December. In which city?
hints: The fair runs from December 25 to 30 and closes the year.
At the same fair, people dance in the Salsódromo.
It is the city of salsa.
questions.description: A parade where the ones walking with the most style have four legs.
questions.fun_fact: The Feria de Cali has been held since 1957, and every year it closes Colombia's calendar with horses, parades and salsa.

questions.question: You're at a street stand buying mango biche. Which of these do they NOT usually put on it?
hints: Mango biche is green and sour.
It's sold in little cups or bags on street corners and outside schools.
What doesn't go on it is something sweet you drink hot at breakfast.
questions.description: A fruit that isn't ripe yet but already has fans on every street corner.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “biche” means a fruit that isn't ripe yet.

questions.question: Sancocho trifásico has yuca, potato and plantain, and is cooked in a big pot on river outings. What does “trifásico” tell you?
wrong_answers: It is served in three bowls
hints: “Tri” means three.
The “three” is about what goes into the pot, not how it is cooked or served.
It has beef, pork and chicken in the same pot.
questions.description: A soup with so much energy, its name sounds like it came off a fuse box.
questions.fun_fact: “Trifásico” comes from electricity: three-phase power has three phases, just as the sancocho has three meats.

questions.question: You go to the market to buy plantain for sopa de plátano. Which of these is NOT a kind of plantain or banana in Colombia?
hints: Three of them grow in bunches.
The odd one out grows underground.
The odd one out is a root that goes into sancocho and looks like a white carrot.
questions.description: A shopping list with something sneaked in that doesn’t wear a yellow peel.
questions.fun_fact: For sopa de plátano, many grandmothers grate the green plantain instead of chopping it.

questions.question: You buy maíz peto at the market. Which of these dishes is NOT made with corn?
hints: The odd one out is typical of the Caribbean coast, especially Córdoba and Sucre.
It's eaten hot and served with white rice.
It's thickened with ñame, a root vegetable.
questions.description: A market where corn is the boss, but someone sneaked onto the list.
questions.fun_fact: In Antioquia, mazamorra made with maíz peto is drunk with milk and a piece of panela or bocadillo.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a pasta you add to soup?
hints: Pasta is made from wheat flour.
The odd one out grows on a plant, inside pods.
The odd one out is a small brown seed.
questions.description: The soup Mom serves before the main course, and you have to finish it before the good stuff arrives.
questions.fun_fact: With alphabet soup, lots of kids play at spelling their names on the spoon.

questions.question: I'm big and round, with a hard rind and orange flesh. In Colombia I'm made into a cream soup for lunch. What am I called in Colombia?
hints: I grow on a vine that creeps along the ground.
I'm a relative of the Halloween pumpkin.
In other countries I'm called zapallo.
questions.description: At lunchtime, Grandma's pot hides a secret from the vegetable garden.
questions.fun_fact: Ahuyama seeds can be eaten too: toasted with salt, they make a tasty snack.

questions.question: This freshwater fish is raised in ponds and served whole and fried with patacón; the red kind is the most famous. What is it called?
hints: It's the favorite on day trips to warm towns near rivers and reservoirs, like Melgar or Girardot.
It's flat and round, about the size of a plate.
Its name starts with “mo”.
questions.description: A fish that arrives at the table in one piece, looking like it has no idea what just happened.
questions.fun_fact: The red mojarra eaten in Colombia is actually a tilapia, a fish that came from Africa.

questions.question: This village in the Sierra Nevada belongs to Valledupar and is the main town of the Kankuamo people. What is it called?
hints: It sits on the slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, on the Cesar side.
The chicote, a traditional dance, is danced there.
Its name starts with A.
questions.description: A town so high up in the Sierra that vallenato arrives there a little out of breath.
questions.fun_fact: Several vallenato songwriters come from Atánquez, where Indigenous music and the accordion met.

questions.question: You're in class and the teacher comes back shouting “¡Se acabó la recocha!” What does the teacher want stopped?
hints: It isn't homework or anything the teacher assigned.
It's about jokes, laughing and paper balls flying.
It's the opposite of sitting quietly and behaving.
questions.description: The teacher's patience has an expiration date, and today is the day.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, someone who is always joking and goofing around is called a “recochero.”

questions.question: You're making a poster for school: “scissors” is to cutting as “colbón” is to…
hints: Colbón comes in a bottle and it's white.
If it gets on your fingers, it dries and peels off like skin.
It keeps the paper shapes from falling off the poster board.
questions.description: The school poster at 10 p.m.: the real test for parents.
questions.fun_fact: “Colbón” started out as a brand name and ended up as every Colombian's word for white glue.

questions.question: I hide under your jeans, you change me every day, and Superman wore me in red over his suit. What do Colombians call me?
hints: Superman wore me over his blue tights.
You put me on before your jeans.
In other countries they call me “calzoncillos”.
questions.description: Nobody sees it, but everybody changes it every day (hopefully).
questions.fun_fact: Depending on the country, underwear is called “calzoncillos”, “chones”, “bombachas” or “bragas”.

questions.question: Rapunzel let me grow longer and longer, Elsa wears me in a braid, and in Colombia anyone who has me is called «mono». What am I?
hints: Rapunzel and Elsa have the same hair color.
My color looks like the sun or gold.
I'm light hair, almost yellow.
questions.description: In Colombia, this nickname has nothing to do with climbing trees or eating bananas.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, babies with very light hair are lovingly called «monitos».

questions.question: Faking being sick, heading to the park with friends and never showing up in the classroom. What do Colombians call that?
hints: It has to do with school.
If the parents find out, a scolding is guaranteed.
It means skipping class in secret.
questions.description: Math first thing in the morning against a sunny day in the park: a very unfair fight.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico it's “irse de pinta,” in Argentina “hacerse la rata” and in Spain “hacer novillos.”

questions.question: You ask someone, “¿Vamos por un tinto?”, and they answer, “¡Hágale!”. What are they telling you?
hints: It's a very Colombian word you hear all day long.
The same word is used to cheer someone on or tell them to go ahead.
It's like saying “¡de una!”.
questions.description: In Colombia, every important conversation starts with a tinto as the excuse.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “hágale” works for everything: saying yes to a plan, cheering someone on or saying “go ahead”.

questions.question: On a trip, which of these plans are chanclas NOT good for?
hints: They're light shoes, almost always made of rubber.
Chanclas leave your toes out in the air.
Look for the plan with snow and lots of cold.
questions.description: The secret weapon of Colombian moms, which you can also wear on your feet.
questions.fun_fact: Nevado del Ruiz rises over 5,000 m (16,400 ft) and has snow all year round.

questions.question: Costumbrismo portrayed ordinary people and their customs in stories and paintings. In which century did it peak in Colombia?
hints: It came after Independence.
In that era, Eugenio Díaz wrote the novel “Manuela.”
It was the century of the civil wars and the Rionegro Constitution.
questions.description: Literature for classy busybodies: what the neighbors eat, how they dress and what they get up to.
questions.fun_fact: The painters of the Comisión Corográfica made watercolors of farmers, miners and street sellers from all over the country.

questions.question: What do you call a man who, like this one, carries loads on mules along mountain trails?
hints: He's a classic figure of Antioquia and the Coffee Region.
He usually wears a sombrero, a carriel (leather shoulder bag) and a poncho over his shoulder.
His name comes from the shout “¡arre!” used to get the animals moving.
questions.description: Before tractor-trailers, freight transport had long ears and a bad temper.
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century, arrieros carried much of Colombia's coffee out along the mountain trails.

questions.question: In the 19th century, Colombia exported tagua, “vegetable ivory,” to Europe and the United States. What was it mainly used for?
hints: It ended up sewn onto clothes.
It was cut into small slices and holes were drilled in them.
Shirts and coats had lots of them.
questions.description: A seed so hard that elephants should thank it.
questions.fun_fact: Plastic killed off the big tagua business, but today it's used again for jewelry and crafts.

questions.question: Why do farmers in Boyacá and Cundinamarca wear this piece of clothing?
hints: It's worn mostly up in the high country.
On the farm, it goes with a hat and alpargatas (rope-soled sandals).
It's nice and warm, and you put your head through a hole in the middle.
questions.description: The piece of clothing that turns any grandpa from Boyacá into a superhero with a square cape.
questions.fun_fact: Nobsa, in Boyacá, is famous for weaving ruanas from sheep's wool.

questions.question: Which of these places was NOT the site of a battle in the Thousand Days' War?
hints: That battle belonged to a different civil war.
It was fought in Valle del Cauca, in 1876.
It happened during the so-called “War of the Schools.”
questions.description: A thousand days of war is enough time to fight almost everywhere… but not quite everywhere.
questions.fun_fact: The Battle of Palonegro, near Bucaramanga, lasted about fifteen days in May 1900.

questions.question: Under President Mariano Ospina Rodríguez, a constitution turned the country into the Granadine Confederation, made of sovereign states. In what year?
hints: It was in the same decade that slavery was abolished in the country.
It replaced the Constitution of 1853 with an even more federal one.
It was three years before Mosquera took Bogotá in 1861.
questions.description: Constitutions in Colombia were like cell phones: every so often a new model came out.
questions.fun_fact: The Granadine Confederation had eight states, including Panama, which was then part of the country.

questions.question: On what day does Colombia remember the Battle of Boyacá?
hints: It's a holiday right in the month of wind and kites.
It's also the day Colombian presidents take office.
It's the seventh day of the eighth month.
questions.description: A teeny little bridge where something huge was won.
questions.fun_fact: The Puente de Boyacá is so small you can cross it in just a few steps.

questions.question: The Panama Railroad, opened in 1855 when Panama was part of Colombia, ran from ocean to ocean. What did its first passengers mostly use it for?
questions.answer: To go looking for gold in California
hints: Many passengers came from the east coast of the United States.
Their final stop was on the west coast of North America.
It was the time of the gold rush.
questions.description: From one ocean to the other in a day, no canal needed.
questions.fun_fact: It was the first railroad to cross the Americas from ocean to ocean, fourteen years before the one in the United States.

questions.question: I was a general of the Independence, of Pijao origin. In 1854, backed by the artisans, I led a coup against Obando. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Tolima.
My government lasted about eight months.
My first two names are the same as José María Córdova's.
questions.description: A general who got tired of waiting his turn to govern.
questions.fun_fact: After leaving Colombia, Melo fought in Mexico on Benito Juárez's side.

questions.question: Its followers are called “godos,” its color is blue, and Mariano Ospina Rodríguez and José Eusebio Caro founded it in 1849. Which party is it?
hints: It's one of Colombia's two traditional parties.
Its historic rival is the red party.
Its name comes from wanting to conserve traditions.
questions.description: In Colombia, politics was all about colors, and not because of fashion.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The core is right: Jan 5 is Día de los Negros, and enslaved people are said to have been given a day off. But the 1607 revolt and the Spanish Crown granting it appear in only some popular sources (Radio Nacional, Sitio Andino). Academic and local sources don't back it up, and El Tiempo gives 1854. The hint 'It was in the 17th century' and the fun fact depend on that shaky date. Some accounts also place the origin in Popayán.

Fact check: uncertain. The answer (enslaved Africans) is consistent across sources. The fun fact is shaky: sources disagree on the origin. One says a 1607 uprising in Remedios, Antioquia, led to the day off. Others say the enslaved people asked for it in Popayán. Others date it to 1854. The question says 'colonial times', but 1854 is after independence. 'Spanish Crown granted it after an uprising in 1607 (in Pasto)' is not well supported. The hint 'It happened in the 17th century' is also not firmly established.

Fact check: uncertain. Answer (enslaved Africans) and the Jan 5 'Día de los Negros' tradition are correct. The 1607 date is documented only in Wikipedia, which says the revolt was in Remedios, Antioquia, not Pasto, and flags the history as needing citations. Other sources call the carnival's origins '17th century' without a specific revolt. The hint 'They didn't have a single day of rest' is awkward but acceptable.

review.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. I found no source for the Colombia-specific belief that holy water in the house corners makes witches run away. The common folk and Catholic accounts say it drives off the devil, evil spirits or bad energy. Witches are plausible, since the question's hints (broomstick, flying at night) point to them. The hints themselves are fine, and the wrong answers (thieves, neighbors, debt collectors) are clearly wrong. The fun fact is plausible but I didn't verify it. Hint 1 is vague. 'Evil spirits' or 'the devil' would be the better-documented answer.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. In Colombian and Latin American tradition, holy water in the corners of a house usually drives away evil spirits, the devil or bad energies. Witches are not the standard answer. I did not verify this by search, so the claim that witches flee is shaky. The hints about broomsticks and night flight are generic witch lore, not Colombian tradition.

The fire takes away the sorrows and bad luck of the last twelve months.
questions.description: Grandpa gave his old clothes to the last party of the year, and the doll ended up looking very sharp.
questions.fun_fact: Many Año Viejo dolls are given the faces of famous people from that year, and some even come with a funny last will.

questions.question: It's a classic Bogotá breakfast with potato and cilantro, nicknamed “levantamuertos.” What animal are the ribs in this soup from?
hints: It's a big farm animal.
Its meat is also used for sobrebarriga.
It moos.
questions.description: A dish that takes breakfast so seriously it's said to bring people back to life.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian grandmothers prescribe caldo de costilla for the flu, for tiredness and even for feeling awful the morning after a party.

questions.question: A Colombian agüero (superstition) for a good day, done as you get out of bed: hence “empezar con buen pie” (start with a good foot). Which foot goes first?
hints: It's just one foot.
According to the superstition, the other foot brings bad luck.
The opposite of left.
questions.description: A very important decision you make before your eyes are even fully open.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombians also step into a new house or into the New Year with their right foot, so luck comes along with them.

questions.question: You're at the stadium in the yellow shirt, painting the flag on your face: yellow, blue and… which color comes next?
hints: It's the same order as Colombia's flag, from top to bottom.
It's the bottom stripe of the flag.
It's the color of ripe tomatoes.
questions.description: When Colombia plays, half the country dresses exactly alike, like a school uniform.
questions.fun_fact: The national team is nicknamed “la Tricolor”, even though it almost always takes the field in yellow.

questions.question: In this stadium on September 5, 1993, Colombia beat Argentina in a World Cup qualifier. How many goals did Colombia score?
hints: It was a thrashing that Argentina still remembers painfully.
Argentina didn't score a single goal.
Freddy Rincón and Tino Asprilla scored two each, and “El Tren” Valencia added another.
questions.description: The night Buenos Aires ended up applauding the wrong team.
questions.fun_fact: Diego Maradona watched the thrashing from the stands of the stadium.

questions.question: It was played in the United States in 2024, and Néstor Lorenzo led Colombia to the final against Argentina, his own country. Which tournament was it?
hints: It is a tournament for national teams, not clubs.
It is the oldest national team tournament in the world.
It is the championship of South America's national teams, run by CONMEBOL.
questions.description: An Argentine coaching Colombia against Argentina: the most awkward family barbecue of the year.
questions.fun_fact: Before coaching Colombia, Néstor Lorenzo was José Pékerman's assistant with the national team at the 2014 and 2018 World Cups.

questions.question: Estadio Centenario is in the Eje Cafetero, hosted the 2011 U-20 World Cup, and its name honors its city's 100th birthday. Which city is it in?
hints: It's a department capital in the Eje Cafetero.
It's the home of Deportes Quindío.
The city shares its name with a country in the Caucasus.
questions.description: A stadium named like a birthday party, with the smell of freshly brewed coffee.
questions.fun_fact: Armenia is nicknamed “the Miracle City” because it grew so fast after it was founded.

questions.question: Which team knocked Colombia out in the quarterfinals of the 2023 Women's World Cup?
hints: That match was played in Sydney, in front of more than 75,000 people.
That's where the dream ended, 2–1.
They were the reigning European champions at the time.
questions.description: A trip to the other side of the world with more joy than hours of sleep.
questions.fun_fact: That World Cup was held in Australia and New Zealand, the first co-hosted by two countries from different confederations.

questions.question: You're in the Colombian Amazon and you see a macaw. Which of these things does it NOT do?
hints: Think about its feathers and its wings.
It's a bird of the trees, not of the rivers.
Fish do it; it doesn't.
questions.description: It has more colors than a chiva bus and screams louder than a fan in the stadium.
questions.fun_fact: A macaw can live more than 50 years, so sometimes it outlives its owners.

questions.question: When a hillside is on fire, firefighters make a “firebreak”. What is that?
questions.answer: A strip of land with no plants that stops the fire
wrong_answers: A plane that drops water on the flames
A special suit that can't catch fire
An alarm that warns you when there is smoke
hints: It is made on the ground, not in the air.
Fire needs something to burn to keep moving forward.
Grass and bushes are cleared along a long line.
questions.description: A name so dramatic it sounds like it came from an action movie.
questions.fun_fact: Firefighting helicopters scoop water from lakes and reservoirs into a giant bucket hanging from a cable.

questions.question: You're in La Guajira watching pink flamingos. Which group do they NOT belong to?
hints: They have beaks and wings.
Their chicks hatch from an egg.
Dogs and cows do belong to that group.
questions.description: It stands on one leg as if waiting for a bus that never comes.
questions.fun_fact: Flamingos are pink because of what they eat: tiny shrimp and algae full of pigments; their chicks are born gray.

questions.question: Which of these statements about sunscreen is NOT true?
wrong_answers: You also use it on cloudy days
You put more on after swimming
It protects your skin from the sun's rays
hints: Three statements are good advice.
Its name already tells you what it protects you from.
The sun isn't out when it's dark.
questions.description: The cream that makes everyone look like a ghost in the beach photos.
questions.fun_fact: Clouds let a good share of the sun's rays through, which is why you can get sunburned on a gray day.

questions.question: The Colombian who races on tracks like this one is called the “Queen of BMX.” In which city was she born?
hints: It's a mountain city, tucked into a valley.
It's famous for its metro and its Feria de las Flores.
It's the capital of Antioquia.
questions.description: A queen with no castle, but with a helmet, knee pads and ramps.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín has a BMX track named after Mariana Pajón.

questions.question: In this sport, which Colombian woman won Olympic bronze at London 2012 and silver at Rio 2016?
hints: She is from Valle del Cauca.
She was judo world champion several times.
She was born in Jamundí and her last name starts with A.
questions.description: A sport where the white uniform is definitely not pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: Yuri Alvear was judo world champion three times: in 2009, 2013 and 2014.

questions.question: My cars have one seat and the wheels on the outside, I race through the streets of Monaco, and a driver from Bogotá won there in 2003. What racing series am I?
hints: My cars sit very low, with wings at the front and back.
The Colombian driver was Juan Pablo Montoya.
My name has a number in it: the very first one.
questions.description: Here nobody follows the speed limit, and everyone cheers.
questions.fun_fact: Juan Pablo Montoya won seven Formula 1 Grands Prix, including Monaco in 2003.

questions.question: It's played barefoot on sand, in pairs, hitting the ball with the hands over a net, and you see it all over El Rodadero in Santa Marta. Which sport is it?
hints: No rackets, and no feet either.
Each team has only two players.
It's the beach cousin of the indoor sport played with six per side.
questions.description: A sport where coming home with sand in your ears is completely normal.
questions.fun_fact: Beach volleyball has been an Olympic sport since the 1996 Atlanta Games.

questions.question: You're at the Édgar Rentería stadium in Barranquilla watching baseball. How many players does the fielding team have on the field?
hints: More than a basketball team, fewer than a soccer team.
That includes the pitcher and the catcher.
The same as the number of innings in a regular game.
questions.description: On Colombia's Caribbean coast, people argue about this sport more passionately than about the price of fish.
questions.fun_fact: Barranquilla's stadium is named after Édgar Rentería, the local hero who was MVP of the 2010 World Series.

questions.question: The sack race is to the sack as the egg race is to…
hints: Both races use something to complete the challenge.
In the egg race, you have to carry the egg without dropping it.
You hold it in your mouth or in your hand.
questions.description: The only sport where climbing into a bag is part of the training.
questions.fun_fact: The sack race is a classic at Colombian school fairs and at paseos de olla, family cookout trips to the river.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer 'Spoon' is right: the egg-and-spoon race is a real, well-known race. The wrong answers (Basket, Plate, Hen) are not the standard implement. I did not run web searches, so this rests on general knowledge. The description ('only sport where climbing into a bag is part of the training') is inaccurate, because the sack race is a game and not training. Hint 3 ('mouth or hand') fits the spoon but is vague. The fun fact about Colombian school fairs and paseos de olla is plausible, and paseo de olla is a real custom, but I could not verify the sack-race link.

questions.question: This trophy is awarded at the Indianapolis 500 and carries the face of every winner. Which Colombian won it in 2000 and 2015?
hints: All four are Colombian drivers who raced at Indianapolis.
He was born in Bogotá and also raced in Formula 1 and NASCAR.
He is the most famous Colombian racing driver in history.
questions.description: A trophy so big it won't even fit in the living room display cabinet.
questions.fun_fact: Montoya won the 2000 Indy 500 on his first try, and won it again 15 years later.

questions.question: We play tennis together. In 2019 we won Wimbledon and the US Open in doubles and became world number one. Who are we?
questions.answer: Juan Sebastián Cabal and Robert Farah
hints: We both grew up in Cali.
