We were the first Colombians to win a Grand Slam men's doubles title.
Our last names start with C and F.
questions.description: They say two heads are better than one, and these two proved it with rackets.
questions.fun_fact: Cabal and Farah knew each other as kids and played together in the junior ranks in Cali.

questions.question: Counting the 2018 Games, how many times has Barranquilla hosted the Central American and Caribbean Games?
hints: The first time was a long time ago, in the 1940s.
Medellín and Cartagena have also hosted them once each.
72 years passed between one time and the next.
questions.description: La Arenosa never gets tired of sporting visitors.
questions.fun_fact: Barranquilla hosted the Central American and Caribbean Games in 1946 and did it again in 2018.

questions.question: A huge bronze cat by Botero arrived in this city in 1987, moved several times and now lives in the Raval neighborhood. What city is it?
hints: The cat has the round, chubby shapes typical of Botero.
It's a European city famous for its architecture and museums.
It's home to Gaudí's Sagrada Família.
questions.description: Nine lives weren't enough to make this cat stay in one place.
questions.fun_fact: Before reaching the Raval, Botero's cat stood in Ciutadella Park and then next to the Olympic Stadium on Montjuïc.

questions.question: Toxicómano Callejero mixes punk style, stencils and posters with political humor, and fills his city's walls with messages. What city is he from?
hints: The city is famous for its graffiti tours.
The city is in the Andean region.
It's the country's capital.
questions.description: His name sounds like trouble, but the walls welcome him with open arms.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá has some of the most graffiti-friendly rules in Latin America, which is why artists from all over the world go there to paint.

questions.question: The churches of Santa Clara and San Francisco in Bogotá shine with golden Baroque altars. From what period are they?
hints: Baroque art came to America with the Spanish.
Bogotá was founded in 1538, so think of the centuries after that.
It was right in the middle of colonial times, before independence.
questions.description: So much gold on one altar that even the sexton needed sunglasses.
questions.fun_fact: The Santa Clara church in Bogotá no longer holds services: today it is a museum with almost all its walls covered in paintings and gold.

questions.question: This giant bronze statue honors “El Pibe” Valderrama, next to the stadium of his hometown. Where is it?
hints: It's on the Caribbean coast.
It is the oldest city in Colombia that still stands.
Its team is Unión Magdalena.
questions.description: A hairstyle so famous they cast it in bronze so it never gets messy.
questions.fun_fact: The statue of El Pibe was made by sculptor Amilkar Ariza and was unveiled with Valderrama himself there.

questions.question: The tiple is heard in many Colombian ensembles. Which of these ensembles does NOT usually include it?
hints: Look for the group with no plucked string instruments.
Its rhythm is set by a scraper and a small drum.
Its star instrument has bellows and buttons.
questions.description: The guitar's tiny, squeaky cousin is out looking for someone to invite it to play.
questions.fun_fact: The classic conjunto vallenato has only three instruments: accordion, caja and guacharaca.

questions.question: Today almost all picks for playing the bandola or the tiple are plastic, but they used to be made from an animal's shell. Which animal?
hints: It's a sea animal.
Its shell is hard and shiny, with brown spots.
Today it's protected and can't be hunted.
questions.description: A tiny little thing, but without it the bandola would go silent.
questions.fun_fact: Because the hawksbill turtle is endangered, picks are now made of plastic that copies the look of its shell.

questions.question: With the Constitution of 1886, the country stopped being federal. What official name did it take then?
hints: The country went from nearly independent states to a central government.
That constitution was pushed by Rafael Núñez, in the period known as La Regeneración.
It's printed on the cover of the Colombian passport.
questions.description: A country with more names than grandma's cat has nicknames.
questions.fun_fact: The Constitution of 1886 lasted more than a hundred years, until the one of 1991 replaced it.

questions.question: At the Battle of Ayacucho, José María Córdova shouted: “Division, arms at will, forward, at the pace of…!” How does it end?
hints: It was a word to fire up the soldiers before the attack.
That battle, in 1824, sealed the independence of South America.
Think of the word “victory.”
questions.description: The most famous military order from a general who was only 25 years old.
questions.fun_fact: The department of Córdoba and the airport in Rionegro are named after this general from Antioquia.

questions.question: The paper of Colombian bills has colored fibers you can't see with the naked eye. How can you see them?
questions.answer: By shining ultraviolet light on it
wrong_answers: By holding it up against the light
By tilting it to one side
hints: They help fight fake bills.
It's the same light that makes white clothes glow at parties.
People call it “black” light.
questions.description: A secret the bill keeps hidden in its own paper.
questions.fun_fact: The fibers go into the paper while it's being made, so they're very hard to copy with a printer.

questions.question: I was president of Colombia in the 1970s, and my dad had been president too. Who am I?
hints: In the 1960s he founded the Movimiento Revolucionario Liberal (MRL).
He was the first governor of Cesar and helped create the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata.
He has the same first name and first surname as his dad.
questions.description: Four years in the Casa de Nariño are good for a whole lot of official photos.
questions.fun_fact: His dad, Alfonso López Pumarejo, was president twice: from 1934 to 1938 and from 1942 to 1945.

questions.question: Every July, this city's bay hosts the Fiestas del Mar, with regattas and a beauty pageant. Which city is it?
hints: It sits at the foot of the Sierra Nevada.
Tayrona National Park is very close by.
Simón Bolívar died there in 1830, at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino.
questions.description: A party where even the sailboats want to wear the beauty queen's sash.
questions.fun_fact: The Fiestas del Mar have been held since 1959 and crown their own Reina Nacional del Mar (National Queen of the Sea).

questions.question: Which white powder do people throw at each other in the parades of the Carnaval de Barranquilla?
hints: You buy it at the supermarket, in the baking aisle.
It's used to thicken natilla and coladas.
It's made from corn.
questions.description: A little white powder that leaves all of Barranquilla looking like happy ghosts.
questions.fun_fact: In 2003, UNESCO named the Carnaval de Barranquilla a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: If January 6 falls on a Wednesday, which day do Colombians get off for the Three Kings’ Day holiday?
hints: In Colombia, many holidays get moved to another day.
That way you get a long weekend.
It’s five days after January 6.
questions.description: Melchior, Caspar and Balthazar don’t get up early when they don’t have to either.
questions.fun_fact: The so-called Ley Emiliani, from 1983, moves several holidays to Monday to create long weekends.

questions.question: I'm a climber from Boyacá. In the first Tour de France with a Colombian team, I was the first from my country to wear the polka-dot jersey. Who am I?
hints: I raced in the 1980s, with the first escarabajos who went to Europe.
My polka-dot jersey lasted a few days, not all the way to Paris.
My first name is the Spanish word for what a company does when it pays for a team.
questions.description: Before Europe knew what an escarabajo was, this one was already scrambling up the Alps.
questions.fun_fact: The Tour has rewarded its best climber since 1933, but the famous polka-dot jersey only appeared in 1975.

questions.question: Egan Bernal won it at the 2021 Giro d'Italia, where it's called the “maglia rosa”. What is it?
hints: It's something the rider wears on his body.
Its color comes from the paper of the newspaper that founded the race.
Whoever wears it after the last stage wins the Giro.
questions.description: Pasta, mountains and three weeks of pedaling: the Giro has a prize for every taste.
questions.fun_fact: Egan Bernal reached Milan in the maglia rosa in 2021 and became the second Colombian to win the Giro, after Nairo Quintana.

questions.question: The Belgian team Quick-Step, where Rigoberto Urán and Álvaro Hodeg rode, is named after a brand. What does that brand make?
hints: It has nothing to do with cycling.
Its products are used inside homes.
You walk on them every day without noticing.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a ballroom dance, even though what it sells stays perfectly still.
questions.fun_fact: For a while the team was even called “Quick-Step Floors”, which gave the game away.

questions.question: I founded the Bavaria brewery, and today I'm a statue in Bogotá's Central Cemetery that people whisper wishes to. Who am I?
hints: I came to Colombia from Europe and became a businessman in Bogotá.
I had the La Perseverancia neighborhood built for my workers.
My surname has just four letters and ends in a double letter.
questions.description: A cemetery resident who gets more visitors than plenty of living people.
questions.fun_fact: Many visitors leave him flowers, coins and little notes with requests, especially on Mondays.

questions.question: I live in the rivers of the Amazon. They say that on party nights I leave the water as an elegant young man in white who wins the girls' hearts. What am I?
hints: My legend is told in Leticia and Puerto Nariño.
I'm a mammal, even though I live in the water.
My hat hides the hole on top of my head that I breathe through.
questions.description: A party charmer who never takes off his hat, not even to dance.
questions.fun_fact: The bufeo colorado, as the pink river dolphin is also called, is the largest river dolphin in the world.

questions.question: In Colombia, kids dress up in costumes and go out asking for candy on Halloween. What day in October is it?
hints: It is in the last week of the month.
The next day is All Saints' Day.
The next day, November begins.
questions.description: A night when superheroes and princesses hit the streets to get paid in candy.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian kids ask for candy by singing “triqui triqui Halloween, quiero dulces para mí” (“I want candy for me”).

questions.question: She's the daughter of Colombians, acted in “Jane the Virgin” and voiced one of the Madrigals in the English version of “Encanto”. What is that character's gift?
hints: Her character is the family's “perfect granddaughter”.
In the end she lets her hair down and bursts into color.
That character is named Isabela.
questions.description: An actress who speaks English on screen but dreams in Colombian.
questions.fun_fact: Diane Guerrero also played Maritza on the series “Orange Is the New Black”.

questions.question: You wake up at the farm and the horse's mane is full of little braids. According to legend, who made them?
hints: They're small and very mischievous.
They also get the blame when keys go missing at home.
They wear big hats and are said to fall in love with long-haired girls.
questions.description: An unlicensed hairdresser who only works at night and never charges.
questions.fun_fact: In the Colombian countryside, people say that if a duende likes a girl, he hides her things and throws pebbles on her roof to get her attention.

questions.question: In the Amazon, healers make pusanga from roots, leaves and forest scents, then rub it on or spray it on clothes. What is it believed to do?
wrong_answers: Bring rain in the dry season
hints: It has to do with the heart, not the body.
You use it with one special person in mind.
They say whoever smells it can't stop thinking about the person wearing it.
questions.description: A jungle perfume you won't find at any mall.
questions.fun_fact: In the markets of Leticia and Iquitos, little bottles of pusanga are sold to tourists as souvenirs.

questions.question: You're in a town square under a giant ceiba tree, and white tufts like cotton fall from it. What were they traditionally used for?
hints: Those tufts are very light and soft.
They were also used in life jackets because they float.
You put them where you rest your head at night.
questions.description: A tree so huge it seems to make it snow in the hot lowlands.
questions.fun_fact: For the Maya, the ceiba was the sacred tree linking the underworld, the earth and the sky.

questions.question: Clay figurines with very expressive faces were made about 2,000 years ago among the mangroves of the Pacific coast. Where?
hints: The same culture also worked gold and platinum.
The culture that made them also lived on land that now belongs to another country.
It's a port in Nariño, also famous for its marimba music.
questions.description: Long before gift shops, people were already making little clay figures that beat any souvenir.
questions.fun_fact: The goldsmiths of the Tumaco-La Tolita culture were among the first in the world to work with platinum.

questions.question: These nursery seedlings are for reforesting in Colombia. Why are native trees preferred over pines and eucalyptus?
questions.answer: They feed and shelter local wildlife
wrong_answers: They give more wood to sell
They bloom all year without fail
hints: Think of the animals that already live in that forest.
Pines and eucalyptus come from other continents.
Colombian birds and insects know their fruits and flowers.
questions.description: A nursery where the babies have leaves instead of diapers.
questions.fun_fact: Eucalyptus trees, so common in the Colombian mountains, are native to Australia.

questions.question: Which of these statements about the rubber tree is NOT true?
questions.answer: It came to Colombia from Africa
wrong_answers: Its seeds were taken to plantations in Asia
Its white sap is called latex
It caused an Amazon rubber boom around 1900
hints: The false statement is about the tree's history, not its sap.
It's true that the British took seeds to plantations in Malaysia and Sri Lanka.
It grows wild in Colombia's own rainforest.
questions.description: A tree that cries rubber, and its tears end up as tires.
questions.fun_fact: “La vorágine” (The Vortex), José Eustasio Rivera's 1924 novel, tells of the hard life of rubber tappers in the jungle.

questions.question: While snorkeling at Corales del Rosario, you see meadows of seagrass. What are they really?
hints: They're not what they seem at first glance.
They have real roots buried in the sand.
They make seeds and, now and then, bloom underwater.
questions.description: An underwater soccer field where the turtles do the mowing.
questions.fun_fact: One of the most common seagrasses in the Caribbean is called “turtle grass” because green sea turtles eat it.

questions.question: The Chuza reservoir sits in a protected páramo, and its water travels through tunnels across the mountains. Who does it supply?
hints: The páramo is in the Eastern Andes range (cordillera Oriental).
It's inside Chingaza National Natural Park.
We're talking about the country's capital.
questions.description: The water in your shower doesn't come from nowhere: it comes from way, way up.
questions.fun_fact: Most of the water people drink in Bogotá comes from the páramos of Chingaza.

questions.question: This rocky island in the Colombian Pacific is a World Heritage Site. What animals is it famous for?
hints: The famous residents don't live on the island, but in the water around it.
Divers travel from all over the world to see them in large groups.
Many of them have heads shaped like a hammer.
questions.description: A lonely rock in the sea that gets more visitors under the water than on top of it.
questions.fun_fact: Around Malpelo, you can see schools of hundreds of hammerhead sharks swimming together.

questions.question: They are the country's big multi-sport festival and were first held in Cali in 1928. Who competes in the Juegos Nacionales?
hints: Each team marches in the opening ceremony under its own flag.
Valle, Antioquia and Bogotá usually fight for first place in the medal table.
Colombia has 32 of them, plus the Capital District.
questions.description: A homemade Olympics, with no passport and no jet lag.
questions.fun_fact: The first Juegos Nacionales, in Cali in 1928, were also the country's first big multi-sport games.

questions.question: In 2021, Cali hosted the first edition of a new Pan American Games, whose champions earned a spot at Santiago 2023. Who competed?
hints: They were a kind of warm-up for the regular Pan American Games.
Many of the athletes were just finishing high school or starting college.
Their official name adds the word “Junior.”
questions.description: A sports party in Cali where the prize was a direct ticket to Chile.
questions.fun_fact: Cali hosted the first Junior Pan American Games in history.

questions.question: You're playing ponchados at recess and you have the ball in your hand. Why do you throw it?
wrong_answers: To shoot it through a hoop
To send it over a net
To kick it into a goal
hints: The players on the other team run and dodge.
It's played by two teams, each on its own side of the court.
Whoever gets hit is out of the game.
questions.description: A recess classic played with more shouting than rules.
questions.fun_fact: Ponchados has many names around the world: in some countries it's called “quemados,” and in English it's dodgeball.

questions.question: Speed skaters train at patinódromos (skating tracks). How long is one lap of the track, usually?
hints: It is shorter than the running track in a stadium.
An elite skater covers it in a little over 15 seconds.
It is half a lap of a running track.
questions.description: Round and round they go, and nobody gets dizzy… well, almost nobody.
questions.fun_fact: Patinódromos have banked curves, tilted inward, so skaters can take them at full speed.

questions.question: You're at the Museo del Oro looking at Muisca pieces. Which of these things did the Muisca NOT do?
hints: The Muisca lived on the high plateau where Bogotá and Tunja stand today.
Their houses and temples were made of wood, mud and straw.
That was more something the Aztecs and the Maya did.
questions.description: A surprise test on the very first neighbors of the sabana.
questions.fun_fact: The Muisca Temple of the Sun in Sogamoso was made of wood, and the Spanish set it on fire by accident in 1537.

questions.question: Manuel María Paz painted watercolors of the country's landscapes and people for Agustín Codazzi's Chorographic Commission. In which decade?
hints: It was after independence.
The country was then called New Granada.
It was around the same time slavery was abolished in the country, in 1851.
questions.description: Before Instagram, this was how you made a travel album of a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: The Chorographic Commission's watercolors are kept today in the National Library of Colombia and are among the first portraits of the country's regions.

questions.question: Look at this building: today it is the Museum of Modern Art of Medellín. What was it used for before?
hints: It stands in Ciudad del Río, near the Medellín River.
Look at how much it looks like a factory hall.
Steel was worked there.
questions.description: This building changed jobs without changing its walls.
questions.fun_fact: The MAMM holds a large collection by Débora Arango, the painter from Antioquia whose nudes shocked the society of her time.

questions.question: The Bunde tolimense became the anthem of Tolima. Who composed its music?
hints: He was a musician who lived and worked in Ibagué.
He founded the Tolima Conservatory.
His surname is also the Spanish name of a region in central Spain.
questions.description: A musical recipe from Tolima: mix well, serve in Ibagué, and stand up to sing it.
questions.fun_fact: The Bunde tolimense is so loved that in Tolima it is sung at official events almost as if it were the national anthem.

questions.question: According to tradition, troops in Nariño were already singing the southern bambuco “La guaneña.” In which century?
hints: It's not a radio or record-era song: it's much older.
It's linked to soldiers and battles in the south of the country.
It's said to have been heard in battles in Bolívar's time.
questions.description: A song with so much history that in Pasto people sing it like an oath.
questions.fun_fact: “La guaneña” is seen as the people's anthem of Nariño and is played at the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos in Pasto.

questions.question: Complete: “Jorge Velosa is to carranga as Darío Gómez is to…”
hints: Darío Gómez was from San Jerónimo, in Antioquia.
His songs are some of the most played in cantinas.
Darío Gómez was called “the king” of this genre.
questions.description: Two men in hats with guitars, and a test of how much small-town radio you've heard.
questions.fun_fact: Darío Gómez wrote “Nadie es eterno”, one of the most sung songs in Colombia's cantinas.

questions.question: “El año viejo” is the anthem of Colombian December music. What kind of rhythms does that music use?
hints: It's music for dancing in couples, not for listening sitting down.
“El año viejo” was written by Crescencio Salcedo, who was born on the coast.
They're the same rhythms people dance to in Barranquilla and Cartagena.
questions.description: The official soundtrack of natilla, buñuelos and the uncle who dances on his own.
questions.fun_fact: “El año viejo” became famous in the voice of Mexican singer Tony Camargo, even though a Colombian wrote it.

questions.question: When the music starts, I’m the first to “tirar paso” and I don’t stop until the party ends. Who am I?
hints: What I do at the party, I do with my feet and hips.
In Colombia, “tirar paso” is what you do out on the floor.
Without me, salsa and cumbia would leave the floor empty.
questions.description: Every party has someone like this, and it’s not exactly the one washing the dishes.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia “tirar paso” means to dance, and someone who does it really well is a “buen bailador” or even “un trompo” (a spinning top).

questions.question: On Colombia's Pacific coast, people sing to the saints and the Baby Jesus with bombo, cununos and guasá. What is this song called?
hints: You hear it a lot at the December festivities in Guapi, Timbiquí and Tumaco.
It is sung mostly by women, gathered around an altar.
In everyday Spanish, its name is the soft song a mom sings while rocking her baby.
questions.description: A serenade for the saints, right in the middle of a Pacific Christmas.
questions.fun_fact: The marimba music and traditional chants of Colombia's Pacific coast are recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: I was born in the neighborhoods of Cartagena and in San Basilio de Palenque, to the sound of African guitars, and Charles King is one of my great voices. Which rhythm am I?
hints: I'm played at full blast on huge, colorfully painted sound systems.
Those sound systems are called picós.
My name comes from a long knife used on the coast.
questions.description: A rhythm that showed up in the neighborhoods without asking and took over the whole party.
questions.fun_fact: Champeta is named after the “champeta,” a knife, because at first the elite used the word to look down on the people who danced it.

questions.question: Look at this instrument from the bandas papayeras. How do you play it?
hints: It needs no sticks and no strings.
You have to put your lips on a mouthpiece.
It's like filling up a balloon with air, but music comes out.
questions.description: If the party is too quiet, this instrument wakes it up in one second.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, bandas papayeras liven up bullfights, fairs and soccer games with trumpets, trombones, clarinets and a big bass drum.

questions.question: In Colombia, someone invites you to “echar un pie.” What are they suggesting?
hints: It's a typical plan for a Friday night or a party.
Your feet work hard, but you don't get anywhere.
You do it when a cumbia or a vallenato is playing.
questions.description: An invitation that sounds like it came from a shoe store, but didn't.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “echemos un pie” is an invitation to dance, just like “tirar paso” or “mover el esqueleto.”

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. "Echar un pie" does mean to dance, but sources place it in the Caribbean, Venezuela and Cuba/salsa contexts. I found no source calling it Colombian. The fun fact says "In Colombia", and I couldn't verify that. "Tirar paso" is Colombian, and "mover el esqueleto" is general Spanish.

questions.question: On the Magdalena River and in the marshes (ciénagas), many fishermen go out by canoe with their atarraya. What is an atarraya?
wrong_answers: A long pole for the canoe
hints: It is used to take something out of the water, not to move through it.
When it hits the water it opens into a circle, and small lead weights pull it down.
It is made of many knots and holes that let the water out, but not the fish.
questions.description: A word that sounds like a witch's spell but smells like fish.
questions.fun_fact: A good fisherman can throw an atarraya so that it opens into an almost perfect circle several meters across.

questions.question: Juanchaco and Ladrilleros, Pacific beaches where you can see humpback whales, are in the highlighted department. Which one is it?
hints: Its capital isn't on the coast but inland.
Colombia's most important Pacific port is in this department.
Its capital is Cali.
questions.description: Whales have a favorite vacation spot too, and they don't ask for a hotel with a pool.
questions.fun_fact: Humpback whales travel thousands of kilometers from Antarctica to give birth in the warm waters of Colombia's Pacific coast, between July and October.

questions.question: On Malpelo Island, in Colombia's Pacific, lives a lizard found nowhere else in the world. What kind of species is it?
hints: Nobody brought it from somewhere else, and it isn't going anywhere.
Biologists use this word for animals and plants found only in one place.
It's the same word used for the birds that live only in Colombia.
questions.description: A reptile with very noisy neighbors: nothing but birds screaming all day.
questions.fun_fact: Malpelo Island is home to several reptile species found nowhere else on the planet.

questions.question: On Colombia's Caribbean beaches, swimmers shuffle their feet through the sand so they don't step on this animal with a spine in its tail. What is it?
hints: It's a fish, even if it doesn't look like one at first.
It's flat and swims by flapping its fins like wings.
It hides buried in the sandy bottom.
questions.description: The beach neighbor nobody wants to step on, and it doesn't want to be stepped on either.
questions.fun_fact: Stingrays have no bones: their skeleton is made of cartilage, just like that of sharks, their relatives.

questions.question: This instrument is heard in almost all the salsa of Fruko y sus Tesos. Listen: which one is it?
hints: It's made of metal and you blow into it.
Its sound is low and can glide from one note to another.
It has a long slide that moves back and forth.
questions.description: The instrument that gets even grandma up to dance salsa.
questions.fun_fact: New York salsa of the 1960s and 1970s made orchestras with trombones fashionable, and Colombian orchestras followed that sound.

questions.question: In Colombia, the company Super sells a famous candy called Trululú. What are they?
hints: They're soft and stretchy.
Many come coated in sugar or a sour powder.
They stretch when you bite them, like sweet rubber.
questions.description: A candy that Grandma swears will leave you with no teeth.
questions.fun_fact: Gummies are stretchy thanks to gelatin, which is made from collagen.

questions.question: You're making a tres leches cake. Which of these is NOT one of the three classic milks?
hints: Think about where each one comes from.
Two of the classic ones come in a can.
The odd one out doesn't come from a cow but from a nut.
questions.description: A cake so soggy it should come with a towel.
questions.fun_fact: Tres leches cake became popular across Latin America in the 20th century, partly thanks to recipes printed on cans of milk.

questions.question: At a corner store in Colombia, you ask for a Jumbo. What do they hand you?
wrong_answers: An ice pop on a stick
hints: It melts if you leave it in the sun.
It's brown and crunchy inside.
It's a cousin of the Jet bar, but with peanuts.
questions.description: It's named like an elephant, but you don't need a truck to carry it home.
questions.fun_fact: Peanuts aren't nuts: they're legumes, relatives of beans.

questions.question: In Colombia many people spread natas on bread, and a sweet is made from them with sugar. What are natas?
questions.answer: The layer that forms on top of milk
wrong_answers: The foam on whisked hot chocolate
hints: You don't have to buy them: they appear on their own in the pot.
They form from the milk's proteins and fat when it is boiled and cools down.
It's that thin film floating on boiled milk.
questions.description: Some people fish it out of their mug looking disgusted, others happily spread it on bread.
questions.fun_fact: Dulce de natas is a traditional Colombian dessert that grandmothers made by saving up the natas from several days.

questions.question: Canned peaches come floating in syrup. What is the syrup made of?
hints: It's just two ingredients from the kitchen.
One is clear and comes out of the kitchen sink.
The other is white, and you add it to juice to make it sweet.
questions.description: Fruit that goes for a swim in a pool that comes in a can.
questions.fun_fact: Syrup helps preserve fruit because the sugar stops many germs from growing.

questions.question: Someone proudly says, “Yo soy bumangués.” Where is this person from?
hints: It's a city in Santander.
It's called “la Ciudad Bonita” and “the city of parks”.
Its fans cheer for the city's Atlético, the “leopard” team.
questions.description: A demonym so odd that even spelling gets nervous.
questions.fun_fact: Strange as it sounds, people born in Bucaramanga are usually called bumangueses rather than “bucaramangueses”.

questions.question: Cartagena earned the nickname “La Heroica” by holding out through a long siege in 1815. Against whom?
hints: It happened during the fight for independence.
They wanted to win back the colonies for the King of Spain.
Their leader was nicknamed “the Peacemaker”.
questions.description: A city that earned its nickname by holding out longer than a grandma waiting for her telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: The siege lasted more than 100 days, and ever since, Cartagena has been known as “La Heroica”.

questions.question: Which actress played Beatriz Pinzón Solano in “Yo soy Betty, la fea”?
hints: She is from Bogotá and started acting very young.
Years later she also worked as an actress in Argentina.
Her father is the actor Luis Fernando Orozco.
questions.description: Glasses, braces and a brain too big for the president's office.
questions.fun_fact: Ana María Orozco put Betty's glasses back on in 2024 for the sequel “Betty la Fea: The Story Continues.”

questions.question: In “Café con aroma de mujer” (1994), Guy Ecker played Sebastián, who falls for Gaviota. Which family was he from?
hints: They were a rich family of coffee growers.
The family's matriarch was against Sebastián's romance with Gaviota.
The name starts with the letter V.
questions.description: A leading man, a coffee harvest and a cup of tinto that turned into a love story.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2021 remake, Sebastián was played by Cuban actor William Levy.

questions.question: In this Caracol telenovela, Brayan Galindo and Andrés Ferreira find out they were switched at birth, and their lives swap. What was it called?
wrong_answers: Hijo de nadie, hijo de rey
hints: It premiered in 2007.
The title describes the two main characters.
In Spanish, someone who suddenly gets rich is called a “nuevo rico.”
questions.description: One day you're asking the corner store to put it on your tab, the next you have a chauffeur.
questions.fun_fact: Babies switched at birth are one of the oldest tricks in melodrama, and they still work!

questions.question: In Colombia, kids play “yermis” in the street with two teams and a rubber ball. What do you have to knock down with the ball?
hints: After knocking it down, you have to build it back up.
It's made of something left over after drinking a soda.
They're small and round, and you stack them on top of each other.
questions.description: A street game where yelling, running and dodging are part of the rulebook.
questions.fun_fact: In yermis, while one team rebuilds the tower, the other tries to tag them out by hitting them with the ball.

questions.question: One team chases and the other runs; those caught go to “jail,” and a free teammate rescues them with a touch. What is the game called?
hints: There are two teams with different roles.
One team plays the “good guys” and the other the “bad guys.”
One side would wear uniforms and badges; the other, masks.
questions.description: A game where your legs are the only thing between you and freedom.
questions.fun_fact: In many parts of Colombia, if the last free robber manages to touch the jail, all the prisoners go free at once.

questions.question: At town fiestas, the vara de premio is a tall pole with prizes at the top, but almost nobody can climb it. Why?
questions.answer: It's smeared with grease or tallow
wrong_answers: You aren't allowed to use your feet
It's shaken with ropes from below
hints: It's a very old contest that is also played at festivals in Europe and Asia.
The problem isn't the rules or the prizes, it's the pole itself.
In many countries it's called the “palo encebado.”
questions.description: At a town fiesta, the easiest prize to see is the hardest one to bring down.
questions.fun_fact: To get up the pole, contestants often build human towers or wipe off the grease with sand and rags as they climb.

questions.question: In the juego de la rana, what happens if your token goes into the frog's mouth?
hints: It's the hardest thing to pull off in the game.
Every player aims right there.
The other holes give fewer points.
questions.description: A metal animal that has spent decades with its mouth wide open in neighborhood corner stores.
questions.fun_fact: The frog game is so old that it has relatives in Peru, Spain and France.

questions.question: Colombia's first TV broadcast was on June 13, 1954. From which building in Bogotá was it sent out?
hints: It happened under the government of General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla.
The first studios were set up in the building's basement.
It's a place full of books.
questions.description: Before series on your phone, it all started with a black-and-white screen.
questions.fun_fact: Television came to Colombia to celebrate Rojas Pinilla's first year in power, and at first there were very few TV sets in the whole country.

questions.question: García Márquez's first short stories, later collected in “Eyes of a Blue Dog,” appeared in El Espectador. In which decade?
hints: Gabo was a law student in Bogotá.
It was about twenty years before “One Hundred Years of Solitude.”
It was shortly before the Bogotazo.
questions.description: Before Macondo, Gabo was already spotting dogs in strange colors.
questions.fun_fact: His first published story, “The Third Resignation,” appeared in El Espectador in 1947, when Gabo was 20.

questions.question: Rafael Pombo published it in New York in 1867 for the Appleton publishing house, with versions of English nursery rhymes. Which book is it?
hints: Pombo lived in the United States for many years as a diplomat.
Two years later, the same publisher put out his “Cuentos morales para niños formales”.
Its title says the stories came with pictures.
questions.description: Made in New York, learned by heart in every school in Colombia.
questions.fun_fact: Two years later, Pombo published another book with the same publisher: “Cuentos morales para niños formales”.

questions.question: When did “Alma llanera”, the song sung across the plains of Colombia and Venezuela, premiere?
hints: It's much older than radio in Colombia.
It premiered in Caracas as part of a zarzuela, a Spanish-style operetta.
It's already more than 100 years old.
questions.description: The song every llanero sings with one hand on his heart and his hat in the other.
questions.fun_fact: “Alma llanera” premiered in Caracas in 1914, and in Venezuela people call it their “second national anthem.”

questions.question: I live among cattle and savanna, I wear a hat and cotizas, and at parties I stomp out zapateo with my partner until dawn. Who am I?
hints: My land is flat, huge, and floods in the rainy season.
I dance joropo to the sound of the harp.
I live in Casanare, Meta or Arauca.
questions.description: Someone who kicks up more dust dancing than a herd in a stampede.
questions.fun_fact: In joropo, the man's zapateo and the woman's escobillao are backed by the beat of the harp, the cuatro and the maracas.

questions.question: The bombo is a big, round drum played with mallets that booms in cumbia and chirimía. What is it traditionally made of?
hints: Its materials come from nature.
One part comes from a tree.
The other part, the one you hit, is animal skin.
questions.description: The one that gets the heart beating at any cumbiamba.
questions.fun_fact: The bombo has two leather heads, one on each side, so it can be played on both sides.

questions.question: Which of these words does NOT describe Lake Tota, in Boyacá?
hints: Think about where Boyacá is on the map of Colombia.
The lake sits more than 3,000 m (9,800 ft) up, surrounded by onion fields.
To reach the sea from there, you'd have to travel hundreds of kilometers.
questions.description: A lake so cold that even the trout ask for a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Lake Tota has its own Playa Blanca, a beach of pale sand more than 3,000 m (9,800 ft) above sea level.

questions.question: The Nazca booby is a white seabird with a black mask that dives headfirst into the sea. On which Colombian island does it have one of the world's largest colonies?
hints: It's in the Pacific Ocean.
It's a rock with almost no trees, very far from the coast.
It's famous among divers for its schools of hammerhead sharks.
questions.description: A bird that jumps into the sea headfirst as if it just spotted a sale on sardines.
questions.fun_fact: Nazca boobies usually lay two eggs, but normally only one chick survives.

questions.question: Quebrada Las Gachas, a creek with round, hot-tub-like holes in a reddish rock bed, is in the highlighted department. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the town of Guadalupe.
It's the land of hormigas culonas and the Chicamocha Canyon.
Its capital is Bucaramanga.
questions.description: A river that came with free hot tubs and no entrance fee.
questions.fun_fact: Quebrada Las Gachas is nicknamed “the Caño Cristales of Santander” because of the colors of its riverbed.

questions.question: The Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta was the first Colombian wetland protected by the Ramsar Convention. In what year was that treaty signed in Iran?
hints: It was long before Colombia joined the treaty in the late 1990s.
Back then, worry about the environment was only starting to grow around the world.
It was in the early 1970s.
questions.description: An international treaty to protect the places where frogs throw their parties.
questions.fun_fact: Ramsar is an Iranian city on the shore of the Caspian Sea, and its name is now forever linked to wetlands.

questions.question: Sidestepper was born in Bogotá in the late 1990s, led by English producer Richard Blair. What did it mix with cumbia and salsa?
hints: Blair had worked at Peter Gabriel's studio in England.
People danced to it in clubs, with DJs and sound systems.
Think synthesizers, beats and drum and bass.
questions.description: An Englishman came to Colombia, heard a drum and was never the same again.
questions.fun_fact: Richard Blair met Totó la Momposina at Peter Gabriel's Real World studio, traveled to Colombia in 1993 and stayed in Bogotá for several years.

questions.question: I sang in Pedro Salcedo's band and wrote lyrics for a Juan Madera cumbia about a red skirt that is now heard all over the world. Who am I?
hints: I was from Magdalena, and the song was recorded around 1960.
The song is “La pollera colorá”.
My surname starts with “Chop…”.
questions.description: A skirt so famous it has done more world tours than many singers.
questions.fun_fact: “La pollera colorá” started out as an instrumental piece by Juan Madera and only later got the lyrics everyone sings.

questions.question: In Colombia, the vinyl records played at viejotecas are also called discos de…
hints: It's the name of a material, even though it isn't the exact material.
Salsa collectors in Cali hunt for them like gold.
It sounds like a chemistry word ending in “-ato”.
questions.description: Your grandfather guards it like a treasure, and you mistake it for a black plate.
questions.fun_fact: Cali has an Encuentro de Melómanos y Coleccionistas, where very rare salsa records change hands.

questions.question: At the parranda, “El año viejo” is playing and everyone awaits the twelve chimes with their grapes ready. What night is it?
hints: The next day, you need a new calendar.
Some people go out for a run with a suitcase.
It's the last night of the year.
questions.description: The parranda nobody wants to miss, not even grandma.
questions.fun_fact: “El año viejo” was written by Crescencio Salcedo, and in it the singer is thankful that the year left him “una chiva, una burra negra” (a goat, a black donkey).

questions.question: Listen: which salsa instrument is this?
hints: It's played standing up, with sticks.
Its drums have metal bodies.
The player also strikes the metal shell: that's called “cáscara”.
questions.description: In Cali, salsa is taken so seriously that even the traffic lights seem to keep the clave.
questions.fun_fact: Tito Puente, the “King of the Timbales”, made this instrument famous by playing it standing up at the front of the orchestra.

questions.question: They're paper-thin, rolled into a little tube or cone, and street vendors sell them alongside ice cream. What are they called?
hints: They're made from a very thin flour batter.
They crunch the moment you bite them.
In Spanish, their name sounds like a tiny boat.
questions.description: The crunchy sidekick no ice cream ever wants to let go of.
questions.fun_fact: Barquillos are cooked on hot griddles, much like the ones used for obleas, and rolled up while they're still warm.

questions.question: It comes as powder in a little packet, sets in the fridge, wobbles on the plate and comes in red, green and yellow. What is it?
hints: It's a cold dessert.
At birthday parties it's served in little cups.
If you shake the plate, the whole thing moves as if it were dancing.
questions.description: The most colorful guest at any kids' birthday party, after the clown.
questions.fun_fact: Gelatin sets because its collagen forms a net that traps the water.

questions.question: Look at the photo: which dessert is this, sold in little cups on the street in Colombia?
hints: It's cold and very sweet.
The fruit is red and has tiny seeds on the outside.
It has white cream on top.
questions.description: The street-food craving that fits in a little cup and disappears in two minutes.
questions.fun_fact: Each “seed” on a strawberry is actually a tiny fruit, and one strawberry has about 200 of them.

questions.question: It's a cold dessert eaten with a spoon, made with cream and condensed milk and topped with yellow pulp and crunchy black seeds. Which fruit is it?
hints: The fruit is quite sour.
Its skin is hard and gets wrinkly as it ripens.
It's a top juice flavor in Colombia, and its English name has a strong feeling in it.
questions.description: A dessert that makes you pull a sour face before you smile.
questions.fun_fact: Spanish missionaries named the maracuyá flower the passionflower because they saw symbols of the Passion of Christ in it, and that's why the fruit is called passion fruit in English.

questions.question: It's a lot like flan, it gets baked until a golden crust forms on top, and it was grandma's dessert. What is leche asada made with?
hints: It has no grain in it.
It sets in the heat of the oven thanks to something a hen lays.
They are the same basic ingredients as flan.
questions.description: The flan that went into the oven and came back with a tan.
questions.fun_fact: Unlike flan, leche asada usually has no caramel, and its top is left to turn golden in the oven.

questions.question: You flip me out of the mold, I'm yellow, I wiggle a little and wear a hat of melted caramel. What am I?
hints: I'm made with milk and eggs.
I'm served cold, in slices.
My name is short: just four letters.
questions.description: A dessert that arrives on the plate upside down and happy.
questions.fun_fact: The caramel goes in the bottom of the mold, which is why it ends up on top when you flip the flan.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this statue in Cartagena honors the Spaniard who founded the city in 1533. Who is he?
hints: He isn’t the founder of Bogotá or of Cali.
Cartagena has a famous theater named after him.
His surname starts with H, like Cartagena’s Teatro ___.
questions.description: Everyone takes photos in Cartagena, but hardly anyone asks the bronze gentleman his name.
questions.fun_fact: Cartagena was founded on June 1, 1533, and was named after Cartagena in Spain, where many of the sailors came from.

questions.question: Look at this detail of a silleta de flores. What is the nickname of the city famous for this tradition?
hints: The silletas parade every August at a big fair.
It's the capital of Antioquia.
The nickname refers to its mild climate all year round.
questions.description: Here people carry entire gardens on their backs and still manage to smile.
questions.fun_fact: Some silletas in the parade weigh more than 70 kilos (155 lb), and the silleteros carry them on their backs for the whole route.

questions.question: You're at a get-together where everyone is from Quindío. Who snuck in because they are NOT from Quindío?
hints: All four cities are in the Eje Cafetero.
Salento, the gateway to the Cocora Valley, is definitely on the guest list.
The gatecrasher is from the capital of Caldas.
questions.description: A get-together with more tinto than guests.
questions.fun_fact: Quindío is one of Colombia's smallest departments, but it's home to the Cocora Valley and the wax palm, the national tree.

questions.question: If you are born in Palmira, Buga or Buenaventura, what are you called, going by your department?
hints: All three cities are in the same department.
It's famous for its huge sugarcane fields.
Its department is named after a valley and a river.
questions.description: Your cédula says where you were born, but your accent shouts it first.
questions.fun_fact: Buenaventura, in Valle del Cauca, is Colombia's most important port on the Pacific Ocean.

questions.question: Which of these words is NOT used for someone from Barranquilla?
hints: In Colombia, people from each region have nicknames for people from the others.
One of the words is used on the Coast for people from the interior.
It's what costeños call bogotanos.
questions.description: “Quien lo vive es quien lo goza,” but not everyone gets to live it from birth.
questions.fun_fact: On the Coast, “cachaco” was used mainly for people from Bogotá, but today it applies to almost anyone from the country's interior.

questions.question: Born in the capital of Valle del Cauca, a city famous for its salsa and its December Feria. What is this person called?
hints: This person's city has a Cristo Rey statue high on a hill.
Next to the river in this person's city stands a giant sculpture of a cat.
This person's city is Cali.
questions.description: Here even babies are born with their feet moving to the beat of the clave.
questions.fun_fact: El Gato del Río, by maestro Hernando Tejada, is joined by many cat “novias” (girlfriends) painted by different artists.

questions.question: RCN's telenovela “Hasta que la plata nos separe” (2006) got a Mexican version in 2009. Which word replaced “plata” in the title?
hints: Televisa made the Mexican version, starring Itatí Cantoral and Pablo Montero.
The word comes from the Latin “denarius,” the name of a Roman coin.
It's what you take out of an ATM, said without slang.
questions.description: Some love can survive anything, except the bank statement.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, money is also called “lana,” but Televisa chose the neutral “dinero” for its version.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Betty, la fea,” Lorna Cepeda played Patricia Fernández. What about her inspired her famous nickname?
hints: The nickname came from the women of the “cuartel de las feas.”
It has to do with something done at the hair salon.
The nickname joins the Spanish word for “hair” with what she did to its color.
questions.description: At Ecomoda there was more gossip than fabric, and this secretary was in almost all of it.
questions.fun_fact: Patricia was always bragging about her “six semesters of Finance and International Relations.”

questions.question: The German telenovela “Verliebt in Berlin” (2005) adapted a Colombian story. In what year did the original premiere in Colombia?
hints: The original premiered in the 20th century.
The original aired on RCN and became one of the most adapted telenovelas in the world.
It was the last year before the turn of the millennium.
questions.description: A secretary with braces who learned German without taking a single class.
questions.fun_fact: In the German version, the heroine wasn't called Betty but Lisa Plenske.

questions.question: In “Pasión de gavilanes”, Norma, Jimena and Sara live at Hacienda Elizondo until the Reyes brothers arrive. In which fictional town is it?
hints: It's not García Márquez's town.
It's named after a saint.
The saint is one of the four Gospel writers.
questions.description: Three sisters, three brothers and a hacienda with more drama than horses.
questions.fun_fact: Although many people think it's Mexican, “Pasión de gavilanes” was filmed in Colombia, co-produced by Telemundo and Caracol.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact says “Pasión de gavilanes” was coproduced by Telemundo and Caracol. As far as I know, the producers were Telemundo and RTI Colombia, and Caracol was only the Colombian broadcaster. The translator flagged the same doubt, and the fact check covered only the town. Correct the source fun fact (e.g. “coproduced by Telemundo and RTI”) or drop the coproducer clause, then re-sync the translation.

questions.question: The channel RCN is named after “Radio Cadena Nacional” and made “Yo soy Betty, la fea.” In which city is its main headquarters?
hints: It's inland, not on the coast.
It's a very high, chilly city.
It's the capital of Colombia.
questions.description: Three letters that have made half of Colombia cry in front of the TV.
questions.fun_fact: RCN's radio network was on the air for decades before its TV channel was born.

questions.question: In Colombia, a brave go-getter is called “berraco” or “berraca.” The word comes from the name of a male animal. Which one?
hints: It's a farm animal.
Its meat is very common in Colombian cooking.
Its female is called a sow, or “marrana” in Spanish.
questions.description: A word Colombians use for the brave, the fierce, and anything that's really great.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “¡qué verraquera!” means something is fantastic.

questions.question: I move very slowly, carry my house on my back and leave a shiny trail. In Colombia, a TV channel is named after me. Who am I?
hints: I like to come out when it rains.
My house is a spiral shell.
The channel that aired “Pedro el escamoso” bears my name.
questions.description: A character who never misses the evening telenovela, even when it's on the other channel.
questions.fun_fact: The name Caracol (Spanish for “snail”) comes from the initials of “Cadena Radial Colombiana,” the Colombian Radio Network.

questions.question: I'm a reggaeton songwriter from Medellín. My songs were stolen, I spent years in prison in New York, and I came back for revenge. Who am I?
hints: Caracol told my story in 2018.
They call me the queen of a music genre.
My enemy is Charly Flow.
questions.description: A songwriter with plenty of flow and an even longer memory.
questions.fun_fact: “La Reina del Flow” was such a hit that it came back for a second season in 2021.

questions.question: Every night you watch a new episode of “Yo soy Betty, la fea,” a love story full of twists. What kind of show is it?
hints: It tells a made-up story.
It has villains, lovers and lots of episodes.
Colombia sells a huge number of these shows to other countries, and each episode ends with a dramatic “to be continued.”
questions.description: The hour when nobody at home talks, nobody answers their phone, and the remote control is sacred.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the countries that sells the most telenovelas to the rest of the world.

questions.question: You're playing with a Spanish deck of cards: the sota is the 10 and the caballo (knight) is the 11. Which figure is the 12?
hints: It's the most important of the three figures.
It wears a crown on its head.
It rules a kingdom and sits on a throne.
questions.description: At grandma's table you play for points, for pride and for the last empanada.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish deck has no queen: its three face cards are the sota, the caballo and the rey (king).

questions.question: Playing parqués, you roll doubles again and again. How many doubles in a row do you need to send a piece straight to the cielo (heaven)?
hints: It's more than two, but not many.
It's an odd number.
It's the number of sides of a triangle.
questions.description: The only game where your own cousin is happy to send you to jail.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian parqués comes from Spanish parchís, which was itself inspired by pachisi, an ancient game from India.

questions.question: In tejo, bursting a mecha scores 3 points and landing in the bocín scores 6. Do both at once and you get 9. What is that shot called?
hints: It's the dream shot of every tejo player.
It scores the most points of any single throw.
Its name sounds like “moño,” the Spanish word for a bow.
questions.description: The “boom!” heard every Saturday at the tejo court that makes the neighborhood dogs jump.
questions.fun_fact: Tejo was declared Colombia's national sport by law in 2000.

questions.question: The púa is the metal tip of a trompo (spinning top): it spins on it and scratches the floor. In street games, what else do kids use it for?
questions.answer: To hit the other player's top
wrong_answers: To hang it on the wall
To measure how long it spins
hints: It has to do with the other players.
It's a rough use, not a gentle one.
In Colombia, that hit is called a “quiña”.
questions.description: A tiny metal tip does all the work while the wood gets all the fame.
questions.fun_fact: Many kids sharpened the púa of their trompo so their “quiñas” would leave a mark on the rival's top.

questions.question: You're making a tail for your kite out of things from home. Which of these does NOT work for the tail?
hints: The tail has to fly along with the kite.
Think about how much each thing weighs.
One of these sinks in water and won't rise with the wind.
questions.description: August in Colombia: the month when the sky fills with colors and the power lines fill with trapped kites.
questions.fun_fact: The tail keeps the kite balanced: without it, the kite spins and dives out of control.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Iron hex nuts are plausible as the heavy wrong item, but I did not search for this one. Kite tails are normally light, so heavy nuts would not work. Some kite makers tie small weights to a tail, so the answer could be argued. August as Colombia's kite month is well known.

questions.question: In the song “Un elefante se balanceaba,” when the elephant sees the spider web holds, who does it go and call?
hints: It's a song that helps kids learn to count.
After that call, the spider web has to hold even more weight.
It's just as big and also has a trunk.
questions.description: A song that never ends, perfect for long car trips.
questions.fun_fact: The song can go on forever: each verse adds one more elephant to the spider web.

questions.question: If the cometa won't fly straight, you have to adjust its frenillo. What is the frenillo?
questions.answer: The strings joining the frame to the line
wrong_answers: The strips that make up the tail
The stick the line is wound around
The paper that covers the frame
hints: It's part of the kite, not the sky or the wind.
It decides the angle at which the kite faces the wind.
It's the point where the long line you hold is tied on.
questions.description: The best-kept secret of veteran kite flyers, right after where they buy their paper.
questions.fun_fact: If the frenillo is set wrong, the kite spins or dives headfirst into the ground, even when the wind is great.

questions.question: On “Yo me llamo”, contestants sing, dress and move exactly like a famous singer. What do you call someone who does that?
hints: They don't sing their own songs, but someone else's.
The judges want them to look and sound as close to the real artist as possible.
They pretend to be another person on stage.
questions.description: Here nobody wants to be themselves, and they still get a round of applause.
questions.fun_fact: Several “Yo me llamo” contestants became so famous that they now give concerts all over Colombia as the artist's look-alike.

questions.question: Which TV host created “Sábados Felices”, the show famous for its joke-telling contest?
hints: The show started in the early 1970s.
Besides creating it, he hosted it for many years.
His last name starts with L.
questions.description: A man who has made Colombia laugh on Saturdays for half a century deserves a serious question.
questions.fun_fact: “Sábados Felices” started in 1972 and is one of the longest-running comedy shows on TV anywhere in the world.

questions.question: She's from Barranquilla, played Gloria on “Modern Family”, and Forbes named her the world's highest-paid TV actress for several years. Who is she?
hints: She started out hosting TV shows in Colombia and Miami.
On US TV she's famous for her humor and her strong accent.
Her last name almost rhymes with “Niagara”.
questions.description: From the Barranquilla Carnival to the red carpet, no layovers.
questions.fun_fact: Sofía Vergara was also a judge on “America's Got Talent”.

questions.question: In what year did “Fake Profile” (Perfil falso), the Colombian series about a dating-app scam that became a global hit, premiere on Netflix?
hints: It's a recent series, from after the pandemic.
It premiered in the middle of the year, and its second season came some time later.
It was the same year the “Barbie” movie hit theaters.
questions.description: Before you swipe right, take a good look at that photo, or things could turn into a telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: “Fake Profile” made Netflix's global top 10 for non-English series shortly after its premiere.

questions.question: Which of these characters was NOT created by the comedian Jaime Garzón?
hints: Three of them appeared on shows like “Zoociedad”, “Quac! El Noticero” or “Lechuza”.
The odd one out belongs to a comedian from Boyacá who was famous on “Sábados Felices”.
The odd one out was played by Pedro González.
questions.description: One of these gentlemen sneaked into another comedian's gallery of characters.
questions.fun_fact: Godofredo Cínico Caspa was a very right-wing old man whom Garzón used to make fun of the politicians of his time.

questions.question: Who teamed up with Martín de Francisco as the comedy duo behind “La Tele” and the animated series “El siguiente programa”?
hints: They were a very famous duo on Colombian television in the 1990s.
In “El siguiente programa”, the two of them voiced the cartoon characters.
He is an actor and comedian from Bogotá, and his first name is also the name of Chile's capital.
questions.description: Two gentlemen, one couch and zero desire to make serious television.
questions.fun_fact: “El siguiente programa” was a cartoon made for grown-ups, in a style often compared to “Beavis and Butt-Head”.

questions.question: Legend says Francisco el Hombre beat the devil in an accordion duel by singing a prayer. Which one?
hints: It's a long prayer said at Sunday Mass.
It lists everything a Catholic believes in.
It begins with the words “I believe in God, the Father”.
questions.description: Not even the bravest accordion player at the parranda would sign up for this midnight concert.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriel García Márquez made Francisco el Hombre a character in “One Hundred Years of Solitude”.

questions.question: Listen: with this instrument, not the accordion, Guillermo Buitrago recorded Caribbean-coast songs in the 1940s. What is it?
hints: It has strings and you play it with your fingers.
It has a wooden body with a round hole in the middle.
Mariachis play it, rockers play it, and so does Miguel from “Coco”.
questions.description: Before the bellows ruled the parranda, someone was already getting Ciénaga's nights dancing.
questions.fun_fact: “La víspera de Año Nuevo” (New Year's Eve), recorded by Guillermo Buitrago, still plays all over Colombia every December.

questions.question: It’s one of the four aires (rhythms) of vallenato: the slowest and most swaying, with the accordion’s bass notes strongly marked. Which one is it?
hints: It’s the most melancholy of the four aires.
“Alicia adorada”, by Juancho Polo Valencia, is played in this aire.
Its name is the same as the Cuban rhythm of Compay Segundo.
questions.description: Four siblings from the same vallenato family, and today just one gets the spotlight.
questions.fun_fact: At the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata, accordion players must play all four aires: paseo, merengue, son and puya.

questions.question: Which of these musicians is NOT part of the traditional vallenato group?
hints: The other three have played together for over a hundred years.
The odd one out plays a wind instrument made from cardón cactus.
The odd one out belongs to cumbia and to San Jacinto, in the Montes de María.
questions.description: Three's company, four's a crowd... and someone crashed the parranda.
questions.fun_fact: Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto won a Latin Grammy in 2007 for Best Folk Album.

questions.question: Many say vallenato was born from the songs that certain workers sang on the job in the savannas of Cesar. Who were they?
hints: They spent very long days working far from town.
Their songs calmed the animals at night.
They drove cattle from one pasture to another.
questions.description: Before stages and festivals, vallenato was rehearsed outdoors with no applause at all.
questions.fun_fact: Those songs were sung with the voice alone: the accordion reached the region much later.

questions.question: Los Diablitos sang me first, then Argentina's Vicentico; I'm about a mom who worked hard to raise her kids. Which song am I?
hints: It was written by Omar Geles.
It's the song many people dedicate to their mom.
The chorus says life isn't the way you thought it would be.
questions.description: A vallenato that can make a whole party cry, accordion and chorus included.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to Vicentico's version, this vallenato became a hit in Argentina and all over Latin America.

questions.question: I founded a town by a river with stones “like prehistoric eggs”. I got hooked on the gypsies' magnets and magnifying glass and ended up tied to a chestnut tree. Who am I?
hints: I am a character in “One Hundred Years of Solitude”.
My wife is Úrsula Iguarán.
I am the founder of Macondo and the head of the family.
questions.description: A dad who would rather invent things than farm the land.
questions.fun_fact: José Arcadio Buendía tried to prove that a giant magnifying glass could turn the sun into a weapon of war.

questions.question: This bar, La Cueva, was where Gabo, Alejandro Obregón and Álvaro Cepeda Samudio met in the 1950s. Which city is it in?
hints: It's on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
A famous literary group named after the city came from there.
It's the city of Colombia's most famous Carnival.
questions.description: A cave with no bats, just journalists, painters and plenty of Caribbean-coast jokes.
questions.fun_fact: Alejandro Obregón painted a picture on one of La Cueva's walls that is now part of the bar's heritage.

questions.question: “Érase una viejecita sin nadita qué comer.” Which of these characters did NOT come from a Rafael Pombo poem?
hints: Three of them come from poems kids read at school in Colombia.
One of them is a cat who throws a party.
The odd one out is famous for trading baby teeth for gifts.
questions.description: Verses Colombian grandmothers can recite by heart without blinking.
questions.fun_fact: According to Pombo, the poor little old lady had plenty of houses, clothes and food, yet complained she had nothing.

questions.question: In “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” which of these has NOTHING to do with Rebeca?
wrong_answers: Sucking her thumb in a rocking chair
hints: Rebeca came to Macondo as a little orphan girl to live with the Buendías.
She carried a bag that went “cloc cloc.”
The odd one out was the colonel’s pastime in his workshop.
questions.description: A visitor who turned up in Macondo unannounced and ended up staying in the Buendía house for good.
questions.fun_fact: Rebeca’s arrival brought the insomnia plague to Macondo, which made people forget the names of things.

questions.question: In what year did Pacho Maturana lead the Colombian national team at his first World Cup?
hints: Colombia hadn't been to a World Cup in 28 years.
That World Cup was played in Europe.
It was the World Cup in Italy, the one with Freddy Rincón's goal against Germany.
questions.description: A soccer coach with more famous one-liners than a wall calendar.
questions.fun_fact: Maturana also won the 1989 Copa Libertadores with Atlético Nacional, the first ever for a Colombian club.

questions.question: A chiva has wooden benches running side to side and a rack on the roof. In country towns, what was carried on that rack?
hints: The chiva linked the countryside with the town market.
Up there went whatever didn't fit among the passengers.
Coffee, plantains and even chickens.
questions.description: A bus with more colors than a brand-new box of crayons.
questions.fun_fact: Today many chivas have become “chivas rumberas,” party buses that tour cities like Cartagena and Medellín at night with music.

questions.question: Joe Arroyo's “La rebelión,” the one that goes “no le pegue a la negra,” plays at every Colombian party. In which decade did it come out?
hints: Before this, Joe Arroyo had already sung with Fruko y sus Tesos.
He recorded it with his band La Verdad.
It came out the same year as Maradona's World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: A song that has been forcing everyone onto the dance floor for decades.
questions.fun_fact: The song tells the story of an enslaved couple in 17th-century Cartagena.

questions.question: At which Olympic Games did Ximena Restrepo win bronze in the 400 meters, the first Olympic medal for a Colombian woman?
hints: The host city lies on the coast.
These Games were held in the Northern Hemisphere.
These were the Games of the mascot Cobi.
questions.description: Four hundred meters that became a chapter of Colombian sports history.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, Ximena Restrepo was elected vice president of World Athletics, the sport's world federation.

questions.question: The 1928 banana workers' strike ended in a square next to the train station. In which town in Magdalena?
hints: It's in the banana zone, near the Caribbean Sea.
It's on the coast, on the highway toward Barranquilla.
It sits on the shore of Colombia's largest coastal lagoon, which shares its name.
questions.description: A chapter of history that Gabo never let anyone forget.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez retold this event in “One Hundred Years of Solitude,” at the Macondo train station.

questions.question: He wrote the poem “La perrilla,” founded the Colombian Academy of Language and was in power when Panama split away. Which party did José Manuel Marroquín belong to?
hints: He governed during the Thousand Days' War.
His party ruled the country without a break from 1886 to 1930.
It was the rival party of Rafael Uribe Uribe.
questions.description: A president who wrote poems about dogs while half his country walked away.
questions.fun_fact: Marroquín is credited with saying “They gave me one country and I'm handing back two,” though there's no proof he ever said it.

questions.question: In Colombia, Tennis is a brand born in Medellín. It doesn’t sell rackets and has stores in many malls. What does it sell?
hints: It is a very popular brand with young people.
It brings out new collections every season.
Jeans, T-shirts and bags.
questions.description: It’s named after a sport, but ask for a racket and you’ll get some funny looks.
questions.fun_fact: Despite its sporty name, Tennis is a fashion brand from Antioquia that sells much more than workout clothes.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a flavor of Papas Margarita?
hints: It's a potato chip brand sold in corner stores all over Colombia.
The real flavors are ones you find at lunch or squeeze over your food.
That flavor belongs in a candy bar, not a bag of chips.
questions.description: The snack that's always in a Colombian kid's lunchbox.
questions.fun_fact: Each Papas Margarita flavor has its own bag color, and many people ask for them by color.

questions.question: In the novena I have my own prayer, I rode a donkey to Bethlehem with my husband Joseph, and I'm the mother of Baby Jesus. Who am I?
hints: In the pesebre (nativity scene), I kneel next to the baby.
My husband is a carpenter.
My name starts with M.
questions.description: The guest of honor at the novena, even though she's never late and never asks for buñuelos.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian homes, Baby Jesus is only placed in the pesebre on the night of December 24.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: in October, Colombian schools get a week off called “semana de…”.
hints: It has nothing to do with Holy Week.
The same word is used for a break in a meeting.
Its English cousin is the name of the school break kids spend on the playground.
questions.description: A little week for parents to discover how long a day is with the kids at home.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's October school break was created in 2007 to boost tourism, and it is usually joined to the October holiday long weekend.

questions.question: In Colombia, the last Saturday in April is celebrated with games, fun activities and gifts. What day is it?
hints: On that day, many parks and malls put on activities.
Schools hold parties, costume contests and games.
Its official name mentions childhood and recreation.
questions.description: A party day with presents, and no birthday required.
questions.fun_fact: A 2001 law set Colombia's “Day of Childhood and Recreation” on the last Saturday in April.

questions.question: At the baptism, I hold the baby next to the font and promise to help look after them all their life. Who am I?
hints: The parents choose me especially for that day.
During the ceremony I stand next to the parents and answer for the baby when the priest asks.
After the baptism, the child calls me “padri”.
questions.description: Holy water, candles, a white dress and a photographer who won't stop taking pictures.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, it's a tradition for the godparents to give the baby a gold chain or medal.

questions.question: There are three of them, they ride camels, and they reach the nativity scene on January 6. What gifts do they bring Baby Jesus?
hints: They were gifts fit for kings, very valuable.
One of them is a shiny metal.
Another is a perfume you burn that gives off a little smoke.
questions.description: Three gentlemen who traveled by camel long before anyone invented traffic jams.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian homes, the Three Kings figures are moved a little closer to the nativity scene each day until they arrive on January 6.

questions.question: At the novena, kids play instruments along with the Christmas carols. Which of these is NOT usually played there?
hints: The ones at the novena are small and easy to play.
You shake or hit almost all of them.
The odd one out is a huge brass instrument you blow into.
questions.description: The novena: the only prayer that comes with its own band.
questions.fun_fact: At many novenas, people make instruments out of soda bottle caps, pots and spoons.

questions.question: You're making a Father's Day card in Colombia. In which month is Father's Day celebrated?
hints: It's not the same month as Mother's Day.
It's in the middle of the year.
It comes just as the mid-year school vacation begins.
questions.description: The day Dad gets his tenth necktie and pretends to love it.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, Father's Day is the third Sunday in June, a month after Mother's Day.

questions.question: On March 8, people in Colombian offices and schools give flowers and chocolates. Who is celebrated that day?
hints: It's celebrated in offices, schools and even on the street.
It's an international day.
Girls, young women and older ladies all celebrate it.
questions.description: The day Colombian flower shops just can't keep up.
questions.fun_fact: The United Nations has officially celebrated International Women's Day since 1975.

questions.question: In 1996, Jorge Alí Triana filmed a García Márquez script about a mayor in a Colombian town torn by violence. Which classic did it adapt?
hints: The original work comes from Ancient Greece.
In the original, an oracle foretells a terrible fate.
The film's title joins the classic hero's name with the main character's job.
questions.description: A classic so famous it ended up working at the town hall of a Colombian village.
questions.fun_fact: “Edipo alcalde” stars Cuban actor Jorge Perugorría and Spanish actress Ángela Molina.

questions.question: My first film, “La Playa D.C.”, went to Cannes in 2012. It follows Tomás, a young Afro-Colombian from the Pacific who cuts designs into hair in Bogotá. Who am I?
hints: He is not the director of “Embrace of the Serpent”.
He went on to direct “X500”.
His initials are J. A. A.
questions.description: From Bogotá to Cannes, with a stop at the barbershop.
questions.fun_fact: “La Playa D.C.” was selected for the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival.

questions.question: Javier Bardem played Florentino Ariza in “Love in the Time of Cholera”, filmed in Cartagena. Which character is NOT from that story?
hints: The intruder comes from another García Márquez novel.
This character lives in Macondo.
He is a colonel who started 32 civil wars.
questions.description: An intruder has sneaked into the longest love story in Colombian literature.
questions.fun_fact: Javier Bardem also played Pablo Escobar in “Loving Pablo” (2017).

questions.question: Which of these films did NOT come out of the Grupo de Cali?
hints: The odd one out is from the 1990s.
Its director is Sergio Cabrera.
It's about tenants in Bogotá who refuse to be thrown out of their building.
questions.description: A gang from Cali who traded salsa for cinema… or rather, mixed the two.
questions.fun_fact: “Oiga vea” (1971), by Luis Ospina and Carlos Mayolo, showed Cali's Pan American Games from the neighborhoods whose people couldn't get in to watch them.

questions.question: Which of these films is NOT by the documentary maker Marta Rodríguez?

hints: The odd one out isn't a real documentary but a fake one.
It mocks filmmakers who filmed poverty to sell it in Europe.

questions.description: A woman who pointed her camera at real life and didn't let go for half a century.
questions.fun_fact: “Chircales,” which she made with Jorge Silva, shows families who made bricks by hand in the south of Bogotá.

questions.question: In “Land and Shade,” winner of the Caméra d'Or at Cannes, a farming family lives surrounded by a crop whose burning covers the house in ash. Which crop?

Panela is made from it.
questions.description: A film where even the sky turns gray from all the burning.

questions.question: I founded a film club in Cali, and with my filmmaker friends the city got the nickname “Caliwood.” I wrote the novel “¡Que viva la música!” Who am I?

questions.description: When Cali wanted to be Hollywood, but with more flavor.
questions.fun_fact: “¡Que viva la música!” was made into a film in 2015 by director Carlos Moreno.

questions.question: Who directed “The Kings of the World,” the Colombian film that won the Golden Shell at San Sebastián in 2022?
hints: The film follows five young men from Medellín who travel to claim a piece of land.
This director's earlier film was “Killing Jesus.”
The director is a woman, the only woman among the options.
questions.description: Five young guys, one road trip and a prize that came all the way from the Basque Country.

questions.question: In November 1985, a lahar from the Nevado del Ruiz rushed down the rivers and reached Armero, Tolima. What is a lahar?

A tremor that warns of an eruption
A river of red-hot lava flowing down

Volcanoes with snow on their peaks are the ones that produce it most.
Think of wet earth: lots and lots of it, on the move.
questions.description: Volcanoes have more words in their dictionary than just “eruption.”
questions.fun_fact: The word “lahar” comes from Javanese, a language of Indonesia, a country full of volcanoes.

questions.question: By tradition, Santa Fe de Bogotá was founded at the Chorro de Quevedo. Where does the word “Bogotá” come from?
questions.answer: From Bacatá, the Muisca name for the area
wrong_answers: From a Spanish conquistador's last name
From a Catholic saint from Andalusia
From a Quechua word brought by the Incas
