questions.question: Who performed the first keratomileusis in Bogotá, the cornea surgery that paved the way for laser correction of nearsightedness?
hints: He was an ophthalmologist, an eye doctor.
He was born in Barcelona and settled in Bogotá in the 1950s.
A famous eye clinic in Bogotá bears his last name.
questions.description: Thanks to him, many Colombians threw away their glasses without a fight.
questions.fun_fact: Keratomileusis is the grandmother of LASIK, the laser surgery that millions of people use today to give up their glasses.

questions.question: I was born in Bogotá, studied engineering in Cambridge, and in 1958 built a pacemaker so big it ran on a car battery. Who am I?
hints: My invention was one of the first of its kind in the world.
My device was worn outside the body and weighed tens of kilograms.
My last name sounds English, though I'm a true Bogotá local.
questions.description: Bogotá doesn't only export tinto and rainstorms: it also sends out inventions that go around the world.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Reynolds's first pacemaker kept an Ecuadorian priest alive, and he lived 18 more years.

questions.question: In Nariño it's eaten roasted, in many homes it's a pet, and its other name also means “test subject.” What else is the cuy called?
hints: It's a South American rodent, even though its other name sounds like it comes from another continent.
In the Andes it was tamed long before the Europeans arrived.
Its English name points to a country in West Africa.
questions.description: A rodent that is a pet in one part of the world and a party dish in another.
questions.fun_fact: The cuy is neither a pig nor from Guinea: it's an Andean rodent that people have kept for thousands of years.

questions.question: At the Vallenato Festival, some dancers act out pounding corn in an object like this one. What are these dancers called?
hints: The dance grew out of women's kitchen work in Cesar.
Their name comes from the object in the photo.
The object is a wooden mortar called a pilón.
questions.description: A dance that works your arms like a kitchen gym.
questions.fun_fact: The piloneras open the Vallenato Legend Festival in Valledupar with a colorful parade through the streets.

questions.question: In many Colombian kitchens, chicharrones are fried in a white fat. What is it?
hints: Grandmas kept it in tins and used it for almost everything.
It's also what makes tamales soft and tender.
It comes from the marrano.
questions.description: A cooking fat that has spent more years in the kitchen than most grandmas.
questions.fun_fact: Before vegetable oil became common, lard was the main frying fat in Colombian kitchens.

questions.question: It's peeled, cooked white corn, served with milk and a bit of panela or bocadillo. Where is this mazamorra typical?
hints: It's a region of mountains and arrieros (mule drivers).
It's a coffee-growing department in the Andes, in the northwest of the country.
It's paisa country.
questions.description: A drink you chew and a meal you sip, all in the same glass.
questions.fun_fact: Mazamorra antioqueña is sold from street carts, and in some towns it's even delivered door to door.

questions.question: They're big, flat, dark cookies made with wheat flour, panela and spices like cinnamon and cloves. What are they called?
hints: They're sold in neighborhood bakeries, often in packs.
They go great with a glass of milk.
Their name has just two syllables and starts with “cu”.
questions.description: Cookies so big they beat the hand that holds them.
questions.fun_fact: Cucas get their dark color from panela, the cane sugar used in almost all traditional Colombian baking.

questions.question: Look at this close-up: it's black, in Colombia it's stuffed with rice, and no picada is complete without it. What is it?
hints: It's a pork sausage.
Its dark color comes from blood.
In some regions it's also called rellena.
questions.description: A sausage that always has a line at the fritanga stand.
questions.fun_fact: In parts of Colombia, morcilla is called “rellena”, and in Bogotá people often eat it with papa criolla.

questions.question: Bocadillo veleño (guava paste) comes from Vélez, Santander, and each slice is wrapped in a leaf that gives it its aroma. What is that leaf called?
hints: It's a big green leaf from a tropical plant.
In some regions it's also used to wrap tamales and fiambres.
Its name starts with “Bi”.
questions.description: It comes gift-wrapped all the way from Santander, no bow needed.
questions.fun_fact: The bijao leaf doesn't just add scent to the bocadillo: it also protects it and helps it last longer without spoiling.

questions.question: Sugarcane is crushed, the juice is boiled in big pailas and then beaten until it turns into panela, in blocks or as powder. Where does all this happen?
hints: It's a place in the countryside, with ovens and pailas.
A machine there squeezes the juice out of the sugarcane.
Its name starts with the same three letters as “travel”.
questions.description: Before it reached the jar in the kitchen, this little powder had a really rough week.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the biggest panela producers in the world, second only to India.

questions.question: It comes in a small dark bottle, a few drops add flavor to a cake or arequipe, and it comes from an orchid first grown by the ancient peoples of Mexico. What is it?
hints: It's one of the most famous ice cream flavors in the world.
The orchid grows long black pods.
The Aztecs mixed it with chocolate.
questions.description: A few drops of this and the whole kitchen smells like someone is making something yummy.
questions.fun_fact: Vanilla is one of the most expensive spices in the world, because on most farms every orchid flower is pollinated by hand.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this famous combination called in Colombia?
hints: One part is white and salty.
The other part is red, sweet and firm, and it's cut into slices.
The sweet part comes wrapped in leaves from Vélez, Santander.
questions.description: A couple so perfect together that nobody dares to split them up in the lunchbox.
questions.fun_fact: In Brazil, this same combination is called “Romeo and Juliet.”

questions.question: You eat a Gansito at recess. Who is the Ramo brand named after?
hints: He founded the company in Bogotá.
The name joins the start of his first name and the start of his last name.
RA from his first name and MO from his last name.
questions.description: A goose that has traveled in lunchboxes for decades and never once flown.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Molano started out selling homemade cakes before creating one of Colombia's best-loved brands.

questions.question: It's thick, very sweet milk, drizzled over raspao and cholado, and invented over 150 years ago so milk would keep without a fridge. What is it?
hints: It comes in a can or a little pouch.
If you boil it in the can for a long time, it turns into something like arequipe.
Almost all the water is taken out of the milk and sugar is added.
questions.description: An ingredient that turns anything into dessert with just a little drizzle.
questions.fun_fact: American Gail Borden patented condensed milk in 1856, and it became famous because it didn't spoil on long trips.

questions.question: It's a ring-shaped sweet bread with sugar on top, filled with arequipe or bocadillo. What is it called in Colombian bakeries?
hints: It has a hole in the middle.
It's usually big and cut into slices to share at onces (afternoon snack).
Its name means a big “rosca”, a ring shape.
questions.description: A bread shaped like a swim ring, so it won't drown in your tinto.
questions.fun_fact: In Spain, the most famous one is the roscón de Reyes, eaten on January 6 with a surprise hidden inside.

questions.question: Villavicencio is called “the Gateway to the Llanos.” It is the capital of which department, highlighted on the map?
hints: The department is named after a river that flows into the Orinoco.
It borders Cundinamarca, down the mountains from Bogotá.
Its name has only four letters.
questions.description: They say that behind this city begins a sea of grass, with cows instead of fish.
questions.fun_fact: Villavicencio is just a few hours’ drive from Bogotá, but more than 2,000 meters (6,600 ft) lower.

questions.question: Jesús María Ocampo, who founded Armenia in 1889, was known to everyone as “el…”. How does his nickname end?
hints: The nickname comes from a reputation he had in the wilderness, before he founded the city.
He earned it for his bravery in a very risky trade in the region's forests.
Country people back then called the jaguar “tigre.”
questions.description: Founding a city is easy; earning a nickname like that in Quindío is the hard part.
questions.fun_fact: Armenia is called “la Ciudad Milagro” (the Miracle City) because it grew so fast after it was founded.

questions.question: I'm made of leather, I hang from the shoulder of the Antioquian arriero, and I hold everything, even in hidden pockets. What am I?
hints: I'm part of the traditional paisa outfit.
The arrieros who crossed the mountains with their mules carried me.
I often have hairy hide on the outside and several compartments.
questions.description: When the arriero and his mule crossed the Andes, not even GPS dared to follow them.
questions.fun_fact: The carriel is also called a “guarniel,” and some have secret pockets for hiding money.

questions.question: You're in Pasto. If people from Bogotá are called “rolos”, what are people from here called?
hints: Pasto is the capital of Nariño.
The word sounds a lot like the city's name.
It ends in “-uso”.
questions.description: A city so cold that even its nickname for locals comes wearing a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Pasto sits at the foot of the Galeras volcano, one of the most active in Colombia.

questions.question: This statue of a naked Bolívar on horseback is the great symbol of the “Perla del Otún.” Who made it?
hints: The artist was from Antioquia.
He was born in Fredonia and became famous for his giant monuments.
He also made the huge monument to the lancers of the Pantano de Vargas, in Boyacá.
questions.description: A national hero showed up in the town square without clothes, and nobody said a word.
questions.fun_fact: The statue was unveiled in 1963, when Pereira turned 100.

questions.question: Rondón, the signature dish of San Andrés, is a stew of fish, conch, cassava and plantain. What is it cooked in?
hints: It's a very common ingredient in Caribbean cooking.
It comes from the fruit of a palm tree.
It's white, made by grating that fruit's flesh with water.
questions.description: An island stew that takes its sweet time while the sea plays the music.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the English “run down”, as the Raizal people of San Andrés call it.

questions.question: The Colombian series “Los caballeros las prefieren brutas” was based on a book. Who wrote it?
hints: She's a Colombian humor writer and columnist.
The book is a tongue-in-cheek guide to relationships.
She shares her last name with one of Colombia's best-known business families.
questions.description: A series with a cheeky title and an author who laughs at stereotypes before anyone else does.
questions.fun_fact: The book was sold as a funny handbook about love before jumping to TV as a series.

questions.question: If you laugh at Andrés López's “La pelota de letras,” whose childhood are you remembering?
questions.answer: People who grew up in the '70s and '80s
wrong_answers: People who grew up in the '50s and '60s
People who grew up in the '90s and 2000s
People who grew up in the '30s and '40s
hints: Andrés López looks back at the toys, TV shows and scoldings from Mom of his own childhood.
TV had only a few channels, and kids played games out in the street.
There was already color TV and the first video game consoles were arriving, but no internet.
questions.description: A comedy show that makes parents feel old in under two hours.
questions.fun_fact: “La pelota de letras” became one of the most-watched comedy shows in Colombia and was released on DVD.

questions.question: It's sold from street carts, topped with sauces and crushed potato chips. What is a “perro caliente”?
wrong_answers: A dog lying in the sun
hints: It's food, not a pet.
You eat it with your hands, wrapped in a napkin, and the sauce drips easily.
There's a sausage inside.
questions.description: Relax: no puppies were harmed in the making of this question.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, hot dogs get pink sauce, pineapple sauce and even quail eggs.

questions.question: Huevos pericos are scrambled eggs eaten for breakfast with arepa. What gets chopped into them to make them pericos?
hints: Two ingredients found in almost every Colombian kitchen, and they add color to the eggs.
One is red, and the other is long and green.
One of them makes you cry when you chop it.
questions.description: A breakfast named after a chatty bird that doesn't make a peep.
questions.fun_fact: They're said to be called “pericos” (parakeets) because their green, red and yellow colors look like a parakeet's feathers.

questions.question: It goes on the bandeja paisa: cooked, dried and ground until it's like a powder. What meat is carne en polvo made from?
hints: It's not the same meat as the chicharrón.
At the butcher's, you ask for cuts like posta or bola.
It comes from a cow.
questions.description: The only meat that could fly off the plate if someone sneezes at the table.
questions.fun_fact: Carne en polvo was born in Antioquia as a way to make meat last and use every bit of it.

questions.question: In the Colombian Amazon it's toasted on big budares (griddles), it's grainy and yellowish, and it goes into fish broth. What is fariña?
hints: Its name comes from Portuguese, because Brazil is right next door.
It's sold by the sack at the Leticia market and eaten daily there, like rice.
It comes from a root that is poisonous if it isn't processed.
questions.description: Golden jungle sand that, luckily, you can actually eat.
questions.fun_fact: Yuca brava has a toxic juice that Amazon peoples learned to squeeze out before toasting it.

questions.question: It goes on top of the round arepa, you buy it at the corner store, and it’s the everyday paisa breakfast. What is “quesito”?
hints: It doesn’t melt like pizza cheese.
It’s white and crumbles a little.
It’s a fresh cheese that isn’t aged.
questions.description: A paisa breakfast favorite whose name comes in a cute little size so it sounds even tastier.
questions.fun_fact: Quesito antioqueño is made from curdled milk and sold fresh, without aging.

questions.question: You open the fridge in the morning to make calentado paisa. Which two leftovers from yesterday are a must?
hints: They're heated together in the pan with a little hogao.
Both come from yesterday's lunch, the everyday meal in paisa homes.
One is a white grain, the other a red bean cooked in a pressure cooker.
questions.description: The breakfast that proves yesterday's leftovers can be today's stars.
questions.fun_fact: Calentado is usually served with a fried egg, an arepa and hot chocolate or tinto (black coffee).

questions.question: Omar Geles and Miguel Morales founded the group Los Diablitos in Valledupar. In which decade?
hints: It was a time when vallenato was reaching radio stations all over the country.
By the early 1990s they were already famous for “Los caminos de la vida”.
It was the same decade as the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: Little devils so nice they got half of Colombia singing.
questions.fun_fact: Omar Geles, the accordion player of Los Diablitos, wrote hundreds of songs, including “Los caminos de la vida”.

questions.question: Listen: which instrument is this?
hints: You play it by opening and closing one part, as if it were breathing.
It has buttons or keys on both sides.
It's the main instrument of vallenato.
questions.description: An instrument that never misses a party and always shows up ready to dance.
questions.fun_fact: The accordion came to Colombia from Europe by ship and ended up as the king of vallenato.

questions.question: You hear someone say “¡ajá!” all the time, coastal style. In which of these cities would that be LEAST typical?
hints: The coastal “ajá” is heard mostly near the Caribbean Sea.
Three of these cities are on the coast or in the Caribbean region.
The answer is an Andean city in the south, near Ecuador.
questions.description: Ajá, so what? Ajá, well… this question.
questions.fun_fact: On the coast, “ajá” works for everything: saying hello, asking, doubting, and even starting a juicy bit of gossip.

questions.question: You reach the last pages of “One Hundred Years of Solitude.” Which of these characters is NOT a parent or grandparent of Aureliano Babilonia?
hints: One of his parents is always surrounded by yellow butterflies.
The character you're looking for is actually his aunt.
With her he has a son with a pig's tail.
questions.description: The Buendía family tree needs its own GPS.
questions.fun_fact: Aureliano Babilonia is the one who finally deciphers Melquíades' parchments, just as Macondo disappears.

questions.question: José Asunción Silva wrote his famous “Nocturno” after the death of his sister Elvira. In which decade?
hints: It was in the 19th century.
Silva was one of the forerunners of modernismo.
It was in the last decade of that century.
questions.description: A poem so sad that even the shadows cry together.
questions.fun_fact: Silva's portrait appeared on the Colombian 5,000-peso bill.

questions.question: In a fishing village, the sea brings in a huge man; the people name him Esteban and paint their houses bright colors for him. Which Gabo story is it?
questions.answer: “The Handsomest Drowned Man in the World”
wrong_answers: “A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings”
“Monologue of Isabel Watching It Rain in Macondo”
hints: It is a short story by García Márquez from the late 1960s.
The main character arrives floating in from the sea.
The village women say he is the best-looking man they have ever seen.
questions.description: A story where a whole village falls in love with someone who never says a word.
questions.fun_fact: The story is part of the 1972 collection “The Incredible and Sad Tale of Innocent Eréndira and Her Heartless Grandmother”.

questions.question: Liberals and Conservatives agreed on the Frente Nacional, which began in 1958. What was it created for?
questions.answer: To take turns holding the presidency
wrong_answers: To give power back to Rojas Pinilla
To replace both parties with a new one
hints: It came after years of violence between the two traditional parties.
Liberal Alberto Lleras Camargo and Conservative Laureano Gómez agreed on it in Spain.
Every four years, the presidency passed to the other party.
questions.description: A political deal with more fine print than a cell phone contract.
questions.fun_fact: Alberto Lleras Camargo was also the first secretary general of the OAS, founded in Bogotá in 1948.

questions.question: In the early 1950s, Colombia's league played outside FIFA and signed stars like Alfredo Di Stéfano. What is that era called?
hints: Clubs paid salaries no other country could match.
Millonarios, with Di Stéfano, was nicknamed “Ballet Azul.”
It was named after the legend of the city of gold the conquistadors searched for.
questions.description: An era when Colombian clubs signed players as if money grew on the stadium goalposts.
questions.fun_fact: Di Stéfano joined Millonarios in 1949 and left Bogotá for Real Madrid in 1953.

questions.question: In 1992, an El Niño drought emptied the reservoirs, the power went out for hours, and the “hora Gaviria” appeared. What was it?
questions.answer: Setting all clocks forward one hour
wrong_answers: Cutting the power for one hour every night
A daily radio speech by the president
The hour when all businesses closed
hints: It had to do with making better use of daylight.
Several countries do something similar in summer.
Overnight, when it was 6 in the morning, the clock already said 7.
questions.description: A time when Colombians learned to do their homework by candlelight.
questions.fun_fact: The hora Gaviria started in May 1992 and ended in February 1993, so many people had to get up while it was still dark.

questions.question: Before it reached your cup as a tinto, the coffee was a red cherry. Where did it grow?
hints: It grows on a plant, up in the mountains.
In Colombia there are lots of them in the Eje Cafetero.
It's a field full of coffee bushes.
questions.description: The official fuel of every Colombian office.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia a tinto is a black coffee, but in Spain it's a glass of red wine.

questions.question: I'm a green insect that lives in the grass of cattle pastures. My back legs are super long, and I use them to make huge jumps. What am I?
hints: I have antennae and wings, but I'd rather jump
People sometimes mix me up with the cricket
My name says I hop around in the grass
questions.description: Green, skinny and always rushing across the pasture.
questions.fun_fact: A grasshopper can jump about 20 times the length of its own body.

questions.question: In the Colombian countryside they call it “cocuyo”: it's tiny, comes out at night, and kids chase it. What is it?
hints: It's a small animal that flies.
You see it best when everything is dark.
It switches its little light on and off like a light bulb.
questions.description: A word you hear on the farm more at night than during the day.
questions.fun_fact: Fireflies make light that gives off almost no heat; it's called bioluminescence.

questions.question: Look at this moray eel from the reefs of San Andrés. Why does it keep opening and closing its mouth?
wrong_answers: To lure fish with its tongue
To swallow sand from the bottom
hints: It has nothing to do with food.
It does it even while resting quietly in its cave.
It's about its gills: this pushes water through them to take out the oxygen.
questions.description: It looks like it's giving you a long lecture, but don't take it personally.
questions.fun_fact: Moray eels have a second jaw in their throat that shoots forward to pull in their prey.

questions.question: Look at this round hole in a tree trunk on the farm. Which animal made it?
hints: It was a bird.
It made it by hitting the wood many, many times.
Knock, knock, knock against the trunk all day long.
questions.description: Someone remodeled this tree without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: A woodpecker can peck about 20 times per second.

questions.question: Look at this pelican from the beaches of Santa Marta. What does it use the pouch under its beak for?
wrong_answers: To store food for several days
hints: It dives headfirst into the water
It works like a net
It lets the water drain out and swallows its catch
questions.description: A bird with more pockets than a pair of cargo pants.
questions.fun_fact: A pelican's pouch can hold about 10 liters (2.5 gallons) of water.

questions.question: Look at this toad. How many legs does it have?
hints: It has legs in the front and in the back
The back ones are longer for jumping
It has the same number as a dog
questions.description: In Colombia a «sapo» is someone who tells on everybody; this one only tells you how far it jumped.
questions.fun_fact: Most toads have 4 toes on their front feet and 5 on their back feet.

questions.question: At the corner store you buy a candy for 1,000 pesos and pay with a 2,000-peso bill. How much change should you get?
hints: You paid more than the candy cost.
Subtract the candy's price from what you paid.
It's exactly half of your bill.
questions.description: The tensest moment at the corner store: when the shopkeeper opens the coin drawer.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia change is called “las vueltas”, but in other Latin American countries it's “el vuelto” or “el cambio”.

questions.question: A heroine of the fight for independence who was a seamstress and a spy was on the old 10,000-peso bill. Who is she?
hints: She is said to have been born in Guaduas, Cundinamarca.
She carried messages to the patriots in Santafé de Bogotá.
People called her “La Pola.”
questions.description: The old money in the drawer can keep secrets from the fight for independence too.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia celebrates the Day of the Colombian Woman on November 14 in her honor.

questions.question: Which of these store chains did NOT start in Colombia?
hints: One of them arrived in the country just over ten years ago.
It began by opening stores in the Eje Cafetero.
Its owner is a Portuguese company.
questions.description: Four supermarkets walk into a party, and one of them shows up with a foreign accent.
questions.fun_fact: Tiendas Ara belongs to Jerónimo Martins, the Portuguese group that owns the Pingo Doce supermarkets in Portugal.

questions.question: You're at the tienda picking out candy. Which of these is NOT made by Colombina?
hints: Three of them come from a company in Valle del Cauca.
The odd one out is made by the same company that makes Corona chocolate.
The odd one out comes with stickers to collect in an album.
questions.description: A family of candies with one cousin who sneaked into the photo.
questions.fun_fact: Colombina was born in La Paila, in Valle del Cauca, and its Bon Bon Bum is sold in many countries around the world.

questions.question: Conchita appears with Juan Valdez in the ads and the famous logo. What is her job?
hints: She's a pack animal.
She walks the coffee mountains with something on her back.
She brings the harvest down from the farm.
questions.description: The most patient coworker in all of Colombian advertising.
questions.fun_fact: Conchita is a mule, the offspring of a donkey and a horse, an animal widely used to climb Colombia's steep coffee farms.

questions.question: In which decade did Víctor Gaviria’s “Sumas y restas” come out? It follows a Medellín engineer who gets into the cocaine business.
hints: The story is set in the 1980s, but it was filmed many years later.
Gaviria made it after “La vendedora de rosas”, which is from 1998.
It came out in the 21st century.
questions.description: A film where the numbers never add up, however big your calculator is.
questions.fun_fact: As in his other films, Gaviria worked mostly with non-professional actors, people from the street with no acting training.

questions.question: I’m from Medellín. My short film “Leidi” won the Short Film Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2014, and later I directed the feature “Amparo”. Who am I?
hints: I studied film in London before coming back to shoot in my home city.
“Amparo” tells the story of a mother trying to get her son out of military service.
My second surname is Soto.
questions.description: A paisa who flew home from France with a little golden palm tucked in his suitcase.
questions.fun_fact: “Leidi” was the first Colombian short film ever to win the Palme d’Or at Cannes.

questions.question: “Soñar no cuesta nada” tells the true story of soldiers who find millions of dollars hidden by guerrillas in the jungle. What year did they find it?
hints: The soldiers were in a counter-guerrilla battalion, and many were poor young men from the countryside.
It happened in Caquetá, shortly before the movie was made.
It was in the first years of the 21st century.
questions.description: Dig a hole in the jungle and find something no backyard garden has ever grown.
questions.fun_fact: It was one of the most-watched Colombian movies of its year.

questions.question: What is the sequel to “Romancing the Stone” (1984), Michael Douglas's adventure in the Colombian jungle, called?
hints: It came out in 1985 with the same stars.
The adventure moves from Colombia to Africa.
It takes place near Africa's longest river.
questions.description: Michael Douglas left the Colombian jungle still hungry for more adventure.
questions.fun_fact: In the film, Kathleen Turner plays a romance novelist who ends up living an adventure of her own.

questions.question: Franco Lolli made his debut in 2014 with “Gente de bien.” What was his next feature, about a Bogotá lawyer caring for her sick mother?
hints: It premiered in 2019 at Critics' Week in Cannes.
The lead is played by Colombian writer Carolina Sanín.
Its title is the Spanish word for someone fighting a case in court.
questions.description: A director from Bogotá who likes family dramas without the soap-opera shouting.
questions.fun_fact: Franco Lolli studied film in Paris, at the La Fémis film school.

questions.question: Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote it, Sebastián Yatra sings it, and it was nominated for the Oscar for Best Original Song. Which film is “Dos Oruguitas” from?
hints: It's a Disney film.
In the film, the song goes with the memory of how a grandmother lost her husband and found a new home.
Mirabel and the Madrigal family's house are in it.
questions.description: Two little bugs that made it all the way to the world's most famous red carpet.
questions.fun_fact: Sebastián Yatra sang “Dos Oruguitas” live at the 2022 Oscars ceremony.

questions.question: “Memoria” (2021), filmed in Colombia with Tilda Swinton hearing a mysterious bang, won the Jury Prize at Cannes. Where is its director from?
hints: This director's movies often show jungles, spirits and dreams.
He had already won the Palme d'Or with “Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives”.
His country's capital is Bangkok.
questions.description: A noise so strange that someone came from the other side of the world to film it.
questions.fun_fact: “Memoria” was the first feature film Apichatpong made outside his home country.

questions.question: Fill in the name Medellín was given at its founding in 1675: “Villa de Nuestra Señora de la ____ de Medellín.”
hints: It's a title of the Virgin Mary honored in many towns in Spain and Latin America, and she is still the city's patron saint.
Her feast day is February 2.
It's the name of the church on Parque Berrío and of a historic neighborhood in Bogotá.
questions.description: A name so long that the city decided to keep only the last part.
questions.fun_fact: The Virgin of Candelaria is still Medellín's patron saint, and her church on Parque Berrío served as the cathedral for years.

questions.question: I was a Pijao chief who fought the Spanish in the early 1600s. Today a town in Quindío, next to Armenia, bears my name. Who am I?
hints: My people, the Pijao, lived between the Central Cordillera and the Magdalena valley.
The town named after me has a famous botanical garden with a butterfly house.
My name starts with “Cal…”.
questions.description: Long before it was a must-stop for a tinto, this name belonged to someone very fierce.
questions.fun_fact: Calarcá, the town, was founded in 1886 and is known as the “Villa del Cacique”.

questions.question: Complete the famous chorus: “Santa Marta tiene tren, pero no tiene…” (Santa Marta has a train, but it has no…).
hints: It's a traditional cumbia from Colombia's Caribbean coast.
Bogotá and Medellín did have one in the early 20th century.
It runs on rails, and its Spanish name rhymes with “moriría”, which comes later in the song.
questions.description: A song that proves public transportation has always given people something to talk about.
questions.fun_fact: The Santa Marta train carried bananas from the Zona Bananera to the port, which is why the song says the city would die without “la zona”.

questions.question: I was a young colonel from Antioquia in the War of Independence and fought alongside Bolívar. Today a hot lowland city on the Magdalena bears my surname. Who am I?
hints: The city named after me is in Cundinamarca, very close to Melgar.
It's famous for its pools and its heat, and people from Bogotá head down there on weekends.
My surname sounds French and starts with “Gir…”.
questions.description: A hero of independence who ended up giving his name to half of Bogotá's favorite long-weekend getaway.
questions.fun_fact: Atanasio Girardot is remembered for carrying the flag at the Battle of Bárbula, in Venezuela, in 1813.

questions.question: In Colombia, Milo is in every lunchbox and kitchen. What is that powder used for?
hints: You can drink it cold or hot.
You stir it into a glass of something white.
It tastes of cocoa and malt.
questions.description: The powder that gets kids out of bed just a little bit faster.
questions.fun_fact: Milo was invented in Australia in 1934 and today people drink it in lots of countries, from Colombia to Malaysia.

questions.question: Look closely: chicha and mazamorra are made with these. What are they?
hints: They grow attached to a cob.
Arepas are made with them too.
When it's young and tender, Colombians call it chócolo.
questions.description: Yellow teeth that never need a toothbrush.
questions.fun_fact: The Muisca people were already making corn chicha long before the Spanish arrived.

questions.question: The smell of fritanga, the sight of mango biche with salt or the sound of chicharrón frying makes your mouth water. Which part of the body makes that “water”?
hints: That water helps start digestion.
They sit under the tongue and near the cheeks and jaw.
They make your spit.
questions.description: A tiny flood that starts with just one whiff of fritanga.
questions.fun_fact: A person makes about 1 to 1.5 liters (2 to 3 pints) of saliva a day.

previous.feedback: Source: this asks the same fact as approved q-4549 (mouth watering comes from the salivary glands, same answer), and the Colombian foods are only decoration. Seeing one question gives the other away. The translation itself is faithful and natural, but the question should be dropped or replaced with a different fact in the source.

questions.question: On the outside it can be green, yellow or red, and inside it has a big, flat seed. What fruit is it?
hints: On the street it's sold cut up, with salt and lime.
Its juice is thick and orange.
When it's green and eaten with salt, it's called “biche.”
questions.description: The fruit that turns any white shirt into a colorful one.
questions.fun_fact: The mango de azúcar is typical of Magdalena, on Colombia's Caribbean coast.

questions.question: Sabajón, a Christmas drink of egg, milk and liquor, has relatives in other countries. Which of these drinks is NOT one of them?
hints: Look for the drink with no egg and no milk.
It's drunk hot on cold nights in the Andes.
It's made with aguapanela, cinnamon and aguardiente.
questions.description: A very creamy family Christmas party, with one cousin who looks like nobody else.
questions.fun_fact: The name “sabajón” comes from zabaione, an Italian cream made of egg yolks, sugar and wine.

questions.question: What is the name of the aluminum pot, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, that every Colombian kitchen has?
hints: A wooden stick goes in through its narrow mouth.
It's used to make what people drink with cheese at onces.
Its name comes from the drink made in it.
questions.description: A pot with a model's waistline and a passion for foam.
questions.fun_fact: The chocolatera's narrow shape helps the molinillo whip up more foam without the hot chocolate spilling.

questions.question: You do it with your lips, it's a tiny bit of drink at a time, and it tells you if the tinto (black coffee) is too hot. What is it called?
hints: It isn't a container.
It's the opposite of gulping it all down at once.
Drinking slowly means taking little ones, one after another.
questions.description: The official technique for not burning your tongue on Grandma's tinto.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the “cuncho” is what's left at the bottom of the pocillo after the last sip.

questions.question: In many Colombian towns, people drink chicha or water from a totuma. What is a totuma made from?
questions.answer: A tree's dried fruit, cut in half
wrong_answers: A cut piece of guadua bamboo
hints: No potter makes it.
It grows hanging from branches, green and round.
The tree is called the totumo.
questions.description: Grandma's favorite cup for chicha, and it tastes better than any glass.
questions.fun_fact: The same totumo fruit is used to make the maracas heard in music from Colombia's Caribbean coast.

questions.question: After three days of rain, an old man who fell from the sky shows up in a yard. They lock him in a chicken coop and charge people to see him. Which García Márquez story is this?
questions.answer: A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings
wrong_answers: The Handsomest Drowned Man in the World
hints: The yard was full of crabs.
A neighbor woman insists the old man is an angel.
The title describes what the old man is like and what he has on his back.
questions.description: A visitor from heaven who ended up charging admission like a circus act.
questions.fun_fact: García Márquez published this story in 1968, and it is one of the most famous examples of magical realism.

questions.question: “La Luciérnaga,” the comedy radio show led by Hernán Peláez, was born during Colombia's big power rationing. In which decade?
hints: Back then, many people in Colombia already listened to the radio in the car, but almost nobody had a cell phone.
The rationing came after a severe drought left the hydroelectric reservoirs almost empty.
It was shortly after Colombia adopted its 1991 Constitution.
questions.description: A show born to light things up just when the whole country went dark.
questions.fun_fact: The show's name (“The Firefly”) was a nod to the blackouts: a firefly shines even when everything is dark.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian actress. In “Birds of Passage” by Ciro Guerra and Cristina Gallego, I played Úrsula, the Wayuu matriarch who defends her clan. Who am I?
hints: The film is set in La Guajira during the bonanza marimbera.
My character guards her Wayuu family's traditions and dreams.
My first name is a diminutive of Carmen.
questions.description: A grandmother nobody in the clan dares to argue with.
questions.fun_fact: “Birds of Passage” was Colombia's submission for the Oscar for best foreign language film.

questions.question: I made people laugh for years on “Sábados Felices” and was married to the comedian Polilla, who I also performed with. Who am I?
hints: I was one of the best-known faces of comedy on Colombian TV.
My husband and I often went on stage together.
My nickname combines an affectionate Spanish word about my figure with my first name.
questions.description: A woman whose house is full of laughter because she married another comedian.
questions.fun_fact: “Sábados Felices” is one of the longest-running comedy shows in the world: it started in 1972.

questions.question: Look at Colombia’s coat of arms. What do the two horns of plenty at the top stand for?
hints: Look at what is spilling out of each horn.
One pours out coins and the other pours out fruit.
It has to do with all the valuable things that Colombia’s soil gives.
questions.description: Two horns that don’t belong to a bull or a cow, just to pure generosity.
questions.fun_fact: One of the horns on the coat of arms pours out gold coins and the other pours out tropical fruit.

questions.question: Colombia's coat of arms shows an open pomegranate with its red seeds visible. What does it recall?
questions.answer: The country's old name, New Granada
wrong_answers: The harvests of the Valle del Cauca
hints: It has nothing to do with food.
It has to do with what the land was called centuries ago.
In colonial times, this land was the New Kingdom of…
questions.description: A fruit with more seeds than there are speeches in a session of Congress.
questions.fun_fact: The New Kingdom of Granada was named after the Spanish city of Granada, whose symbol is also this fruit.

questions.question: You're in Bogotá's Plaza de Bolívar. Which of these places is NOT on the square?
hints: The square is the city's historic heart, where Bogotá was founded.
The place that isn't there lies several kilometers north of La Candelaria.
Millonarios and Santa Fe play there.
questions.description: A square where the pigeons have more power than many politicians.
questions.fun_fact: The square's Bolívar statue, made by the Italian Pietro Tenerani, was Bogotá's first public statue.

questions.question: Complete the name: in Colombian schools, the ceremony that honors the homeland and rewards the best students is the “izada de…”.
hints: It takes place in the schoolyard, with students standing in rows.

It's yellow, blue and red.
questions.description: The one time of the week when the whole school gets up early without complaining… much.
questions.fun_fact: At izadas de bandera in Colombian schools, the national anthem is almost always sung, and often the anthems of the department and the school too.

questions.question: Many presidents lived in the Palacio de San Carlos in Bogotá, and Bolívar escaped through one of its windows in 1828. What is there today?
hints: The presidents moved to the Casa de Nariño.
Today ambassadors from other countries are received there.

questions.description: A house with so many stories that even its windows have a biography.
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar survived the assassination attempt of September 1828 thanks to Manuela Sáenz, who helped him jump out of the window.

questions.question: I hosted the 1972 Olympic Games, where Colombia won its first medals: a silver in shooting and two bronzes in boxing. Who am I?
hints: Those Games had the first official Olympic mascot, a little dachshund.
I am a European city.
I am the capital of Bavaria, in Germany.
questions.description: The place where Colombia finally got to fill its Olympic trophy cabinet.
questions.fun_fact: The Munich silver was won by Helmut Bellingrodt from Barranquilla, in running target shooting.

questions.question: Which of these would you NOT take to go diving on the reefs of San Andrés?
hints: Three of these things are used underwater.
The odd one out is used on a field.

questions.description: Packing for the beach is easy, until someone sneaks in something that doesn't belong.
questions.fun_fact: Around San Andrés and Providencia lies Seaflower, one of the largest marine biosphere reserves in the Caribbean.

questions.question: Which of these Colombian cities has NEVER hosted the Central American and Caribbean Games?
hints: Between them, the three cities that did host them held the Games in 1946, 1978, 2006 and 2018.

questions.description: A roll call to see which cities have had to keep the host's medal tucked away in a drawer.
questions.fun_fact: Cali hosted the 1971 Pan American Games, the biggest multi-sport event Colombia had ever organized up to then.

questions.question: In which decade was Miguel “Happy” Lora, from Montería, the WBC bantamweight world champion?
hints: It was after the days of Kid Pambelé.
He won the title in the middle of the decade and defended it several times.
He took the belt from Daniel Zaragoza in 1985.
questions.description: The boxer from Córdoba who proved you can punch hard and still be called “Happy.”

questions.question: I'm a 16th-century colonial house in Boyacá. On my painted ceilings, Greek gods share space with an elephant and a rhinoceros copied from Dürer. What am I?
questions.answer: Casa del Escribano Juan de Vargas

questions.description: A house where staring at the ceiling beats watching TV.
questions.fun_fact: The painters in Tunja had never seen a rhinoceros: they copied the famous 1515 print by Albrecht Dürer, who had never seen one either.

questions.question: In 1819, after the Battle of Boyacá, I painted Bolívar with an Indigenous woman who stands for America. My sons carried on my workshop in Bogotá. Who am I?
wrong_answers: Gregorio Vásquez de Arce y Ceballos
hints: I worked between the end of colonial times and the first years of the Republic.
My painting is called “Bolívar, Liberator and Father of the Nation”.
I share my surname with a colonial painter, Baltasar de…
questions.description: A portrait painter who had to work fast, because the nation had just been born.
questions.fun_fact: That portrait is considered one of the first ever painted of Bolívar in New Granada.

questions.question: Which writer and philosopher from Antioquia, nicknamed “el brujo de Otraparte,” lived in the house that is now the Casa Museo Otraparte in Envigado?
hints: He wrote “Viaje a pie.”
The Nadaístas admired him as a master.
He shares a first name with Botero.
questions.description: A house whose name means “somewhere else,” even though it is right there in Envigado.
questions.fun_fact: Otraparte also has a café that hosts talks and tertulias, just as its owner would have liked.

questions.question: In 2000, Botero gave Bogotá a large collection that you can now see for free in La Candelaria. Besides his own works, what does it include?
questions.answer: Works by masters like Picasso, Monet and Dalí
hints: Botero was a collector as well as a painter.
Many of those works come from Europe.
There are paintings by French Impressionists and by a famous painter with a twisted mustache.
questions.description: The gift any city would dream of getting, and it wasn't even its birthday.
questions.fun_fact: Botero made it a condition that entry to his donation be free, so anyone could see those works.

questions.question: Juan Antonio Roda came to Colombia in 1955, taught art in Bogotá and became a master of printmaking there. What country was he born in?
hints: He crossed the Atlantic Ocean to reach Colombia.
Before coming to Colombia, he lived and studied art in Paris for a few years.
His home country was ruled by Franco when he left.
questions.description: A painter who made Colombia his home, though his accent gave him away.
questions.fun_fact: Roda became a Colombian citizen, and his work ranks among the most important Colombian art of the 20th century.

questions.question: Born in Medellín, I worked at Discos Fuentes as a boy, I play bass, and my orchestra recorded the salsa hit “El preso.” Who am I?
hints: I have been a legend of Colombian salsa since the 1970s.
Joe Arroyo became famous singing in my orchestra.
My orchestra is called “… y sus Tesos.”
questions.description: A man who has been getting Colombians to dance for half a century without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Great voices like Joe Arroyo and Wilson Saoko, who sang “El preso,” came through Fruko y sus Tesos.

questions.question: You’re in line with the first Colombian women ever to vote, a dream Ofelia Uribe de Acosta fought for. What year is it?
hints: It’s in the second half of the 20th century.
It was a plebiscite that gave birth to the Frente Nacional.
It was the same year Rojas Pinilla’s government fell.
questions.description: A line that took decades of fighting, and it wasn’t for concert tickets.
questions.fun_fact: In 1944, Ofelia Uribe de Acosta founded the newspaper “Agitación Femenina” in Tunja.

questions.question: I have pages of animals, planets and landscapes, filled with stickers that come inside a chocolate bar. Kids trade their duplicates at school. What am I?
hints: I’m Colombian, and several generations have filled me.

The chocolate bar that feeds me has a three-letter name, like a fast airplane.
questions.description: Collecting with discipline and eating chocolate guilt-free: the perfect plan.
questions.fun_fact: Jet stickers have fun facts on the back, so you learn while you collect.

questions.question: Betty wears huge glasses and braces, is brilliant with numbers and works at Ecomoda. In which city does her story take place?
hints: Ecomoda is a fashion company in one of Colombia’s biggest cities.
It’s a chilly city, high up in the mountains.
It’s the capital of Colombia.
questions.description: Giant glasses, braces and a heart of gold: the most famous office on TV.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” has been remade in dozens of countries, including the US series “Ugly Betty.”

questions.question: Colombia's largest monument, by Rodrigo Arenas Betancourt, shows 14 lancers on horseback and honors an 1819 battle. Where is it?
hints: It stands out in open country, not on a city square.
The hero of that battle was Colonel Juan José Rondón.
It's near Paipa, in Boyacá.
questions.description: So much bronze in one place that you could melt down every pot in Grandma's kitchen with it, and the whole neighborhood's too.
questions.fun_fact: Arenas Betancourt lived in Mexico for many years, and several of his sculptures are there too.

questions.question: I'm a lady in a lullaby: they ask me why the baby is crying, and it's because he lost an apple. Who am I?
hints: Grandmothers sing it to get babies to sleep.
In the song, they promise the baby another apple so he'll stop crying.
According to tradition, I'm the mother of the Virgin Mary.
questions.description: The song that has put more Colombian babies to sleep than any other, and never charged a single peso for it.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, Saint Anne was Jesus's grandmother, and this lullaby came from Spain and is now sung across almost all of Latin America.

questions.question: His stories came from West Africa, are told in Creole on San Andrés and Providencia, and he always tricks the strongest. What kind of animal is Anansi?
hints: His stories come mostly from present-day Ghana.
He lives in a web he makes himself.
He has eight legs.
questions.description: A trickster who crossed the ocean and ended up telling tales by the sea of seven colors.
questions.fun_fact: In a tale from Ghana, Anansi buys all the world's stories from the sky god, which is why many folktales are called “Anansi stories”.

questions.question: Rafael Pombo was a member of the Colombian Academy of Language, the oldest such academy in the Americas. In what year was it founded?
hints: Colombia had already been independent for several decades.
Its founders included Miguel Antonio Caro and Rufino José Cuervo.
It was just one year after Charles Dickens died in 1870.
questions.description: The official guards making sure nobody ever says “haiga” or “nadien.”
questions.fun_fact: Rufino José Cuervo, one of its founders, started a dictionary so huge that it was finished almost a century after his death.

questions.question: In the famous Spanish tongue twister, who were swallowing wheat in a wheat field?
hints: It’s one of the best-known tongue twisters for kids in every Spanish-speaking country.
They’re big animals that live in the forests of Asia.
They have orange and black stripes.
questions.description: A tongue twister that leaves your tongue tired from all that chewing.
questions.fun_fact: “Tres tristes tigres” is also the title of a famous novel by Cuban writer Guillermo Cabrera Infante, known in English as “Three Trapped Tigers.”

questions.question: It comes at the end of fables, sometimes in a couple of verses, and Rafael Pombo put it in his «Fábulas y verdades». What is the moraleja?
hints: It has to do with right and wrong.
It answers the question “What did we learn?”
It comes from the word “moral.”
questions.description: Every fable saves something special for the very last line.
questions.fun_fact: Fables with a moral are ancient: Aesop's were already being told in Greece more than 2,500 years ago.

questions.question: In many folktales from Colombia and the Caribbean, a country boy takes everything literally and always messes up. Who is he?
hints: He isn't an animal.
Unlike Pedro Rimales, he isn't clever at all.
His nickname tells you how slow-witted he is.
questions.description: A country boy with more stories than harvests.
questions.fun_fact: In Puerto Rico, Juan Bobo is famous for a story where he dresses a pig in his mom's clothes and jewelry to take her to Mass.

questions.question: In «El renacuajo paseador», Rin Rin sings at doña Ratona's party. Who suddenly shows up and ends the party?
hints: They arrive uninvited and very hungry.
Mice are terrified of them.
They purr when they're happy.
questions.description: The party was going great until someone knocked on the door.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo took his idea from an old English song, “A Frog He Would A-Wooing Go,” about a frog who goes to court a mouse.

questions.question: You're listening to Shakira's session with Bizarrap. In the lyrics, “Ferrari” is to “Twingo” as “Rolex” is to…
hints: Shakira compares very expensive things with much cheaper ones.
In the song, the cheap watch stands for the new partner, who is worth far less than she is.
It's a brand famous for its calculators and the digital watch lots of students wear.
questions.description: A recording session that ended up costing more than a divorce.
questions.fun_fact: Shakira's BZRP Music Session #53 broke several YouTube records in its first 24 hours.

questions.question: In Colombia, if you really like something, you say it's “bacano.” Which of these expressions is NOT used there with that meaning?
hints: You'll hear three of them in any Colombian city.
The odd one out comes from across the ocean.
It's the favorite word of YouTubers from Spain.
questions.description: The paisa-rolo-costeño dictionary of things we love.
questions.fun_fact: “Bacano” is also used in Venezuela and other Caribbean countries, but in Colombia it's almost a national word.

questions.question: Whose 2018 album “Vibras” includes hits like “Ambiente” and “Machika”?
hints: He's a man, a reggaeton artist from Medellín.
He's called “the Prince of Reggaeton” and loves dyeing his hair.
“Mi gente” is on that same album.
questions.description: An album that could get even grandma dancing reggaeton, with her doctor's permission.
questions.fun_fact: “Vibras” won the Latin Grammy for Best Urban Music Album in 2018.

questions.question: In which city was the singer of “Dos Oruguitas” born? It's the Spanish-language song Lin-Manuel Miranda wrote for Encanto.
hints: The singer is Sebastián Yatra.
It's a mountain city, famous for its spring-like weather all year.
It's the capital of Antioquia.
questions.description: Two little bugs that made half the planet cry at the movies.
questions.fun_fact: “Dos Oruguitas” was nominated for the Oscar for Best Original Song, and Yatra sang it at the 2022 ceremony.

questions.question: In what year did Shakira's line “Las mujeres ya no lloran, las mujeres facturan” become famous?
hints: It was after the World Cup in Qatar.
It came out in January, in a session with an Argentine producer.
It was one year before Shakira released an album named after part of that same line.

questions.fun_fact: The following year, Shakira named her album “Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran.”

questions.question: “We Don't Talk About Bruno” is a song from a Disney movie. In which country is that movie set?
hints: It's a country of coffee, mountains and yellow butterflies.
The family lives in a magical house among coffee-growing mountains.
Its capital is Bogotá.
questions.description: A song about someone nobody talks about… that nobody can stop singing.
questions.fun_fact: “We Don't Talk About Bruno” reached number one on the US charts, something no Disney song had done since the 1990s.

questions.question: Which Andean rhythm is the song “Soy colombiano” by Rafael Godoy?
hints: It's one of the most traditional rhythms of the Andean region.
Couples dance it with a handkerchief, and it's often written in 6/8 time.
Its name starts almost like the plant used to make flutes and houses: bamboo.
questions.description: The song that makes any Colombian abroad cry, even if they only left yesterday.
questions.fun_fact: Rafael Godoy was from Huila, and his song became almost a second national anthem at patriotic celebrations.

questions.question: Carranga musicians sing in a ruana and a light, hand-woven hat that keeps off the sun. What is that hat made of?
hints: It's a material that comes from plants.

It's yellow and is also used to stuff scarecrows.
questions.description: The only roof a farmer wears on his head.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. I couldn't confirm the hat is straw. Sources confirm the ruana and hat are the carranga look and that Jorge Velosa wears both. Some sources mention a straw campesino hat (e.g. the jipa). Boyacá campesino hats are also often felt (wool). Velosa's own hat is usually a dark felt one, which would make 'Wool' arguably correct. No source I found says what the carranga hat is made of. The question's 'light, hand-woven' wording favours straw. The fun fact is broadly true.

questions.question: Alberto Castilla founded the music school in Ibagué that is now the Conservatorio del Tolima, but he wasn't from Tolima. Where was he born?
hints: He was born in the 19th century in an Andean city.
When he was born, it was already one of the most important cities in the country.
It's the capital of Colombia.
questions.description: A musician who fell so hard for Tolima that he moved in for good.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to his conservatory, Ibagué is known as the “Musical City of Colombia”.

questions.question: Los Tolimenses became famous for funny country songs. How many members did the group have?

questions.fun_fact: Luis Carlos González wrote the lyrics of “La ruana”, one of the most sung bambucos in Colombia.

questions.question: You're on a farm in the Eje Cafetero and “Mi cafetal” comes on the radio. Who wrote this song?

questions.description: A song that smells like freshly brewed tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Crescencio Salcedo is remembered as “the barefoot composer” because he refused to wear shoes.

questions.question: If you go out with a couple and you're the extra person, Colombians say you are “tocando…”. Which instrument completes the phrase?
hints: It's a string instrument.

It rests between the shoulder and the chin.
questions.description: When the couple holds hands and you hold your juice, all alone.

previous.feedback: The fun fact doesn't say what the source says. The source calls «tocar violín» very Colombian and says other countries use «hacer mal tercio» or «ser el chaperón». The translation instead says the phrase is also used in Chile and Peru, and that Spain uses «hacer de carabina» or «hacer mal tercio». The Chile and Peru claim is plausible, so the source's "very Colombian" may be overstated (source: worth checking). But the claim that Spain says «hacer mal tercio» can't be confirmed, since Spain typically says «hacer de carabina» or «sujetar la vela». Bring the fun fact back in line with the source, or keep only claims that can be confirmed (for example the Colombian saying plus the English "third wheel").

questions.question: In Colombia, if someone says “me toca camellar todo el sábado,” what do they have to do all Saturday?
hints: It has nothing to do with riding an animal.

questions.question: In the Llanos, what do they call the guide who knows every stream, every trail and every crossing of the savanna?

questions.description: The GPS of the plains: it wears a hat and its battery never dies.
questions.fun_fact: In Argentina and Uruguay they spell it «baqueano», and it means the same guide who knows the land by heart.

questions.question: In Colombia, this word describes a shirt in loud colors, a living room full of gold ornaments and someone showing off huge chains. What is it?
hints: It's a criticism, not a compliment.
It's the opposite of elegant.
It's also an animal that howls at the moon.
questions.description: In Bogotá fashion, this is worse than going out in your pajamas.
questions.fun_fact: Something in really bad taste is also called “una lobería.”

questions.question: In Colombia, who is most likely to say “¡qué calor, oís!” or “oís, ¿me vas a ayudar?”?
hints: In their city, people dance incredibly fast.
People there eat chontaduro and drink lulada.
They live in the “World Capital of Salsa”.
questions.description: A question that expects no answer, just your full attention.
questions.fun_fact: Cali calls itself the “World Capital of Salsa” and holds its Feria every December.

questions.question: It's noon and you haven't had lunch. Three of these phrases mean you're hungry. Which one does NOT?
hints: One of the four sounds like it's about food, but it's a trick.

questions.fun_fact: In Antioquia, being “tragado” with someone means being head over heels in love.

questions.question: The plebiscite of December 1, 1957, the first in which Colombian women voted, approved the Frente Nacional. What share voted Yes?
hints: Both big parties asked people to vote Yes.

questions.description: An election where millions of Colombian women stood in line to vote for the very first time.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian women won the right to vote in 1954, under Rojas Pinilla's government, but first used it in this plebiscite.

questions.question: It's sold from carts on the street and comes in lots of colors. What is a Bon Ice?
questions.answer: A flavored ice in a little tube

A frozen fruit pop on a little stick
An ice cream sandwich in a little wrapper
hints: It's sweet, and mostly kids eat it.

You bite off one end and squeeze it up as you eat.

questions.question: Many people call the Amazon rainforest “the lungs of the planet.” Why did it get that nickname?
wrong_answers: Because it looks like a lung on the map
Because all the winds start there
Because its rivers clean the seawater
hints: It has to do with the air we breathe.
Trees do something with sunlight.

questions.question: Hardly anyone sees them now, but the Colombian peso is divided into centavos. How many centavos make one peso?
hints: It's a round number.
The dollar and the euro are split into cents the same way.
It's a 1 followed by two zeros.
questions.description: So tiny that in Colombia not even the piggy bank wants them anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Because of inflation, centavo coins stopped being used in Colombia decades ago, and today the smallest coin in use is the 50-peso coin.

questions.question: You're having Corona hot chocolate for breakfast. How long ago was its maker, the Compañía Nacional de Chocolates, founded in Medellín?
hints: Your grandparents were already drinking this company's chocolate as kids.

It was founded in 1920.
questions.description: A company that has been sneaking into your breakfast for decades without asking.
questions.fun_fact: The Compañía Nacional de Chocolates is now part of Grupo Nutresa, one of Colombia's largest food companies.

questions.question: You’re at the laundry sink with a bottle of Límpido. Which of these should you NOT wash with it?
hints: Límpido is a chlorine bleach.
Chlorine removes stains… and other things too.
It can leave pale spots where there used to be dye.
questions.description: The laundry bottle your mom keeps on the highest shelf for a reason.
questions.fun_fact: Bleach should never be mixed with other cleaners like ammonia, because together they release dangerous gases.

questions.question: Savital, famous in Colombia for its sábila (aloe vera), is sold even in little packets at the corner store. What product is it?
hints: You use it in the bathroom.
You put it on with water and it makes foam.
It's for your head.
questions.description: A desert plant that became the star of the corner store.

questions.question: I directed “Pura sangre” (1982), about a tycoon who needs young blood, and the documentary “Todo comenzó por el fin.” Who am I?

questions.question: In which decade was the Cinemateca Distrital de Bogotá, now called Cinemateca de Bogotá, founded?

questions.question: On a Holy Thursday, an earthquake destroyed much of Popayán’s historic center. In which year?

questions.question: The Carnaval del Diablo in Riosucio, Caldas, isn't held every year. How often does it take place?

questions.question: Tourists come to Minca, in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, to look for the animal group in which Colombia has more species than any other country. Which group is it?

questions.question: The name Chapinero, in Bogotá, comes from the nickname of a Spanish craftsman who lived there in colonial times. What did he make?
hints: It was something people used every day to go out on the street.

questions.question: This statue in front of the San Felipe Castle in Cartagena honors the admiral who defended the city from the English in 1741. Who is he?
hints: He was a Spanish sailor born in the Basque Country.
