questions.description: In the Eje Cafetero, even the mountains wake up smelling of tinto.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has two coffee harvests a year: the main one and a smaller one called the “traviesa” or “mitaca.”

questions.question: At the school snack shop, you buy a 1,500-peso empanada and a 2,000-peso juice and pay with a 5,000-peso bill. How much change do you get?
hints: First, add up what you bought.
The empanada and the juice cost 3,500 pesos together.
Now subtract 3,500 from 5,000.
questions.description: The only store where the line is longer than recess.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian school snack shops, the empanada with ají is the undisputed queen of recess.

questions.question: It's December 31, minutes before midnight, and in many Colombian homes people sweep from inside toward the door. Why?
questions.answer: To get rid of the year's bad luck
wrong_answers: To make it rain in January
hints: It's one of the New Year's agüeros, like the grapes or the yellow underwear.
It's about what you don't want to carry into the new year.
The bad stuff from the old year goes out the door with the dust.
questions.description: When the year runs out, even a broom gets superpowers.
questions.fun_fact: Another Colombian New Year's agüero is carrying lentils in your pocket or wallet so you never run short of money.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: in Colombia, on sports day you don't wear your everyday uniform to school, but your…
hints: It's the PE uniform.
It's comfy for running and jumping in class.
It has long pants made of soft fabric and a sports jacket.
questions.description: A student's closet has two personalities.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian schools, seniors in grade 11 show off a “prom jacket” with their names embroidered on it.

questions.question: It stays at the bottom of the rice pot, comes out toasted and crunchy, and families fight over it. What do Colombians call it?
hints: Its name tells you where it ends up.
You can't serve it with a ladle: you have to scrape it off.
It stays stuck to the pot.
questions.description: The kitchen's greatest hidden treasure isn't in a chest, it's in a pot.
questions.fun_fact: Electric rice cookers leave almost no pegao, which is why many people still prefer to cook rice in a regular pot.

review.feedback: Source: the translation is faithful, but the fact check is uncertain on points I can't confirm either. "Cuncho" is Colombian for residue or dregs at the bottom of a pot, so it may be a defensible name for the same thing, and the claim that rice cookers leave almost no pegao, "which is why" people prefer pots, is unverified. The source needs a clearly wrong replacement for "Cuncho" and a softer or sourced fun fact; "pegao" itself is fine as a Colombian word, though "pega" and "cucayo" are also regional names. Fact check: uncertain. "Pegao" is used in Colombia, but sources mostly give cucayo/cucallo (Caribbean coast) and pega (Andean region) as the Colombian names. Pegao is the usual name in Puerto Rico. The wrong answer "Cuncho" could not be ruled out: the Spanish dictionary may list it in Colombia for the rice stuck to the pot, but I found no source for that. The fun fact about rice cookers was not verified. One source mentions a rice cooker designed to make pegao.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact is unverified. Neither the fact check nor I can confirm that electric rice cookers leave almost no pegao, or that this is why many people still cook rice in a regular pot. The source should soften or replace it, for example with a fact about the regional names pega and cucayo. The answer itself is fine: pegao is a widely used Colombian word, and the regional variants pega and cucayo are not among the options. Fact check: wrong. The main weakness is that Colombia has several regional names for this, so the question has more than one defensible answer. Cucayo (Caribbean coast) and pega (Andean region) are the most common; pegao is also used on the coast. The wrong answers are fine: chicharrón and calentado are different foods, and I found no source that lists 'cuncho' in Colombia (it looks like a variant of the Panamanian 'concho' or of 'concón'). Hint 1 ('Its name tells you where it stays') is inaccurate, because 'pegao' means 'stuck', not 'at the bottom'. Hint 3 ('stuck to the pot') gives the answer away. I couldn't verify the fun fact about electric rice cookers.

Fact check: uncertain. 'Pegao' (or 'pega') is a valid Colombian name for the rice crust, mainly in Antioquia, Bogotá and the Andean region. The Caribbean coast says 'cucayo', so the answer is region-dependent. 'Cuncho' is listed as a wrong answer, but it is a documented Latin American word for dregs or residue at the bottom of a pot. My searches did not confirm or rule out its use for rice crust in Colombia, so it may be a valid alternative. The question also says 'What do Colombians call it?', which implies a single name. The 'Cuncho' distractor is risky, and 'Calentado' (reheated leftovers) is fine.

Fact check: uncertain. Pegao is the standard Colombian term. But "cuncho" is also reported as a regional word for the rice crust or dregs in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, so it may not be clearly wrong. My search did not confirm or rule this out. Other regional names are cucayo (Caribbean coast) and pega.

questions.question: A delivery arrives at the portería (front gate) of your conjunto. What device rings in your apartment to let you know?
hints: It hangs on the wall, near the door or the kitchen.
You can only use it to talk to the front gate.
Its Colombian name, citófono, sounds a lot like the Spanish word for telephone.
questions.description: A gatekeeper that saves no goals, only your dinner order.
questions.fun_fact: In many other Spanish-speaking countries, like Spain, the citófono is called an interfono or a portero eléctrico.

questions.question: At a Colombian school, you're sent to talk to the person in charge of the whole school. Which office do you go to?
hints: The person in charge of the school has an office of their own.
Universities have a post with the same name.
In Colombia, universities are also led by someone with this title.
questions.description: The office where even the bravest kids walk very slowly.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, universities have a rector too, just like schools.

questions.question: It's a Colombian government survey that sorts households into groups with letters and is used for subsidies and subsidized health care. What is it?
hints: A surveyor visits homes and asks how the family lives.
The groups go from A to D.
Its name sounds like “see-ben.”
questions.description: A survey that comes to your house and doesn't ask your favorite color.
questions.fun_fact: In Sisbén IV, group A covers households in extreme poverty and group D those that are not poor.

questions.question: It's always on the preschool supply list: it comes in colored sticks, you knead it with your hands and make little figures with it. What is it?
hints: It's a cheap supply that kids love to use in art class.
It doesn't dry out, so you can use it again and again.
You roll it into little snakes and balls.
questions.description: What starts on the supply list ends up on the sofa, in your hair and even on the dog.
questions.fun_fact: Plasticine was invented in England in 1897, and it doesn't dry out even if you leave it out.

questions.question: You go to the Registraduría to get your cédula. The Registraduría is to the cédula as the Cancillería is to the…
hints: The Cancillería handles relations with other countries.
You need it to travel outside Colombia.
It gets stamped at the airport.
questions.description: Every document has its own window, and every window has its own line.
questions.fun_fact: The Registraduría also runs the elections in Colombia.

questions.question: In the name of the YouTube channel “Calle y Poché,” what is “Calle”?
questions.answer: The last name of one of them
wrong_answers: The Bogotá street where they filmed
The name of their first pet
hints: “Poché” is the nickname of María José, the other half of the duo.
Each of them put something of her own into the channel's name.
The other member is named Daniela, and on her ID card “Calle” comes right after her first name.
questions.description: Two friends, one camera, and the hardest decision of all: what to name the channel.
questions.fun_fact: Calle y Poché went from YouTube videos to music and also appeared on TV shows.

questions.question: This man governed New Granada from Santafé on July 20, 1810, and a few days later was arrested and banished. Who is he?
hints: He held the post of viceroy.
He was the last viceroy before the Grito de Independencia.
His second surname is the name of the Spanish royal family.
questions.description: On July 20, 1810, he got up as the boss and went to bed with his job up in the air.
questions.fun_fact: The viceroy's wife, Francisca Villanova, was also arrested, and the crowd insulted her on the way to jail.

questions.question: Pablo Morillo created me during the Reconquista to take the patriots' houses, estates and goods and hand them to the Crown. What was my name?
hints: I was one of the three courts of the Reign of Terror.
My job was to seize property.
My name uses a Spanish word that today makes people think of kidnapping.
questions.description: A lost-and-found office, except nothing had been lost.
questions.fun_fact: The Consejo de Purificación tried suspect officials and the Consejo de Guerra tried patriot leaders: Morillo had a court for everything.

questions.question: July 20, 1810, was a Friday and market day, and the criollos took advantage of a crowded spot in Santafé. Which one?
hints: It was the city's main square.
Back then it was called the Plaza Mayor.
Today the Capitol and the Primatial Cathedral stand around it.
questions.description: If you want half the town to see you, pick your day and your spot carefully.
questions.fun_fact: The house that held Llorente's shop, on a corner of that square, is now the Museo de la Independencia – Casa del Florero.

questions.question: This town on the banks of the Magdalena River declared full independence from Spain on August 6, 1810. Which one is it?
hints: It's in the department of Bolívar.
Bolívar said he owed it his glory.
It's famous for its gold filigree and its Holy Week.
questions.description: A town so peaceful today that it's hard to believe it once shouted so loud.
questions.fun_fact: Bolívar said, “If to Caracas I owe my life, to Mompox I owe my glory,” because he recruited many of his first soldiers there.

questions.question: Which popular leader from Pasto kept fighting for the King of Spain until 1824, when independence had already been won?
hints: He came from a humble background and rose to colonel in the king's army.
In 1824 he attacked the town of Barbacoas, on the Pacific coast.
His surname begins with the Spanish word for water.
questions.description: While half the continent shouted “Long live independence!”, someone in the south was shouting something else.
questions.fun_fact: Today many people in Pasto remember him as a local hero, and he even has a monument in the city.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: in the Patria Boba, in New Granada, the “carracos” and the “pateadores” were…
wrong_answers: Two battalions of the patriot army
hints: They fought over how to organize the new country.
One of them followed Antonio Nariño.
They were nicknames for centralists and federalists.
questions.description: Nicknames about as affectionate as the ones rival fans give each other.
questions.fun_fact: The rivalry between centralists and federalists led to civil war, which is why the period earned the name “Patria Boba” (Foolish Fatherland).

questions.question: In February 1816, the Battle of Cachirí, in Santander, left the road to Santafé wide open. Which side won it?
hints: It was fought on a cold páramo, on the road from the country's northeast to the capital.
The beaten army had been retreating from the north and broke apart after the battle.
The winners served Ferdinand VII.
questions.description: A cold páramo where they settled who would reach the capital first.
questions.fun_fact: After Cachirí, the king's troops marched into Santafé in May 1816 with almost no resistance.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what do people in Colombia call this plant that grandma uses for burns and for hair?
hints: Its leaves are thick, with little spines along the edges.
Inside, it has a clear, cool gel.
In other countries it's called aloe vera.
questions.description: Grandma has more plants on the patio than the corner drugstore has remedies.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian homes, a sábila leaf tied with a red ribbon hangs behind the door to bring good luck and keep bad energy away.

questions.question: The peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta call themselves “older brothers” because, by their tradition, their task is to…
questions.answer: …look after the balance of the world
wrong_answers: …be the first to reach the sea
hints: The Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa and Kankuamo call themselves this.
Their spiritual guides are called mamos and train for many years.
For them, the Sierra is the heart of the world and must be protected.
questions.description: Being the older sibling was never just about age… or about keeping the TV remote.
questions.fun_fact: For the peoples of the Sierra Nevada, whatever happens in those mountains affects the whole planet, which is why they call it “the heart of the world.”

questions.question: “Se va el caimán” tells of a man who turned half caiman, and his town holds a Caiman Man Festival every year. Which town?
hints: It's in the department of Magdalena.
It sits on the banks of the Magdalena River.
Its name is the Spanish word for the dish you serve food on.
questions.description: A song that gets everyone dancing, even though it tells the story of a man with very bad life choices.
questions.fun_fact: “Se va el caimán” was written by José María Peñaranda and became so famous that bands all over Latin America have recorded it.

questions.question: In Colombian villages, if you twist your ankle, who do they take you to so it gets put back in place?
hints: You find one in almost every village, and many people trust them more than the hospital.
Fixes sprains and twisted joints with massages that hurt.
The name comes from the Spanish verb “sobar”, to rub.
questions.description: A village specialist with no white coat, no office and no waiting room.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombian villages, a sobandero is often famous across the whole region, and people travel for hours to have a bone “put back in place.”

questions.question: They speak Damana, were once called “Arsarios” or “Malayos,” and live in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. Which people are they?
hints: They are one of the four peoples of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
They live mainly on the slopes facing La Guajira and Cesar.
Their name has only two syllables, and both start with the same letter.
questions.description: The Sierra Nevada has four elder brothers, and today you have to guess one of them.
questions.fun_fact: The four peoples of the Sierra Nevada see themselves as “elder brothers” whose task is to keep the world in balance.

questions.question: You're in the main square of San Basilio de Palenque, facing a statue of a man breaking his chains. Who founded the palenque?
hints: He was an enslaved African who escaped near Cartagena more than 400 years ago.
He was called “the King of Arcabuco.”
His name starts with “Ben…”.
questions.description: A king who needed no crown, only the will to be free.
questions.fun_fact: San Basilio de Palenque is seen as the first free town in the Americas, and UNESCO has listed it as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: Many communities in Colombia are bilingual, speaking Spanish and their own language. Which of these languages is NOT one of them?
hints: Three of these languages are heard in La Guajira, near Cartagena and on the Caribbean islands.
The odd one out is an official language in another South American country.
It is spoken mainly in Paraguay.
questions.description: Speaking two languages is like having two keys to the same house.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has about 65 Indigenous languages, plus Palenquero, Creole and Romani.

questions.question: Colombia’s Ministry of Culture coordinates the law that protects the country’s native languages. In which decade was that ministry created?
hints: Before it existed, culture was handled by a smaller institute called Colcultura.
It was created by the General Law of Culture.
It came a few years after the 1991 Constitution.
questions.description: Even culture needs someone to do its paperwork.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia’s Ministry of Culture was born with Law 397 of 1997.

questions.question: In Colombia you can call a friend «socio». Which of these words is NOT used in Colombia to mean the same?
hints: You hear three of these words on any street corner in Colombia.
The odd one out is heard a lot in another country’s films and telenovelas.
It’s the typical way to say “friend” in Mexico.
questions.description: In Colombia there are more words for “friend” than actual friends.
questions.fun_fact: «Cuate» comes from the Nahuatl «cóatl», meaning “snake” and also “twin”, which is why in Mexico «cuate» can also mean a twin.

questions.question: You're celebrating a goal by the national team and get sprayed with espuma carioca (party foam). What does the word “carioca” mean?
hints: It's a word that comes from Portuguese.
It's what people call the residents of a Brazilian city famous for its carnival.
That city is home to Christ the Redeemer and Copacabana beach.
questions.description: Carnival's most dangerous weapon: it leaves everyone white, sticky and happy.
questions.fun_fact: People from Rio de Janeiro are called cariocas, while people from the city of São Paulo are called paulistanos.

questions.question: Jorge Carrascal played for CSKA and Dynamo, two big clubs from the same capital city. In which country are they?
hints: It's a European country with very cold winters.
It's the largest country in the world by area.
Both clubs are from Moscow.
questions.description: A midfielder who has traveled the world more than a suitcase lost at the airport.
questions.fun_fact: Before joining River Plate, Carrascal had already played in Ukraine for Karpaty Lviv as a teenager.

questions.question: The 2021 Copa América was supposed to be played in Colombia and Argentina, but it moved in the end. Which country hosted it?
hints: That country had also hosted the previous Copa América, in 2019
Colombia finished third there
The final was played at the Maracanã stadium
questions.description: A tournament that packed its bags at the last minute, like someone leaving on a trip without telling anyone.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia beat Peru 3–2 for third place, with a stunning last-minute goal by Luis Díaz from outside the box.

questions.question: At this stadium in La Paz, about 3,600 m (11,800 ft) up, Colombia's national team runs short of air. Who was Hernando Siles, the man it's named after?
hints: He wasn't an athlete
He lived in the early 20th century
He governed from the Palacio Quemado in La Paz
questions.description: A stadium where even running to the bathroom counts as high-performance training.
questions.fun_fact: Hernando Siles was president of Bolivia from 1926 to 1930, and his son Hernán Siles Zuazo also became president.

questions.question: At the 2014 World Cup, goalkeeper Faryd Mondragón became the oldest player ever to play at a World Cup. How old was he?
hints: He had already played at the 1998 World Cup in France
He was over forty
He had had his birthday just three days before the match
questions.description: A goalkeeper who proved that gloves don't come with an expiration date.
questions.fun_fact: His record lasted until 2018, when Egypt's Essam El-Hadary played at a World Cup at age 45.

questions.question: I'm a stretch of rapids and rocks on the Orinoco River in Vichada, next to El Tuparro park. Alexander von Humboldt called me “the eighth wonder of the world.” What am I?
hints: I'm on the border between Colombia and Venezuela.
My name comes from an Indigenous people who lived in that part of the Orinoco.
My name starts with “Mai…”.
questions.description: A stretch of river so wild that even a German scientist was left speechless.
questions.fun_fact: Humboldt passed through these rapids in 1800, during his famous journey along the Orinoco.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this fog covers the páramo almost every day. What does it give plants like the frailejones?
hints: Páramos are high, cold places where it's almost never hot.
The fuzzy leaves of the frailejones catch something the fog brings.
It's the same thing that later flows down the rivers to the cities.
questions.description: A cloud that got tired of flying and lay down for a nap on the páramo.
questions.fun_fact: Frailejones catch water from the fog and release it little by little, which is why páramos are like water factories.

questions.question: Tayrona Park closes several times a year so nature can rest. About how many days a year is it closed in total?
hints: For most of the year, the park does welcome tourists.
It usually closes three times: in February, in June, and between October and November.
Each closure lasts about two weeks.
questions.description: Even paradise needs to take a vacation now and then.
questions.fun_fact: The closures are agreed with the Indigenous peoples of the Sierra Nevada, who use them for rituals to spiritually cleanse the land.

questions.question: About how many protected areas are in Colombia's National Natural Parks System?
hints: There are more than you can count on one hand.
It includes parks, flora and fauna sanctuaries, and reserves.
More than 50 but fewer than 100.
questions.description: A sticker album that collects jungles, páramos and reefs instead of soccer players.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park was Cueva de los Guácharos, in Huila, created in 1960.

questions.question: You're on the páramo in a thick jacket. The jacket is to you as what is to the frailejón?
hints: Think about why you put on the jacket.
It's what protects it from the cold and the frost.
If you touch its leaves, they feel as soft as a blanket.
questions.description: On the páramo, even the plants got dressed before going out.
questions.fun_fact: Some frailejones grow only about 1 centimeter (less than half an inch) a year, so a tall one can be more than 100 years old.

questions.question: In the triple jump, Caterine Ibargüen landed in a place like this one. What is it called?
hints: Long jumpers and triple jumpers land here.
After each jump, a judge measures the mark you left.
It ends up full of footprints, like a beach.
questions.description: This is where Olympic dreams land… and sometimes faces too.
questions.fun_fact: Before each jump, officials smooth the sand with a rake so the new mark shows up clearly.

questions.question: In an Olympic BMX final, like the ones Mariana Pajón races, how many riders start together from the ramp?
hints: It's an even number.
It's more than six.
It's the same number as a spider's legs.
questions.description: A race where rolling down a ramp is only the start of the scare.
questions.fun_fact: The start ramp on Olympic BMX tracks is about 8 m (26 ft) high, almost as tall as a three-story building.

questions.question: At the Olympics held in this stadium, which Colombian woman won a bronze medal in wrestling?
hints: The stadium is the famous “Bird's Nest” of Beijing 2008.
Four years later, at London 2012, she won bronze again.
Her first name starts with J.
questions.description: A stadium that looks like it was built by a bird with a huge budget.
questions.fun_fact: At those same Beijing Games, weightlifter Diego Salazar gave Colombia a silver medal.

questions.question: In this sport, which Colombian won the silver medal in the light flyweight class at Rio 2016?
hints: It was at the same Games where Ingrit Valencia won bronze.
In the final he lost to a boxer from Uzbekistan.
His first name is very rare and starts with “Yuber”.
questions.description: A weight class named after an insect, but with very real punches.
questions.fun_fact: At Rio 2016, light flyweight was the lightest class in men's Olympic boxing, with a limit of 49 kg (108 lb).

questions.question: In which of these sports did Colombia NOT win a medal at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics?
hints: Colombia won five medals at those Games.
Anthony Zambrano in the 400 meters and Sandra Arenas in race walking both won silver.
Colombia's men's national team in this sport didn't even qualify.
questions.description: Japan, 2021: a Games that showed up a year late, like the bus at rush hour.
questions.fun_fact: The Tokyo 2020 medals were made from metal recycled from old cell phones and other electronics.

questions.question: I have four wheels and an engine, I ride close to the ground, and I have no roof or doors. Juan Pablo Montoya started racing me as a kid in Bogotá. What am I?
hints: There are tracks for me in several Colombian cities, even in some shopping malls.
Many Formula 1 drivers start out with me as kids.
Mario and Luigi race me too in a very famous video game.
questions.description: A real car that shrank in the wash but still goes super fast.
questions.fun_fact: Montoya started karting at age 6 and went on to win Formula 1 races in Monaco and Monza.

questions.question: You're watching Sebastián Muñoz from Bogotá win his first PGA Tour event in Mississippi, in a playoff. What year is it?
hints: Before turning pro, Muñoz played college golf at the University of North Texas.
It was in the 2010s.
It was one year before the COVID-19 pandemic began.
questions.description: Golf: the only sport where whoever hits the ball the least wins.
questions.fun_fact: With that win, Muñoz became the second Colombian to win a PGA Tour event, after Camilo Villegas.

questions.question: Alongside the National Games, Colombia holds another competition between departments, with sports like boccia and goalball. Who is it for?
hints: It is usually held in the same year and region as the National Games.
Its best athletes can go on to other games held after the Olympics.
Goalball is played blindfolded, with a ball that has bells inside.
questions.description: A competition where the medals weigh the same, but the stories weigh double.
questions.fun_fact: In goalball the crowd must stay silent, because the players find the ball by the sound of its bells.

questions.question: Which of these figures from Cartagena's history was NOT a sailor?
hints: Three of them are linked to sea battles or attacks on Cartagena.
The one you want became famous for something he wrote, not for a ship.
He translated the Rights of Man into Spanish.
questions.description: A question that smells of salt, cannon smoke and tales from the high seas.
questions.fun_fact: The Colombian Navy has a training ship called “Gloria” that has sailed around the world several times.

questions.question: Which art critic, born in Argentina, founded the Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá and championed Obregón and Botero?
hints: She was no painter: words were her weapon.
She also hosted art programs on Colombian television.
She was born in Buenos Aires and also wrote novels.
questions.description: This lady told painters what nobody else dared to tell them.
questions.fun_fact: Marta Traba was also a novelist: her book “Las ceremonias del verano” won the Casa de las Américas Prize in 1966.

questions.question: You're at the Casa del Florero in Bogotá, which remembers July 20, 1810. Which of these did NOT happen that day?
hints: Look for something that happened years later.
One of these was a fight between armies, far from Bogotá.
It happened in 1819, near a bridge.
questions.description: It all started because someone wouldn't lend out a table decoration.
questions.fun_fact: The famous Llorente vase can still be seen in the museum, even though it's broken.

questions.question: I'm an artist from Córdoba, Colombia: I fill whole rooms with soil mixed with cinnamon and cloves, as I did at the 2022 Venice Biennale. Who am I?
hints: You smell my works as well as look at them.
I was born in Tierralta, Córdoba.
My installation in Venice was called “Earthly Paradise.”
questions.description: An artist who filled an entire museum without hanging a single painting on the wall.
questions.fun_fact: Her mountains of soil mix mud, spices and even cassava flour, and the smell fills the whole room.

questions.question: Look at the department highlighted on the map. Its capital is famous as “the City of Parks.” Which city is it?
hints: It's a department in the eastern Andes, famous for its hormigas culonas (big-bottomed ants).
Its people are called santandereanos.
The city sits on a plateau, not far from the Chicamocha Canyon.
questions.description: A city with so many parks that even the squirrels have to wait in line for a bench.
questions.fun_fact: Bucaramanga is also called “the Pretty City of Colombia.”

questions.question: Look at this pedestrian street in downtown Bogotá. When people stroll along it with no rush, watching artists and street vendors, what do they call that outing?
hints: It's a very long street that crosses Bogotá from south to north.
It runs past the Plaza de Bolívar.
The name of the outing comes from the street's number.
questions.description: Strolling with no rush, buying mango biche and watching a mime: the perfect Sunday plan.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries, the Carrera Séptima was the old road that led out of Bogotá toward Tunja.

questions.question: Johnny Cay is a small cay a few minutes by boat from San Andrés, full of palm trees and white sand. What is it made of?
hints: It formed little by little in the sea.
Tiny living things built it.
Its sand comes from the reefs around it.
questions.description: An island so tiny you can walk around it before your raspado melts.
questions.fun_fact: The San Andrés islands are part of the Seaflower Biosphere Reserve, declared by UNESCO in 2000.

questions.question: The Torre Colpatria in downtown Bogotá has 50 floors, stands 196 m (643 ft) tall and glows with colored lights at night. What is it mainly used for?
hints: It was built by a financial group that gave it its name.
Thousands of people go there from Monday to Friday.
Inside you'll find desks, computers and meeting rooms.
questions.description: Bogotá's tallest Christmas tree, switched on all year round.
questions.fun_fact: Every year there is a race to run up its nearly 1,000 steps.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. The fun fact is off. The Torre Colpatria stair race is usually quoted as 980 steps over 48 floors, so 'nearly 1,000' is about right for that source. questions.question: Look at the photo: it's the India Catalina monument in Cartagena. A small replica of this figure is the trophy for some awards. Awards for what?

questions.question: Near Villa de Leyva there's a field of stone columns once used to track the sun, called El Infiernito. Which people built it?

questions.question: Look at this hat that farmers on the Caribbean coast wear to work in the fields. What does it mainly protect them from?

questions.question: It's called Colombia's “river star”: the Magdalena and Cauca rivers start there, near San Agustín. What place is it?

questions.question: I'm round and flat, people made me from corn before the Spanish arrived, and you eat me for breakfast with butter and cheese. What am I?
hints: I'm cooked on a grill or on a clay griddle called a tiesto.

questions.question: Look at this flag: which country is it from?

questions.question: According to tradition, how long has tejo been played in Colombia?

questions.question: Which Colombian landscape is on the back of the 100,000-peso bill, the one with Carlos Lleras Restrepo?
hints: It's a green, cold place in the mountains.

The wax palm, the national tree, grows there.

questions.fun_fact: The Quindío wax palm can grow over 50 meters (160 ft) tall, higher than a 15-story building.

questions.question: Your December prima (the bonus every employer must pay) arrives, but it's only half of the year's prima. In which month do you get the other half?
hints: It's in the first half of the year.

questions.description: The extra cash that shows up just in time for natilla and buñuelos.
questions.fun_fact: By law, the December prima must be paid by December 20 at the latest.

questions.question: In which decade was Leonisa, the underwear and swimwear brand from Medellín, founded?
hints: It's older than most of the parents who buy it.
It was born shortly after television arrived in Colombia.
It was born in the middle of the 20th century.
questions.description: Paisa fashion that has seen a whole lot of beach seasons come and go.
questions.fun_fact: Leonisa started in Medellín and today sells its clothes in many countries across the Americas and Europe.

questions.question: Besides the big Carnival, Barranquilla has another one with its own queen, dance groups and parade. Who dances in it?
hints: It's been a tradition of the Carnaval de Barranquilla for decades.
The queen of this carnival can't vote or drive a car.

questions.fun_fact: Barranquilla's Carnaval de los Niños also crowns a child queen, who joins the queen of the grown-ups' carnival.

questions.question: At the Feria de Manizales, a queen is crowned in the International Pageant of… what?
hints: Manizales sits high in the Andes mountains.
It's one of the products Colombia sells most to other countries.
Juan Valdez carries it on his mule.
questions.description: Manizales picks a queen, and half the planet sends a contestant.
questions.fun_fact: Contestants from coffee-growing countries on several continents come to the International Coffee Pageant.

questions.question: It's “Faltan cinco pa' las doce” (five to midnight) on December 31 and, as the song says, you run home. Why?
hints: The song is about getting there on time, before the year ends.

questions.description: On December 31, everyone turns into an Olympic sprinter for the last five minutes of the year.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian homes, as soon as the clock strikes twelve, the family lines up so everyone can hug everyone.

questions.question: They're made of colored paper, set out on sidewalks and windows in December, with a small candle inside. Besides decorating, what are these lanterns for?

To wrap the presents from Niño Dios
To mark the homes that pray the novena

Think about what happens to a candle outdoors.
The paper works as walls around the flame.
questions.description: A colorful little house that lights up only one night a year.
questions.fun_fact: Every December, Quimbaya, in Quindío, holds a festival famous for its giant paper lanterns lit with candles.

questions.question: Its Holy Week processions date back to the 16th century and are on UNESCO's heritage list. Which Colombian city holds them?
hints: It's the capital of Cauca, in the country's southwest.

Its name starts with P.
questions.description: One week when the whole city walks very slowly, candle in hand.
questions.fun_fact: Popayán's processions were added to UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2009.

questions.question: It has the child's name and the date, sometimes a drawing of a chalice, and guests get one at a first communion. What is it called?
hints: Guests take it home with them.
It's small and almost always made of paper or card stock.

questions.description: The official souvenir of a day when everyone behaves like a little angel.
questions.fun_fact: Many families keep the recordatorios from their children's and nephews' first communions for decades.

questions.question: They call me the “West Indian cherry,” and I have far more vitamin C than an orange. What fruit am I?
hints: I grow on a shrub in hot climates.

Health food stores sell me as a powder, as a vitamin C supplement.

questions.question: You're eating guanábana and picking out the black seeds. What does the plant need those seeds for?
hints: If you plant them in soil, something happens.

Trees, flowers and vegetables all start from one of these.

questions.question: In Colombia, about how old are students when they graduate from once, the last grade of school?

questions.question: In Colombia, what is a “morral”?

questions.question: Panama became independent from Spain on November 28, 1821. Which country did it join soon after, of its own free will?

questions.question: On July 4, 1810, in Pamplona, a woman stood up to the Spanish magistrate and took away his staff of command. Who was she?

previous.feedback: The answer "the dactylological alphabet" copies the Spanish "alfabeto dactilológico" word for word. questions.question: Gorgona Island, in the Pacific, is a national park today, but it used to be a prison. In which decade was the prison closed?

questions.question: In the markets of Putumayo and Caquetá, they sell little bottles of “sangre de drago.” It's red and thick, and people use it to heal wounds. What is it?

questions.question: Look at this mola made by the Gunadule people. How is it made?

questions.description: In Cali on a Saturday night, there's no empty dance floor and no neighbor asleep.
questions.fun_fact: People say that in Cali, 33 rpm records were played at 45 rpm, and that's why Cali salsa is danced so fast.

questions.question: El Rey de Rocha is huge, painted in bright colors and makes champeta boom at parties on Colombia's Caribbean coast. What is it?
hints: It doesn't sing or play instruments, but it's incredibly loud.
It has giant speakers and a DJ who runs it.
It's a sound system typical of Barranquilla and Cartagena.
questions.description: It wears a crown, but instead of a castle it lives at a neighborhood street party.
questions.fun_fact: Picós compete to have the most exclusive records, and sometimes they scratch the label off the vinyl so rivals can't tell what the song is.

questions.question: Evan in “Embrace of the Serpent” is based on Richard Evans Schultes, who searched the Amazon in World War II for trees that give…
hints: Japan had cut off access to the big plantations in Asia.
It was a key material for the war, and the United States paid for trips to find it growing wild in South America.
It comes out as a white latex when you cut the tree's bark.
questions.description: A gringo from Harvard walked into the Colombian jungle and took twelve years to come back out.
questions.fun_fact: Schultes is seen as the father of modern ethnobotany, the study of how peoples use plants.

questions.question: Which priest and botanist founded the Bogotá Botanical Garden in 1955?
hints: He was born in Medellín in the late 19th century.
He wrote the book “Plantas útiles de Colombia” (Useful Plants of Colombia).
He studied botany in Munich, Germany, and fought to protect Colombia's forests and soils.
questions.description: A priest who, instead of counting rosary beads, counted orchids.
questions.fun_fact: Even though he founded it, the garden is named after José Celestino Mutis, the director of the Royal Botanical Expedition.

questions.question: “Carros de balineras” are homemade carts you brake with the soles of your shoes, named after their wheels. What are “balineras”?
hints: They're taken out of old machines or cars.
Inside, they hide tiny metal balls.
They're metal rings that spin smoothly thanks to little balls.
questions.description: Neighborhood Formula 1: a downhill engine and shoe-powered brakes.
questions.fun_fact: Several Colombian cities hold carro de balineras festivals on their steepest streets.

questions.question: In parqués, what is the square called where nobody can capture your piece?
hints: There are several spread around the board
They usually have a different mark from the other squares
In Spanish, it's the same word as the insurance you pay to protect your car or house
questions.description: The only spot on the board where a game piece can sleep soundly.
questions.fun_fact: Pieces of different colors can share that square without any of them capturing another.

questions.question: Héctor Ulloa was “Don…” in an '80s series. In Spanish, the nickname is also a biting insect and a thumbtack. What is it?
hints: The series took place in a Bogotá neighborhood, and he was the handyman who fixed everything.
The insect hides in old mattresses and bites you at night.
In Colombia, you use one to pin a paper to a corkboard.
questions.description: A nickname that bites, pins things up, and fixes pipes too.
questions.fun_fact: “Don Chinche” was on the air for about seven years, from 1982 to 1989, and is one of the best-remembered comedies on Colombian TV.

questions.question: RTVC runs Colombia's public media. Señal Colombia is to TV as which station is to radio?
hints: It belongs to the same house, RTVC, as Señal Colombia.
It was born in 1940, long before Colombian television.
It's the country's oldest public radio station, and it carries the country's name.
questions.description: A public family with one sibling you can watch and another you can only hear.
questions.fun_fact: Radio Nacional de Colombia began broadcasting in 1940, fourteen years before the country's first TV signal.

questions.question: Laura Restrepo won the 2004 Alfaguara Novel Prize with “Delirio” (Delirium). Which of these Colombians has NOT won that prize?
hints: In its current form, the prize has been awarded since 1998.
The three Colombian winners on the list all received the prize in this century.
He won the Nobel Prize in 1982.
questions.description: A novel whose title sounds like a diagnosis from the emergency room.
questions.fun_fact: Before becoming a novelist, Laura Restrepo was a journalist and served on a peace commission in the 1980s.

questions.question: Jairo Aníbal Niño, from Boyacá, wrote it in the 1980s, and Colombian schools read it a lot. What is “La alegría de querer”?
questions.answer: A book of love poems for children
wrong_answers: A young-adult love novel set in the jungle
A play about an impossible love
A collection of love stories for teenagers
hints: It has no long chapters.
Its texts are very short, and each one fits on a page.
It's about first crushes, written in verse.
questions.description: A book that has spent decades in Colombian school backpacks and still makes parents sigh.
questions.fun_fact: Jairo Aníbal Niño also wrote “Zoro,” a novel widely read by young Colombians.

questions.question: It has been awarded every year since the 1970s to the best work in Colombian journalism. What is this traditional prize called?
hints: It is run by a Colombian company, not a journalists’ foundation.
It is named after a historical figure, not a journalist or the symbol of a city.
It is named after the Liberator.
questions.description: The trophy every Colombian journalist dreams of placing next to their voice recorder.
questions.fun_fact: The prize has a lifetime achievement category, which has gone to great figures of Colombian journalism.

questions.question: Born in Magangué, she married García Márquez in 1958 and stayed by his side to the end. What pet name did Gabo have for Mercedes Barcha?
hints: The nickname has nothing to do with his novels.
The nickname compares her calm, unshakable character to an animal.
It's a river reptile with lots of teeth… and divine, too.
questions.description: Behind every great Nobel winner stood a great woman, and a nickname only he dared to use.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexico, Mercedes pawned things from their home so Gabo could finish “One Hundred Years of Solitude.”

questions.question: Bogotá-born Ivar Da Coll writes and illustrates picture books for little ones, with almost no words. Which animal stars in his most famous series?
hints: It's a very calm Colombian animal.
It loves water and lives in the Llanos.
It's a big, chubby rodent that lives in groups near rivers and lagoons.
questions.description: Books with very few words and a whole lot of heart.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia this animal is called chigüiro, in Venezuela chigüire, and in Brazil capivara.

questions.question: Jairo Varela founded Grupo Niche and wrote “Cali pachanguero,” but he wasn't from Cali. In which city was he born?
hints: He was born in Colombia's Pacific region.
It's the capital of a very rainy department.
It's the home of chirimía music, on the banks of the Atrato River.
questions.description: He gave Cali so much salsa that the city returned the favor with some giant trumpets.
questions.fun_fact: Cali has a monument to Jairo Varela made of giant metal trumpets, honoring his music.

questions.question: The redoblante of marching bands and chirimía is a drum with two heads, played with sticks. What on its bottom head gives it that “rattly” sound?
hints: It's nothing you could eat.
They are stretched tight against the bottom head.
They are coiled, like the ones inside a mattress.
questions.description: A drum that sounds like it caught a cough.
questions.fun_fact: Many redoblantes have a lever that lifts those springs off the head, so it sounds like a plain drum.

questions.question: Look at this waterfall: it's the Salto de Bordones, dropping almost 400 m (1,300 ft) through a canyon. Which department is it in?
hints: It's in the south of the country, in the Andes.
It's near the Colombian Massif, where the Magdalena River begins.
It's in the town of Isnos, very close to the San Agustín Archaeological Park.
questions.description: A river that got tired of walking and decided to dive in headfirst.
questions.fun_fact: The Salto de Bordones is one of the tallest waterfalls in Colombia, and the stone statues of San Agustín are just a few kilometers away.

questions.question: Buenaventura, on its bay, is Colombia's biggest Pacific port. Which of these places is NOT on the Pacific?
hints: Three of them are in Chocó, Cauca and Nariño, facing west.
The odd one out is in Antioquia.
It's on the Gulf of Urabá, on the Caribbean Sea.
questions.description: Some ports watch the sunset, and others watch the sunrise.
questions.fun_fact: A large share of Colombia's trade with Asia, across the Pacific Ocean, passes through the port of Buenaventura.

questions.question: Almost 50 years ago in Antioquia, a valley and even the old town of El Peñol were flooded to create a huge reservoir beside the famous rock. What for?
wrong_answers: To bring water to the desert
hints: It has to do with something you use at home every day.
The dammed water turns big machines called turbines.
Thanks to it, lots of light bulbs turn on across Colombia.
questions.description: A town that went for a swim and never came back out.
questions.fun_fact: The people of old El Peñol moved to a new town, where they built a replica of the town left underwater.

questions.question: In the swamps and rivers of Colombia, what is a babilla?
questions.answer: A reptile similar to a crocodile
hints: It has scales and lays eggs.
It spends hours motionless in the water with only its eyes showing.
It has many teeth, a long strong tail and skin like leather.
questions.description: Its name sounds a little like “baby”, but it doesn't sleep in any crib.
questions.fun_fact: Some people call the babilla the “spectacled caiman”, because of the bony ridge between its eyes.

questions.question: The orchestra Son de Cali was formed in 2002 by musicians who used to sing in another famous group. Which one did they come from?
hints: It was a salsa orchestra, not a cumbia or chucu-chucu one.
Although it's a symbol of Cali, that orchestra was formed in Bogotá in the late 1970s.
It was founded by Jairo Varela.
questions.description: When an orchestra has children, the children come out dancing too.
questions.fun_fact: Willy García, one of the voices of Son de Cali, had sung Grupo Niche hits before founding the new orchestra.

questions.question: Cali-born Nubia Muñoz helped prove that the human papillomavirus causes a cancer. What does the vaccine given to girls from age 9 prevent?
hints: The virus behind it passes from person to person, and the vaccine works best before the teen years.
In Colombia it is one of the most common cancers among women.
Only women can get it, and doctors check for it early with a Pap smear.
questions.description: A vaccine that stings for a second and protects for decades.
questions.fun_fact: German scientist Harald zur Hausen won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Medicine for discovering this link, and Nubia Muñoz's studies helped confirm it around the world.

questions.question: Diana Trujillo, from Cali, led the team behind this Mars rover's robotic arm. What does the robot use that arm for?
questions.answer: To collect and study rocks and soil
wrong_answers: To get back up if it tips over
hints: The robot is like a lab on wheels.
At the tip of the arm there is a drill and several tools.
With it, the rover takes small bits of Martian ground to analyze them.
questions.description: A tourist on another planet who hasn't asked for a vacation in years.
questions.fun_fact: Curiosity has no solar panels: it runs on a nuclear battery that has powered it for more than a decade.

questions.question: The Instituto Geográfico Agustín Codazzi makes Colombia's official maps. Why is it named after Codazzi?
wrong_answers: He mapped the route of the Panama Canal
hints: Codazzi was an Italian soldier and geographer.
He worked in the country in the mid-19th century.
His team traveled the provinces drawing maps and landscapes.
questions.description: If you ever got lost in Colombia, now you know who to complain to.
questions.fun_fact: Codazzi died in 1859 in the middle of the expedition, near a town in Cesar that is now called Agustín Codazzi in his honor.

questions.question: It is common in jungles like those of the Chocó, is spread by a mosquito, and its name comes from the Italian for “bad air.” What disease is it?
hints: People once believed it came from the bad smells of swamps.
In Spanish it is also called paludismo.
It is caused by a parasite called Plasmodium.
questions.description: A mosquito with very bad intentions and even worse aim.
questions.fun_fact: For centuries it was treated with the bark of the quina (cinchona) tree, which grows in the Andes.

questions.question: It's the giant wheel with cabins at fairs. George Ferris built the first one in 1893, and in Colombia it's named after the city where it opened. Which city?
hints: It's in the United States.
It sits on the shore of a huge lake.
It's famous for its skyscrapers and the Bulls basketball team.
questions.description: The only wheel that spins all night long and never gets anywhere.
questions.fun_fact: The first wheel opened at the World's Columbian Exposition, which celebrated 400 years since Columbus's voyage.

questions.question: Finish the circle song: “Juguemos en el bosque mientras el … no está” (“Let's play in the woods while the … isn't here”).
hints: It's an animal with fangs.
It howls at the moon.
It's the same one that chases Little Red Riding Hood.
questions.description: A circle game where everyone prays someone takes a really long time getting dressed.
questions.fun_fact: In the game, the character says which piece of clothing they're putting on, until they shout that they're coming out and everyone runs.

questions.question: The children's ring song “Mambrú se fue a la guerra” makes fun of a real English general. In which century was the song born?
hints: It's from before Colombia's independence.
At that time, France still had kings.
“Mambrú” is how the French said “Marlborough,” a duke who fought in 1709.
questions.description: A children's song about a man who left, and nobody knows when he'll be back.
questions.fun_fact: It became fashionable at the French court when the nanny of Marie Antoinette's son sang it to the baby.

questions.question: You're about to play golosa on the sidewalk and you're holding this. What do you use it for?
questions.answer: To draw the squares on the ground
wrong_answers: To keep your balance hopping on one foot
To write the winner's name in a notebook
To dust powder on your shoes
hints: Golosa doesn't come ready-made: you have to set it up
You use it before anyone takes the first hop
Without it, you wouldn't know where to hop
questions.description: The school supply that escaped the classroom to go play in the street.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish word for chalk, «tiza», comes from the Nahuatl «tizatl», a white earth the Aztecs used.

questions.question: In December it's built with moss and little figures, and at midnight on the 24th the Niño Dios is placed in it. Which two animals are with him in the pesebre?
hints: They are farm work animals.
One of them has horns.
The other is the child of a donkey and a mare.
questions.description: The Niño Dios's first neighbors couldn't talk, but they were very cozy and warm.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, these two animals kept the baby warm with their breath on that cold night.

questions.question: They're metal, you flatten them with a hammer and string them on a wire to play along with the carols at the novena. What are they?
hints: Many families save them at home all year long
They have a crinkly edge
You take them off with a bottle opener
questions.description: A Christmas orchestra with a budget of zero pesos.
questions.fun_fact: A crown bottle cap has 21 little teeth around its edge.

questions.question: One player counts against the wall while the others hide. To save yourself you shout “¡un, dos, tres por mí!” Where must you get to?
questions.answer: The spot where the seeker counted
hints: It's not far away: it's inside the play area.
The seeker has to guard that place while looking for you.
It's the wall or post where the counting happened.
questions.description: The only game where losing means you got found.
questions.fun_fact: If the last player shouted “¡por mí y por todos mis compañeros!” (for me and all my friends), the whole team was set free.

questions.question: You're playing dominoes at the neighborhood corner store and someone slams the table and shouts “¡Dominó!” When do you say that?
questions.answer: When you play your last tile
wrong_answers: When you play the double six
When you have no tile to play
hints: It means the round is over.
That person won the hand.
They have nothing left in their hand.
questions.description: The battle cry of grandpas in the park.
questions.fun_fact: If the last tile fits on both ends, it's called “capicúa,” which means “head and tail” in Catalan.

questions.question: You're watching Greeicy Rendón as Daisy, the girl who turns into a vampire, in “Chica vampiro”. What year did it premiere on RCN?
hints: It was in the 2010s.
It came out a few years after the worldwide “Twilight” craze.
It was the year after 2012.
questions.description: A teenager with fangs and dreams of the stage: the perfect high-school drama.
questions.fun_fact: “Chica vampiro” was a hit outside Colombia too, especially in countries like Italy and France.

questions.question: In what year did Canal RCN air the first season of “La casa de los famosos Colombia”?
hints: It's a fairly recent reality show.
It came out after the pandemic.
It was the same year as the Paris Olympics.
questions.description: Celebrities locked in, cameras everywhere, and the whole country gossiping from the couch.
questions.fun_fact: The format comes from “La casa de los famosos”, Telemundo's reality show in the United States, which started in 2021.

questions.question: I was born in Medellín and wrote “Paraíso Travel”, about Marlon and Reina, two young people who go to New York without papers. It became a film in 2008. Who am I?
hints: Another of my novels was also made into a film and a TV series.
That other novel tells the story of a dangerous woman from the poor hillside neighborhoods of Medellín.
I wrote “Rosario Tijeras”.
questions.description: A one-way ticket to New York, no papers, lots of literature.
questions.fun_fact: The film “Paraíso Travel” was one of the biggest box-office hits of Colombian cinema in its time.

questions.question: For the 2007 Hollywood film “Love in the Time of Cholera,” starring Javier Bardem, I wrote and sang two songs in Spanish. Who am I?
hints: I was born on Colombia's Caribbean coast, like the novel's author.
Gabo and I were friends and met at several events.
I'm from Barranquilla and sang “Hips Don't Lie.”
questions.description: A romance that waited half a century and still got a five-star soundtrack.
questions.fun_fact: One of those songs, “Despedida,” was nominated for a Golden Globe for Best Original Song.

questions.question: One morning I went out all stiff and dapper, in short pants and a ribboned hat, even though my mom told me not to go. Who am I?
hints: I appear in a poem by Rafael Pombo.
I live near the water.
My mom is a frog.
questions.description: A stroll that started out very fancy and ended very badly.
questions.fun_fact: Pombo was inspired by an old English nursery song about a frog who goes courting.

questions.question: The Colombian poetry group Piedra y Cielo (Stone and Sky) took its name from the title of a book. Who wrote that book?
hints: He was a Spanish poet.
He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1956.
He wrote “Platero and I”.
questions.description: Poets who named themselves after geology with a view of the heavens.
questions.fun_fact: Eduardo Carranza and Jorge Rojas were among the founders of Piedra y Cielo.

questions.question: “Manuela,” by Eugenio Díaz, portrays life in a hot lowland town. In which decade did it start coming out in installments?
hints: It is a 19th-century novel of customs (costumbrista).
It came out in installments in El Mosaico, the magazine of Bogotá's costumbrista writers.
Its author died in 1865.
questions.description: A novel that reached its readers in installments, like a fridge bought on credit.
questions.fun_fact: Many critics consider “Manuela” the first great Colombian novel of customs.

questions.question: His only book, “Morada al sur,” made him one of Colombia's great 20th-century poets. In which department was Aurelio Arturo born?
hints: His home region is in the Andes in the south of the country.
His department shares a border with Ecuador.
Its capital is Pasto.
questions.description: A poet who earned his place in history with a single book.
questions.fun_fact: Aurelio Arturo was born in La Unión and worked for much of his life as a lawyer and civil servant.

questions.question: Who is this Colombian writer?
hints: He was born in Aracataca, Magdalena.
His face is on the 50,000-peso note.
He wrote “One Hundred Years of Solitude.”
questions.description: A famous mustache that isn't Juan Valdez's.
questions.fun_fact: To receive the Nobel Prize in 1982, Gabo skipped the tailcoat and wore a white liquiliqui, a traditional Caribbean suit.

questions.question: Who is this Colombian singer?
hints: She was born in Barranquilla.
Her father has Lebanese roots.
In 2020 she performed the Super Bowl halftime show with Jennifer Lopez.
questions.description: Today the question goes in through your eyes, not your ears.
questions.fun_fact: She released her first album, “Magia,” in 1991, when she was 14.

questions.question: In 1929 I traveled to the banana zone, then spent several days in Congress denouncing what happened to the strikers in Ciénaga. Who am I?
hints: I was a young Liberal lawyer and politician.
My speeches filled entire town squares.
My face was on the old 1,000-peso bill.
questions.description: There was a time when a speech in Congress was the plan for the whole week.
questions.fun_fact: Gaitán was also mayor of Bogotá, from 1936 to 1937.

questions.question: During which years was Misael Pastrana Borrero president of Colombia?
hints: He was the last president of the National Front.
His disputed election on April 19 gave the M-19 its name.
He handed power to Alfonso López Michelsen.
questions.description: A surname that came back to the Casa de Nariño a generation later.
questions.fun_fact: His son Andrés Pastrana was also president, from 1998 to 2002.

questions.question: In many Colombian classrooms, first graders use the Nacho workbook. What do they learn with it?
hints: It starts with the vowels.
It has syllables like “ma, me, mi, mo, mu.”
Its full title is “Nacho lee.”
questions.description: Many Colombians' very first book is named like a kid from the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: It's published by a Medellín publisher, and several generations of Colombians have learned with it.

questions.question: Many Colombian kitchens have a plastic jug: you drop the whole bag in, snip off a little corner and pour. What comes in that bag?
hints: You keep it in the fridge.
People drink it at breakfast, on its own or with hot chocolate.
Brands like Alpina and Colanta sell it.
questions.description: A kitchen gadget for pouring from a floppy bag without spilling a drop.
questions.fun_fact: In Canada, especially Ontario, it is also sold in bags that go into a jug.

questions.question: If you followed the Cerrejón coal train from the mine in La Guajira to Puerto Bolívar, how far would you travel?
hints: The mine and the port are in the same department.
It's much more than crossing a city, but not enough to cross the country.
It's roughly the drive from Bogotá to Tunja.
questions.description: A mine so big its coal needs its own train to reach the sea.
questions.fun_fact: Cerrejón trains can pull more than 100 cars loaded with coal.

questions.question: The spectacled bear appears on one of Colombia's coins. How many of those coins do you need to make 200 pesos?
hints: It's the lowest-value coin in use today.
It's worth half the coin with the frailejón plant on it.
Two of them make 100 pesos.
questions.description: A bear that wears glasses and still fits in your pocket.
questions.fun_fact: The spectacled bear is the only bear in South America, and the pale markings on its face are different on every bear.

questions.question: Which of these names does NOT belong to the same company that owns Alkosto?
hints: Three of them belong to Corbeta, a company founded in Pasto.
One of them is Alkosto’s own brand of TVs and home appliances.
The odd one out is a home improvement store linked to Falabella.
questions.description: A family of stores where all the siblings look alike… except one.
questions.fun_fact: Kalley is Alkosto’s own brand: its TVs, fridges and cell phones are sold in the company’s own stores.

questions.question: This viaduct over the Otún River starts in Pereira. Which neighboring municipality does it lead to?
hints: It's in Risaralda, just like Pereira.
It's the second most populous municipality in the department.
Its name talks about two streams.
questions.description: A bridge so long that if you're not paying attention, you end up in another town without noticing.
questions.fun_fact: Dosquebradas was a district of Santa Rosa de Cabal until 1972, when it became a municipality of its own.

questions.question: This cat sculpture stands by the river in a Colombian city. What is that city's nickname?
wrong_answers: La Ciudad de la Eterna Primavera
hints: The sculpture is by Hernando Tejada.
The city is famous for salsa.
Its nickname says it's like a branch office of paradise.
questions.description: A cat that chases tourists with cell phones instead of mice.
questions.fun_fact: The Gato del Río later got feline “girlfriends,” each decorated by a different artist.

questions.question: Every year-end, the Christmas lights (alumbrados) fill the Medellín River with color. In which month are they switched off?
hints: They're still on after December 24.
You can still see them on New Year's Day.
They go off in the first month of the year.
questions.description: So many light bulbs in one place that even Medellín’s moths are asking for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín’s alumbrados have been a tradition since the 1960s, and National Geographic listed them among the most beautiful in the world.

questions.question: In Colombia, homes are ranked into estratos (social levels) based on the neighborhood. How many estratos are there?
hints: The lowest one is estrato 1.
They are used to work out how much you pay for water, power and gas.
More than five and fewer than ten.
questions.description: The favorite question of anyone about to rent you an apartment.
questions.fun_fact: Homes in estratos 5 and 6 pay more for water, power and gas to help cover the bills of estratos 1, 2 and 3.

questions.question: Which of these towns in the Eje Cafetero is NOT in Quindío?
hints: Three of them are close to Armenia.
The odd one out lies between Manizales and Pereira.
It's in Caldas.
questions.description: In the Eje Cafetero all the towns look alike, but each one knows its own department.
questions.fun_fact: Chinchiná is home to Buencafé, the freeze-dried coffee factory of Colombia's National Federation of Coffee Growers.

questions.question: This gold figure comes from the same Indigenous culture that gives its name to a municipality in Quindío. Which culture made it?
hints: They lived in what is now the Eje Cafetero.
They made the famous poporo in the Museo del Oro.
Their name sounds like that of a coffee-growing department.
questions.description: Gold so fine that even a modern jeweler would ask for the recipe.
questions.fun_fact: The so-called Quimbaya Treasure was given to Spain in 1893 and is now in the Museo de América in Madrid.

questions.question: These rides are at the Parque Nacional del Café in Quindío. Which municipality is the park in?
hints: It's near the city of Armenia.
It's west of Armenia.
It has the same name as a country in the Balkans.
questions.description: A park where your tinto goes up and down on a roller coaster.
questions.fun_fact: The Parque del Café opened in 1995 and began as a museum telling the story of Colombian coffee.

questions.question: This town in western Antioquia had gold mines so rich that the Spanish founded Santa Fe de Antioquia nearby, and it still has a big mine today. Which town is it?
hints: Indigenous people were already mining gold in its hills before the Conquest.
It lies a short distance from Antioquia's old capital.
Its name starts with “Buri.”
questions.description: A town with so much gold that the hens should be laying bars of it.
questions.fun_fact: Buriticá's gold was one of the reasons Jorge Robledo came to the region in 1541.

questions.question: Every July 20 there are parades, flags everywhere and no school. What does Colombia celebrate?
hints: It's a national holiday.
It recalls the cry for freedom of 1810 in Bogotá.
On that day Colombia began breaking away from Spain.
questions.description: The one day a year when the whole country puts on its yellow, blue and red uniform.
questions.fun_fact: It all started with a fight because a Spanish merchant refused to lend a flower vase in the main square of Bogotá.

questions.question: In Colombia people say: «Hay que estirar los pies hasta donde alcance la cobija» (“stretch your feet only as far as the blanket reaches”). What does it mean?
questions.answer: Spend only what you can afford
wrong_answers: Share with people who are cold
hints: It's advice for everyday life
If the blanket is short, it won't cover your whole body
It's the opposite of going into debt just for fun
questions.description: Grandma's advice that keeps you warmer than a ruana.
questions.fun_fact: Sheep's wool keeps you warm even when it's a little damp, which is why it rules the cold highlands.

questions.question: In Colombia they call me “el Patas”, “el Mandinga” and “el Enemigo”. They say I show up when someone swears. Who am I?
hints: I'm the most feared one in all the stories.
One of my nicknames comes from what my feet are like.
I have horns, a tail and a pitchfork.
questions.description: Grandma has a scary story ready for every bad word that slips out of your mouth.
questions.fun_fact: “Mandinga”, another of his nicknames, comes from the name of a people of West Africa.

questions.question: According to a very Colombian superstition, what do you summon if you whistle at night?
hints: It's nothing good.
That's why grandmas tell you to hush at midnight.
One of the spooks of the Llanos has a name that comes from the Spanish word for whistling.
questions.description: A song with no words that's better saved for daytime.
questions.fun_fact: According to the legend of the Llanos, when El Silbón's whistle sounds far away, it means he is close.

questions.question: “El Desafío” is to Caracol as “Protagonistas de Nuestra Tele” is to…
hints: It's a national channel based in Bogotá that airs reality shows and telenovelas.
It's the channel of “Yo soy Betty, la fea”.
Its name is three letters, and it's Caracol's eternal rival.
questions.description: No easy money here: either you fly across a canyon on a tarabita or you cry at a casting call.
questions.fun_fact: On “Protagonistas de Nuestra Tele”, the contestants lived together in a house and competed for a lead role in a telenovela.

questions.question: In what year did the first season of MasterChef Colombia air, with Jorge Rausch as a judge?
hints: It was in the 2010s.
Paulina Vega had just been crowned Miss Universe that year.
It was the middle of the decade, one year before the peace agreement with the FARC.
questions.description: A judge so strict that even the rice is scared of sticking to the pot.
questions.fun_fact: In Bogotá, Jorge Rausch runs the restaurant Criterión, which he founded with his brother Mark.

questions.question: At Miss Universe 1994 in Manila, what place did Colombia's Carolina Gómez finish in?
hints: She was Señorita Colombia in 1993 and later became an actress and TV host.
That year's winner was Sushmita Sen from India.
Just one tiny step away from the crown.
questions.description: Crown, sash and smile: the basic survival kit of any Colombian beauty queen.
questions.fun_fact: The first Colombian to win Miss Universe was Luz Marina Zuluaga, in 1958.

questions.question: Tucano is the most widespread Indigenous language in this department, where it lets peoples who speak different languages understand each other. Which department is it?
hints: It's in the Amazon region, on the border with Brazil.
A river with the same name runs through it.
Its capital is Mitú.
questions.description: A corner of the country where the dictionary would need several extra volumes and a pocket translator.
questions.fun_fact: In Vaupés, many Indigenous people marry someone who speaks another language, so three or four languages can be spoken in a single home.

questions.question: They are a nomadic people of the Guaviare rainforest. In 1988 a group of them walked into Calamar, and the country learned they existed. Who are they?
hints: They live between the Guaviare and Inírida rivers.
For centuries they roamed the rainforest, hunting with blowguns.
The group that reached Calamar showed up out of nowhere: almost no one outside the forest knew they existed.
questions.description: Neighbors who never stayed put in the same house.
questions.fun_fact: The Nukak are among the last nomadic peoples of Colombia and know hundreds of rainforest plants by name.

questions.question: I'm spoken in a desert by the Caribbean Sea and across the border in Venezuela; I'm Colombia's most spoken indigenous language. What am I?
hints: The weavers of colorful mochila bags speak me.
My people live in La Guajira.
I'm the language of the Wayuu.
questions.description: A language that handles sun, wind and sand without a hair out of place.
questions.fun_fact: In Wayuunaiki, the word “wayuu” means “person.”

questions.question: Which of these statements about the Colombian island of Providencia is NOT true?
questions.answer: It lies in the Pacific Ocean
wrong_answers: A bridge links it to Santa Catalina
It has a national natural park
hints: It is San Andrés's neighbor.
Its bridge is called the “Lovers' Bridge”.
Its sea is the same one as Cartagena's.
questions.description: An island so calm that even the crabs walk slowly.
questions.fun_fact: The bridge linking Providencia to Santa Catalina is called the Puente de los Enamorados, the Lovers' Bridge.

questions.question: Colombia protects its native languages: the indigenous ones, its two creoles and Romani. How many are there in total, according to the Ministry of Culture?
hints: Far more than twenty.
Most of them are indigenous languages from many different families.
The indigenous ones number 65; add the other three.
questions.description: If every language were an arepa, this country would have breakfast for a long, long time.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's 2010 Native Languages Law says anyone may use their native language when dealing with the state.

questions.question: In Boyacá and the Bogotá savanna, farmers fear the “heladas.” What is a helada?
questions.answer: A pre-dawn cold that freezes the crops
wrong_answers: A downpour of small falling balls of ice
A snowfall that turns the towns white
A very strong wind that knocks plants over
hints: It happens mostly on clear nights with no clouds.
It usually comes in the dry season, from December to February.
At dawn the grass looks white and the plants' leaves look burned.
questions.description: An enemy of Boyacá's potatoes, feared even more than the worms.
questions.fun_fact: Cloudless nights are the most dangerous: without that “blanket,” the ground's heat escapes to the sky and the temperature can drop below freezing.

questions.question: This desert of reddish earth and deep gullies lies in Ráquira, Boyacá, next to a 17th-century Augustinian monastery. What is it called?
hints: Ráquira is famous for its clay crafts.
The nearby monastery has the same name as the desert.
It's also the name of the colonial neighborhood in downtown Bogotá.
questions.description: A desert with monks for neighbors: peace and quiet guaranteed.
questions.fun_fact: Ráquira, very close to the desert, is known as Colombia's craft capital for its pottery.

questions.question: In the páramo, what are the stretches of tall, tough, yellowish grass that grows in tufts called?
hints: Along with the frailejones, it is the most common landscape of the páramo.
Farmers once used these dry grasses to thatch the roofs of their houses.
Its name comes from «paja», the Spanish word for straw.
questions.description: The messy-haired páramo that has never been to a barber.
questions.fun_fact: The tufts of the pajonal shelter insects, frogs and other little páramo animals from the cold.

questions.question: Colombia's two highest peaks, in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, are Simón Bolívar and which other?
hints: Both are about 5,700 m (18,700 ft) high, and people still argue over which is taller.
The other peak is named after someone who lived centuries before Bolívar.
This person reached America in 1492.
questions.description: Two neighbors in the Sierra Nevada who have been arguing for years about who's taller.
questions.fun_fact: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is the world's highest coastal mountain range: its snowy peaks are only about 42 km (26 miles) from the Caribbean Sea.

questions.question: Because of its colors, Colombia's flag has a nickname that the national soccer team uses too. What is it?
hints: Fans and commentators shout this name at every national team game.
Ecuador and Venezuela could use the same nickname, because their flags have the same colors.
It starts with “tri,” like tricycle or triangle.
questions.description: Soccer commentators have a nickname for everything, even a piece of cloth.
questions.fun_fact: The flags of Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador all come from the same three-color flag designed by Francisco de Miranda.

questions.question: Venezuela's flag has the same colors as Colombia's, but with an arc of white stars. What do those stars stand for?
questions.answer: The provinces that signed for independence
wrong_answers: The states the country has today
hints: They have to do with the year 1811.
Each star matches a territory from colonial times.
These territories joined together to break away from Spain.
questions.description: A neighbor's flag that seems to bring its own night sky along.
questions.fun_fact: One of the stars, for the province of Guayana, was added in 2006, following an 1817 decree by Bolívar.

questions.question: You're wearing a cap at the stadium, watching Colombia's national team. When should you take it off?
wrong_answers: When the referee ends the game
hints: It happens before the ball starts rolling.
The players line up and look at the flag.
It's when everyone sings “¡Oh gloria inmarcesible!”.
questions.description: Caps have manners too, even if they don't look like it.
questions.fun_fact: By custom, men take off their caps or hats as a sign of respect while the anthem plays.

questions.question: I was born in Maicao, La Guajira. At Tokyo 2020, I ran one full lap of the track flat out, and only one runner finished ahead of me. Who am I?
hints: I won a silver medal.
My event is the 400 meters.
My first name starts with A.
questions.description: Just one lap, but by the end your tongue is hanging out.
questions.fun_fact: The 400 meters is exactly one lap of an Olympic track in the inside lane.

questions.question: On the rocks of Suesca, near Bogotá, people go up stone walls wearing a harness, a rope and a helmet. Which sport are they doing?
hints: You use your hands and feet to grip the rock.
It joined the Olympic Games at Tokyo 2020.
Spider-Man does it up buildings, no rope needed.
questions.description: For people who think elevators are for cowards.
questions.fun_fact: The rocks of Suesca have hundreds of climbing routes and are one of climbers' favorite spots in Colombia.

questions.question: Colombia's Evelis Aguilar competes in the heptathlon. Which of these events is one of its seven?
hints: The heptathlon has three races, two jumps and two throws.
The two throws are the shot put and one more.
The object thrown is long and has a pointed tip.
questions.description: Seven events in two days: the perfect plan for anyone who gets bored fast.
questions.fun_fact: The heptathlon events are the 100 m hurdles, high jump, shot put, 200 m, long jump, javelin and 800 m.

questions.question: I was named after a Brazilian star, shone at Porto and Atlético Madrid, and I'm the all-time top scorer for Colombia's national team. Who am I?
hints: My dad was a soccer player too.
In 2024 I came back to Colombia to play for Millonarios, the team I grew up loving.
They call me “El Tigre.”
questions.description: He celebrated every goal as if it were the first one of his life.
questions.fun_fact: Falcao was named after the Brazilian Paulo Roberto Falcão, his dad's idol.

questions.question: In the 1970s, humor columnist Daniel Samper Pizano founded the first investigative unit in Colombian journalism. At which newspaper?
hints: It is a Bogotá daily.
For decades it belonged to the Santos family.
Its name has to do with clocks and calendars.
questions.description: A journalist who made readers laugh in his column and made politicians sweat in his investigations.
questions.fun_fact: Samper Pizano is also a vallenato expert and wrote the book “100 años de vallenato” with Pilar Tafur.

questions.question: He sings música popular and became famous with “Dulce pecado”. What city is Jessi Uribe from?
hints: He isn't paisa, even though many people think so.
His city is in the Eastern Range of the Andes.
It's the capital of Santander, the “Ciudad Bonita” (Beautiful City).
questions.description: It would be a sweet sin not to know where this singer comes from.
