questions.fun_fact: “Dulce pecado” came out in 2018 and made him one of the most-played voices in Colombian música popular.

questions.question: Which Colombian duo sang “Ricardo Semillas”, a protest song from the 1970s?
hints: They played social and protest songs on guitar.
They sang Latin American nueva canción at university peñas.
They also sang “Café y petróleo”.
questions.description: Two voices, one guitar and plenty of opinions about the world.
questions.fun_fact: This duo was part of the Latin American nueva canción wave, the same movement as Mercedes Sosa and Víctor Jara.

questions.question: I was born as a country dance in England and became elegant in France and Spain. They say «La vencedora», one of my pieces, played at the Battle of Boyacá. What am I?
hints: I was the fashionable ballroom dance in the time of Independence.
My name comes from the English “country dance.”
My Spanish name starts with a word that means “against.”
questions.description: A dance with more passport stamps than a retired flight attendant.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, Simón Bolívar loved dancing contradanzas at parties to celebrate his victories.

questions.question: Bogotá has two letters after its name, isn't part of Cundinamarca and is split into 20 localities. What is Bogotá on the political map?
hints: It has its own mayor and its own city council.
The two letters are the same ones Washington has in the United States.
The letters are D.C.
questions.description: It's the capital of a department, but it doesn't pay that department any rent.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it isn't part of Cundinamarca, Bogotá is still that department's capital.

questions.question: It was born on August 25, 1951, when the De Mares Concession in Barrancabermeja passed from Tropical Oil to the Colombian state. What company is it?
hints: Today it is the biggest company in Colombia.
Its main refinery is in Barranca.
Its name joins Colombia with what it pulls out from underground.
questions.description: A city as hot as an oven and very interested in what lies beneath the ground.
questions.fun_fact: Barrancabermeja is known as “the oil capital of Colombia.”

questions.question: General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla fell from power on May 10, 1957. Who took power in his place?
hints: Elections didn't come right away.
They governed until August 1958, when Alberto Lleras Camargo took office.
They were four generals and a rear admiral, led by Gabriel París.
questions.description: One May when Colombia changed governments without waiting for an election.
questions.fun_fact: Those days are remembered as the “Jornadas de Mayo” (May Days), with strikes by students, banks and shops.

questions.question: Someone hands you a bill and you suspect it's chimbo. Which of these does NOT help you tell if it's fake?
wrong_answers: Holding it up to the light
hints: Real bills hide details that are very hard to copy.
The Banco de la República teaches a quick check that uses your hands and eyes.
Your nose is no help at all for this.
questions.description: Some bills look real until you take a really close look.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “chimbo” means fake or poor quality, so a fake bill is a “billete chimbo.”

questions.question: It comes in flavors like blackberry, mango or lulo, and just a little makes a whole jug. In what form is Frutiño sold?
hints: You have to mix it with water and stir well.
It comes in a tiny packet that fits in your pocket.
It's a lot like Tang.
questions.description: The magician that turns a jug of water into blackberry juice without peeling a single fruit.
questions.fun_fact: Frutiño is made by Quala, a Colombian company that also created brands like Savital and Bonice.

questions.question: It's a company born in Medellín in 1949, and its logo is yellow. What is Éxito?
hints: Its parking lots are packed on Saturdays.
It belongs to the same business group as Carulla.
It's like a giant supermarket that sells a bit of everything.
questions.description: Its name is what every parent wishes you before an exam, at least in Spanish.
questions.fun_fact: The first Éxito opened in Medellín in 1949 as a small shop selling fabric and clothes.

questions.question: Alquería is a Colombian milk brand, but the word comes from Arabic. What is an alquería in Spain?
hints: There are more hens than people around it.
In Colombia, a similar place would be called a finca.
It is a house in the countryside with its land all around it.
questions.description: A word with a thousand years of history that ended up in the fridge.
questions.fun_fact: The word alquería comes from the Arabic “al-qarya”, which means “the little town” or “the village”.

questions.question: Falabella came to Colombia from Chile and sells clothes and electronics, and it even has a bank. Where does its name come from?
wrong_answers: From a river in Argentine Patagonia
hints: It started as a very small business in Santiago, Chile, in the 19th century.
Its founder came to Chile from Europe.
The founder was named Salvatore and made custom-tailored suits.
questions.description: A store that crossed the Andes and hasn't stopped growing since.
questions.fun_fact: Salvatore Falabella opened a tailor shop in Santiago in 1889, and it grew into one of the biggest department stores in South America.

questions.question: Soledad, in Atlántico, is Barranquilla's neighbor. Roughly how many people live there?
hints: It's much more than a small town.
It has more people than several department capitals.
Its population is counted in hundreds of thousands.
questions.description: A very lonely name for such a party-loving neighbor of Barranquilla.
questions.fun_fact: Soledad is one of the most populated municipalities in Colombia that is not a department capital.

questions.question: “Oiga, mire, vea” is a very Cali expression, and Guayacán Orquesta turned it into a song. What kind of song is it?
hints: It's danced in pairs, with lots of fast footwork.
It features trumpets, timbales and congas.
It's the same genre as Grupo Niche.
questions.description: Three words that work for getting attention, saying hello and showing off your city.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali, “oiga, mire, vea” is used to get someone's attention before telling them something.

questions.question: In 1821, the Congress of Cúcuta passed the Law of Manumission. What does “manumission” mean?
hints: The word comes from Latin.
The law was passed as Gran Colombia was being born, with Bolívar as president.
That 1821 law applied to children born from then on to enslaved women.
questions.description: A very long word that sounds like a craft you do with your hands, but you won't need glue or scissors for it.
questions.fun_fact: Slavery was finally abolished completely in Colombia on January 1, 1852, under a law signed in 1851.

questions.question: An English seaman captured Cartagena in 1586 and only left once he was paid a huge ransom. Who was he?
hints: On the same voyage he also attacked Santo Domingo.
Queen Elizabeth I of England knighted him.
He was the first Englishman to sail around the world (1577–1580).
questions.description: An Englishman who came to Cartagena, and not exactly for a tan.
questions.fun_fact: After Drake’s attack, Spain set out to surround Cartagena with the walls that tourists walk along today.

questions.question: In San Basilio de Palenque, people say enslaved women wore braids tight against the head. What were they for?
wrong_answers: To protect them from the sun
To carry baskets on their heads
hints: San Basilio de Palenque was founded by people who escaped slavery.
The patterns held a secret message the masters couldn't read.
They showed routes through hills and rivers to freedom.
questions.description: A hairstyle with more history than any beauty salon.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, seeds and gold nuggets were also hidden in the braids to survive after the escape.

questions.question: Arriería moved gold, coffee and goods by mule along mountain trails, and today the arriero is a symbol of one region’s culture. Which one?
hints: It’s a region in the northwest of the country.
Its traditional outfit includes a poncho, a sombrero aguadeño and a carriel.
Its people are called “paisas.”
questions.description: Long before trucks, the mountain freight had four legs and long ears.
questions.fun_fact: The carriel, the arriero’s leather bag, had lots of pockets to keep even the last coin of the journey safe.

questions.question: In 1808 my troops entered Spain and I left King Ferdinand VII without a throne. With no king, governing juntas sprang up in New Granada. Who am I?
hints: I wasn’t Spanish.
I made my brother Joseph King of Spain.
I was Emperor of France and lost at Waterloo.
questions.description: A throne sat empty across the ocean, and over here everyone suddenly wanted to run things themselves.
questions.fun_fact: Spaniards nicknamed Joseph Bonaparte, the brother Napoleon put on the throne, “Pepe Botella” (“Joe Bottle”).

questions.question: The asiento gave a foreign power Spain’s monopoly on shipping enslaved people to ports like Cartagena. In what year did Britain get it, by the Treaty of Utrecht?
hints: It was early in a century.
That treaty ended the war over who would inherit the Spanish throne.
That peace left Philip V, the first Bourbon, as king of Spain.
questions.description: A peace treaty with some very unpeaceful fine print.
questions.fun_fact: Before the British, the asiento had been held by the Portuguese and the French.

questions.question: You're in a colonial house in Popayán and someone says, “Vamos al patio.” What is the patio?
questions.answer: The open space in the middle of the house
hints: From there you can see the sky.
It often has plants, flowers and sometimes a stone water basin.
All the rooms open onto it, all the way around.
questions.description: An everyday word that, in Popayán, carries centuries of history.
questions.fun_fact: The Spanish brought the central patio with them, and they had learned it from Arab and Roman houses.

questions.question: In the sugarcane fields of Valle del Cauca, what do you call the worker who cuts down the cane with a machete?
hints: This person works in the fields under the sun.
What gets cut ends up at the sugar mills.
The name comes from the Spanish verb for “to cut.”
questions.description: A job where the gym membership comes included with the paycheck.
questions.fun_fact: Valle del Cauca is the region of Colombia that grows the most sugarcane.

questions.question: In the countryside they say some witches are village ladies by day and turn into a bird screeching over the rooftops by night. Which bird?
hints: It sees very well at night.
It can turn its head almost all the way around.
In Harry Potter, one delivers the letters.
questions.description: A very friendly neighbor by day who has other plans at night.
questions.fun_fact: Real owls don't bring bad luck: they eat loads of mice and help farmers.

questions.question: The Inquisition in Cartagena put women from Tolú on trial for going to “aquelarres”, witches' night meetings. What language does that word come from?
hints: It's a language older than Spanish.
It's so old that nobody really knows where it came from.
It's spoken in Bilbao and San Sebastián.
questions.description: A neighborhood meeting where nobody takes the bus: everyone flies in on a broom.
questions.fun_fact: The best-known explanation is that “aquelarre” comes from “akelarre”, which would mean ‘meadow of the billy goat’ in Basque.

questions.question: The person you were just talking about walks in. Which animal completes the saying “Hablando de Roma, y el… que se asoma”?
hints: It's an animal you see a lot on farms.
It's known for being very stubborn.
It brays.
questions.description: You got caught talking behind someone's back and need a quick line.
questions.fun_fact: The Roman Empire built about 80,000 km (50,000 miles) of roads, and many of them started in Rome.

questions.question: In Colombia's Deaf community, what is a person who isn't deaf called?
hints: You don't need to know sign language to be one.
Most people are one without realizing it.
It has to do with the ears.
questions.description: A label you wear without even knowing it.
questions.fun_fact: In sign language, each person gets a “name sign” that works as their name.

questions.question: On the Caribbean coast, a beach vendor fondly calls a lady “mi reina”. What does he call a man?
hints: It’s the highest title in a palace.
The queen marries him.
It’s the partner of “mi reina”.
questions.description: On the beach nobody wears a crown, but everyone has a title.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali and on the coast, people say “mi rey” and “mi reina” even to someone they’ve just met.

questions.question: The most important Muisca temple stood in Sogamoso, Boyacá, and it gave the city its nickname. What was it dedicated to?
hints: The Muiscas called it Sué.
The Spanish burned that temple in 1537.
Sogamoso's nickname is “the City of the…”.
questions.description: A town in Boyacá that earned its nickname more than 500 years ago.
questions.fun_fact: The Sogamoso Archaeological Museum has a rebuilt version of the Muisca temple.

questions.question: At the Casa de Nariño, the Presidential Guard lines up, presents arms and plays the anthem when a foreign head of state arrives. What is this salute called?
hints: It's a way of showing respect with soldiers.
The flag and great figures at their funerals receive them too.
National heroes are buried with “full” ones.
questions.description: A greeting so elegant it takes a whole battalion to deliver it.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's Presidential Guard wears uniforms inspired by those of the independence era.

questions.question: It plays on every radio station and TV channel in Colombia at 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., because a law says so. What is it?
hints: In many places, people stand up when they hear it.
Every Colombian learns it by heart at school.
It begins with “¡Oh gloria inmarcesible!”
questions.description: A daily radio appointment more punctual than any wall clock.
questions.fun_fact: Law 198 of 1995 requires radio and TV to broadcast the national anthem at 6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.

questions.question: In Colombia, many holidays are moved to Monday, making a three-day weekend. What is that long weekend called?
hints: The same word also names a piece of engineering.
Highways fill up with cars heading out of town.
Several of these cross the Magdalena River.
questions.description: The most beloved Monday of all is the one nobody works.
questions.fun_fact: The Ley Emiliani of 1983 is the law that moves several holidays to Monday in Colombia.

questions.question: In the Olympic opening ceremony parade, teams usually enter in alphabetical order. Which team always enters last?
wrong_answers: The one with the most athletes
The one with the most past golds
hints: It's the team the stadium cheers for the loudest.
It's the one that had the shortest trip to the Games.
It's the country organizing the Games that year.
questions.description: The longest parade in the world, and nobody complains about their shoes.
questions.fun_fact: Greece always leads the parade because the Olympic Games were born there.

questions.question: In blind soccer, the ball has something inside it. What is it?
hints: The players wear blindfolds.
What's inside helps them know where the ball is.
It makes a sound every time the ball rolls.
questions.description: Real soccer, with goals, goalkeepers and one rule that changes everything.
questions.fun_fact: In blind soccer the goalkeeper can actually see, and a guide behind the goal shouts directions to the team.

questions.question: In Rafael Pombo’s poem, Simón el bobito sits for hours and hours in front of a bucket of water. Why?
hints: What Simón is trying to do usually happens in a river, a lake or the sea.
It takes lots of patience and sitting very still while you wait.
He’s waiting for something to bite.
questions.description: Endless patience, zero logic.
questions.fun_fact: In the same poem, Simón makes a snow cake and puts it on the hot coals to bake… and it melts!

questions.question: Look at the map: which natural region of Colombia is highlighted?
hints: It sits out in the Caribbean Sea, far from the coast.
San Andrés and Providencia are there.
It is made up of islands.
questions.description: A part of Colombia where the black crab is more famous than most singers.
questions.fun_fact: San Andrés is closer to Nicaragua than to the Colombian coast.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department on the Caribbean coast is highlighted?
hints: It is one of the smallest departments in Colombia.
It lies where Colombia's longest river reaches the sea.
Its capital is Barranquilla, the city of the Carnival.
questions.description: Put your finger on the map, right up against the sea, and don't move it until you're sure.
questions.fun_fact: Despite its name, the department of Atlántico has its coast on the Caribbean Sea.

questions.question: At the old-time parties and carnivals of Colombia's Caribbean coast, what was a «caseta»?
questions.answer: A fenced dance area with a band and an entry fee
wrong_answers: A small drum played with two sticks
A palm hat worn by cumbia dancers
A slow vallenato style sung as a duet
hints: It was the star of grandma and grandpa's party nights, when carnival was the most awaited event of the year.
It was put up for a few days with boards, palm leaves and canvas.
It was like a temporary nightclub where the town danced to big bands.
questions.description: A word from the Coast that your grandpa says with a nostalgic look on his face.
questions.fun_fact: During Carnival, the casetas of Barranquilla brought in famous bands that played until sunrise.

questions.question: The Battle of Flowers at the Barranquilla Carnival began as a way to celebrate the end of the Thousand Days' War. In what year was the first one?
hints: The war it celebrated had ended only a short time before.
It was the same year Panama split from Colombia.
The Thousand Days' War ended in 1902.
questions.description: A battle where the only weapons are paint, music and a burning need to dance.
questions.fun_fact: The Battle of Flowers is the oldest parade of the Barranquilla Carnival.

questions.question: The Dagua River flows down through Valle del Cauca to the sea. Into which bay does it empty?
hints: It empties into the Pacific Ocean.
The road from Cali to the sea follows its canyon.
It is home to the largest port on Colombia's Pacific coast.
questions.description: This river comes down from the mountains eager to see some ships.
questions.fun_fact: The old Pacific Railway, which linked Cali with the sea, was built along the canyon of the Dagua River.

questions.question: The giant otter of the Amazon and the Orinoco plains lives in big families and hunts fish in groups. What do Colombians call it?
hints: It's named after another animal that lives and hunts in a pack.
That other animal also howls.
It's the animal from the story of Little Red Riding Hood.
questions.description: An animal that bathes with the whole family and never eats alone.
questions.fun_fact: The giant otter can grow to about 1.8 meters (6 ft) long, making it the longest otter in the world.

questions.question: “I flow out of Lake Fúquene, run down through Boyacá and Santander, and when I meet the Chicamocha I form the Sogamoso River.” Which river am I?
hints: I'm part of the Magdalena River basin.
I flow past Barbosa, in Santander.
I share my name with a famous Uruguayan goal scorer.
questions.description: A river that starts out calm in a lake and ends up changing its name.
questions.fun_fact: The Fonce River, famous for rafting in San Gil, ends up flowing into the Suárez River.

questions.question: His orchestra had an English name, played in Caracas and packed dance floors in Colombia. In what country was Billo Frómeta, founder of Billo's Caracas Boys, born?
hints: He wasn't born in the city his orchestra is named after.
His country is on a Caribbean island.
He was born in the city of Santo Domingo.
questions.description: An orchestra that got half a continent dancing every December.
questions.fun_fact: Billo Frómeta led his orchestra for more than four decades, until he died in 1988.

questions.question: What does the saying “del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho” mean?
questions.answer: Promising is easy, but keeping it is hard
wrong_answers: The road is short in good company
You should think before you speak
hints: “Trecho” means a distance.
Italian has an almost identical saying that talks about the sea.
It's said to someone who promises a lot and does nothing.
questions.description: A saying with more miles on it than an intercity bus.
questions.fun_fact: This saying already appeared in Spanish collections of proverbs more than 400 years ago and reached Colombia along with the language.

questions.question: In corner stores and bakeries you often hear “¿me regala un tinto?” What is that “me regala” used for?
wrong_answers: To ask for something for free
To ask for something on credit
To treat someone to a coffee
hints: Nobody expects to get it without paying.
It’s another way of saying “deme” or “me vende.”
In the end, the person who says it takes out their money.
questions.description: Two little words that can leave a visitor very confused at the bakery counter.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, a “tinto” is a black coffee, nothing to do with vino tinto (red wine).

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this street food called?
hints: It's sold from food carts and fast-food stands.
It comes with French fries.
Its name joins the Spanish words for its two ingredients, and one is salchicha (sausage).
questions.description: Food-cart fare you eat with a toothpick, a napkin and plenty of pink sauce.
questions.fun_fact: Salchipapa is famous in Colombia, but it's also hugely popular in Peru, where many say it was born.

questions.question: It's crunchy, turns golden in the paila and is always on a bandeja paisa. What is chicharrón?
questions.answer: Fried pork belly with the skin on
hints: It comes from an animal.
It's also eaten on its own, with arepa or in a picada.
It comes from the same animal as ham.
questions.description: It sounds like applause when you bite into it.
questions.fun_fact: On a bandeja paisa, chicharrón shares the plate with beans, rice, ground beef, egg, arepa, ripe plantain and avocado.

questions.question: The avena sold in Colombian bakeries is a thick, cold drink made from oats. What kind of food are oats?
hints: It doesn't grow inside a pod or under the ground.
It's related to wheat and barley.
It's harvested as grain, just like rice.
questions.description: The shake that sticks by the pandebono like a cold bodyguard.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian bakeries, cold avena with a pandebono or buñuelo is the favorite afternoon snack.

questions.question: In many bakeries, pandebono comes filled with a firm, reddish, sweet paste that's cut into slices. Which one?
hints: It's also used to fill roscones and obleas.
It's sold in blocks or small bars that you cut with a knife.
With cheese, it becomes a classic of the onces (afternoon snack).
questions.description: A cheese bread that decided it wanted to be dessert too.
questions.fun_fact: Pandebono is made with cassava starch, cheese and egg, with no wheat flour at all.

questions.question: Who goes around the neighborhood pushing a cart full of ice and sells frozen fruit treats on a stick?
hints: What he sells melts if you take too long.
He sells mango, blackberry and lime flavors.
His name comes from what he sells: paletas.
questions.description: He rings a little bell and every kid on the block comes running.
questions.fun_fact: The ice pop on a stick was invented by accident: a boy left a cup of soda with a stick in it outside on a freezing night, and the next day it was frozen solid.

questions.question: At a Colombian bakery, you order an alfajor. What do you get?
questions.answer: Two soft cookies joined with arequipe
wrong_answers: A round bread roll filled with bocadillo
A sponge cake roll filled with jam
A puff pastry cake with cream
hints: You eat it in one or two bites.
Sometimes the outside is covered in grated coconut or powdered sugar.
It has two little lids with a brown filling in the middle.
questions.description: The treat nobody eats just one of, even when they swear they will.
questions.fun_fact: The word alfajor comes from Arabic, and the treat reached the Americas from Spain.

questions.question: They steal cookies from the cupboard, always ask for dessert and never say no to a bocadillo. In Colombia, what is that person called?
hints: It has to do with wanting to eat tasty things.
This person loves sweets.
The word starts with “go”.
questions.description: The reason some homes hide the chocolate behind the lentils.
questions.fun_fact: The word “goloso” comes from “gula”, Spanish for eating more than you should.

questions.question: Look at the map: the capital of the highlighted department is Colombia’s “Ciudad Milagro.” Which city is it?
hints: It's right in the heart of the Eje Cafetero.
It's the capital of the smallest department in that region.
It shares its name with a country in the Caucasus.
questions.description: A city that grew so fast it earned a nickname worthy of a telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: It's called the “Ciudad Milagro” (Miracle City) because in a few decades it went from a jungle hamlet to a department capital.

questions.question: Many manizaleños use this transport to go up and down their city's steep hills. What is it?
hints: It doesn't run on the ground.
It has run in Manizales since 2009 and also reaches neighboring Villamaría.
It travels through the air, hanging from strong steel ropes.
questions.description: In Manizales, climbing a hill on foot is an extreme sport.
questions.fun_fact: By 1922, a cargo cable line of about 72 km (45 miles) was already running between Manizales and Mariquita, one of the longest in the world.

questions.question: Which Spanish conquistador founded Anserma, Cartago and Santa Fe de Antioquia between 1539 and 1541?
hints: He traveled north along the Cauca River valley.
He worked under Belalcázar's orders.
In Spanish, his last name means “oak grove.”
questions.description: A man who founded cities the way other people hand out business cards.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Fe de Antioquia was the capital of Antioquia until 1826, when Medellín took over.

questions.question: On the Caribbean coast, the hicotea lives in swamps and buries itself in the mud when the dry season comes. That's why it stands for resilience. What is it?
hints: It's a reptile.
It lays its eggs on land, near the water's edge.
It has a shell.
questions.description: An animal that knows the trick of sitting still until the storm passes.
questions.fun_fact: Sociologist Orlando Fals Borda wrote about the “hombre hicotea”: the costeño who endures everything and still keeps going.

questions.question: A lemon is related to an orange the way the caracolí, a giant tree of Colombian rivers, is related to which tree?
hints: Its relative is a fruit tree from hot lowlands.
Its relative has a curved seed that hangs outside the fruit.
That kidney-shaped seed is sold roasted as one of the world's favorite snack nuts.
questions.description: A tree so big it never fits in the family photo.
questions.fun_fact: There is a town in Antioquia called Caracolí, named after this tree.

questions.question: What Colombian word describes someone who flatters the boss to win favors?
hints: This is someone who is always trying to look good to the people on top.
In other Latin American countries they would say “chupamedias.”
It comes from “lamber,” which is how many Colombians say “lamer” (to lick).
questions.description: Some coworkers bring the boss a tinto before anyone even asks.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, people also say “lambonería” for the habit of flattering others.

questions.question: The regional channel Telepacífico broadcasts to southwestern Colombia. In which city is it based?
hints: It is the capital of a department.
It is one of the three largest cities in the country.
It is known as the world capital of salsa.
questions.description: A channel that brings the flavor of the Pacific right into your living room.
questions.fun_fact: Telepacífico went on the air in the late 1980s and covers Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Nariño and Chocó.

questions.question: I was an actress and scriptwriter, and I created and starred in “Yo y tú,” one of the longest-running comedies on Colombian TV. Who am I?
hints: My show started in the early years of Colombian television.
Besides acting, I wrote the scripts.
My last name starts with “del.”
questions.description: A comedy that ran so long that its viewers grew up, got married and kept on watching.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo y tú” stayed on the air for about 20 years, from the mid-1950s, which is almost unheard of on Colombian TV.

questions.question: QAP was a 1990s newscast, and Gabriel García Márquez was one of its partners. Its name is a radio code. What does it mean?
hints: It's a code used by ham radio fans and radio operators.
In Colombia it became an everyday expression.
Someone who tells you “quedo QAP” is keeping an eye out for you.
questions.description: A newscast that talks in code, like taxi drivers on the radio.
questions.fun_fact: Q codes like QAP were created in the early 1900s so telegraph operators from different countries could understand each other without sharing a language.

questions.question: The bajero style of vallenato, from the lowlands of Magdalena and Cesar, has one great star: an accordion player from El Paso. Who?
hints: People called him “el Negro Grande del vallenato.”
He was the first Rey Vallenato, in 1968.
He made “Alicia adorada,” a song by Juancho Polo Valencia, famous.
questions.description: Low doesn't mean worse: here it means downriver and full of flavor.
questions.fun_fact: Alejo Durán won the very first crown of the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata in 1968, and at the 1987 Rey de Reyes contest he walked off in the middle of his performance.

questions.question: Which of these towns is NOT in the department of Cesar?
hints: It's in a neighboring department.
It's in southern La Guajira, near Villanueva.
Its name comes from the river, which also named the neighboring department.
questions.description: A question for anyone who knows the map of Colombia's Caribbean coast by heart.
questions.fun_fact: San Juan del Cesar is a land of vallenato songwriters, and its village of La Junta is where Diomedes Díaz grew up.

questions.question: Which marimba player born in Guapi founded Grupo Bahía, which took the Pacific's currulao to stages around the world?
hints: He's from Cauca and is also a composer and producer.
He's not a mid-20th-century pioneer: his career took off in the 1990s.
His second given name sounds like “candela,” Spanish for fire.
questions.description: A man who gets more music out of wood than a carpenter with the hiccups.
questions.fun_fact: The keys of the marimba de chonta are made from chonta palm wood, and its resonators from guadua bamboo tubes.

questions.question: The La Chorrera waterfall, in Choachí (Cundinamarca), is considered the tallest in Colombia. Roughly how tall is it?
hints: It is much taller than any building in Bogotá.
But it doesn't reach the height of a mountain several kilometers tall.
It is more than twice the height of Torre Colpatria, which is about 190 meters (620 feet) tall.
questions.description: A shower so tall that the water is worn out by the time it reaches the floor.
questions.fun_fact: Right beside La Chorrera falls another waterfall, El Chiflón, and you can see both on the same hike from Choachí.

questions.question: Look at this village on Colombia's Caribbean coast: it's Sapzurro, in Chocó. If you hike up the hill from here, which country can you walk into?
hints: It's one of Colombia's neighbors.
It lies to the northwest, in Central America.
It's famous for its canal.
questions.description: A little village so close to the edge of the map it almost falls off.
questions.fun_fact: From Sapzurro you can hike up to the border and down the other side to La Miel, a beach in Panama.

questions.question: In Tumaco Bay, the sea rises and falls several meters every day, leaving mudflats exposed, so many houses stand on stilts. What causes it?
hints: It happens twice a day, every day.
It has to do with the Moon.
That's why people talk about the sea being “high” or “low”.
questions.description: The sea in Tumaco is like an elevator: up and down all day long.
questions.fun_fact: On Colombia's Pacific coast the tides are much bigger than in the Caribbean, where the sea barely rises or falls.

questions.question: Emilio Fortou founded it in 1945. It recorded Pacho Galán and was a rival of Discos Fuentes. In which city was the Discos Tropical label born?
hints: It is a city on the Caribbean coast.
In the 1940s and 1950s, it was a big center for orchestras and radio stations.
It is the city of Colombia's most famous Carnival.
questions.description: Before Spotify, music from the coast lived on black plates that went round and round.
questions.fun_fact: Discos Fuentes started in Cartagena and later moved to Medellín, but Discos Tropical always stayed a Barranquilla label.

questions.question: You're at a December party and a “14 Cañonazos Bailables” record is playing. Since which decade has a new volume come out every year?
hints: It has livened up the December parties of several generations of Colombian families.
Discos Fuentes has released it since the days of vinyl records.
The first volume came out at the start of the Beatles' decade.
questions.description: In some homes, December doesn't start with the calendar but with a brand-new record.
questions.fun_fact: For many Colombian families, the release of the new “14 Cañonazos” is the sign that the holiday season has begun.

questions.question: Boogaloo was born in New York in the 1960s and drove the dancers of Cali wild. It mixed Latin rhythms with which African American music?
hints: It was the music of Black neighborhoods in the United States at the time.
James Brown and Ray Charles were big stars of that world.
One of the two has “blues” in its full name.
questions.description: A New York musical recipe that Cali gobbled up, plate and all.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali, DJs played boogaloo records faster than normal speed, and that is how Cali-style dancing got so fast.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The answer is right: boogaloo (Latin boogaloo) blended Latin rhythms with soul and R&B. The wrong answers are wrong, and the hints are true. The fun fact is unverified: Cali DJs are widely said to have sped up records, but usually salsa records played at 45 rpm instead of 33. Tying this specifically to boogaloo is not well sourced. The question also says "which African American music" (singular) but the answer names two genres. I did not run a search.

questions.question: You're at a New Year's Eve party and “Ay cosita linda”, Pacho Galán's merecumbé, comes on. In which decade was it written?
hints: It's older than the first Moon landing.
Nat King Cole recorded it on a Spanish-language album.
It's from the same decade Elvis Presley became famous.
questions.description: A song so lovely that even grandma gets up from her chair.
questions.fun_fact: Pacho Galán created the merecumbé, a mix of merengue and cumbia, and Nat King Cole took “Ay cosita linda” around the world.

questions.question: I'm not on any field, but I work hard and defend my team or company as if they were my own. Who am I?
questions.answer: El que se pone la camiseta
wrong_answers: El que se hace el de la vista gorda
hints: The expression comes from soccer.
It has to do with what the players on a team wear.
It's the piece of clothing with the crest and the number that each player puts on.
questions.description: Not on the national team, but sweats through every office meeting like it's the World Cup final.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombian companies you often hear “hay que ponerse la camiseta” as a call for commitment, even though nobody wears a uniform.

questions.question: Which Colombian saying encourages you to save instead of spending all your money?
wrong_answers: Al que madruga Dios lo ayuda
Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente
No hay mal que por bien no venga
hints: It’s about not spending everything at once.
Its main verb means “to keep” or “to put away.”
It starts with “El que guarda…”.
questions.description: The little clay piggy banks applaud this one with their tiny clay ears.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia the most traditional piggy bank is the clay “marranito,” which often has to be broken to get the money out.

questions.question: Paisas use it all the time. It's short for a longer word and means “friend.” What is it?
hints: It's very typical of Antioquia.
Colombian TV shows and songs made it famous around the world.
It's the short form of “parcero”.
questions.description: The word you hear most on the Medellín metro, right after “next station”.
questions.fun_fact: The word got so famous that tourists from all over the world now say “¡quiubo, parce!” when they arrive in Medellín.

questions.question: It's said about the first level of a video game, a super easy test or a match against the worst team in the tournament. Which expression is it?
hints: It describes something that takes no effort at all.
It has to do with something people eat at breakfast.
Once food has been eaten, it's no more work.
questions.description: In Colombia, there's a ready-made saying even for telling people how your day went.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the opposite of something that's “pan comido” is “un camello”: that's what people call a really tough job.

questions.question: When a player lifts the ball over an opponent's head and collects it on the other side, Colombians say they pulled off a…
hints: The move humiliates the defender a little.
The ball goes over, not under.
It's something you wear on your head, in diminutive form.
questions.description: A move so elegant that the opponent ends up staring at the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: The chalaca, another famous move, is named after the port of Callao in Peru, where it is said to have been born.

questions.question: In a Spanish saying, everything I know I learned more from being old than from being bad. Who am I?
hints: The saying claims that experience teaches more than cunning.
I show up in many legends as a trickster who makes deals.
They say I have horns and a tail.
questions.description: A character from a saying who didn't learn it all in college, just by piling up birthdays.
questions.fun_fact: The full saying is “más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo”, used to say that the years teach more than any trick.

questions.question: You walk into the neighborhood tienda and say «¡Buenas!». Why do you say it?
hints: You say it as soon as you arrive.
It's the short form of «buenos días» or «buenas tardes».
It means the same as «hola».
questions.description: The shortest word for getting on the shopkeeper's good side.
questions.fun_fact: «¡Buenas!» works at any time of day, morning, afternoon or night, so you never have to check the clock.

questions.question: Guama is a long pod whose seeds are wrapped in white pulp that looks like cotton candy, and it's sold from carts. Where is it originally from?
hints: Its wild relatives grow near very big rivers.
Indigenous peoples were already eating it before the Spanish arrived.
It grows wild in the Amazon.
questions.description: A fruit that comes in its own green case, no plastic wrap needed.
questions.fun_fact: Guama trees are planted on coffee farms to give shade to the coffee plants.

questions.question: In Colombian bakeries, pan francés is long, with a crunchy crust and a soft inside. Which famous bread from France is it like?
hints: It's the bread French families buy every day.
In France, people carry it under their arm, fresh from the oven.
It's a long, thin stick of bread.
questions.description: A bread with a European passport that has never left the corner bakery.
questions.fun_fact: In 2022, UNESCO added the craft and culture of the French baguette to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

questions.question: Obleas are two thin, round wafers. What classic sweet gets spread in the middle?
hints: It's sweet, not salty.
It's light brown and sticky.
It's made by cooking milk with sugar for a long time.
questions.description: Two wafers so thin they need glue to keep from flying away.
questions.fun_fact: Obleas can also get grated cheese, blackberry jam and even cream, all at once.

questions.question: You buy a bunch of mamoncillos on the street. Which of these do you NOT do to eat them?
questions.answer: Cut them into slices with a knife
wrong_answers: Crack the peel with your teeth
hints: It's a tiny fruit, about the size of a grape.
Almost the whole fruit is seed.
There's hardly anything there to cut.
questions.description: Buying fruit on the street is a sport you play with sticky fingers.
questions.fun_fact: In Puerto Rico the mamoncillo is called quenepa, and in Venezuela, mamón.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these little eggs they put on top of salchipapas and hot dogs come from which bird?
hints: The bird is much smaller than a chicken.
Before peeling, the shell has little brown speckles.
It's a tiny, plump bird that runs along the ground.
questions.description: Pocket-size eggs for family-size salchipapas.
questions.fun_fact: It takes about five quail eggs to match the weight of one chicken egg.

questions.question: I'm green and round. They cook me in panela syrup, cut me in half and fill me with arequipe. What am I?
hints: I'm related to the fig.
People often serve me in December with cheese.
My name starts with “Br”.
questions.description: A fruit that goes on vacation in the paila and comes back sweeter.
questions.fun_fact: The breva is the fig tree's first crop of the year, which is why Colombians say “no caerá esa breva” (that breva won't fall) when something good just won't happen.

questions.question: Philip II gave Popayán its coat of arms in 1558. In the center are a golden city, rivers and snowy mountains, with a blue border with four crosses. Which crosses?
hints: They are gold crosses on a blue background.
Their name comes from a city that was key in the Crusades.
It is the holy city where, according to the Bible, Jesus was crucified.
questions.description: A coat of arms so fancy that the king himself signed off on it.
questions.fun_fact: The 1558 royal decree described the coat of arms in detail, right down to the green trees around the golden city.

questions.question: Which of these does NOT appear on the flag of Cartagena?
hints: The flag has three colors in rectangles, one inside the other.
Barranquilla has an almost identical flag.
Its colors are red, yellow and green.
questions.description: A flag that stacks boxes inside boxes, like a Russian nesting doll.
questions.fun_fact: This flag is nicknamed “la cuadrilonga,” and it flew during Cartagena's independence in 1811.

questions.question: It's brown, a little sweet, sometimes has raisins, and on the coast it comes with fried mojarra and patacón. What is it called?
hints: It's a classic side dish on the Caribbean coast: made in a caldero and served at beach restaurants.
The rice turns brown and sweet because something toasts in the pot until it caramelizes.
That fruit has a hairy shell and water inside.
questions.description: On the coast, no fried fish leaves the kitchen without its sidekick.
questions.fun_fact: “Titoté” is the name for the toasted bits of coconut that give the rice its brown color.

questions.question: People from Antioquia and the Eje Cafetero are called “paisas”. That word is a shortened form of a longer one. Which one?
hints: The longer word names a type of person.
In Mexico people also use it a lot to greet someone from their home region.
Take the ending “-no” off it and you get the short word.
questions.description: A word so affectionate that people cut it short to say it faster.
questions.fun_fact: “Paisano” came from the French “paysan”, which comes from “pays”, meaning country.

questions.question: “Ugly Betty,” the US version of “Yo soy Betty, la fea” starring America Ferrera, premiered in which year?
hints: It came several years after the original Colombian telenovela.
It premiered in the same decade as the Mexican version, “La fea más bella.”
It was the same year as the World Cup in Germany.
questions.description: Betty moved from Bogotá to New York without even standing in the visa line.
questions.fun_fact: “Ugly Betty” was produced by Salma Hayek, and America Ferrera won an Emmy and a Golden Globe for the role.

questions.question: In what year did Caracol premiere “Escobar, el patrón del mal”, starring Andrés Parra?
hints: It was in the 2010s.
It came out a few years after “El capo”.
It premiered the same year some people said the world was going to end.
questions.description: A telenovela with more bodyguards than heartthrobs.
questions.fun_fact: For the role, Andrés Parra gained weight and spent months studying real recordings and interviews.

questions.question: In 2001, which telenovela continued the story of Betty and Armando after the ending of “Yo soy Betty, la fea”?
hints: Its title doesn't include any character's name.
It has the same name as a very important place in the original show.
It's the name of the fashion company where Betty worked.
questions.description: When a happy ending isn't enough, it's time for another season at the office.
questions.fun_fact: Terramoda, one of the wrong options, was the front company Betty used to protect the firm's assets.

previous.feedback: source: the fun fact is inaccurate, and the translation repeats it faithfully. Terramoda was a shell company set up by the Ecomoda executives (Armando and Mario) to absorb Ecomoda and keep it from the banks, with Betty only its figurehead manager; she did not use it herself to protect assets. Suggested text for the source: “Terramoda, one of the wrong options, was the shell company created to absorb Ecomoda and shield it from the banks, with Betty named as its general manager.” Fact check: uncertain. The answer (Ecomoda) is right. The fun fact is inaccurate: Terramoda was a shell company set up by the Ecomoda executives to absorb Ecomoda and stop the banks seizing it. Betty was only its figurehead general manager, and she did not use it to protect assets.

questions.question: In the Netflix series “Siempre bruja”, Carmen is a young witch from 17th-century Cartagena who travels to the present. Which actress plays her?
hints: She is a young Colombian actress.
This was her first major leading role.
She shares a surname with a former president of Colombia.
questions.description: A witch who travels through time without a broomstick, but with plenty of drama.
questions.fun_fact: “Siempre bruja” is based on the novel “Yo, bruja” by Colombian writer Isidora Chacón.

questions.question: You’re on a trip through La Guajira, vallenato country. Which of these cities will you NOT find there?
hints: Look for the city far from the Caribbean Sea, up in the mountains.
Three of them are in the desert and on the coast of the north.
It’s the city of the paisas, home of the Feria de las Flores.
questions.description: A trip with heat, goats, dunes and an accordion playing in the background.
questions.fun_fact: Uribia, in La Guajira, is known as the Indigenous capital of Colombia for its large Wayuu population.

questions.question: In which century did Francisco de Paula Santander, the “Man of the Laws,” govern?
hints: He was a friend and later a rival of Simón Bolívar.
He governed when the country had just won independence from Spain.
It’s the same century as the Battle of Boyacá, in 1819.
questions.description: A statue so patient it has stood still in the same park for generations.
questions.fun_fact: The department of Santander is named after him, though he was born in Villa del Rosario, which is now in Norte de Santander.

questions.question: Look at this portrait: this general from Popayán was president four times and in 1861 seized much of the Church's property. Who is he?
hints: He came from a very powerful family in Cauca.
People called him “the Great General.”
A town in Cundinamarca, next to Bogotá, bears his surname.
questions.description: A portrait of a very serious man who clearly never learned to smile for the camera.
questions.fun_fact: A decree by Mosquera in November 1861 adopted the yellow, blue and red flag with horizontal stripes, almost the same as today's.

questions.question: It's 1863 in Rionegro: the Liberals who won the 1860–1862 civil war write a new constitution. What do they name the country?
hints: The country was split into nine sovereign states.
Its great promoter was General Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera.
It copies the official name of the country whose capital is Washington.
questions.description: A country that changed its name more often than its president.
questions.fun_fact: The country kept that name for 23 years, until the Constitution of 1886 changed it to Republic of Colombia.

questions.question: In the 19th century, on the steep Quindío trail, the silleteros carried a chair strapped to their backs. What did they carry in that chair?
hints: It was a muddy track where mules could barely get through.
Sometimes the load complained about the trip.
Today, for that same service, you would pay a fare.
questions.description: A job where your back was the vehicle and your legs were the engine.
questions.fun_fact: The flowers came much later: since 1957, silleteros have paraded with their silletas at Medellín's Feria de las Flores.

questions.question: Your mesada (allowance) is 3,000 pesos a week and you spend none of it. How much money do you save in 4 weeks?
hints: It's a simple multiplication.
It's 3,000 pesos, four times over.
It's what a 10,000 bill and a 2,000 bill add up to.
questions.description: The most eagerly awaited paycheck in the house, and it's not your parents'.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the word “mesada” is also used for the monthly pension that retired grandparents receive.

questions.question: The red 10,000-peso bill shows the Amazon. Which of these places is NOT in the Colombian Amazon?
hints: Look for the one with no jungle around it.
The other three are in the Amazonas department, in the south of the country.
It's an island in the Caribbean Sea.
questions.description: A bill so jungly you almost have to keep it next to the bug spray.
questions.fun_fact: The Amazon is home to the pink river dolphin, which swims in rivers, not in the sea.

questions.question: In Colombia, if people say they “echaron la casa por la ventana” for a cousin's quinceañera, what did they do?
questions.answer: Spent a fortune on the party
wrong_answers: Held the party in the street
hints: It has nothing to do with real windows.
You also hear it a lot about weddings and graduations.
They didn't save on anything: food, music and decorations all went big.
questions.description: A saying that scares window repairers and thrills the guests.
questions.fun_fact: The saying is thought to come from an old Spanish custom of throwing a lottery winner's furniture out the window.

questions.question: This is what bills look like before they're cut. What are the bills printed by the Banco de la República mainly made of?
hints: It isn't the same paper as in your notebooks.
That's why they hold up better if you forget them in a pocket and they go through the wash.
It's the same fiber your T-shirts are made of.
questions.description: Literally making money, and it's not even a crime.
questions.fun_fact: The Banco de la República has its own banknote printing plant in Bogotá.

questions.question: The discount store chain Justo & Bueno spread across Colombia’s neighborhoods. In which decade did it start?
hints: It is a fairly recent chain.
It came to compete with D1 and Ara, which were already in the neighborhoods.
It started about ten years ago and closed a few years later.
questions.description: A store that arrived, filled the block with cheap groceries and vanished faster than a paycheck.
questions.fun_fact: Justo & Bueno grew to hundreds of stores around the country in just a few years, before it fell into crisis and closed.

questions.question: They’re crisp crackers made by Noel, eaten with cheese or tinto (black coffee), and their name comes from a title of nobility. Which one?
hints: The cracker’s name almost spells out the title.
It ranks higher than a count.
His wife is called a duchess.
questions.description: A cracker so elegant it should be eaten wearing a crown, with your pinky raised.
questions.fun_fact: “Ducal” means “of a duke”, just as a ducal palace is the home of a duke.

questions.question: Envigado is nicknamed “la Naranja Mecánica” (the Clockwork Orange), like the Netherlands team that dazzled at a World Cup. Which one?
hints: It was the era of Johan Cruyff.
That World Cup was played in Germany.
It was in the 1970s.
questions.description: A nickname that traveled from the land of windmills all the way to a town in Antioquia.
questions.fun_fact: The 1974 “Clockwork Orange” reached the final unbeaten, but lost it to the hosts, West Germany.

questions.question: Finish the sentence: Bogotá's blue club got the name “Millonarios” because in the 1940s…
questions.answer: …it spent a lot of money signing and paying players
wrong_answers: …its stadium was built with gold coins
…it was founded by a bank in the capital
hints: It has to do with money, but not with a lucky prize.
A journalist of the time made fun of how much the club was spending.
A few years later it brought in stars like Di Stéfano.
questions.description: A name that sounds like a bank account but gets shouted from the stands.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname became so popular that the club ended up adopting it as its official name.

questions.question: Colombian coach Jorge Luis Pinto led Costa Rica to the quarterfinals of a World Cup. Which one?
hints: At that World Cup, goalkeeper Keylor Navas started becoming famous worldwide.
Costa Rica topped a group with Uruguay, Italy and England.
It was played in South America.
questions.description: A man from Santander who got a whole Central American country dancing.
questions.fun_fact: Costa Rica left that World Cup unbeaten: it was knocked out on penalties by the Netherlands.

questions.question: “A striker earns me by scoring three goals in one game, and in the Colombian league many take the match ball home for it. What am I?”
hints: It's more than two and less than four.
The name was born in cricket, not in soccer.
Part of my name is something you wear on your head.
questions.description: The day a striker's teammates have to admit he was carrying the whole team.
questions.fun_fact: The term was born in English cricket, where a player who pulled off the feat was given a hat.

questions.question: At a Colombian league game, the coach, the backup goalkeeper and the players waiting to come on sit there. What is it called?
hints: It's next to the field, not under it or above it.
It often has a small see-through roof.
In Colombia it's also called “la banca”.
questions.description: Ninety minutes in which even grandma turns into the head coach.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, a player who goes many games without playing is said to be “calentando banca”: warming the bench.

questions.question: The Pact of Lima set an end date for El Dorado, the era when world stars played in the Colombian league. In what year was it signed?
hints: Colombia had left FIFA, so its clubs could bring in stars without paying transfer fees.
The deal gave the clubs a few more years with their stars before sending them back.
It was in the early 1950s.
questions.description: A deal signed in another country that switched off the lights on Colombia's big soccer party.
questions.fun_fact: With the pact, Colombia returned to FIFA and the clubs promised to send the foreign players back to their original teams.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these brightly colored mochilas are hand-woven by women of an Indigenous people. In which Colombian department do they live?
hints: It's a department at the country's northern tip.
It has desert, salt flats and lots of wind by the Caribbean Sea.
Cabo de la Vela is there.
questions.description: A bag so colorful that even the rainbow asks the weaver for her number.
questions.fun_fact: A large Wayuu mochila can take between two weeks and a month to weave by hand.

questions.question: Why do the potters of Ráquira put their clay pots in the wood-burning oven?
questions.answer: To fire them so they turn hard
wrong_answers: To soften the clay for shaping
To stick on the handles and lids
To test if they work for cooking
hints: Before it goes in the oven, the piece already has its shape.
Raw clay falls apart in water.
Strong heat turns it into tough ceramic.
questions.description: An oven that has never roasted a chicken, yet it's always busy.
questions.fun_fact: A potter's kiln can go past 800 °C (1,470 °F), much hotter than a kitchen oven.

questions.question: I was a Liberal general in the Thousand Days' War. The so-called Indigenous capital of Colombia, in La Guajira, bears my name. Who am I?
hints: He was a politician in the early 20th century, long after Independence.
The town is famous for its Wayuu mochilas and its Wayuu culture festival.
That town is called Uribia.
questions.description: Some people get a street named after them; this man got a whole town.
questions.fun_fact: Uribia was founded in 1935 and is one of the largest municipalities in La Guajira by area.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these flower pots are made of reddish fired clay with no glaze. What is this material called?
hints: It's a type of ceramic.
Its name comes from Italian and means something like “baked earth.”
China's famous clay army of warriors, guarding an emperor's tomb, is made of it.
questions.description: Grandma's plants live better than most of us, each in its own little clay house.
questions.fun_fact: Clay pots let the soil breathe, because water and air pass through their tiny pores.

questions.question: In Usiacurí, Atlántico, people weave famous colorful crafts. From which fiber?
hints: The fiber is cut into thin strips and dyed in bright colors.
Hats are woven from this same fiber in Sandoná, Nariño.
Ecuador's famous “Panama” hat is woven from this same palm.
questions.description: In this town in Atlántico, hands work faster than the ceiling fan.
questions.fun_fact: The poet Julio Flórez spent his last years in Usiacurí, and his house is now a museum.

questions.question: Look at the photo: many pre-Hispanic chest pieces like this one aren't pure gold but gold mixed with copper. What is that mix called?
hints: It's an alloy used all over pre-Hispanic America.
Bronze has no gold; this mix does.
Its name starts with “tum”.
questions.description: All that glitters is not gold, and pre-Hispanic goldsmiths knew it well.
questions.fun_fact: Goldsmiths treated tumbaga with plant acids so the surface turned into shiny gold.

questions.question: The Serranía de Chiribiquete has tens of thousands of red rock paintings showing jaguars and deer. What was the red color made from?
questions.answer: An iron-rich mineral from the earth
hints: The ancient painters used whatever they found around the tepuis.
That's why it has lasted thousands of years without fading.
It's called ochre.
questions.description: Colombia's first decorated wall, and nobody got fined for drawing on it.
questions.fun_fact: Chiribiquete was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018, for both its nature and its culture.

questions.question: When you peel the mandarin from your lunchbox, it splits into little pieces. What are those pieces called?
hints: You don't need a knife to get them out.
They are shaped like a half-moon.
Oranges and lemons have them too, and the word starts with S.
questions.description: The fruit that comes already shared out so nobody fights at recess.
questions.fun_fact: A mandarin usually has between 8 and 13 segments.

questions.question: In Colombia it's called patilla: big, green and striped outside, red with black seeds inside. What is it almost entirely made of?
hints: There's a reason people eat so much of it in the hot lowlands.
When you bite into it, it drips down your chin.
It's the same thing that comes out of the faucet.
questions.description: A fruit so big you have to carry it like a baby.
questions.fun_fact: Patilla is about 92% water, which is why it quenches your thirst almost as well as a glass of water.

questions.question: At the market, mora, uchuva and tomate de árbol are sold by the pound: half a pound, one pound, two pounds. What does the pound tell you?
hints: Before handing it over, the seller puts it on a device.
That device is the scale.
A bag full of feathers would have very little of this.
questions.description: The market has its own language, and this word is one of the first you learn.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia a pound is 500 grams, while the English pound weighs about 454 grams.

questions.question: In Colombia, guacamole is eaten with patacones. Which of these ingredients does NOT go in guacamole?
hints: Guacamole is made from mashed avocado.
Three of these options are chopped into little pieces and mixed with the avocado.
The odd one out is sweet and has no business being in a dip.
questions.description: A green dip that gets jealous whenever someone brings the mayonnaise near.
questions.fun_fact: Guacamole comes from Mexico: its name comes from a Nahuatl word meaning “avocado sauce.”

questions.question: Look at the photo: after blending the mora, you pour the juice through this. What gets caught?
hints: It's something you don't want to find in your glass.
It's tiny and hard.
If you plant it, a new plant can grow.
questions.description: A kitchen tool full of holes that still does its job really well.
questions.fun_fact: Mora has so many seeds that in many Colombian homes the juice is always strained before it's served.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what do Colombians call the little seeds in the middle of this fruit?
hints: You scoop them out with a spoon before eating it.
They're tiny and flat, and lots of them come together.
It's the same word used for the seeds of a patilla (watermelon).
questions.description: A fruit that keeps its secrets right in the middle.
questions.fun_fact: Melon pepas can be toasted and eaten, just like ahuyama (squash) seeds.

questions.question: The priest blesses it on Palm Sunday, you take it home, and people put it behind the door. What is that palm for?
questions.answer: To protect the house from harm and storms
hints: It's a “contra” (a protective charm), like holy water.
In heavy downpours, some grandmothers burn a little piece of it.
People say that with it, no ghosts or lightning get in.
questions.description: The only plant in the house that went to Mass better dressed than the family.
questions.fun_fact: To save the wax palm, Colombia's national tree, people were asked not to use its leaves on Palm Sunday.

questions.question: I am a wise man of the Indigenous peoples of Putumayo: I lead ceremonies with sacred plants and heal with chants and leafy branches. Who am I?
hints: You'll find me in the Sibundoy Valley, among the Kamëntsá and the Inga.
I prepare yagé.
In the countryside, my name is also an affectionate way to say “dad”.
questions.description: A doctor with no white coat, no office and no online appointments.
questions.fun_fact: In Sibundoy, the Kamëntsá celebrate the Bëtscnaté, or Carnival of Forgiveness, a big festival of reconciliation.

questions.question: At night on a country road, a dog and the famous ghost Mule of Colombian legend walk by. How many legs do they have together?
hints: A dog has four legs.
This ghost mule doesn't walk like normal mules: you hear a strange, limping trot.
It's called the Mula de Tres Patas, the Three-Legged Mule.
questions.description: An easy sum, as long as you don't run away before you finish it.
questions.fun_fact: A real mule is the foal of a female horse and a male donkey, and it can almost never have babies of its own.

questions.question: In the Llanos, at night on the road, a very tall woman in a white saya appears: it's the Sayona. What is a saya?
hints: It is a piece of clothing.
Women and girls used to wear one every day; the word is still heard in the countryside.
Cumbia dancers wear a very wide one to dance.
questions.description: A ghost named after something from grandma's closet.
questions.fun_fact: The Sayona also scares people in Venezuela, where the llaneros tell the same legend.

questions.question: I'm not a prayer or a charm, and I cost nothing: if a spook leads you astray in the wild hills, I break the spell and you find your way. What am I?
hints: It works against the duende and the Madremonte.
You do it to yourself, with what you're wearing.
The seams end up on the outside.
questions.description: The countryside's free GPS for when the spooks hide the path from you.
questions.fun_fact: In the Colombian countryside, people say the duende especially likes long-haired girls and children.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The folk remedy of wearing clothes inside out against the duende and the Madremonte is plausible and widely reported in Colombian and Latin American folklore, but I did not run a search to confirm it. The fun fact (the duende likes long-haired girls and small children) also matches general folklore and was not verified. The wrong answers are not real remedies.

Fact check: uncertain. Turning clothes inside out is the well-known remedy against the duende and Madremonte when lost. The duende is said to like children and long-haired girls, which is plausible. I did not run a search, so I couldn't confirm that every wrong answer is absent from the folklore (e.g. shoes on the wrong feet).

questions.question: Every December, floats of the Madremonte, the Patetarro and other spooks roll in the Desfile de Mitos y Leyendas, which opens the Christmas alumbrados. In which city?
hints: It's one of the three most populated cities in Colombia.
Its Christmas lights stretch along the river.
It's the city of the Feria de las Flores.
questions.description: A city where even the spooks line up to see the lights.
questions.fun_fact: Medellín's Christmas lights are put on by EPM, the city's public utility company.

questions.question: Which of these roles has Colombian actress Natalia Reyes NOT played?
wrong_answers: Lady in “Lady, la vendedora de rosas”
hints: Natalia Reyes shared the screen with Arnold Schwarzenegger.
She also worked with director Ciro Guerra in La Guajira.
The odd one out is a hired killer from Medellín, taken from a novel by Jorge Franco.
questions.description: Her résumé has more twists than a 200-episode telenovela.
questions.fun_fact: In “Terminator: Dark Fate” (2019), Natalia Reyes plays Dani Ramos, the young woman a robot from the future comes to hunt.

questions.question: Grandma gives you this hot drink when you have a cold: a brown block made from sugarcane, boiled in water, with lime squeezed in. What is it called?
hints: It is sweet and a little sour.
The brown block is sold at the corner store.
In the hot lowlands people also drink it cold with ice.
questions.description: The official syrup of every Colombian grandma, no prescription needed.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia is one of the world's biggest producers and consumers of panela.

questions.question: In the legend from Antioquia, the Sombrerón rides out at night on a black horse with two chained dogs. Who does he chase?
hints: He appears at night in the streets of Antioquia's towns.
His victims are people who've gone down the wrong path.
He throws his hat at those leaving the bar or betting money.
questions.description: A man whose hat is so big it needs its own parking spot.
questions.fun_fact: They say the Sombrerón's hat grows as it lands on its victim until it covers them completely.

questions.question: In the Llanos, they say El Silbón roams the plains at night, whistling. If you hear his whistle very close, what does it mean, according to the legend?
wrong_answers: That he's looking for someone else
hints: The legend plays with the opposite of what you'd expect.
His whistle tricks your ears.
The dangerous thing is hearing it soft and distant.
questions.description: The only ghost who knows the whole musical scale and uses it to scare people.
questions.fun_fact: They say El Silbón's whistle climbs up the notes do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti.

questions.question: You go out with binoculars. In which of these places in Colombia would you NOT see a condor flying free?
wrong_answers: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
hints: The condor needs high mountains and strong winds.
Its full name, “Andean condor,” tells you where it lives.
One of these places is low, hot jungle.
questions.description: A bird so big that if it landed on your balcony, you'd have to ask it to scoot over.
questions.fun_fact: The Andean condor's wings can measure more than 3 meters (10 ft) from tip to tip.

questions.question: A Colombian saying warns that on Tuesday the 13th you should neither get married nor… what?
hints: In Colombia this is the unlucky day, like Friday the 13th in other countries.
It has to do with a trip.
Long journeys used to be made by ship.
questions.description: A day so unlucky that even the black cats stay home.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia and much of Latin America, the unlucky day is Tuesday the 13th, not Friday the 13th.

questions.question: In which century was Colombia's national anthem first sung in public?
hints: It happened after Colombia's independence.
When it premiered, radio didn't exist yet.
It was in the 1800s.
questions.description: A song so old your great-great-grandparents already knew it, and still nobody skips the chorus.
questions.fun_fact: The anthem was first sung in public on November 11, 1887, in Bogotá.

questions.question: Look at the photo: when the anthem plays at school, many people put their hand like this. What are they showing with it?
hints: People also do it when the flag is raised.
It's a way to honor your country.
It's the same thing you show when you listen carefully to your teacher.
questions.description: A gesture that doesn't say a single word, and still everyone understands it.
questions.fun_fact: The right hand goes over the left side of the chest, where the heart is.

questions.question: The red stripe on Colombia's flag honors certain people from history. Who are they?
hints: They are celebrated on July 20 and August 7.
They fought so that Colombia could be free.
Simón Bolívar is one of them.
questions.description: The bottom stripe of the flag belongs to someone, and it's not the kids in the back row.
questions.fun_fact: The red of the flag is also explained as a symbol of the courage and honor of the Colombian people.

questions.question: You're watching TV as the presidential sash is placed on the new president in Bogotá. What date is it?
hints: It's a national holiday.
The day commemorates a battle.
It was the Battle of Boyacá, in 1819.
questions.description: A three-colored outfit that only gets a new wearer every four years.
questions.fun_fact: The presidential sash has the colors of the flag and Colombia's coat of arms embroidered on it.

questions.question: They come in July and August, flags hang from houses and there are independence parades. What are these celebrations called?
hints: Schools hold flag-raising ceremonies for these dates.
One is on July 20 and the other on August 7.
They celebrate the Grito de Independencia and the Battle of Boyacá: the birth of the nation.
questions.description: The time of year when the flag goes out for a stroll through every window.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, July 20 and August 7 are public holidays that are never moved to a Monday.

questions.question: In November 2023 in Barranquilla, Colombia beat Brazil in World Cup qualifying for the first time, with two goals by Luis Díaz. How did he score both?
hints: Brazil took the lead, and Colombia came back to win.
Both goals came late in the match.
Two crosses came in from the wing, and he jumped higher than the Brazilian defenders.
questions.description: Four minutes that people in Barranquilla still talk about as if they lasted four years.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won 2-1, and Luis Díaz scored both goals in just four minutes after Brazil had taken the lead.

questions.question: In what year did Colombia play its first final of a FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup, in India, against Spain?
hints: It was after the pandemic.
Linda Caicedo was already playing for the senior national team that year.
It was the year Argentina won the World Cup in Qatar.
questions.description: A bunch of teenage girls who went further than plenty of grown-ups.
questions.fun_fact: Spain won that final 1–0 and Colombia finished runner-up, with Linda Caicedo just 17 years old.

questions.question: I was born in Quibdó in 1999, came up through Atlético Nacional and played several years for Genk in Belgium. I'm a center back for Colombia. Who am I?
hints: I'm the youngest of the four.
After Belgium I played for Galatasaray in Turkey.
My last name is the Spanish word for a steep slope.
questions.description: A wall that came from the Pacific coast and learned to defend in Belgium.
questions.fun_fact: Quibdó, the capital of Chocó, is one of the rainiest cities in the world.

questions.question: From 1968 I managed Colombia's natural resources and created many national parks; in 1993 the Ministry of the Environment replaced me. What was my name?
hints: I was a government institute.
My name was an acronym that started with “In”.
My acronym included “recursos naturales renovables” (renewable natural resources).
questions.description: An acronym that sounds like a tongue twister and looked after half the country.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's first national park, Cueva de los Guácharos, was created in 1960, before this institute even existed.

questions.question: A Ramsar wetland in Guainía is named after the Inírida, Guaviare and Atabapo rivers, which meet there. Which great river do its waters flow into?
hints: It's one of the longest rivers in South America.
Alexander von Humboldt traveled along it and studied it in 1800.
It gives its name to one of Colombia's great natural regions, the Llanos.
questions.description: A star that doesn't shine in the sky but flows through the jungle.
questions.fun_fact: Nearby rise the Mavecure hills, giant rocks that are among the oldest on the planet.

questions.question: In Colombia's national parks, like Tayrona, who pays the highest entrance fee?
hints: Not everyone pays the same.
It depends on where the visitor comes from.
They come from other countries.
questions.description: Nature is free, but taking care of it costs a bit of plata.
questions.fun_fact: The money from entrance fees helps pay for trails, park rangers and conservation programs.

questions.question: It's a red flower that lasts a very long time without wilting, grows on sandy savannas and is named after a jungle capital. Which department is it from?
hints: It's a department in eastern Colombia, on the border.
It borders Venezuela and Brazil.
Its capital is Inírida.
questions.description: A flower that flat-out refuses to wilt.
questions.fun_fact: It's called the “eternal flower” because even after it's cut, it keeps its color for a long time.

questions.question: In 2018, Caterine Ibargüen became the first Colombian to receive a major international award. Which one?
hints: In 2018 she won almost every competition she entered.
Usain Bolt received it several times.
It goes to whoever had the best track and field season on the planet.
questions.description: A trophy you don't win by jumping for joy… although in this case, it helped quite a bit.
questions.fun_fact: That same year, the men's award went to Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge, who had just broken the marathon world record.

questions.question: Weightlifter María Isabel Urrutia is one of the great stars of Colombian sport. Which department is she from?
hints: It's a department with a coast on the Pacific Ocean.
She was born in Candelaria, a town very close to the department's capital.
Its capital is the city of salsa, the “Sucursal del Cielo”.
questions.description: Some people lift weights, and some people lift a whole country.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, María Isabel Urrutia became Colombia's Minister of Sport.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian weightlifter. At Rio 2016 I got bronze after a rival was disqualified, and at Tokyo 2020 I won silver. Who am I?
hints: I compete in one of the lightest weight classes.
In Tokyo I competed in the 67 kg class.
My last name is also the name of a town in Cundinamarca.
questions.description: A man who can lift more than a whole stadium's spirits.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won no gold at Tokyo 2020: it came home with four silvers and one bronze.

questions.question: Which Colombian tennis player won the 2017 Australian Open mixed doubles with American Abigail Spears?
hints: He is a doubles specialist.
He was born in Cali in 1986.
He shares his first names with the navigator Elcano.
questions.description: In January, Melbourne burns, and not just from the sun: the rackets are on fire too.
questions.fun_fact: That mixed doubles title in Melbourne was the first Grand Slam of his career.

questions.question: At town festivals, people put up a very tall pole covered in grease, with prizes at the top, and try to climb it. What is it called?
hints: Almost everyone slips before reaching the top.
Contestants stand on each other's shoulders to make it.
In Spanish, “sebo” is another word for grease.
questions.description: A game where butter is your worst enemy.
questions.fun_fact: Games like the palo encebado exist in many countries, from the Philippines to Italy.

questions.question: Its creator was a painter born in Medellín, and in this style everything looks huge and round: people, fruit and even horses. What is it called?
hints: Its sculptures stand in squares of cities all over the world.
Its creator gave many sculptures to a square in downtown Medellín.
The painter's first name was Fernando.
questions.description: A paisa paintbrush that has been to more museums than most tourists.
questions.fun_fact: Botero said he didn't paint fat people: he painted volume, because he loved how big shapes fill a canvas.

questions.question: In what year did Justin Bieber spray-paint graffiti on a wall on Bogotá's Calle 26 during a concert tour?
hints: It was during a world tour that took him through several Latin American countries.
It happened in the 2010s.
It was the same year Pope Francis was elected.
questions.description: A pop idol, a can of spray paint and a national scandal: the perfect recipe for the evening news.
questions.fun_fact: It caused an uproar because Bieber painted with a police escort, while many Bogotá graffiti artists complained that police chased them for doing the same.

questions.question: I'm an artist from Bogotá. In 2007 I opened a 167 m (548 ft) crack in the floor of London's Tate Modern and called it “Shibboleth.” Who am I?
hints: My works deal with memory and the victims of violence.
In 2018 I made a floor from melted-down FARC weapons, called “Fragmentos.”
My first name starts with D.
