questions.description: A work of art that literally hit the floor.
questions.fun_fact: The crack of “Shibboleth” was filled in after the exhibition ended, but the scar is still visible in the Tate's floor.

questions.question: During Holy Week in Popayán, what are the men called who carry floats like the one in this photo on their shoulders?
hints: Popayán's processions have gone out at night since colonial times and are UNESCO heritage.
They walk under the float's poles, with a cushion on the shoulder.
Their name comes from the Spanish verb “cargar”, meaning “to carry”.
questions.description: A job for strong shoulders, slow steps and a lot of devotion.
questions.fun_fact: In Popayán, being a carguero often passes from father to son, and some families carry the same float for generations.

questions.question: El Pibe Valderrama played in three World Cups in a row for Colombia's national team. In which decade were they?
hints: It was in the 20th century.
One of those World Cups was played in the United States.
They were Italy, the United States and France, one every four years.
questions.description: A head of hair that deserves its own sticker album.
questions.fun_fact: In 1987, El Pibe became the first Colombian named South American Footballer of the Year.

questions.question: I was a philanthropist from Antioquia, lived in a Medellín castle that is now a museum, and gave Itagüí its first library. Who am I?
hints: My family was behind some of Antioquia's big textile companies.
I bought the castle in the 1940s and filled it with European art and furniture.
The library in Itagüí carries my full name.
questions.description: A man who lived in a castle without being a king or a fairy-tale character.
questions.fun_fact: Museo El Castillo, in El Poblado, copies the medieval castles of France and has gardens open to the public.

previous.feedback: Fact check: wrong. Answer is right (Diego Echavarría Misas, Coltejer family, Itagüí library bears his name). But hint 2 is false: he did not buy the castle in the 1940s. He had it built (c. 1930–1932) as a home with his wife Benedikta Zur Nieden, and filled it with European art.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the carbonero flower looks like a red pom-pom. What are those red “hairs” really?
hints: They have to do with how the plant reproduces.
At the tip of each “hair” there's a tiny bit of pollen.
They are the male part of the flower.
questions.description: A flower that got its hair done for the party, and now every strand is standing on end.
questions.fun_fact: The carbonero's petals are so tiny and greenish that hardly anyone notices them.

questions.question: Colombia is one of the countries with the most orchid species in the world. About how many does it have?
hints: Colombia is one of the most biodiverse countries on the planet.
A single cloud forest reserve can have hundreds of orchid species.
It's thousands, but not tens of thousands.
questions.description: A flower so elegant it has more cousins than a paisa family in December.
questions.fun_fact: More than 1,500 of Colombia's orchids grow in no other country.

questions.question: I’m a woman from Colombia’s Pacific coast: in the arrullos I sing the lead and the others answer me in chorus, to the cununo drum. What am I?
hints: You find me at wakes and saints’ festivals in Guapi, Timbiquí or Tumaco.
The women who answer me in the chorus are called “respondedoras.”
My name comes from the Spanish verb for what I do with my throat.
questions.description: In Guapi, the marimba, the cununo and the downpour never take a day off.
questions.fun_fact: In 2010, UNESCO declared the marimba music and traditional chants of Colombia’s South Pacific region an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: In Pombo's poem, Mirringa Mirronga, la gata candonga, is throwing a party. What does she ask all the cats not to eat for lunch?
hints: It's something a cat hunts on its own.
She also doesn't want them eating the mice's bigger cousins for dinner.
They love cheese and are scared of cats.
questions.description: A cat party you have to show up to on an empty stomach.
questions.fun_fact: «Candonga» is an old word for someone sweet-talking and crafty, perfect for a flirty cat.

questions.question: It came out in 2018, J Balvin and Nicky Jam sing it, and its title is a single letter of the alphabet. Which letter?
hints: It's one of the least used letters in both Spanish and English.
In math, it stands for the unknown.
On pirate maps, it marks where the treasure is.
questions.description: A song with a title so short it fits on a soda bottle cap.
questions.fun_fact: The song is also listed as “X (Equis)”, and a remix with Maluma and Ozuna came out the same year.

questions.question: In what year did Karol G and Shakira release their song together, “TQG”?
hints: It was in the 2020s.
It came out on the album “Mañana Será Bonito.”
It was the same year as Shakira's session with Bizarrap.
questions.description: Two Colombian women, one microphone and a message for someone who just wasn't up to it.
questions.fun_fact: “TQG” stands for “Te Quedó Grande.”

questions.question: Karol G and Nicki Minaj sang about this in 2019. Complete it: in Colombia, having “tusa” means being…

hints: It has to do with the heart.
Time heals it… and so does despecho music.
It happens when your boyfriend or girlfriend leaves you.
questions.description: A word you hear at every reggaeton party in Colombia, even though nobody wants to have it.
questions.fun_fact: “Tusa,” by Karol G and Nicki Minaj, came out in 2019, and its video passed 1 billion views on YouTube.

questions.question: You're in Cali, the marimba de chonta is playing and everyone is at the Petronio Álvarez Festival. What month is it?
hints: It's not during the end-of-year holidays.
It's in the second half of the year.
It's the month for flying kites in Colombia.
questions.description: When Cali swaps salsa for marimba for a few days… and nobody complains.
questions.fun_fact: The festival celebrates the music of the Pacific coast and is named after Petronio Álvarez, who wrote the famous currulao “Mi Buenaventura.”

questions.question: In what year did Andrea Echeverri and Aterciopelados release the album “El Dorado,” with the song “Bolero falaz”?
hints: It was in the golden age of Spanish-language rock in the nineties.
It was their second album: the first had come out two years earlier.
It was right in the middle of the decade.
questions.description: A bolero called “deceitful” that turned out to be faithful to Bogotá forever.
questions.fun_fact: Besides being a singer, Andrea Echeverri is a ceramic artist: she studied art and makes clay pieces.

questions.question: Jorge Villamil, the doctor from Huila who wrote “Los guaduales” and “Espumas”, died in 2010. In which decade was he born?
hints: He was from Neiva, on the banks of the Magdalena River.
His most famous songs were on the radio in the 1960s and 1970s.
He was born the same year as the great New York stock market crash.
questions.description: A doctor who prescribed bambucos and pasillos for a broken heart.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Villamil was an orthopedic surgeon who wrote songs in his spare time; many of them sing about the landscapes of Huila.

questions.question: I'm the paisa word for when you feel so at home in a new place that you don't want to leave. What word am I?
hints: It's a good thing: it describes someone happy where they are.
It's often used when someone moves to a new city and things go well.
It comes from “maña”, as when you get used to something.
questions.description: You came for a weekend and you're already asking how much the rent is.
questions.fun_fact: When a paisa says someone “se amañó” in another city, it almost always means they don't plan to come back.

questions.question: On the Pacific coast of Chocó, a “potrillo” is carved from a single tree trunk, carries plantains and children steer it from a young age. What is it?
hints: It's not an animal, even if the name sounds like one.
It's made of wood and used for carrying things.

questions.description: In Chocó it rains so much that even the bunches of plantains ask for an umbrella.
questions.fun_fact: Many towns in Chocó have no roads: the rivers are the highways, and almost everything travels by canoe.

questions.question: It comes from Quechua, you hear it in Pasto and in Ecuador, and it means a baby still carried in arms. What's the word?
hints: Grandmothers in southern Colombia use this word all the time.
In Cuba, this same word means a bus.
It sounds almost like a baby crying.
questions.description: Sleeps all day, eats every three hours and runs the whole house.
questions.fun_fact: In Cuba and the Canary Islands a “guagua” is a bus, so if you ask for one in Havana, nobody will hand you a baby.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what is this traditional Colombian dish called?
hints: It's cooked in a really big pot, sometimes over a wood fire.
It's a thick soup with yuca, plantain and corn on the cob.
There's a chicken one, a fish one and even a “trifásico” one.
questions.description: Sunday at Grandma's: the whole family shows up hungry, and nobody wants to leave.

questions.question: It's part of the Eje Cafetero, its capital is Pereira, and it's named after a river. Which department is it?
hints: It's in the Andean region, between Caldas and Valle del Cauca.
Its capital has a soccer team nicknamed “Matecaña”.
Its name starts with “Risa”.
questions.description: A department so into coffee that its mountains wake up already wide awake.
questions.fun_fact: The Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, which includes part of Risaralda, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.

questions.question: You're touring the capitals of the Caribbean departments. Which of these cities is NOT on your route?
hints: Three of them have coastal heat; the other has jungle heat.
The odd one out sits at the gateway to the Amazon.
It's the capital of Caquetá, and its name is Spanish for a famous Italian city.
questions.description: A road trip with a sea breeze that someone crashed wearing rubber boots.
questions.fun_fact: Florencia, the capital of Caquetá, is known as “the golden gateway to the Colombian Amazon.”

questions.question: It lies south of Cartagena, it has the famous Playa Blanca, and the Canal del Dique separates it from the mainland. Which island is it?
hints: It belongs to the department of Bolívar.
The Islas del Rosario lie just off its coast.
Its name has only two syllables and ends in “ú.”
questions.description: An island that cheated: it didn't used to be one.

questions.question: Which of these natural wonders is NOT in the department of Guainía?
hints: Three of them are near Puerto Inírida.
The odd one out lies between Caquetá and Guaviare.
Its tepuis hide thousands of very old rock paintings.

questions.fun_fact: The Cerros de Mavecure are rocks more than a billion years old that rise like towers out of the jungle.

questions.question: It is the widest of Colombia's three mountain ranges, and both Bogotá and the Sierra Nevada del Cocuy are in it. Which is it?
hints: It is the one closest to the Llanos.
It splits in two, and one branch runs into Venezuela.
It's on the side where the sun rises over Colombia.

questions.question: Bolívar won the Battle of Carabobo on June 24, 1821. In which present-day country was it fought?

questions.question: Long before the peso, the Muisca traded salt for cotton blankets without using coins. What is this kind of exchange called?
hints: It's one of the oldest ways of trading in the world.
Some fairs in Colombia still do it today.
It's like swapping album stickers with a classmate.
questions.description: The oldest business deal in the world: no card reader, no cash, no Nequi.
questions.fun_fact: Salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón was one of the most valuable goods the Muisca traded with other peoples.

questions.question: You're watching the Baloto draw on TV. Where do the winning numbers come from?
hints: They get mixed well before every draw.
They roll around inside a see-through machine.
The game's name comes from the Spanish word «balota».
questions.description: Dreaming is free; the ticket, not so much.
questions.fun_fact: In many lotteries around the world, the balls are weighed and checked before use so that none has an advantage.

questions.question: In which decade did Colombia's two-color 500-peso coin with the Samán de Guacarí start circulating?
hints: It was before the year 2000.
Your parents probably used it when they were young.
It came out shortly after the 1991 Constitution.

questions.question: Fruko y sus Tesos plays the salsa you dance to. Fruco makes a sauce, or “salsa” in Spanish. What kind?
hints: Fruco is a brand you find in the kitchen, not at the dance club.
It goes great with French fries and hot dogs.
It's red and comes from a fruit many people think is a vegetable.
questions.description: One with a “K” plays at the party, the other with a “C” waits in the fridge: don't mix them up.
questions.fun_fact: Today Fruco belongs to Unilever, the same multinational that sells soap and ice cream in many countries.

questions.question: Deportivo Pasto's nickname comes from the landscape around the city. Complete it: “los…”
hints: Pasto sits at the foot of a very special mountain.
It's the most famous mountain in Nariño, and it sometimes makes the news.
It's called Galeras, and now and then it puffs out smoke and ash.

questions.question: Deportivo Pereira, in yellow and red, won the Colombian league for the first time in 2022. Roughly how many years had it waited since its founding?

It was founded in the 1940s.

questions.question: Coach Santiago “Sachi”, who managed Atlético Nacional, is the brother of a famous Colombia defender from the 1990s. Who?
hints: That defender spent almost his whole career at Atlético Nacional.
He was nicknamed “el Caballero del fútbol” (the Gentleman of Soccer).
He won the 1989 Copa Libertadores with Nacional.
questions.description: Two brothers, one shade of green, and a jersey worn close to the heart.
questions.fun_fact: Atlético Nacional won the Copa Libertadores in 1989, the first ever for a Colombian club.

questions.question: Wool comes from sheep the way fique comes from…
hints: It comes from a plant, not an animal.
That plant has long, thick, pointed leaves.
That plant looks a lot like the agave used to make tequila.
questions.description: The toughest “wool” in Colombia, and not a single sheep got sheared.
questions.fun_fact: Cauca, Nariño and Santander are among Colombia's biggest fique producers.

questions.question: It's part of the paisa arriero's outfit and its name comes from “escápula.” What is the escapulario?
questions.answer: A religious cloth worn around the neck
wrong_answers: A leather strap for carrying the machete
A rosary of beads used for praying

questions.question: The loom is to the ruana as what is to the Wayuu mochila?
hints: It's a small tool that fits in your hand.
You use just one, not two as in knitting.
Its curved tip catches the yarn.

questions.question: Look at the photo: what covers the skin of this fruit?
hints: Touch it with your fingertips.

questions.question: You're in the kitchen and take a bag of frozen maracuyá pulp out of the freezer. What are you going to make with it?

questions.fun_fact: In Colombia you can buy frozen pulp of loads of fruits, from mora and lulo to guanábana and corozo.

questions.question: Many Colombians carry the prayer of the Justo Juez (Just Judge) in their wallet to protect them from enemies and spirits. Who is the Justo Juez?
hints: He is the central figure of the prayer.
In Christian tradition, he is the one who will judge everyone at the end of time.
He was born in Bethlehem.
questions.description: A pocket lawyer who never charges a fee.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombian drivers hang holy cards or rosaries from the rearview mirror to protect them on the road.

questions.question: I was Señorita Colombia in 1991 and Miss Universe runner-up the next year. Later I hosted TV shows and acted in US series. Who am I?
hints: My family has Lebanese roots.
I went back to the national beauty pageant in Cartagena, but as a host of several editions.
I share my last name with a 20th-century Colombian president.

questions.fun_fact: The 1992 Miss Universe pageant, where Paola Turbay came second, was held in Bangkok, Thailand.

questions.question: I came to Bogotá as a singer with an opera company and set to music the verses that begin “¡Cesó la horrible noche!”. Who am I?
hints: I didn’t write the anthem’s words: a president took care of that.
I stayed in Bogotá and taught music for many years.
My name sounds very Italian and starts with O.
questions.description: Some verses were wandering around without a tune until someone with an ear for opera showed up.
questions.fun_fact: Síndici stayed in Colombia for the rest of his life and died in Bogotá in 1904.

questions.question: What does the gallinazo have on its head?
hints: In this way, it looks like its big cousin, the condor.
It helps the bird stay clean when it eats dead animals.
If you look closely, it seems to be bald.
questions.description: A bird that's always dressed for a funeral, yet goes through life completely relaxed.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, the gallinazo is also called “chulo” or “golero,” depending on the region.

questions.question: According to the best-known explanation, what does the name “Cundinamarca” mean?
hints: The name is said to come from Quechua, the language of the Incas.
It has to do with an animal of the Andes.

questions.question: They are private protected areas: a landowner chooses to conserve the land, registers it with Parques Nacionales, and Law 99 of 1993 recognizes it. What are they called?
questions.answer: Reserva Natural de la Sociedad Civil

hints: It is not created by the government, but by private individuals.
Its name refers to ordinary people, not the government.
Its name contains the word “civil”.
questions.description: Owning a farm and planting nothing can also be very serious work.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia has hundreds of these private reserves, and some are farms of only a few hectares.

questions.question: Bogotá wetlands like La Conejera and Juan Amarillo are rest stops on long journeys. For which animals?
hints: They come from very far away, sometimes from North America.
They travel through the air.
They have feathers and move to a different place depending on the time of year.
questions.description: Right in the middle of the city, there are free hotels for travelers who never book ahead.
questions.fun_fact: The tingua bogotana (Bogotá rail) is a bird that lives only in the wetlands of the Bogotá high plateau and the area around it.

questions.question: How many gold medals did Colombia win at the Rio 2016 Olympics?
hints: It was Colombia's best gold haul in its whole Olympic history.
One of those gold medals came in weightlifting.
They were won by a weightlifter, a female BMX rider and a female triple jumper.
questions.description: A trip to Brazil with samba, beaches and plenty to celebrate.
questions.fun_fact: In total, Colombia brought home 8 medals from Rio: 3 gold, 2 silver and 3 bronze.

questions.question: In 2013, Cali hosted a big event with roller skating, lifesaving and tug of war. What was it called?
hints: They are held every four years by an association backed by the International Olympic Committee.
Some sports that went through them, like karate, later made it to the Olympics.
The name sounds like the whole planet is playing, not just one continent.
questions.description: A sports party in the Sucursal del Cielo, with sports you don't see every day.
questions.fun_fact: Cali was the first city in Latin America to host the World Games.

questions.question: For years, Catalina Peláez has been one of Colombia's top athletes in a racket sport. Which one?
hints: It is played indoors.
Catalina Peláez has represented Colombia at the Pan American and Bolivarian Games.
The ball is hit against the front wall of an enclosed court.
questions.description: A racket sport where you're guaranteed to sweat from the very first point.
questions.fun_fact: Squash was born in England, at Harrow School, around 1830.

questions.question: You shake me before using me, I let out colored paint, and graffiti artists use me on the walls of Bogotá. What am I?
hints: I'm made of metal.

Press the little button on top and the paint comes out as a fine mist.

questions.fun_fact: Spray paint cans have a little ball inside that mixes the paint when you shake them: that's why they go “clack, clack”.

questions.question: The yipao is a Willys jeep loaded to the roof with coffee, plantains or a family’s furniture, and it has its own parade. In which department did that parade begin?
hints: It’s one of Colombia’s smallest departments.
The Cocora Valley, with its wax palms, is there.
Its capital is Armenia.
questions.description: A car that carries more than a mule and never asks for a break.
questions.fun_fact: In the Coffee Axis, “un yipao” is also a unit of measure: whatever fits in a fully loaded Willys.

questions.question: In many versions of the tale, a doll is placed on Tío Conejo’s path to catch him. What is it made of?
hints: The rabbit hits the doll because it doesn’t answer his greeting.
With every blow he gets more stuck: his paws won’t come loose.
It’s the sticky black stuff once used to seal wooden ships.
questions.description: Tío Conejo learned the hard way that not everyone who stays quiet is a friend.
questions.fun_fact: The same tale exists in the southern United States, where the doll is called the “Tar-Baby” and the one who falls for the trap is Br’er Rabbit.

questions.question: Paisa trovadores got their name from Europe’s singing poets, the troubadours. When did those first troubadours appear?
hints: It was long before Columbus reached the Americas.
Around the same time, the first Gothic cathedrals were going up.
We’re talking about the 11th to 13th centuries, in southern France.
questions.description: Long before rap battles there were rhyme duels, only with a ruana and a carriel.
questions.fun_fact: The first troubadours didn’t sing in French but in Occitan, a language of southern France.

questions.question: It’s said softly and repeated again and again in a well-known Colombian song. What is “arrurrú” used for?
questions.answer: To put a baby to sleep
hints: It’s sung at night.
It goes with gentle rocking in someone’s arms.
It’s the word that fills lullabies.
questions.description: A word so soft it sounds like a cat purring.
questions.fun_fact: In other countries the same lullaby is sung with “arrorró” instead of “arrurrú”.

questions.question: I'm a paisa, and in 2022 I released a song named after a famous nightlife area of El Poblado, in Medellín. Who am I?
hints: As a teenager, I took part in a talent show on Colombian TV.
In 2023 I released a worldwide hit with Shakira.

questions.description: A song named after a neighborhood, so that half of Colombia would learn the address.
questions.fun_fact: Provenza is an area of bars and restaurants in the El Poblado neighborhood of Medellín, and it became even more famous after the song.

questions.question: It's the name of Carlos Vives's band, it's in the title of his 1993 album “Clásicos de la…” and it names vallenato country. What word is it?
hints: It's a single word that refers to a place, not a rhythm.
On the Caribbean coast, people use it to talk about Valledupar and the area around it.
In Spanish, it's what Argentina and Ecuador call their main divisions.
questions.description: A word that came by donkey from Valledupar and ended up being heard all over the world.
questions.fun_fact: With “Clásicos de la Provincia,” Carlos Vives recorded old vallenatos with a rock and pop sound and took them around the world.

questions.question: Camilo released “Vida de rico” (“A Rich Man's Life”) in 2020. What does the song's title mean?
questions.answer: That love makes him feel rich

hints: Camilo is known for his cheerful, simple style.

What makes him rich is being with the person he loves.

questions.fun_fact: Camilo sings many of his love songs with Evaluna, his wife, in mind, and she also appears in his videos.

questions.question: In Jorge Velosa's carranga, “merengue” isn't the egg-white dessert. What is it?
hints: Velosa's music grew out of the rural traditions of Boyacá.
On carranga records, this word appears next to the titles of many songs.

questions.description: In Boyacá, even something that sounds like dessert gets played with a ruana on.
questions.fun_fact: Although it shares its name with the famous Dominican merengue, carranga merengue sounds like the Boyacá countryside, not the Caribbean.

questions.question: This charro in the photo is a must at every Colombian party. Who is he?
hints: He was born in Jalisco and sang for more than 50 years.
He is known as “the King of ranchera music.”
His version of “El rey” by José Alfredo Jiménez is the most famous one.
questions.description: At Colombian parties, around midnight, this Mexican guest always shows up.
questions.fun_fact: His most famous line was that as long as the audience kept clapping, he would keep singing.

questions.question: I’m a pasillo paisa heard at every wedding, graduation and birthday, and I make parents cry. What song am I?
hints: I’m sung above all as a tribute to parents.

My lyrics travel through childhood, youth, love, children and old age.

review.feedback: source: the error is in the Spanish source and the translation copies it faithfully. It calls “El camino de la vida” a pasillo, but the fact check found sources calling it a bambuco (El Comercio) or a vals (Portafolio). The source should drop the genre (“a paisa song”), then the translation can follow. Fact check: wrong. The song is not a pasillo. Sources call "El camino de la vida" a bambuco (El Comercio); Portafolio calls it a vals. The composer (Héctor Ochoa), the theme and the "Colombian Song of the 20th century" title (1999 poll) check out. The wrong answers are fine: Pueblito viejo, Los guaduales and Espumas are different songs.

questions.question: In Spain, people address a group of friends as “vosotros”. What word is used in Colombia instead?
hints: It's for speaking to several people at once.
In Colombia it works the same with friends and with strangers.
It's the plural of the word you use to address a teacher.
questions.description: Cross the Atlantic and even the way you address your friends gets a new passport.
questions.fun_fact: In Latin America almost nobody says “vosotros”: you mostly hear it in the Bible, in prayers and in some old dubbed films.

questions.question: Colombian law protects a language spoken in Bogotá and Girón as a native language, even though it came from Europe. Which one?
questions.answer: The language of the Roma people
hints: Its roots go back much farther than Europe.
Its speakers are a people famous for centuries for moving from place to place.
Their communities are organized in kumpañy.
questions.description: A language that reached Colombia with more miles on it than a long-haul truck driver.
questions.fun_fact: Romani was born in India more than a thousand years ago and traveled across Asia and Europe before reaching the Americas.

questions.question: In Cali, wandering around with no plan, on foot or by car, and ending up with a champús (a cold corn drink) is called “dar un…” what?
hints: It's a plan for relaxing, not for working.
You also hear it in the Coffee Region (Eje Cafetero).
It rhymes with the Spanish word for “round”: “redondo.”
questions.description: The favorite plan of anyone who leaves home saying “be right back” and returns three hours later.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali, a good afternoon borondo often ends with a champús or a lulada, a drink made from the lulo fruit.

questions.question: You hear it a lot in Boyacá, usually with a “sumercé” attached. What does “mi Dios le pague” mean?
hints: You say it after you receive something, not before.
Whoever says it feels they owe a favor they can't repay on their own.
It's what you're taught to say when someone gives you a present.
questions.description: A phrase so polite it even brings heaven into the conversation.
questions.fun_fact: The idea behind the phrase is that since you can't repay the favor yourself, you ask God to repay it for you.

questions.question: A sock without its partner is called a “media chulla,” from a Quechua word. In which Colombian department do people say it?
hints: It's in the south of the country.
It borders Ecuador.
It's home to the Carnival of Blacks and Whites (Carnaval de Negros y Blancos).
questions.description: The washing machine ate a sock, and one part of Colombia even has a word for the survivor.
questions.fun_fact: In Ecuador, people say “chulla vida” to remind you that you only live once.

questions.question: Look at the map: which department of Colombia is highlighted?
hints: It's in the north of the country.
Its capital is Montería, on the banks of the Sinú River.
It shares its name with a city in Spain and another in Argentina.
questions.description: A department that, seen from above, thinks it's one of a kind… just like all its neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The sombrero vueltiao, a cultural symbol of Colombia, is woven mainly in Tuchín, Córdoba.

questions.question: Juanchito, in Candelaria, lies just across the bridge over the Cauca River, and caleños have gone there on weekends for decades. What is it famous for?
hints: What people do there has a lot to do with Cali's fame.
People who go there usually come back at dawn with tired feet.
You go there to dance to timbales, trumpets and congas.
questions.description: A place where caleños lose all track of time every weekend.
questions.fun_fact: Juanchito is sometimes called “the cradle of Cali's rumba”, and although it belongs to another municipality, it's only minutes from downtown Cali.

questions.question: In the brass bands of the Córdoba savannas, one rhythm has the bombero (bass drummer) hit the drum's wooden rim, not the skin. Which one?
hints: It's played by brass bands with clarinets, trumpets and euphoniums.
You hear it at town festivals in the Sinú River valley.
Its name comes from «palito» (little stick), said the coastal way.
questions.description: A rhythm that makes the town band pull even the tuba out of the closet.
questions.fun_fact: Porro has two main styles: palitiao and tapao, where the bombero mutes the drum skin with his hand.

questions.question: In the Caribbean I mean “ruckus” or “a huge mess,” and in northern Cali I'm a famous salsoteca (salsa bar). What word am I?
hints: It's a word you hear in salsa songs from Cuba and Puerto Rico.
It's a cousin of “bochinche” and “zafarrancho.”
It rhymes with “loco.”
questions.description: A word with so much flavor it should be served with ice and lime.
questions.fun_fact: Cali's salsotecas have no live band: the star is the DJ with his old salsa records.

questions.question: My son Viviano Torres founded Anne Swing and sang champeta in my own Creole language, mixed with Spanish. What town am I?
hints: I'm in Bolívar, near Cartagena.
I was founded by enslaved people who escaped and made themselves free.
UNESCO declared me a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
questions.description: A town where the music pours out of the picó and the pride is heard at full volume.
questions.fun_fact: Champeta mixes rhythms of the Colombian Caribbean with African music, such as soukous from the Congo.

questions.question: Gustavo Quintero, nicknamed “el Loco” for his moves and shouts on stage, sang chucu-chucu in Medellín. With which band?
hints: Its records play every December at paisa parties.
Its name is a single plural word after “Los.”
Its name sounds like finishing high school or college.
questions.description: A singer who moved so much on stage that the microphone asked for a vacation.
questions.fun_fact: Around the same time, Rodolfo Aicardi was a hit in Medellín with Los Hispanos, another chucu-chucu star.

questions.question: It's held in Cali, salsa schools from around the world compete, and one of its categories is called “cabaret.” What does that category feature?
questions.answer: Lifts and acrobatics in the air
wrong_answers: A single dancer with no partner
hints: It's the most spectacular category of the Festival Mundial de Salsa.
This category takes a lot of strength and a lot of trust between the two dancers.
The couples do circus-like stunts.
questions.description: In Cali, salsa is taken so seriously that it even has its own world championship.
questions.fun_fact: Cali's salsa schools have won many world championships thanks to their lightning-fast footwork and their acrobatics.

questions.question: In 1804 a Spanish expedition reached Cartagena with a vaccine passed from arm to arm among children. Which disease was it against?
hints: It left marks on the skin of those who survived.
No mosquito spreads it.
It was the first human disease wiped off the planet, in 1980.
questions.description: A trip across the Atlantic where the smallest passengers were the most important ones.
questions.fun_fact: The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow, because the first one was made from cowpox.

questions.question: “Tarde lo conocí” told the life of Patricia Teherán. After singing with Las Musas del Vallenato, which group did she found?
hints: It was an all-female group, like the one before.
The new name also came from Greek mythology.
Like Athena or Aphrodite, who lived on Mount Olympus.
questions.description: An accordion, a caja and a guacharaca walk into a telenovela… and come out crying.
questions.fun_fact: Patricia Teherán was one of the first women to succeed in vallenato, a genre sung almost only by men for decades.

questions.question: In Bogotá, the word “ñero” came from clipping “compañero.” What does it mean today?
questions.answer: A rough, street-smart person with crude manners
wrong_answers: An elegant person from a good family
A person who is stingy with money
hints: It's not exactly a compliment.
You hear it in everyday Bogotá slang, never in a formal speech.
It's pretty close to what a gamín is.
questions.description: A word that went on a diet and lost two syllables along the way.
questions.fun_fact: “Ñero” started as a friendly short form of “compañero” and over the years came to mean someone rough and street-wise with bad manners.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Betty, la fea”, what is the name of Beatriz Pinzón Solano's strict, very protective father?
hints: He's an old-fashioned man who lives with his family in a Bogotá neighborhood.
He was played by actor Jorge Herrera.
He shares his name with the messenger of the Greek gods, the one with winged sandals.
questions.description: The most protective dad on Colombian TV: not even the clock in his house dared to go past ten.
questions.fun_fact: His role as the grumpy dad, always watching what time Betty got home, became one of the show's best-loved memories.

questions.question: I'm made of wood and shaped like a pear, my four strings are played with a pick, and in joropo I carry the melody next to the harp. What am I?
hints: I come from the plains that Colombia shares with Venezuela.
They don't strum me like the cuatro: they pluck me note by note.
In Colombia's Andean region there's an instrument with the same name as me, but with many more strings.
questions.description: The lead singer of the group, even though it never opens its mouth.
questions.fun_fact: The bandola llanera sometimes replaces the harp in a llanero group and carries the whole joropo melody on its own.

questions.question: What sets apart paso caleño, Cali's style of dancing salsa?
wrong_answers: Slow turns in a close hold
hints: Watch the dancers' legs in Cali's salsa shows.
It's said to have been born when people in Cali played records faster than normal.
The feet move so fast you can barely see them.
questions.description: A dance you have to warm up for, just like a soccer game.
questions.fun_fact: As the story goes, people in Cali played 33 rpm records at 45, and dancing to that sped-up music gave birth to paso caleño.

questions.question: Marimba is to the currulao of the Pacific as which instrument is to the cumbia of the Montes de María?
hints: It's a wind instrument.
There is a “female” one and a “male” one, and they are played as a pair.
It's made from cactus, with a beeswax head and a duck feather mouthpiece.
questions.description: A love match between an instrument and a rhythm.
questions.fun_fact: The female gaita carries the melody, while the player of the male gaita often shakes a maraca with his other hand.

questions.question: You arrive at a fandango in the savannas of Córdoba or Sucre. What will you NOT find there?
hints: The fandango is a party of the Caribbean coast.
There you hear porros played on trumpets, euphoniums and snare drum.
One of these belongs to another region: the land of joropo.
questions.description: A party where the musicians sweat more than the dancers.
questions.fun_fact: Every year San Pelayo, Córdoba, holds the Festival Nacional del Porro, where wind bands get the whole town dancing.

questions.question: At the Vallenato Festival, the accordion player announces an aire with the same name as the Dominican Republic's famous dance rhythm. Which one?
hints: It's one of the aires played in the competition in Valledupar.
It's cheerful and lively, but not the fastest of them all.
In the Dominican Republic it's played with güira and tambora.
questions.description: A rhythm with dual citizenship, or at least a double name.
questions.fun_fact: The Vallenato Legend Festival has been held in Valledupar since 1968, and the best accordion player is crowned the Vallenato King.

questions.question: I was born in Barranquilla, grew up in Argentina and worked at NASA. I helped find the ring of cenotes that reveals the Chicxulub crater in Mexico. Who am I?
hints: I'm a planetary geologist.
The crater I studied was left by the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.
My last name is very common in Antioquia and Valle, and it starts with O.
questions.description: A costeña who went looking for rocks… and ended up looking at other planets.
questions.fun_fact: As a girl, Adriana Ocampo turned her dolls into astronauts and pretended to build spaceships on her rooftop.

questions.question: Fernando Gómez Agudelo organized Colombia's first television broadcast. In what year was it?
hints: It was in the 1950s.
General Gustavo Rojas Pinilla was in power.
It was on June 13, exactly one year after Rojas Pinilla took power in 1953.
questions.description: Before this, Colombians could only hear their telenovelas, not watch them.
questions.fun_fact: Almost nobody in Colombia owned a TV for that first broadcast, so the government put sets in shop windows for people to watch from the street.

questions.question: I'm a Colombian actor. In the country's most famous telenovela I was the president of Ecomoda, Marcela Valencia's fiancé, and I fell in love with my assistant. Who am I?
hints: My character's first name was Armando.
I worked alongside Ana María Orozco.
My character's last name was Mendoza.
questions.description: A boss who spent the whole telenovela with his tie too tight and his heart in a knot.
questions.fun_fact: Jorge Enrique Abello played Armando Mendoza again in 2024, more than 20 years later, in the new season of Betty.

questions.question: It's the most typical shout of vallenato singers, heard right before a verse: “¡Ay, …!” What completes it?
hints: You hear it in almost every vallenato song, old or new.
On the coast people shorten their words, and this one lost a letter along the way.
It's “hombre,” said the coastal way, without the r.
questions.description: The official sigh of every heartbroken singer with an accordion by his side.
questions.fun_fact: “Hombe” is the coastal way of saying “hombre” (man), and in vallenato it can express joy, longing or heartbreak, depending on how it's sung.

questions.question: Which singer and actor played Diomedes Díaz in the 2015 TV series “Diomedes, el Cacique de La Junta”?
hints: The series aired on Canal RCN.
The lead actor is also a vallenato singer, born in the Caribbean region.
His last name starts with L.
questions.description: Stepping into the Cacique's shoes isn't easy: you have to sing, act and put up with the comparisons.
questions.fun_fact: The nickname “el Cacique de La Junta” comes from La Junta, the village in La Guajira where Diomedes Díaz was from.

questions.question: García Márquez called “One Hundred Years of Solitude” “a 350-page vallenato”. What did he mean?
questions.answer: That the novel tells stories the way vallenato songs do
wrong_answers: That he wrote it in Valledupar during a festival
That the novel should be read with music playing
That each chapter is named after a song
hints: Gabo grew up in Aracataca listening to minstrels who traveled from town to town.
Old vallenato songs were like sung newscasts.
Think of vallenato as a way of telling a story.
questions.description: A book so long the accordion would need a spare battery.
questions.fun_fact: Gabo admired Rafael Escalona so much that he put him in “One Hundred Years of Solitude” as a character.

questions.question: “Valledupar is to Cesar as Santa Marta is to…”. Which department completes the phrase?
hints: It's about capitals and their departments.
Santa Marta is the capital of this department.
It has the same name as Colombia's most important river.
questions.description: A logic puzzle with a taste of sea, mountains and green mango.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Marta, founded in 1525, is the oldest Colombian city still standing.

questions.question: Nobody has recorded me or played me on the radio; at the Vallenato Festival I compete to be the best new song. What am I?
hints: My songwriter performs me in public for the first time.
If I had already been recorded, I'd be disqualified.
My category's name in Spanish, «inédita», means “never published.”
questions.description: In Valledupar, even a songwriter's nerves sound like accordion and caja.
questions.fun_fact: Several vallenato hits were heard for the first time in the unreleased-song contest of the Festival de la Leyenda Vallenata.

questions.question: You open a classic Jet chocolate bar to fill your album. How many stickers come inside?
hints: That's why filling the album takes so long.
You have to buy lots of chocolate bars to complete it.
It's not a full pack: it's a single surprise.
questions.description: Got it, got it, got it… need it!
questions.fun_fact: Swapping duplicate Jet stickers at recess is a habit shared by several generations of Colombians.

questions.question: The Desfile Magno, with its giant floats, closes the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos on Día de Blancos. What day in January is it?
hints: First comes Día de Negros, then Día de Blancos.
It falls in the first week of January.
It’s the same day as Three Kings’ Day.
questions.description: The biggest floats in southern Colombia, and not one of them fits in the garage.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, UNESCO added the Carnaval de Negros y Blancos to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: I dress in white, with a sombrero vueltiao and a red scarf around my neck. At carnival I dance to drums and gaitas, and my partner wears a pollera and carries lit candles. Who am I?
hints: I'm from Colombia's Caribbean coast.
My dance was born on the banks of the Magdalena River.
My name comes from the rhythm I dance: cumbia.
questions.description: A character who doesn't need a gym: one night of carnival does the job.
questions.fun_fact: Cumbia mixes Indigenous, African and Spanish roots, and today people dance it from Mexico to Argentina.

questions.question: It studies the remains of ancient peoples, digs carefully into the ground, and has uncovered hundreds of stone statues in San Agustín, Huila. Which science is it?
hints: It doesn't study dinosaurs or raw rocks, but what people left behind.
Its scientists look for pots, tombs, tools and statues.
Its name comes from the Greek “archaios”, which means “ancient”.
questions.description: People who get more excited about an old stone than a new cell phone.
questions.fun_fact: San Agustín Archaeological Park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995.

questions.question: They're made from tree bark, worn at the Pelazón festival of Ticuna girls, and stand for forest spirits. Which department are they from?
hints: It's a region of jungle and huge rivers.
The Ticuna live where Colombia meets Peru and Brazil.
Its capital is Leticia.
questions.description: Faces that don't hide behind anyone, but behind a whole tree.
questions.fun_fact: The bark cloth the Ticuna use is called yanchama: the bark is beaten until it's as thin and soft as a canvas.

questions.question: It's a white powder that comes in a bottle and smells nice. On Día de Blancos at the Carnaval de Pasto, people throw it at each other. What is it?
hints: The day before, people paint themselves black; on this day, white.
It's soft and doesn't stick like wet flour does.
People also put it on their feet so they don't sweat.
questions.description: In Pasto on January 6, nobody leaves home with clean clothes… or a clean face.
questions.fun_fact: Pasto's Carnaval de Negros y Blancos has been on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since 2009.

questions.question: It goes on the living room floor or next to the bed, it's woven from wool or other fibers, and it's what Colombians call a small rug. What's the word?
hints: It keeps your feet off the cold floor when you get up.
People shake it outside to get the dust out.
It starts with “ta.”
questions.description: That thing in the house everyone swears they shook out last week.
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known knotted rug, the Pazyryk carpet, is about 2,400 years old and was found frozen in the Altai Mountains of Siberia.

questions.question: Commentators say Egan Bernal “won the general” at the 2019 Tour de France. What does that mean?
questions.answer: He had the lowest total time across all stages
wrong_answers: He won more stages than anyone else
He finished first on the final stage
He scored the most points at the sprints
hints: It looks at the time for the whole race, not just one day.
The hours, minutes and seconds of every stage are added up.
The winner is whoever took the least time overall.
questions.description: A sum so long that not even the corner store's calculator can handle it.
questions.fun_fact: Egan won that 2019 Tour without winning a single stage.

questions.question: In the Vuelta a Colombia, a car from each team follows the riders, with bikes on the roof and the director inside. What is it for?
questions.answer: To give spares, water and instructions
wrong_answers: To keep the official race time
To close the road to traffic
hints: It belongs to the team, not the organizers.
If a tire goes flat, this is where help comes from.
It carries extra wheels and drink bottles.
questions.description: A car with more bikes on its roof than seats inside.
questions.fun_fact: Sometimes a rider holds on to the car while taking a bottle: commentators call it a “sticky bottle.”

questions.question: John Leguizamo, born in Bogotá, is the original voice of Sid in “Ice Age.” In how many of the saga's theatrical movies did he play him between 2002 and 2016?
hints: The saga released a new movie roughly every three or four years.
After the first one came “The Meltdown,” “Dawn of the Dinosaurs” and more.
The last theatrical movie with Sid was “Collision Course,” in 2016.
questions.description: A guy from Bogotá who became the most famous sloth in prehistory, even though he never sits still.
questions.fun_fact: John Leguizamo was born in Bogotá and moved to New York with his family as a child; years later he also voiced Bruno in “Encanto.”

questions.question: It sailed from Cádiz in 1815, was led by Pablo Morillo and besieged Cartagena for over 100 days. What was this army called?
questions.answer: The Expeditionary Army of Costa Firme
wrong_answers: The Liberation Army of New Granada
The Army of the Southern Provinces
hints: It was a royalist army sent to win the land back.
It crossed the Atlantic Ocean to get there.
Its name says it came on an expedition to the coast.
questions.description: A Caribbean vacation that nobody in Cartagena asked for.
questions.fun_fact: It is considered the largest military expedition Spain ever sent to the Americas: over 10,000 soldiers on dozens of ships.

questions.question: Many European volunteers who fought alongside Bolívar came from a great war that had just ended in Europe. Which one?
hints: Bolívar's Liberation Campaign was in 1819.
That European war ended a few years earlier, in 1815.
Its great loser was a famous French emperor.
questions.description: Soldiers who crossed an ocean because back home they had run out of work.
questions.fun_fact: The Battle of Waterloo in 1815 left thousands of soldiers out of work, and many sailed to Venezuela to join Bolívar.

questions.question: I was born in Popayán, and in 1830 Congress chose me as president of Colombia after Bolívar, but Urdaneta overthrew me a few months later. Who am I?
hints: My family from Popayán produced several famous politicians.
My younger brother was also president, several times.
I share a last name with my brother Tomás Cipriano.
questions.description: A presidency that barely outlasted a school vacation.
questions.fun_fact: His brother Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera was president of Colombia four times.

questions.question: In December 1814, who led the Congress’s troops to take Santafé and forced Cundinamarca to join the United Provinces?
hints: He had recently arrived in New Granada after losing a war.
He came from fighting in Venezuela.
Since 1813 people had already been calling him the Liberator.
questions.description: When the neighbors couldn’t agree, someone showed up to knock on the door with an army.
questions.fun_fact: Cundinamarca was then governed by Manuel de Bernardo Álvarez, Antonio Nariño’s uncle.

questions.question: The word “jaibaná” names the wise person who heals with chants and talks with spirits. Which Indigenous people does it come from?
hints: They are a people of the rainforests of Colombia's Pacific coast.
Many of their communities live in Chocó, near the Atrato River.
Their women are famous for bead necklaces and body paint made from jagua fruit.
questions.description: A doctor who prescribes no pills, only chants and spirits.
questions.fun_fact: Emberá jaibanás use wooden staffs carved with figures to talk with the spirits.

questions.question: Finish the Colombian superstition: “If someone sweeps over your feet…”
hints: Colombian grandmothers repeat it while cleaning the house.
That's why, when someone sweeps, many people lift their feet fast.
It has to do with staying single.
questions.description: A broom has more power than you think, and not just against dust.
questions.fun_fact: The same superstition exists in Mexico, Puerto Rico and other Latin American countries.

questions.question: I'm a very beautiful woman with long blond hair. I live where rivers begin, and I enchant children who come near. Who am I?
hints: I'm not looking for my children, and I don't have just one leg.
Children who see me get sick from wanting so badly to go back and find me.
My name says what I watch over.
questions.description: A neighbor by the river who won't let anyone make a mess of her home.
questions.fun_fact: In some versions of the legend, the Madre de agua has backward feet, so nobody can follow her tracks.

questions.question: When a Colombian says «¿Quiubo, mano?», the word «mano» is short for…
hints: You say it to someone you're very close to.
It's part of the family.
It's the son of your mom and your dad.
questions.description: A word so friendly it lost half of itself along the way.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, «mano» and «manito» are used even when the other person isn't family at all, just out of affection.

questions.question: We're two short words of respect that go before a name: you greet the shopkeeper or the older lady next door with us. What are we?
hints: They're used with older people, even if they aren't family.
You use them with a first name, like “___ Ramón”.
One has three letters and the other has four.
questions.description: Two little words that make anyone instantly older and more respectable.
questions.fun_fact: “Don” comes from the Latin “dominus”, which means “lord” or “master”.

questions.question: Look at the map: the department marked is home to the Cueva de los Guácharos, Colombia’s first national park. Which one is it?
hints: It is in the south of the Andean region.
The Magdalena River is born here and runs through it for its first stretch.
Its capital is Neiva.
questions.description: A park that has been turning off the lights for over 60 years so its neighbors can sleep in peace.
questions.fun_fact: Cueva de los Guácharos National Natural Park was declared in 1960 and is the oldest in the country.

questions.question: Which of these animals does NOT live in the Alta Guajira?
hints: The Alta Guajira is dry, hot and right by the sea.
The odd one out lives in the cold, damp mountains of the Andes.
It's the only bear in South America.
questions.description: Here the wind blows so hard and the sun beats down so strongly that even the clouds just keep moving.
questions.fun_fact: The Alta Guajira is home to Punta Gallinas, the northernmost point of all of South America.

questions.question: It's a large, cold plain at about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft) in the Cordillera Oriental, where the Muisca lived and many flowers are grown today. What is it called?
hints: It's flat, but it's not in the hot lowlands.
Towns like Chía, Cota and Mosquera are there.
It's named after the country's biggest city.
questions.description: A plain so classy that it moved up to live in the mountains.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of years ago the Sabana de Bogotá was a big lake, which is why its ground is so flat.

previous.feedback: Source: the fact check is uncertain, and I can't confirm two claims from my own knowledge. One is the fun fact that Ariza was "one of the first Latin American artists to study in Japan" and that it "shaped all his work". The other is the question's "in the style of Japanese prints"; sources describe a looser Japanese influence. The source should soften both, for example "with a Japanese-influenced eye" and "Ariza was the first Colombian to exhibit in Japan". The translation follows the source faithfully and reads naturally. Fact check: uncertain. Ariza (Bogotá, 1912–1995) did live in Japan and was the first Colombian to exhibit there. Sources disagree on the dates: one says he returned in 1938, another says he stayed until 1958. A Banco de la República article says Japanese influence on his work is faint and more philosophical than stylistic, so "in the style of Japanese prints" is doubtful. I found no source for the fun fact that he was one of the first Latin American artists to study in Japan, or that the experience "shaped all his work".

hints: It had to do with the port and the ships.
Goods arriving by sea passed through it.
Taxes were charged there on everything coming into the city.
questions.description: A building with more history than Grandma, and that's saying a lot.
questions.fun_fact: The museum holds works by great artists from Colombia's Caribbean coast, such as Alejandro Obregón and Enrique Grau.

questions.question: Bogotá-born artist María Fernanda Cardoso, who lives in Australia, ran a real circus with tiny performers she trained herself. What animals were they?
hints: They were insects.
They have no wings, but they jump a huge distance.
They often live in the fur of dogs and cats.
questions.description: A show where the performers are so tiny it's hard to know where to clap.
questions.fun_fact: The fleas in Cardoso's circus pulled little carts and walked the tightrope, and the show was seen in museums in several countries.

questions.question: I'm an artist from Bogotá: I made sculptures in the style of pre-Columbian figures, but with the faces of cartoon characters like Mickey Mouse and Bart Simpson. Who am I?
hints: My work mixes Indigenous art with US pop culture.
My pieces look straight out of the Museo del Oro, but they date from the 1990s.
I share my last name with a former president and a famous goalkeeper of Colombia's national team.
questions.description: Archaeology of the future: what archaeologists will dig up a thousand years from now.
questions.fun_fact: Some of these sculptures were made by craftsmen who produce replicas of pre-Columbian pieces, which makes them even harder to tell from the originals.

questions.question: I was born in Barranquilla, I was one of Junior's first idols and captain of the national team. Today the Metropolitano bears my name. Who am I?
hints: I played long before Colombia had television.
The stadium that honors me opened in 1986.
My first name is Roberto.
questions.description: Some people carve their name on a tree; this man left his on an entire stadium.
questions.fun_fact: The Metropolitano was built with the 1986 World Cup in mind, which Colombia was supposed to host but in the end did not.

questions.question: Roughly how long, in total, are the walls around the historic center of Cartagena?
hints: It's not even enough for a half marathon.
It's about what a good amateur runner covers in an hour.
It's more than 10 km (6 miles) but less than 15 km (9 miles).
questions.description: A stroll with a sea view, past walls that have watched pirates go by.
questions.fun_fact: The walls of Cartagena took about two centuries to finish.

questions.question: At the Medellín Botanical Garden, giant wooden “trees” shaped like flowers shelter a collection of plants. Which plants?
hints: They're sold in pots and make a very elegant gift.
In Medellín, they're shown off in a big exhibition during the Feria de las Flores.
One of their genera is called Dracula, and another has flowers shaped like little slippers.
questions.description: Wooden trees that never need watering and still give shade to a whole collection.
questions.fun_fact: The wooden “flower-trees” of the Orquideorama collect rainwater.

questions.question: Complete the title of Juanes's famous 2002 song: “A Dios le…”
hints: It's a single word: a verb in the first person.
It's what you do when you want someone to give you something.
It's the same word you'd use ordering at a Colombian restaurant: “Yo … una bandeja paisa.”
questions.description: Juanes in 2002: guitar in hand, heart wide open and a title that sounds like a prayer.
questions.fun_fact: “A Dios le pido” was one of the biggest Latin rock hits of the early 2000s and was played all over the world.

questions.question: In Nariño, when something is lovely or delicious, people exclaim “¡ananay!”. That word comes from the language of which people?
hints: You can hear similar words across the border in Ecuador.
Their rule reached what is now southern Colombia shortly before the Spanish arrived.
They spoke Quechua, the language that gave us “guagua” and “chulla”.
questions.description: A southern exclamation with a family tree older than colonial times.
questions.fun_fact: In Quechua, “añañay” says that something is beautiful or tasty, and from it comes Nariño's “¡ananay!”.

questions.question: What is the area at the far southern tip of Colombia's map called, where the city of Leticia is?
hints: There, Colombia borders two countries at once: Brazil and Peru.
The river that carries more water than any other in the world flows through it.
On the map it has a four-sided shape with two parallel sides.
questions.description: The corner of the map where Colombia stretches out to dip its toes in the water.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia won this access to the Amazon River through a treaty signed with Peru in 1922.

questions.question: Mangroves cover much of Colombia's Pacific coast. What is a mangrove?
questions.answer: A forest that grows in salt water
wrong_answers: A beach of black volcanic sand
A freshwater lagoon in the jungle
hints: It's where a river meets the sea.
Crabs, pianguas and lots of little fish live there.
Its roots stick out of the water as if the trees were walking on stilts.
questions.description: It rains so much on this coast that even the crabs are asking for umbrellas.
questions.fun_fact: Mangroves protect the coast from strong waves and serve as a nursery for many fish.

questions.question: The Cordillera Central, home of the Nevado del Tolima and the Nevado del Huila, lies between two great Colombian rivers. Which two?
wrong_answers: The Atrato and the San Juan
hints: Both rise in the south of the country, in the mountains of the Macizo Colombiano.
Both head for the Caribbean Sea, and one ends up flowing into the other.
One shares its name with the department whose capital is Popayán.
questions.description: A mountain range squeezed like the cheese in a sandwich, only with water on each side.
questions.fun_fact: The Cauca flows into the Magdalena, which then reaches the Caribbean Sea at Bocas de Ceniza, next to Barranquilla.

questions.question: The northernmost point of South America is in La Guajira. What kind of landform is La Guajira?
hints: It has sea on almost every side.
On one side it is still joined to the mainland, so it isn't an island.
Its name comes from Latin and means “almost an island”.
questions.description: A desert so windy that even the hammocks rock themselves.
questions.fun_fact: La Guajira has the Taroa dunes, where the desert sand runs straight down into the sea.

questions.question: Lake Calima, in Valle del Cauca, is famous for its windsurfing winds. What kind of body of water is it?
hints: It didn't exist a hundred years ago.
People made it to store water and produce electricity.
It's the same word used for the one at Guatapé, in Antioquia.
questions.description: A lake so windy that the sails have more fun here than the fish.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to its strong, steady winds, Lake Calima welcomes kitesurfers and windsurfers from many countries.

questions.question: Swing Latino, from Cali, performed in the 2020 Super Bowl halftime show. What is it?
hints: It was founded by Luis Eduardo Hernández, whom everyone calls “el Mulato.”
Its members train for hours every day for their shows.
Its shows have lots of people on stage, but no instruments.
questions.description: In Cali, this is taken more seriously than the weather forecast.
questions.fun_fact: Swing Latino has won several world salsa championships.

questions.question: Which of these songs was NOT written by José Barros?
hints: Three of them are by a songwriter who grew up on the banks of the Magdalena River.
The odd one out is by a bandleader who brought coastal music to the grand ballrooms.
It was written by Lucho Bermúdez.
questions.description: A songwriter with so many songs that someone else's sometimes sneaks onto the list.
questions.fun_fact: José Barros was born in El Banco, Magdalena, where the Festival Nacional de la Cumbia that bears his name is held every year.

questions.question: Complete the title of this mapalé by Lucho Bermúdez: “Prende la…”.
hints: It's something you light.
It's usually lit with a match.
It's made of wax and slowly melts.
questions.description: A song that gets the shoulders moving on even the stiffest guest at the party.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Bermúdez was born in El Carmen de Bolívar and took porro and cumbia to the country's grand dance halls.

questions.question: Carmelo Fernández was born in Venezuela, was a nephew of José Antonio Páez, and joined the Chorographic Commission in 1850. What was his job there?
hints: In the mid-1800s, the Commission traveled through the provinces of New Granada to get to know the country.
It was led by the Italian Agustín Codazzi and set out to describe the regions and the people who lived there.
His main tool was the brush.
questions.description: A Venezuelan traveled all over New Granada and didn't come back empty-handed.
questions.fun_fact: The Chorographic Commission's plates are kept at the National Library of Colombia.

questions.question: Which anthem begins with “¡Oh libertad que perfumas las montañas de mi tierra!”?
wrong_answers: The anthem of Valle del Cauca
hints: It's the anthem of a department, not of the country.
Its lyrics come from a poem by Epifanio Mejía.
Paisas from the land of the carriel sing it with pride.
questions.description: A chorus so passionate that even the cows on the farm stop to listen.
questions.fun_fact: The lyrics come from Epifanio Mejía's poem “El canto del antioqueño,” and Gonzalo Vidal wrote the music.

questions.question: Its anthem says “blanca estrella que alumbra en los Andes” and was written by Pedro Medina Avendaño. Which city is it from?
hints: It's a very large city in the Andes.
It sits on a high plateau, about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft) up.
It's the capital of Colombia.
questions.description: A song so chilly it makes you want to sing it in a ruana with a tinto in your hand.
questions.fun_fact: The anthem's music is by the composer Roberto Pineda Duque.

questions.question: This typical dish from Tolima is a whole animal stuffed with peas and its own meat. Which animal is it?
hints: It's served at big parties, with arepa and insulso.
It's brought to the table whole, with golden, crispy skin on top.
Its young is called a lechón.
questions.description: The dish that turns any birthday into a party for the whole neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: Lechona is baked for many hours, sometimes all night, in a wood-fired oven.

questions.question: On which day of the week did “Especiales Pirry” air on Canal RCN?
hints: It aired at night, in prime time.
It wasn't a school day.
Many families watched it just before a new week began.
questions.description: A reporter who went where nobody else dared, with half the country following him, remote control in hand.
questions.fun_fact: “Pirry” is the nickname of Guillermo Prieto La Rotta, a journalist from Bogotá who traveled the world making adventure and investigative reports.

questions.question: Profesor Yarumo teaches about farm life on Colombian TV. What is the yarumo his name comes from?
hints: It is very common in the Colombian mountains.
Sloths love to eat it.
It has big leaves, like open hands, silvery underneath.
questions.description: A teacher who knows more about the countryside than a retired cow.
questions.fun_fact: The white yarumo has silvery leaves you can spot from far away on the mountainsides, and it is one of sloths' favorite foods.

questions.question: I was born in Cartagena, founded one of Colombia's most famous record labels in 1934, and later moved it to Medellín. Who am I?
hints: I didn't become famous for singing, but for recording other people.
Los Corraleros de Majagual, Fruko y sus Tesos and La Sonora Dinamita all recorded at my label.
My label is named after me: Discos ...
questions.description: Long before Spotify, this man already had the playlist for the whole Caribbean coast.
questions.fun_fact: Discos Fuentes started out recording in Cartagena and over the years became one of the biggest tropical music labels in all of Latin America.

questions.question: “A car is to gasoline as the old Magdalena River steamboat was to…” What completes the sentence?
hints: To make steam, you have to heat water with fire.
They got it on the riverbank, from the forests along the river.
They stopped at towns to load cut logs.
questions.description: Before highways, traffic jams on the Magdalena were all steam and whistles.
questions.fun_fact: The steamboats burned so many logs that whole forests along the Magdalena were cut down to feed them.

questions.question: “An umbrella is to rain as the Bocachica fort, on Tierra Bomba island, was to…” What completes the sentence?
hints: The fort guarded the entrance to the bay of Cartagena.
It had cannons pointing out to sea.
Pirates and the English tried to get in that way.
questions.description: An island with an explosive name and cannons that have long since retired.
questions.fun_fact: Bocachica was the only navigable entrance to the bay of Cartagena after the Spanish closed off Bocagrande with an underwater wall.

questions.question: The Chicamocha River carved a huge canyon in Santander, now crossed by the Panachi Park cable car. About how long is that ride?
hints: It goes down to the river and climbs back up the other side.
The full trip takes about 20 minutes.
It's longer than a 5K race, but not by much.
questions.description: A river so hardworking it dug a giant hole, and now people cross it through the air.
questions.fun_fact: The Chicamocha cable car links two mountains, passing hundreds of meters above the river.

questions.question: Around Malpelo Island, divers see schools of hammerhead sharks. How many come together in the biggest schools?
hints: It's one of the best places in the world to see them.
Divers say they block out the sunlight.
They number far more than a hundred.
questions.description: A fish that went to the hardware store and walked out wearing the tool.
questions.fun_fact: Malpelo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, partly because of its huge schools of sharks.

questions.question: Playa Blanca, on Barú near Cartagena, has almost white sand and clear water. What is that white sand made of?
hints: Many Caribbean beaches are this light for the same reason.
The waves grind it down over thousands of years.
Nearby there are reefs full of colorful fish.
questions.description: The perfect sand for building castles and burning your feet at noon.
questions.fun_fact: Parrotfish bite off coral and poop it out as sand: part of the Caribbean's white beaches came out of their bellies.

questions.question: You're at a marsh along the Magdalena River, watching a manatee eat water plants. How much can it eat in one day?
hints: It's a very heavy, slow animal.
It spends a large part of the day eating.
Roughly what a 12-year-old child weighs.
questions.description: If it had a wallet, it would spend it all at the vegetable market.
questions.fun_fact: The manatee is called a “sea cow” because it spends the day grazing on plants, like a cow in a pasture.

questions.question: In the 2000s, Fonseca, Fanny Lu and Mauricio & Palodeagua mixed radio-friendly ballads with gaitas and accordion. What was that style called?
hints: The name joins two words.
One of them is a genre played on radio stations all over the world.
The other part comes from “tropical.”
questions.description: The soundtrack of school field trips at the start of the century.
questions.fun_fact: Carlos Vives is seen as a forerunner: back in 1993 he was already mixing vallenato with rock and pop on “Clásicos de la provincia.”

questions.question: In the 1940s, Lucho Bermúdez's porros played on victrolas. What were they recorded on?
hints: They were made of shellac, a hard and brittle material.
They spun much faster than the LPs played at viejotecas.
Their name includes a number: how many turns they made per minute.
questions.description: Before Spotify, music was stored on things that needed a lot of care.
questions.fun_fact: Each side of a 78 rpm record held only about three minutes of music, which is why songs back then were short.

questions.question: I'm in Medellín, next to Parque Explora. I have a giant dome, and when the lights go out I show you the night sky in broad daylight. What am I?
hints: I'm named after a Jesuit priest who studied earthquakes.
My shows are projected on the ceiling and you watch them lying back.
Here you learn about planets, stars and constellations.
questions.description: The perfect paisa outing to keep even the most restless kids quiet and open-mouthed for a good while.
questions.fun_fact: Its official name is Planetario Jesús Emilio Ramírez, honoring a priest from Antioquia who was an expert on earthquakes.

questions.question: In 1907, yellow fever broke out in the jungle of Muzo, where the city mosquito didn't live. Which Colombian doctor first described this jungle yellow fever?
hints: He is seen as the pioneer of tropical medicine in Colombia.
He was the first professor of tropical medicine at the Faculty of Medicine in Bogotá.
His surname is the same as that of a famous 20th-century Spanish dictator.
questions.description: A disease detective who found the culprit where nobody was looking.
questions.fun_fact: Jungle yellow fever passes between forest monkeys and is spread by mosquitoes that live in the treetops.

questions.question: At the Astronomical Observatory of Bogotá, there's a tower designed by Friar Domingo de Petrés, one of the first in the Americas. What year was it finished?
hints: Petrés had come to Santafé as a Capuchin friar in 1792.
Francisco José de Caldas was its first director.
It was finished a few years before the Grito de Independencia.
questions.description: A friar who looked up at the sky, and not just to pray.
questions.fun_fact: Domingo de Petrés also designed the Catedral Primada on Bogotá's Plaza de Bolívar.

questions.question: In which year did the Colombian Air Force launch FACSAT-1, its first satellite, into space?
hints: It is more recent than Libertad 1, the satellite from Universidad Sergio Arboleda.
It went up on a rocket launched from India.
It was the year of the World Cup in Russia.
questions.description: A satellite so small it would fit in your carry-on, if the airline doesn't make a fuss.
questions.fun_fact: FACSAT-1 is a CubeSat-type nanosatellite that took photos of Colombian territory from orbit.

questions.question: In what year did the chikungunya epidemic reach Colombia?
hints: That year there were also huge numbers of cases on the Caribbean islands.
The virus had reached the Americas late the year before, on the island of Saint Martin.
That year James Rodríguez was the top scorer at the World Cup in Brazil.
questions.description: A disease with a tongue-twister name that left half the country walking like a grandpa.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Makonde language of Tanzania and means roughly “the one that bends up,” because of the joint pain.

questions.question: Té de Bogotá is an infusion made from an Andean plant. Which scholar proposed it as a replacement for tea from China?
hints: He was a priest and a doctor, born in Cádiz.
He arrived in Santafé in 1761 as the viceroy's doctor.
A genus of flowers, Mutisia, is named after him.
questions.description: A tea so rolo it surely comes with an almojábana on the side.
questions.fun_fact: The scientific name of té de Bogotá is Symplocos theiformis, which means “tea-shaped.”

questions.question: Since 2015, mosquitoes like this one have been released carrying Wolbachia bacteria to fight dengue. In which Colombian metro area did the program start?
hints: It's in the Andean interior, not on the coast.
Its main city has a metro and cable cars that climb up the mountains.
It's the city of eternal spring.
questions.description: Mosquitoes that, instead of stirring up trouble, show up to fix it.
questions.fun_fact: Wolbachia lives in a huge number of insects, and inside the mosquito it makes it very hard to pass on the dengue virus.

questions.question: When you ride a bike without falling, your cerebellum is at work. Which Colombian neuroscientist became world-famous for studying its neurons?
hints: He was born in Bogotá and led a neuroscience department in New York for decades.
He was part of the 1994 Science, Education and Development Mission, alongside García Márquez.
He wrote the book “I of the Vortex” (in Spanish, “El cerebro y el mito del yo”).
questions.description: Someone had to figure out who's in charge of your balance when you're out on your cicla.
questions.fun_fact: Llinás studied medicine at the Javeriana University and then did his PhD in Australia under Nobel Prize winner John Eccles.

questions.question: People from Casanare, Meta and Arauca are called “llaneros”. Where does that word come from?
questions.answer: From the llanos, flat and open lands
wrong_answers: From llamas, animals of the Andes
From llantas, the tires on cars
From lana, the wool of sheep
hints: The word comes from the place where they live, not from something they have or use.
It's a huge region, ideal for raising cattle and riding horses.
Think of land that is flat, flat as a table.
questions.description: People who stomp out joropo in spurs and sing to the cows before breakfast.
questions.fun_fact: The Llanos Orientales continue into Venezuela, which is why joropo is a dance of both countries.

questions.question: Look at the photo: until 2021, this statue stood on a hill in Cali, honoring the conquistador who founded the city in 1536. Who is it?
hints: He came from the south, from the lands that are now Ecuador.
He also founded Popayán and Quito.
He took his surname from the name of his hometown in Córdoba, Spain.
questions.description: A bronze gentleman who has been pointing at something for decades, and nobody has asked him what.
questions.fun_fact: The statue is the work of Spanish sculptor Victorio Macho and was for years one of the city's favorite lookout points.

questions.question: In 1813, the Free State of Cartagena made me a town and gave me a coat of arms as a reward for backing independence. Which city am I?
hints: I sit on the banks of the Magdalena River.
The motto on my coat of arms is “Premio al patriotismo” (Reward for Patriotism).
Today I'm the capital of Atlántico.
questions.description: A coat of arms handed out like a gold star for good patriotic behavior.
questions.fun_fact: The coat of arms was granted by Manuel Rodríguez Torices, president of the Free State of Cartagena, while Santa Marta was still on the king's side.

questions.question: Pereira was founded in 1863 with a Mass among the ruins of old Cartago. Who said that Mass?
hints: He came from nearby Cartago.
He isn’t the founder of Armenia or of Santa Rosa de Cabal.
He was the priest of Cartago who came up to bless the new settlement.
questions.description: A city born among the rubble that still came out in great shape.
questions.fun_fact: The city is named after Francisco Pereira Martínez, a patriot who hid on those lands during the fight for independence.

questions.question: In the biographical telenovela “Pambelé,” Antonio Cervantes becomes Colombia's first world boxing champion. In what year did that really happen?
hints: It was more than 50 years ago.
It happened in the 1970s, in a fight in Panama.
It was two years after the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.
questions.description: A knockout of a story that had the whole country yelling at the TV.
questions.fun_fact: Kid Pambelé was born in San Basilio de Palenque, considered the first free town in the Americas.

questions.question: Gabriel García Márquez called himself one, and on Colombia's Caribbean coast you hear it every day. What is a “mamagallista”?
questions.answer: Someone who is always joking and teasing
wrong_answers: Someone who gets up before dawn
Someone who never spends a single peso
hints: It's someone you have a good time with.
It's the opposite of a grump.
If they tell you something serious, better check it isn't a joke.
questions.description: A word that, on the Caribbean coast, describes half the neighborhood.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “mamar gallo” can also mean stalling and keeping someone waiting with excuses.

questions.question: Which of these TV channels is NOT Colombian?
