hints: Three of them broadcast to one region or to the whole country.
The odd one out broadcasts in Spanish, but from another country.
Its headquarters are in Miami, in the United States.
questions.description: Changing the channel has never been this hard.
questions.fun_fact: “Pasión de gavilanes” (2003) was a coproduction between Caracol and Telemundo.

questions.question: You're at an old-school parranda vallenata, with an accordion and friends. When does it usually end?
hints: It starts once it's already dark.
People say it lasts “until the accordion player gets tired”... and he doesn't tire quickly.
The roosters start crowing and the sky starts getting light.
questions.description: A get-together where the accordion works overtime and nobody pays it.
questions.fun_fact: In the vallenato region, some famous parrandas went on for several days in a row, with the musicians taking turns to rest.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the main ingredient of one of these snacks comes from here. Which one?
hints: It’s yellow and crunchy.
Its ingredient is also used to make arepas.
Its name sounds like “choclo,” the word for fresh, tender corn.
questions.description: The snack that always shows up at the family outing before you do.
questions.fun_fact: One of the most famous Choclitos flavors is lime.

questions.question: Santa Rosa de Cabal, in Risaralda, is famous for its hot springs, has its own festival for this product and sells it on every corner. What is it?
hints: It's a kind of sausage.
It's eaten with arepa and cooked on the grill.
People call it “santarrosano,” and it's reddish.
questions.description: A town where you soak in warm water and come out hungry for something really tasty.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Rosa de Cabal calls itself the “world capital of chorizo” and throws a festival for it every year.

questions.question: If you want to see the Festival Folclórico y Reinado Nacional del Bambuco in Neiva, which month do you travel?
hints: It's in the middle of the year.
The streets fill with parades, bambuco music and asado huilense.
It's the month when the mid-year school vacation starts at many Colombian schools.
questions.description: A party where queens are crowned not just for their looks, but also for how they move their feet.
questions.fun_fact: In the pageant, every candidate has to dance the sanjuanero huilense in front of the judges.

questions.question: Which of these nicknames does NOT belong to Millonarios, the blue-and-white club from Bogotá?
hints: Three of the nicknames speak of its color or its history.
The odd one out belongs to Millonarios' great rival, the other half of the Bogotá derby.
That nickname belongs to Independiente Santa Fe and comes from the red bird.
questions.description: In the fridge of Bogotá nicknames, someone has put their label on the wrong lunch.
questions.fun_fact: It's called “el Embajador” (the Ambassador) because in 1952 it traveled to Madrid and beat Real Madrid 4-2 at Real Madrid's 50th-anniversary tournament.

questions.question: In Colombian soccer, student is to “profe” as player is to…
hints: He's the one who teaches the players and gives them instructions.
He picks the lineup and decides the substitutions.
In Colombia, players call him “profe” in interviews.
questions.description: There's a classroom where the board is green and 100 meters long.
questions.fun_fact: Francisco “Pacho” Maturana, one of Colombia's most famous coaches, studied dentistry before he started coaching.

questions.question: In a Colombian league match, how many substitutions can each team make?
hints: A few years ago it was only three.
They're made in no more than three stoppages, not counting halftime.
As many as the fingers on one hand.
questions.description: Eleven take the field, but not all of them make it to the final whistle.
questions.fun_fact: The five-substitution rule began in 2020, during the pandemic, so players wouldn't get so worn out.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do you call the number 10 position that plays behind the strikers and sets up goals, like el Pibe Valderrama?
hints: My spot is in the middle of the field.
I’m not the one who wins the ball back: I hand it out.
In other countries they call me “enganche” or “armador”; in English, a playmaker.
questions.description: Some jerseys weigh more than others, even when they’re made of the same fabric.
questions.fun_fact: The 10 became the number of soccer magicians thanks to Pelé, who wore it almost by chance at the 1958 World Cup.

questions.question: The chapolera wears a colorful skirt, a headscarf and a basket tied at her waist. What did she put in that basket?
hints: It was the work outfit of women pickers on mountain farms.
Her name comes from “chapola”, the word for butterfly in that region.
What she picked gets roasted and drunk as tinto.
questions.description: Work clothes so pretty they ended up dancing at festivals.
questions.fun_fact: They were called chapoleras because in their colorful skirts among the coffee plants they looked like chapolas, that is, butterflies.

questions.question: Which of these characters does NOT go with the queen at the Carnaval de Barranquilla?
hints: One of them belongs to another holiday of the year.
That character doesn't dance on the Vía 40: he lives far away, where it's very cold.
He arrives in December with presents.
questions.description: A party with so many people in costume that someone sneaked in uninvited.
questions.fun_fact: Every year the Carnaval de Barranquilla has its queen and also its Rey Momo, usually a much-loved carnival maker.

questions.question: I'm a region of flat savannas, my rivers flow to the Orinoco, and my men wear a liqui liqui and a hat to parties. Which region am I?
hints: I share these savannas with Venezuela.
Joropo is danced here with harp, cuatro and maracas.
Villavicencio is my gateway.
questions.description: An outfit so elegant it works for herding cattle and for accepting a Nobel Prize.
questions.fun_fact: The liqui liqui is typical of the plains of Colombia and Venezuela, and in Venezuela it's considered the national men's outfit.

questions.question: In the traditional outfit of the paisa arriero (muleteer), what is the poncho?
questions.answer: A cloth worn over the shoulder
wrong_answers: A leather bag with many pockets
A white hat made of straw
A pair of sandals woven from fique
hints: It doesn't go over your head the way it does in other countries.
It is made of cotton, almost always white or in small checks.
The arriero used it to wipe away his sweat.
questions.description: Same name, different story: paisas just have to do things their own way.
questions.fun_fact: The arriero used his poncho for everything: wiping away sweat, keeping off the sun, shooing flies and even as a pillow.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. Sources agree that the poncho is worn on the shoulders. One says it is called a ruana in Antioquia. They do not clearly say it is a cloth. The wrong answers (carriel, hat, alpargatas) are correct as wrong answers.

questions.question: It's white with a black band, woven from iraca palm in a town in Caldas and worn by paisa arrieros. What is it called?
hints: Its town is in northern Caldas, near Antioquia.
That town holds the Festival Nacional del Pasillo.
Its name comes from the municipality of Aguadas.
questions.description: The accessory that turns any head into an arriero's head.
questions.fun_fact: A good iraca hat is woven by hand, strand by strand, and can take several days to finish.

questions.question: Among Indigenous peoples of the Colombian Amazon, the macaw-feather crown is worn at ceremonies and dances. What does it show about the wearer?
questions.answer: That they are an important person
wrong_answers: That it is their birthday today
That rain will come very soon
That they are leaving on a trip
hints: Not just anyone can put it on.
It is often worn by the shaman or the community's leaders.
It means something similar to a king's crown.
questions.description: A headdress so colorful it would make a parrot cry with envy.
questions.fun_fact: Macaws, whose feathers adorn these crowns, can live for more than 50 years.

questions.question: At Laguna de Fúquene, people cut reeds, dry them in the sun and weave them into esteras. What is an estera?
questions.answer: A flat weave to spread on the floor
wrong_answers: A basket with a handle for the market
A hat with a wide brim
A bag to carry on the shoulder
hints: Families around the lake have woven them for generations.
It used to be common in farmhouses, and today it's sold as a craft at markets.
When it's not in use, you roll it up.
questions.description: Out of the lake come fish, ducks and… this craft.
questions.fun_fact: The reeds and cattails of Fúquene are also woven into baskets, placemats and even furniture.

questions.question: In the villages they say that at midnight a silent line of figures with candles passes down the street, praying. Who are they?
hints: They are no longer of this world.
They ask people to pray for them.
In Colombia they're called the ánimas del purgatorio.
questions.description: A parade with no floats, no music, and nobody who wants to go and watch it.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that if someone accepts a candle from the procession, by the next morning it has turned into a bone.

questions.question: Grandmas say that to keep a witch out of the house, you leave a metal object opened into a cross behind the door. Which one?
hints: Almost every home has them in a drawer somewhere.
Two metal parts joined in the middle.
They have two holes for your fingers.
questions.description: The cheapest security system in the world: no alarm, no cameras, just one of Grandma's tricks.
questions.fun_fact: Some people also put them in a cross under the pillow to sleep without nightmares.

questions.question: At the Barranquilla Carnival, the Garabato dancers fight against Death. What is the garabato they carry in their hand?
hints: The dancers hold it up high and wave it as they dance.
It is decorated with flowers and colorful ribbons.
Its tip is bent, like a question mark.
questions.description: A dance where Death joins the party and keeps losing.
questions.fun_fact: In the Garabato dance, Life beats Death, so the dance ends in a big party.

questions.question: In 1812, during the Patria Boba, Antonio Baraya, the hero of Palacé, switched sides. Whom did he turn against?
hints: He was the centralist leader of Cundinamarca.
He translated and printed the Declaration of the Rights of Man.
Later, in 1814, he was captured in Pasto.
questions.description: A general who switched sides faster than a fan whose team is losing.
questions.fun_fact: In 1811 Baraya won the Battle of Bajo Palacé, one of the first patriot victories in New Granada.

questions.question: I was born in Caracas, served as foreign minister of Gran Colombia, was a delegate to the 1826 Congress of Panama and, in old age, president of Venezuela. Who am I?
hints: My job was dealing with other countries, not commanding troops.
I signed treaties with Mexico, Peru and Central America.
My first name is the same as the first pope’s.
questions.description: While others fought with sabers, this gentleman fought with letters and seals.
questions.fun_fact: The 1826 Congress of Panama, promoted by Bolívar, was one of the first attempts to unite the countries of the Americas.

questions.question: In which patriot woman's house in Santafé did Policarpa Salavarrieta live while plotters against the Reconquista met there?
hints: Like other patriot women, she took risks to help the cause of independence.
She was married to a Lozano.
Her last name is the same as a hero of San Mateo.
questions.description: The most dangerous house in Santafé had no cannons, just needles and thread.
questions.fun_fact: Policarpa got into royalist homes as a seamstress and gathered information for the patriots that way.

questions.question: I was born in La Guaira, served as Bolívar's chief of staff in the 1819 Liberation Campaign and was later president of Venezuela twice. Who am I?
hints: I didn't command the vanguard or the rear guard at Boyacá.
Later I was a Venezuelan minister and diplomat.
I governed Venezuela in the 1830s and 1840s.
questions.description: Somebody had to do the paperwork while Bolívar posed for paintings.
questions.fun_fact: Soublette died in 1870 at age 80, one of the few heroes of independence who lived to old age.

questions.question: Every August 11, Antioquia remembers when Juan del Corral declared its complete independence from Spain. What year was it?
hints: It was during the Patria Boba.
It was before Pablo Morillo arrived.
It was the same year as Bolívar's Admirable Campaign.
questions.description: Antioquia didn't wait for anyone's permission to say “that's it, we're done.”
questions.fun_fact: Juan del Corral also pushed for a “free womb” law in Antioquia: children born to enslaved women would be born free.

questions.question: Guadalupe Hill, with its big statue of the Virgin Mary, watches over Bogotá from the eastern hills. Roughly how high is its summit?
hints: Bogotá itself is already very high: about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft) above sea level.
From the top you can see the whole city, and up there it's often cold and foggy.
Its summit is over 3,000 meters, but nowhere near as high as the snowy peaks.
questions.description: Bogotá has two guardians on the mountain, and one of them wears a Virgin on its head.
questions.fun_fact: The statue of the Virgin of Guadalupe on the summit is about 15 meters (49 ft) tall and can be seen from much of Bogotá.

previous.feedback: source: The fun fact calls the summit statue "the statue of the Virgin of Guadalupe". The fact check says the 15 m statue by Gustavo Arcila Uribe (1946) shows the Immaculate Conception, and only the chapel is dedicated to Guadalupe. The Spanish source has the same error, so it needs fixing there first. Change the fun fact to something like "The statue of the Immaculate Conception on the summit is about 15 m (49 ft) tall…", then translate it again. Otherwise the translation is faithful and reads naturally. Fact check: wrong. Answer (~3,300 m; sources say 3,317 m) and the 15 m statue height are right. But the fun fact calls it the statue of the Virgin of Guadalupe. The statue shows the Virgin of the Immaculate Conception. Only the small chapel is dedicated to Guadalupe.

questions.question: The Las Lajas sanctuary, in Ipiales, rises over the canyon of the Guáitara River. Why was it built right there?
questions.answer: Because of an image of the Virgin in the rock
wrong_answers: Because of a gold mine at the bottom
To keep watch over the border with Ecuador
hints: Every year thousands of visitors come from Colombia and Ecuador.
According to legend, a mother and her daughter saw something on a stone in the canyon in the 18th century.
The church rests against the canyon wall, and that stone became its altar.
questions.description: A church with vertigo: it lives hanging over an abyss and never complains.
questions.fun_fact: The current church, in Gothic style, was finished in 1949 and is counted around the world among the most beautiful churches.

questions.question: Look at the photo: spikes hanging from a cave ceiling, like in the caves of Santander. What are they made of?
hints: They don't melt in the heat.
They form from drops of water carrying dissolved minerals.
That's why they are rock-hard and don't bend.
questions.description: A cave with a full set of teeth and not a dentist in sight.
questions.fun_fact: A stalactite can take about 100 years to grow just 1 centimeter (less than half an inch).

questions.question: In Bogotá it can rain in one neighborhood while the sun shines in another, as the hills and wind give each area its own climate. What is such a small-area climate called?
hints: It's a climate in a small size.
A valley, a neighborhood or even a garden can have one.
Its name starts with a prefix that means “very small.”
questions.description: Bogotá: the only place where you leave home in sunglasses and need an umbrella three blocks later.
questions.fun_fact: Because of its mountains, Colombia has neighboring towns with very different climates, one cold and one hot.

questions.question: The Juan Curí waterfalls, near San Gil, are among the most visited in Santander. About how tall are they?
hints: They are much taller than a two-story house.
They are taller than a 40-story building.
They are close to 200 meters.
questions.description: A natural shower in Santander, except the showerhead is up in the clouds.
questions.fun_fact: At Juan Curí you can go down the wall of the waterfall hanging from a rope, rappelling.

questions.question: Bogotá’s flag has just two horizontal stripes of the same size. What colors are they?
hints: Its colors date back to the days of independence in Bogotá.
One of its colors is also on the flag of Colombia.
They are the colors of the sun and of fire.
questions.description: A capital-city flag that doesn’t need three stripes to show off.
questions.fun_fact: Its colors come from the yellow and red armbands that patriots wore in Bogotá on July 20, 1810.

questions.question: You're watching the 2024 Copa América in your yellow shirt. Which of these players was NOT on Colombia's national team?
hints: He doesn't wear the yellow shirt, but a striped one.
He ended up lifting that Copa with his own team.
He wears Argentina's number 10.
questions.description: A sticker album where an intruder sneaked in.
questions.fun_fact: Even though Colombia lost the final, James Rodríguez was named the best player of that Copa América.

questions.question: I'm a goalkeeper, I played for Arsenal in England and Napoli in Italy, and I was Colombia's starter at the 2014 and 2018 World Cups. Who am I?
hints: I was born in Medellín in 1988.
I have played more games for the Selección than anyone in its history.
I share my first name with the boy who beat the giant Goliath.
questions.description: A man whose whole job is making sure nothing happens.
questions.fun_fact: Ospina played more than 120 games for Colombia, more than any other player.

previous.feedback: source: Hint 2 and the fun fact say Ospina has more caps than anyone in Colombia's history. That record can change, and after the 2026 World Cup cycle I can't confirm it still holds: James Rodríguez was close to Ospina's total and may have passed it. Rephrase both in the source as a fact that can't go out of date (e.g. "one of the most-capped players" or "more than 120 matches"). The translation itself is faithful and natural.

source: Hint 2 and the fun fact say Ospina has the most caps in Colombia's history. That record changes over time, and by late 2026, after the 2026 World Cup, James Rodríguez has probably passed Ospina's 128 caps. Both the source and the translation should drop the record claim: hint 2 could become another clue (for example Atlético Nacional or Copa América 2021), and the fun fact a stable fact. The rest of the translation matches the source and reads naturally.

Source: hint 2 and the fun fact say Ospina has played more matches for Colombia than anyone else. That record can change, and by late 2026 James Rodríguez may have passed his roughly 128 caps, so I can't confirm it is still true. Rephrase it in the source (for example "one of the most-capped players in Colombia's history" or "more than 120 matches"), then translate it again. Apart from that, the translation is faithful and reads naturally.

questions.question: For Colombia, the number 10 shirt has been worn by el Pibe Valderrama and James Rodríguez. What does the player with that number usually do?
questions.answer: Create plays and set up goals
wrong_answers: Guard the box as last defender
hints: He plays in the middle, close to the strikers.
People call him the “brain” or the “playmaker” of the team.
He's the one who serves the ball on a plate to the goal scorer.
questions.description: Two digits on the back that weigh more than a school backpack.
questions.fun_fact: Giving the 10 to the team's star became famous with Pelé, who wore it at the 1958 World Cup.

questions.question: You're watching Colombia vs. England at the 2018 World Cup, and in the 93rd minute a center back ties it with a header. Who is he?
hints: He's a very tall defender, born in Guachené, Cauca.
He scored three goals at that World Cup, all headers.
He celebrates his goals by dancing.
questions.description: When the clock had already reached the end, someone refused to go home.
questions.fun_fact: Yerry Mina scored three headed goals at Russia 2018: against Poland, Senegal and England.

questions.question: This is José Pékerman, the coach who took Colombia to the 2014 and 2018 World Cups. In which country was he born?
hints: Before Colombia, he coached this country's national team at the 2006 World Cup.
With this country, he won three Under-20 World Cups.
It's Messi's country.
questions.description: A man who coached from the sideline looking like he was sitting through Sunday Mass.
questions.fun_fact: With Pékerman, Colombia went back to a World Cup in 2014 after 16 years away.

questions.question: You're on a trip to Tayrona Park. Which of these things should you NOT do?
questions.answer: Leave your trash on the beach
wrong_answers: Watch the animals without touching them
hints: Three of these things protect nature.
The thing you shouldn't do can harm the animals and the sea.
You have to take your bags and bottles back with you.
questions.description: Tayrona has rules, and they're not there to bore you.
questions.fun_fact: In Tayrona, visitors must carry out of the park all the trash they bring in.

questions.question: In 1995 a bomb wrecked this Botero sculpture in Medellín. He donated a new one and asked to leave the broken one beside it. Why?
questions.answer: To remember the violence and call for peace
wrong_answers: Because the broken one was too heavy to move
To repair it later with the pieces
To sell it to a museum later
hints: Botero made several works about Colombia's history.
Think about what Medellín was going through in the 1990s.
The new sculpture has the opposite of war in its name.
questions.description: Medellín's most famous artist never met a figure he couldn't make rounder.
questions.fun_fact: The new sculpture is called “Pájaro de paz” and stands in Parque San Antonio, in downtown Medellín.

questions.question: It's a big carved and gilded wooden structure at the front of the church, filling the wall, with niches for saints. The one in San Francisco church, Bogotá, is famous. What is it called?
hints: You see it straight ahead as soon as you walk into many colonial churches.
It often has levels and columns, like a building front stuck to the wall.
Its English name joins the word for the church's holy table with the word “piece”.
questions.description: At the front of the church, the saints get their own apartment building.
questions.fun_fact: The main altarpiece of San Francisco church in Bogotá is one of the jewels of Colombian colonial art.

questions.question: I spin round and round on the Kokoriko rotisserie until I’m golden, and I’m served with potatoes and arepa. What am I?
hints: I’m an animal with feathers.
Before the rotisserie, I lived on a farm and scratched at the dirt.
The name “Kokoriko” sounds like a rooster’s crow.
questions.description: For many Colombians, Sunday lunch smells of charcoal and family.
questions.fun_fact: The name Kokoriko imitates a rooster’s crow as it sounds in some languages, a cousin of English “cock-a-doodle-doo.”

questions.question: I was born in Cúcuta, played for Real Madrid and wore the number 10 for Colombia's national team. Who am I?
hints: I'm a left-footed midfielder famous for my passes and free kicks.
I became famous around the world at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.
People call me “Jamesito,” and I was the best player of the 2024 Copa América.
questions.description: A kid from Cúcuta who turned the number 10 shirt into a superhero suit.
questions.fun_fact: Even though Colombia lost the final, James was named the best player of the 2024 Copa América.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Bogotá was founded in this colonial neighborhood, La Candelaria, in 1538. Who founded it?
hints: He was a Spanish conquistador who came from Santa Marta, up the Magdalena River.
He was the first to reach the savanna where the Muisca lived.
His first name is Gonzalo.
questions.description: Steep streets, colorful houses and a tinto on every corner: this is where it all began.
questions.fun_fact: The founding is said to have happened near the Chorro de Quevedo, a little square in La Candelaria that is now full of artists and storytellers.

questions.question: This town in Boyacá has white colonial houses, a kite festival in August and the largest cobblestone square in Colombia. Which town is it?
hints: It's about three hours from Bogotá by road.
Many fossils have been found around it, and it even has a fossil museum.
Its name starts with the word “Villa”.
questions.description: A town where cars suffer and kites fly happily.
questions.fun_fact: The main square of Villa de Leyva covers about 14,000 square meters, almost as much as two soccer fields!

questions.question: The accordion, the caja and the guacharaca play together in one kind of Colombian music. In which city is its most famous festival held?
hints: It's a city in Cesar, near the Sierra Nevada.
Every year, the Vallenato King is crowned there.
The festival is called the Vallenato Legend Festival.
questions.description: Three instruments, lots of parrandas and zero desire to go to bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2015, UNESCO added traditional vallenato music to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

questions.question: The Spanish built it on San Lázaro Hill in Cartagena, with sloping walls and tunnels inside. What for?
questions.answer: To defend the city from pirates and enemy armies
wrong_answers: To house the viceroy and his family
To store gold before shipping it to Spain
hints: From the top you could see everything arriving by land and by sea.
Its name recalls a king of Spain, Philip IV.
It has cannons pointing outward.
questions.description: A castle with no princesses or dragons, but a very unfriendly face.
questions.fun_fact: It is said to be the largest fortress the Spanish built in their American colonies.

questions.question: I was born in Ecuador in 1919, my voice filled Colombian jukeboxes with “Temeridad”, and I said goodbye to this world in Tuluá, Valle, in 1991. Who am I?
hints: I'm a singer of the boleros and pasillos you hear in cantinas.
I share my home country with the famous “Ruiseñor de América”.
My first name recalls the mountain of the Greek gods.
questions.description: The voice that coaxed the most coins out of a jukebox on a Sunday afternoon.
questions.fun_fact: Olimpo Cárdenas spent so many years in Colombia that many Colombians thought of him as one of their own.

questions.question: I was born in Ginebra, Valle del Cauca, played the tiple all my life, and my town's great Andean Colombian music festival bears my nickname. Who am I?
hints: The festival has been held since the 1970s.
My nickname refers to my light-colored hair.
They called me “el Mono”.
questions.description: A nickname from the corner store ended up naming the most important festival of Andean music.
questions.fun_fact: The Festival Mono Núñez is so prestigious that winning it is like earning an honors degree for Andean musicians.

previous.feedback: Fact check: uncertain. The person and the festival are right: Benigno "Mono" Núñez was born in Ginebra, Valle, and the festival bears his name. But "played the tiple all my life" is shaky. Sources say he began on the accordion, then played tiple, guitar and bandola, and he is mostly known as a bandola player. The hint that the nickname refers to his light hair is plausible ("mono" means blond) but I couldn't verify it. The festival start year of 1974/75 fits "since the 1970s". The description about a "corner store" nickname is also unverified.

questions.question: You do it on the couch or in bed, best when it rains in Bogotá: snuggling up close to someone under the cobija (blanket). What is the word?
hints: It’s a plan for cold days, with no hurry at all.
You do it with someone you love, or with the dog.
It starts with “arru…”.
questions.description: The favorite plan of people in Bogotá when the sky turns gray at three in the afternoon.
questions.fun_fact: “Emparamarse,” on the other hand, means getting soaked and frozen by the rain, which is very easy on the Bogotá savanna.

questions.question: In Colombia, what do people call the loud, blunt, direct way of talking of people from Santander?
hints: If you're not used to it, it feels like you're being told off.
It's the exact opposite of a soft, sing-song way of talking.
It sounds as if every word lands a punch.
questions.description: Some accents sound like a scolding even when they're offering you lunch.
questions.fun_fact: Many people from Santander explain that they're not angry at all: that's just how they talk.

questions.question: You hear a man tell his dog “¡Sumercé, quédese quieto!” Where is he most likely from?
hints: It's cold, mountain country.
People there say “usted” to everyone, even children and animals.
His home region borders Cundinamarca, and its capital is Tunja.
questions.description: A place where even the cows get spoken to with respect.
questions.fun_fact: “Sumercé” comes from “su merced” (“your grace”), a respectful way of addressing someone in colonial times.

questions.question: On a hato (cattle ranch) in Arauca, everyone calls the new ranch hand “el catire”. Why?
hints: It has to do with how he looks.
The word is used the same way in Venezuela.
In the rest of Colombia they'd call him “mono”.
questions.description: On the llano, a nickname goes on faster than a saddle on a horse.
questions.fun_fact: In the Llanos and in Venezuela, “catire” is such a common nickname that many people carry it all their lives.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: “On the road through Huila we stopped to buy achiras, which are…”
hints: They're sold at roadside stands in Huila and Tolima.
They go very well with a tinto or a kumis.
They contain cheese and butter, are baked and are shaped like a little ring or stick.
questions.description: A trip to southern Huila isn't over without a full bag for the road.
questions.fun_fact: Achira is made from the starch in the root of a plant with the same name, which has red flowers.

questions.question: Look at the map: the highlighted department is home to El Totumo volcano, where people float in mud. Which one is it?
hints: It's on the Caribbean coast.
Mompox, the town by the Magdalena River, is in this department too.
Its capital is Cartagena, the walled city.
questions.description: A natural spa where the mud mask covers you from head to toe.
questions.fun_fact: It's almost impossible to sink in El Totumo's mud: it's so thick that you float like a cork.

questions.question: You want to swim in the sea without leaving the city. Which of these capitals of the Colombian Caribbean WON'T work?
hints: Its department has a coastline, but the city doesn't.
It lies inland, in the middle of the savannas.
It is the capital of the department of Sucre.
questions.description: A question for people who pack their swimsuit before their toothbrush.
questions.fun_fact: From Sincelejo to the beaches of Tolú is only about 40 kilometers (25 miles).

questions.question: Which of these groups is NOT an Indigenous people of Colombia?
hints: Their home is surrounded by sea.
Besides Spanish, they speak an English-based creole language.
They live on San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina.
questions.description: Four groups in the family photo, and one of them has a different story.
questions.fun_fact: The Raizal people speak San Andrés Creole, a language that mixes English with words from Africa.

questions.question: Look at the map: this department is named after a river on the border with Ecuador and Peru. What is the river called?
hints: It flows east through the rainforest all the way to Brazil.
The Fin del Mundo (End of the World) waterfall is in this department.
Puerto Asís, one of the most important ports in southern Colombia, sits on its banks.
questions.description: A river so important that it lent its name to a whole department.
questions.fun_fact: When it enters Brazil, the Putumayo River changes its name to Içá.

questions.question: You're having breakfast in Santa Marta and you're served a green banana mash with queso costeño and butter. What is it called?
hints: It is typical of Magdalena and La Guajira.
It isn't fried: the bananas are boiled and mashed.
Its name starts with “ca” and ends in “ye.”
questions.description: A coastal breakfast that sets you up to survive the midday heat.
questions.fun_fact: In Santa Marta, cayeye usually comes with egg, suero costeño or fried fish.

questions.question: Mitú, the capital of Vaupés, takes its name from an Indigenous language. What is a mitú?
questions.answer: A bird similar to a turkey
hints: It lives in the Amazon rainforest.
The Indigenous peoples of Vaupés hunted it for food.
It's the paujil (curassow), with black feathers and an eye-catching beak.
questions.description: A capital so deep in the jungle that the GPS asks for a guide.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists use “Mitu” as the name of a group of curassows, such as Salvin's curassow.

questions.question: Look at the photo: one of these packaged snacks is made from this green fruit. Which one?
hints: It comes in thin, crunchy slices.
This fruit, green and fried, also becomes patacón.
Its name means “little plantains” in Spanish.
questions.description: A snack that crunches louder than an old creaky door.
questions.fun_fact: Green plantain is barely sweet: it's full of starch, which turns into sugar as the fruit ripens.

questions.question: Look at the photo: these flakes are the main ingredient of an Alpina drink that's served ice-cold. Which one?
hints: It's a thick, creamy drink.
The flakes in the photo are a grain that many moms cook with milk and cinnamon.
The drink has the same name as the grain in the photo, in Spanish.
questions.description: The snack that fits in your lunchbox and in your heart.
questions.fun_fact: Oats are a cereal grain, a relative of wheat and barley.

questions.question: Which pier on Colombia's Caribbean coast opened in 1893 and was the country's main gateway for years?
hints: A train linked it to a large nearby city to carry goods inland.
Many immigrants arrived through it before Bocas de Ceniza existed.
It's a few minutes from Barranquilla, in a town named after the country.
questions.description: A structure that walks out into the sea as if trying not to get its feet wet.
questions.fun_fact: The pier was built by Cuban engineer Francisco Javier Cisneros and stretched more than a kilometer (over half a mile) out to sea.

questions.question: It often wears its alternate jersey, and in several Colombian clásicos its fans aren't allowed into the stadium. What is it called?
hints: It doesn't play at its own home.
When its barra is let in, it goes in a separate stand.
It's the opposite of the team hosting the game.
questions.description: It shows up at the stadium and nobody saved it a seat.
questions.fun_fact: In the Copa Libertadores, until 2021 an away goal counted for more when breaking a tie in a series.

questions.question: You're in Riohacha and see little colorful woven bands with Wayuu patterns, tied around the wrist. What are they called in Colombia?
hints: You wear them on your wrist.
They're a popular gift to bring back from a trip.
The name comes from the Spanish word for “hand.”
questions.description: The easiest souvenir to pack from the whole trip to La Guajira.
questions.fun_fact: The geometric patterns in Wayuu weaving are called kanaas, and each one has its own meaning.

questions.question: In the countryside, people say that when an owl calls at night on top of the roof, it brings news. What does it announce?
hints: People make the sign of the cross when they hear it.
It is one of the bad omens.
It is the opposite of a blessing.
questions.description: A night-time neighbor who pays no rent and has enormous eyes.
questions.fun_fact: Owls don't bring bad luck: every night they eat lots of mice and help farmers.

questions.question: Which journalist, born in the Cauca department, presented Noticias Caracol for years?
hints: She is from the southwest of the country.
She became a role model for many Afro-Colombian women in journalism.
Her first name starts with M, and her last name has just four letters.
questions.description: While the family eats lunch, she tells everyone what happened in the country, and nobody dares change the channel.
questions.fun_fact: Mábel Lara is one of the best-known Afro-Colombian faces on Colombian TV.

questions.question: Wilmer Valderrama, whose mother is Colombian, played Fez on “That '70s Show”. Where does that nickname come from?
wrong_answers: The red hat he wore when he arrived
The Moroccan city where he was born
A typo when writing his real name
hints: On the show, nobody can pronounce the character's real name.
Fez lives with a Wisconsin family that isn't his own.
It's three letters, F, E and S, from three words.
questions.description: A three-letter nickname that none of his friends ever thought twice about.
questions.fun_fact: The show never reveals which country Fez comes from, and that mystery became one of its running jokes.

questions.question: In 1811 in Santafé, Antonio Nariño launched “La Bagatela”, which harshly criticized Jorge Tadeo Lozano's government. What was La Bagatela?
hints: Nariño was a forerunner of independence, famous for spreading ideas.
It was read aloud at tertulias (social gatherings).
Nariño wrote nearly everything in each issue.
questions.description: Its name promises next to nothing, but it toppled a whole president.
questions.fun_fact: The criticism in La Bagatela helped push Lozano to resign and put Nariño in charge of Cundinamarca.

questions.question: Antonio Nariño marched south against the royalists of Popayán and Pasto, but ended up a prisoner in Pasto. In what year was he captured?
hints: It happened in the middle of the Patria Boba.
It was before Pablo Morillo arrived.
It was four years after the Grito (the 1810 cry of independence).
questions.description: A trip south that ended without a return ticket.
questions.fun_fact: After his capture, Nariño was sent as a prisoner to Cádiz, in Spain, where he spent several years in jail.

questions.question: During the Reconquista, patriots were executed by firing squad in Santafé on a plot called the Huerta de Jaime. Today it's a park with an obelisk. Which park?
hints: It's in downtown Bogotá.
It's next to Avenida Caracas, west of La Candelaria.
Its name honors those who died for the patriot cause.
questions.description: Today pigeons peck at corn where a piece of the nation's history was once written.
questions.fun_fact: The park's obelisk was put up in the 19th century in memory of the patriots executed there.

questions.question: In 1816 a Permanent Council of War was set up in Santafé and decided the fate of many patriot leaders. Which Spanish commander created it?
hints: He arrived from Spain in 1815 at the head of a large army.
Before reaching Santafé, he besieged Cartagena for more than 100 days.
He was nicknamed “The Pacifier”.
questions.description: A council whose advice nobody wanted to hear, least of all in person.
questions.fun_fact: Before coming to the Americas, Morillo had fought Napoleon's troops in Spain.

questions.question: The Río Claro, in Antioquia, carved a canyon with pale, smooth walls. What rock are they made of?
hints: It forms when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
It's a rock used for statues, floors and elegant countertops.
Michelangelo used it to carve his famous statue of David.
questions.description: A river with a lot of patience and very fine taste in home decor.
questions.fun_fact: The Río Claro reserve has marble caves that are home to guácharos (oilbirds), birds that fly at night and find their way by sound.

questions.question: “I live in the Tatacoa Desert, in Huila. At night, people come to look at the stars with me.” What am I?
hints: My work starts when the sun goes down.
From me you can see planets, the Moon and shooting stars.
Inside, I have telescopes.
questions.description: There's not much to see in the desert by day, but at night the show is free and has millions of lights.
questions.fun_fact: La Tatacoa is one of the best places in Colombia for stargazing because there are few clouds and almost no city lights reach it.

questions.question: Look at the photo: the battle of August 7, 1819, was won next to this bridge. Who led the patriot army?
hints: He was born in Caracas.
He reached Boyacá after crossing the Andes from the plains.
People call him “the Liberator.”
questions.description: A tiny bridge with a giant story.
questions.fun_fact: The Battle of Boyacá lasted only about two hours and opened the way to independence.

questions.question: This giant bamboo grows in Colombia's Coffee Region. What do people there use it for a lot?
hints: It's very strong and very long.
It bends without breaking and stands up very well to earthquakes.
Architects and carpenters love it.
questions.description: A grass that grew so tall it forgot it was grass.
questions.fun_fact: Guadua can grow more than 10 centimeters (4 inches) in a single day.

questions.question: Colombian Éider Arévalo became world champion in 2017 in the track and field event shown in the photo. Which one is it?
hints: The judges watch very closely how the athletes move their legs.
Its classic Olympic distances were 20 km and 50 km.
Both feet must never leave the ground at the same time.
questions.description: A sport for people in a big hurry with even bigger patience.
questions.fun_fact: In race walking, the supporting leg must stay straight from the moment it touches the ground until it passes under the body.

questions.question: Which of these things does a track bike, like the ones Colombian track cyclists ride in the velodrome, NOT have?
hints: It's missing something almost every street bike has.
On the track everyone rides in the same direction and nobody has to stop suddenly.
To slow down, the rider pushes backward on the pedals.
questions.description: A bike that went to the velodrome and left something behind at home.
questions.fun_fact: A track bike has a fixed gear: if the wheel turns, the pedals turn too, so the rider can never stop pedaling.

questions.question: Who is this Colombian singer?
hints: He's from Antioquia and almost always sings with an electric guitar.
He sang “La camisa negra” and “A Dios le pido”.
His stage name joins his two first names: Juan and Esteban.
questions.description: A singer so famous that even your grandma has belted out his songs on the bus.
questions.fun_fact: Before going solo, Juanes played in Ekhymosis, a heavy metal band from Medellín.

questions.question: Bogotá's main square faces the Capitol and the Cathedral. Who is it named after?
hints: He is a hero of Independence.
He is called “the Liberator.”
A department on the Caribbean coast carries his surname.
questions.description: The living room of every Colombian's home, pigeons included.
questions.fun_fact: The Bolívar statue in the middle of the square dates from 1846 and is Bogotá's oldest public monument.

questions.question: The Rosario Islands are coral islands inside a national park. From which city do almost all the boats leave to visit them?
hints: It's a city on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
A famous international film festival is held there every year.
It's known as “the Walled City”.
questions.description: Water so clear the fish have nowhere to hide.
questions.fun_fact: The Rosario Islands are part of the Corales del Rosario y San Bernardo National Natural Park, created in 1977.

questions.question: I have colorful wings, and at the Quindío Botanical Garden I live with hundreds of others in a huge house. What am I?
hints: I love drinking nectar from flowers.
Before I could fly, I spent some time sitting still inside a chrysalis.
Before I had wings, I was a caterpillar.
questions.description: A glass house where the tenants pay no rent and fly in through the door.
questions.fun_fact: Seen from above, the butterfly house at the Quindío Botanical Garden in Calarcá is shaped like a butterfly.

questions.question: Arelys Henao is one of the queens of Colombian música popular. In which department was she born?
hints: It's a mountain department with many singers of música popular and heartbreak songs.
Its capital is a city famous for the Feria de las Flores.
People from there are called paisas.
questions.description: A voice you hear in every cantina, from the corner store to your uncle's finca.
questions.fun_fact: Colombian música popular mixes Mexican ranchera, tango and the country music of the mountains.

questions.question: I have four thick strings, I'm almost as tall as a person, I'm played standing up, and I have the lowest sound in the string orchestra. What am I?
hints: You'll also find me in lots of jazz bands.
I can be played with a bow or by plucking the strings.
My name starts with a word that means “twice.”
questions.description: In the orchestra everyone follows the conductor, though some pretend they can't see him.
questions.fun_fact: In many Colombian estudiantinas, the double bass joins tiples, bandolas and guitars to add the low notes.

questions.question: If a person is “ibaguereño” or “ibaguereña,” which Colombian department are they from?
hints: It's a department in central Colombia, in the Magdalena River valley.
The Colombian Folk Festival is held there, and lechona is queen.
Its name starts with T, and it shares it with a snow-capped volcano.
questions.description: The demonym: the fancy way of asking “so where are you from, then?”
questions.fun_fact: Ibagué, the capital of Tolima, is called the “Musical Capital of Colombia.”

questions.question: In Colombia, many moms call their baby “usted.” What does that “usted” almost always show?
hints: “Usted” isn't always about keeping your distance.
It often comes out while the mom is cuddling the baby and singing to it.
It's the same feeling the mom has when she kisses her baby.
questions.description: In Colombia, one little word works for the teacher, the boss and even the cat.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Colombia, some couples call each other “usted” their whole lives, out of pure affection rather than respect.

questions.question: In Cali, if people say a child is running around “viringo,” what is the child like?
hints: Something very important is missing.
The kid just got out of the bath and is running all over the house, laughing.
The kid looks just like the day they were born.
questions.description: A word from Cali that sends any mom running right as the guests arrive.
questions.fun_fact: Peru has a hairless dog breed that is also called the “perro viringo.”

questions.question: It comes from Quechua and you hear it a lot in Pasto and in Ecuador. What is a “guambra”?
hints: People often say it with affection.
It works for boys and girls alike: “el guambra” or “la guambra”.
In Bogotá they would say “sardino”.
questions.description: A word that crossed the Andes from the Inca Empire and settled down in Pasto.
questions.fun_fact: “Guambra” comes from the Quechua “wampra”, which means boy or girl.

questions.question: In the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago there is a place called Quitasueño. What is it?
hints: It lies far from the inhabited islands, north of Providencia.
Almost all of it is underwater.
Ships fear it because they can run aground there.
questions.description: A name that sounds like the herbal tea grandma makes you before bed.
questions.fun_fact: In 2012, the International Court of Justice confirmed that Quitasueño belongs to Colombia, in its dispute with Nicaragua.

questions.question: Colombian Crescencio Salcedo wrote “El año viejo.” Who recorded it in 1953 and made it a hit across the Americas?
hints: He was a singer, not a bandleader.
He recorded it in Mexico with Rafael de Paz's orchestra.
His last name is also the name of a city in Chihuahua.
questions.description: The unofficial anthem of the twelve midnight chimes, party hat and all.
questions.fun_fact: Many people in Colombia believe the singer of “El año viejo” was Colombian, but Tony Camargo was Mexican.

questions.question: At the party, someone crosses the room, holds out a hand and leads you to the dance floor. What do Colombians call that?
hints: It happens at weddings and quinceañeras.
It almost always starts with a one-word question.
It’s the opposite of staying in your seat the whole party.
questions.description: A moment of courage that begins on the far side of the room.
questions.fun_fact: In Cali, the capital of salsa, there are schools where children learn to dance from a very young age.

questions.question: In soccer, what do Colombian commentators call a spectacular goal?
hints: The whole stadium jumps up to celebrate.
Commentators shout it, stretching out the last letter.
It’s the word “gol” with an ending that makes it bigger.
questions.description: The commentators’ favorite word, shouted until they run out of air.
questions.fun_fact: James Rodríguez’s goal against Uruguay at the 2014 World Cup won the Puskás Award for the most beautiful goal of the year.

questions.question: As you leave the corner store, the shopkeeper says “¡Que le vaya bien!”. What do people usually reply?
hints: It's a single word.
You give the shopkeeper the same wish back.
It means “same to you.”
questions.description: Words that in Colombia come out all by themselves as you walk out the door.
questions.fun_fact: Many Colombians stretch out the goodbye: “que le vaya bien, que esté bien, saludes en la casa.”

questions.question: CIAT, in Palmira, keeps the world's largest collections of two staple foods in its seed bank. Which two?
hints: Both are staple foods in the tropics, from Latin America to Africa.
One grows in pods and the other is a thick root underground.
One goes in bandeja paisa and the other in sancocho.
questions.description: A pantry so big it could replant half the planet after a disaster.
questions.fun_fact: CIAT's seed bank holds tens of thousands of bean varieties brought from a great many countries.

questions.question: It records brain activity millisecond by millisecond with superconducting sensors near absolute zero, and Rodolfo Llinás used it. What is it called?
hints: It doesn't measure electricity directly with electrodes on the scalp.
It doesn't take pictures of tissue with radio waves either, like another famous scan.
Its name joins “magnet” with “brain recording.”
questions.description: The brain thinks so fast that it takes a very expensive machine to catch it in the act.
questions.fun_fact: The brain's magnetic fields are hundreds of millions of times weaker than Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: Bogotá-born Ana María Rey, a MacArthur “genius grant” winner, studies laser-cooled atoms in the world's most precise devices. What are they for?
hints: She works at JILA in Colorado, an institute famous for these devices.
The GPS on your phone depends on them.
They're the most precise version of what you wear on your wrist.
questions.description: A rola who makes atoms shiver with cold so they'll behave.
questions.fun_fact: The best atomic clocks would lose less than one second over the entire age of the universe.

questions.question: The Perseverance rover, which Colombian Diana Trujillo worked on, landed in Jezero Crater. Why did NASA choose it? Because long ago there was…
hints: NASA was looking for a place where tiny life might have existed long ago.
From orbit you can see a delta, like the one a river makes where it ends.
Still water sat there billions of years ago.
questions.description: To pick a landing spot on Mars, NASA had to look very, very far back in time.
questions.fun_fact: Perseverance stores rock samples in sealed tubes so a future mission can bring them back to Earth.

questions.question: In Bogotá and Medellín, depending on the day of the week, some cars can't be driven at the busiest hours. What is this rule called?
hints: It changes with the day of the week.
It depends on the numbers on the front and back of the car.
Its name joins the Spanish for “rush hour” with the Spanish for what shows a car's number.
questions.description: The rule that makes your dad check the calendar before taking the car out.
questions.fun_fact: Bogotá started pico y placa in 1998, and many other Colombian cities later copied the idea.

questions.question: Carlos Vives was born in Santa Marta. What do you call someone from that city?
hints: The word doesn't look much like the city's full name.
Carlos “el Pibe” Valderrama is one too, and says so proudly.
It joins a little piece of “Santa” with a little piece of “Marta”.
questions.description: Born looking at the Sierra Nevada and the sea at the same time, like someone who can't make up their mind.
questions.fun_fact: Santa Marta, founded in 1525, is the oldest Colombian city still standing.

questions.question: I'm an actress from Cali and also a dancer. I played Rosario in “La hija del mariachi” and Policarpa Salavarrieta in “La Pola.” Who am I?
hints: I trained in dance before I became an actress.
Years later, I starred in a reggaeton series that was a big hit on Netflix.
I starred in “La reina del flow.”
questions.description: An actress who switches characters like switching steps on the dance floor.
questions.fun_fact: Before acting, Carolina Ramírez studied ballet at Incolballet, the Colombian Ballet Institute in Cali.

questions.question: Listen: this instrument joined the accordion, the caja and the guacharaca in modern vallenato. Which one is it?
hints: It sounds low, like a rumble underneath the melody.
You play it by plucking thick strings.
It looks like a guitar, but longer and with a much deeper sound.
questions.description: The musician almost nobody watches on stage, until the band tries to play without one.
questions.fun_fact: The electric bass took off in 1951, when Leo Fender launched his famous Precision Bass.

questions.question: Which style of vallenato did Rafael Orozco and El Binomio de Oro make famous from the late 1970s?
hints: It doesn't tell town chronicles or cowboy stories.
It's what plays most when someone is in love... or heartbroken.
Its name comes from the same word as “romance”.
questions.description: A group so good that even its name sounds like a jewelry store.
questions.fun_fact: El Binomio de Oro was founded in 1976, and its name comes from the duo of singer Rafael Orozco and accordion player Israel Romero.

questions.question: Look at this sea turtle. It nests on beaches of Colombia's Caribbean coast, and the plates of its shell overlap like roof tiles. What is it called?
hints: It is critically endangered.
It is usually seen around coral reefs.
Its shell was once used to make combs and eyeglass frames.
questions.description: An elegant swimmer wearing a suit of luxury armor.
questions.fun_fact: The hawksbill eats mostly sea sponges, even some that are poisonous to other animals.

questions.question: You're at the Feria de Cali, held every year from December 25 to 30. In which decade was the first one held?
hints: It's older than the Salsódromo.
Your grandparents could have gone to the first one when they were young.
Television had just arrived in Colombia a few years earlier, in 1954.
questions.description: A party so good it has been repeating itself every December for decades.
questions.fun_fact: The first Feria de Cali, in December 1957, had bullfights, a horse parade and a beauty pageant.

questions.question: Porro was born in the village brass bands of Córdoba and Sucre. Which bandleader took it to Bogotá's elegant clubs in the 1940s?
hints: He played the clarinet.
His wife, Matilde Díaz, sang with his orchestra.
He wrote “Carmen de Bolívar” and “Colombia tierra querida.”
questions.description: From the cattle pens of the savanna to a ballroom with crystal chandeliers: quite a musical move.
questions.fun_fact: Lucho Bermúdez played the clarinet and wrote hundreds of songs, including porros, cumbias and gaitas.

questions.question: I was born in Chocó, played trombone and wrote arrangements for Grupo Niche in its early days, then founded Guayacán Orquesta. Who am I?
hints: I was not the founder or the leader of Grupo Niche.
I was born in Quibdó, just like Jairo Varela.
My first name is Alexis.
questions.description: A trombone that left one famous band to start another just as famous.
questions.fun_fact: Guayacán Orquesta is the band behind “Oiga, mire, vea,” which became almost an anthem of Cali.

questions.question: I live on the farm, lay eggs and look after my chicks. If someone is scared of everything, people say they're like me. What am I?
hints: I have feathers and can't fly very high.
My soup is what they give you when you have the flu.
I'm the rooster's wife.
questions.description: A saying that left the farm and moved into the schoolyard.
questions.fun_fact: Hens are not cowards at all: a mother hen will peck at anyone who threatens her chicks.

questions.question: At a party, if someone shouts “¡A mover el esqueleto!” (move your skeleton!), they want you to…
hints: There’s music playing.
You do it on the dance floor.
Salsa, cumbia or vallenato are perfect for it.
questions.description: An order you hear at every Colombian wedding right after the cake.
questions.fun_fact: An adult has 206 bones, and dancing puts a good number of them to work.

questions.question: Grandma says it when she makes you take an umbrella, a jacket and a helmet: “más vale prevenir que lamentar.” What does it mean?
questions.answer: Better to take care before something happens
wrong_answers: Crying helps when everything goes wrong
You never need to worry about anything
Scolding someone never does any good
hints: It’s about thinking ahead, before the problem arrives.
It’s like carrying an umbrella in case it rains.
Better to be careful beforehand than to regret it afterward.
questions.description: Grandmothers say this even more often than “¿ya comió?”
questions.fun_fact: Many languages have a similar saying; in English it’s “better safe than sorry.”

questions.question: I work on the street with a rag in my hand. When you go to park, I wave and shout “¡siga, siga, siga!” Who am I?
hints: You find me outside shops and restaurants.
At the end, you give me a few coins.
I tell you when to stop before you crash.
questions.description: A character of the Colombian streets who never needed GPS.
questions.fun_fact: In Colombia, “siga” is also the polite way to say “come in” when someone arrives at your home.

questions.question: It rains on the day of the family outing and your mom says “al mal tiempo, buena cara.” Why does she say it?
questions.answer: To cheer you up even if things go wrong
wrong_answers: To get you to put on your raincoat
To tell you the outing is canceled
To scold you for getting wet
hints: It has nothing to do with clothes.
It’s about attitude.
It’s like saying: smile even if things don’t go the way you wanted.
questions.description: A saying that comes with its own weather forecast.
questions.fun_fact: This saying came from Spain and is used all over Latin America, not only when it rains.

questions.question: A mutation in the PSEN1 gene causes Alzheimer's before age 50 in thousands of relatives studied by Francisco Lopera. Where do they live?
hints: It's the Colombian region with the most families in the world affected by this mutation.
Neurologist Francisco Lopera worked at that region's public university.
The mutation was nicknamed after what people from Medellín are called.
questions.description: A family inheritance nobody wants, and scientists have been chasing it for over 30 years.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists see these families as a unique chance to test treatments that could slow Alzheimer's before any symptoms appear.

questions.question: Born in Bayamo, Cuba, he ran the Royal Library of Santafé and founded the Papel Periódico de Santafé de Bogotá. Who was he?
hints: He came to Santafé as a librarian, not as a politician or soldier.
He is considered the father of Colombian journalism.
His middle name is also a title of the Virgin Mary.
questions.description: Before social media, the news in Santafé arrived on paper with the ink still fresh.
questions.fun_fact: The Royal Library he ran is the forerunner of the Biblioteca Nacional de Colombia.

questions.question: When you pay with a new 10,000-peso bill, you see the face of the anthropologist who studied the families of Colombia's regions. Who is she?
hints: She was one of the country's first anthropologists.
She wrote “Familia y cultura en Colombia.”
She was born in El Socorro, Santander.
questions.description: A scientist who studied Colombian families and now lives in all of their wallets.
questions.fun_fact: Her 1968 book “Familia y cultura en Colombia” showed that the family changes enormously from one region of the country to another.

questions.question: I was born in the capital of Norte de Santander, by the bridge that crosses into Venezuela, and I love pasteles de garbanzo. What am I?
hints: My city is one of the hottest in the Santanders.
Right next to my city, the congress that created Gran Colombia met in 1821.
The name of my city starts with “Cú”.
questions.description: A character who, the moment they say hello, is already telling you where they're from and why their land is the best.
questions.fun_fact: In Villa del Rosario, right next to Cúcuta, the Constitution of Gran Colombia was written in 1821.

questions.question: In 1848, settlers from Neira and Salamina made the “Expedición de los Veinte” to pick the site for a new city. Which city was founded there in 1849?
hints: It's part of the Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero).
Today it's the capital of a department created in 1905.
Its January fair has a famous international coffee beauty pageant.
questions.description: Twenty Antioquians, machetes and mules: the most ambitious weekend plan in history.
questions.fun_fact: In the 19th century, the Antioquian colonization founded dozens of towns in the mountains of west-central Colombia.

questions.question: Who donated the land on which the city of Cúcuta was founded in 1733?
hints: The donated land lay in the valley of the Pamplonita River.
She gave it so the neighbors could build a church dedicated to Saint Joseph.
That's why people say Cúcuta was founded by a woman.
questions.description: A city that exists because someone gave away a plot of land, and not for a parking lot.
questions.fun_fact: The donation was signed on June 17, 1733, the date taken as Cúcuta's founding.

questions.question: Which Colombian telenovela has the opening song “¿Quién es ese hombre?”?
hints: It premiered in 2003 and became famous in many countries.
It tells the story of three brothers who come to a hacienda for revenge.
The Reyes brothers fall in love with the Elizondo sisters.
questions.description: A song that made half the country sigh in front of the TV at dinnertime.
questions.fun_fact: There were three Reyes brothers in the telenovela: Juan, Óscar and Franco.

questions.question: Julio Jiménez wrote “Las aguas mansas,” the telenovela later remade as “Pasión de gavilanes.” In which decade did it first air?
hints: It came out before Caracol and RCN became private channels.
Its remake, “Pasión de gavilanes,” came out about nine years later.
It went on the air in the middle of that decade, in 1994.
questions.description: A writer who knew revenge is a dish best served over many episodes.
questions.fun_fact: Julio Jiménez also wrote “En cuerpo ajeno,” which was remade in the United States as “El cuerpo del deseo.”

questions.question: The 1988 series “Los pecados de Inés de Hinojosa” was based on a real woman from Tunja. In which century did she live?
hints: It was during the Spanish colonial era.
Tunja was a newly founded city back then.
Her story took place a few decades after Gonzalo Suárez Rendón founded Tunja in 1539.
questions.description: A scandal so old the gossips of the day wrote with goose quills.
questions.fun_fact: Her story already appeared in “El carnero”, the chronicle Juan Rodríguez Freyle wrote in the 17th century.

questions.question: It's measured in points every night, and if it's too low, a telenovela can be taken off the air. What is it?
hints: It shows up in the entertainment news the next day.
Caracol and RCN fight over it every night.
It's how many people are tuned in to a TV show.
questions.description: Telenovela producers bite their nails the morning after every premiere because of this.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” reached some of the highest ratings in the history of Colombian television.

questions.question: In “Yo soy Betty, la fea,” what is the name of Ecomoda's vice president of sales, Armando Mendoza's best friend?
hints: He sits on Ecomoda's board and almost always takes Armando's side.
He was played by the actor Ricardo Vélez.
His first name is the same as Nintendo's mustached plumber.
questions.description: An executive who can sell anything at Ecomoda, except loyalty to the secretaries.
questions.fun_fact: “Yo soy Betty, la fea” has been remade in dozens of countries, from Mexico to India, and made Guinness World Records as the most successful telenovela.

questions.question: I show up in the middle of the song: over the accordion, the singer names friends, family and even whoever paid for the parranda. What am I?
hints: I’m not part of the song’s original lyrics.
Some people pay to be mentioned in me.
I’m named after what you do when you say “¡quiubo!” to someone.
questions.description: A parranda where the accordion never rests, the sancocho never runs out and nobody remembers to check the time.
questions.fun_fact: Some vallenato saludos became so famous that people know them by heart, just like the lyrics of the song.

questions.question: It's in Disney's “Encanto”, Carlos Vives sings it, and it mixes vallenato with cumbia. What song is it?
hints: It plays while the townspeople dance through the streets.
It has an accordion, like vallenato songs.
Its title includes the name of the country where the film takes place.
questions.description: A family with magic powers, and still the most magical thing was the soundtrack.
questions.fun_fact: The song was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who also wrote the rest of the songs in “Encanto”.
